t: Most patients who initially failed the 10-minute standing test due to orthostatic intolerance were able to complete it after rTMS treatment.
Heart rate and blood pressure responses during the 10-minute standing test, and prevalence of postural tachycardia/orthostatic hypotension, did not significantly change after rTMS treatment.
Most patients with disequilibrium (instability standing with feet together, eyes closed) had this resolved after rTMS treatment.
Disequilibrium was strongly associated with orthostatic intolerance: most OI-positive patients had disequilibrium, whereas OI was rare among patients without disequilibrium.
Tender point counts markedly decreased in most ME patients with comorbid fibromyalgia or neuropathic pain after rTMS treatment.
Low grip power improved to above 10 kg in half of the patients who had muscle weakness at baseline.
At the group level, median PS scores and tender point counts were significantly lower, and OI and disequilibrium significantly less prevalent, after rTMS treatment than before.
Lower rTMS stimulation intensity (below 60% of resting motor threshold, required in 7 patients due to intolerance) was associated with a lower rate of favorable therapeutic effect.
Sensory impairment (numbness, dysesthesia, paresthesia, sensory loss) was the most frequent persistent symptom after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, affecting 34 of 121 patients (28.1%).
General fatigue was the second most common persistent symptom, reported in 30 of 121 patients (24.8%).
Fever/low-grade fever and headache were each reported in 21 of 121 patients (17.4%), tied as the third/fourth most frequent persistent symptoms.
Female patients were disproportionately represented among those with persistent post-vaccination symptoms, comprising 63.6% of the cohort versus 36.4% male.
The frequencies of the top four persistent symptoms (sensory impairment, general fatigue, fever/low-grade fever, headache) did not differ significantly between female and male patients.
The predominant persistent symptom differed by vaccine type: sensory impairment was most common after BNT162b2 (32.8%), whereas general fatigue was most common after mRNA-1273 (41.7%).

Most persistent symptoms had an onset between 1 hour and 1 week after vaccination, with sensory impairment and general fatigue specifically beginning 12 hours to 1 week post-vaccination in all affected patients.

Many persistent symptoms, including sensory impairment, general fatigue, fever, headache, weakness, rash, joint pain, abdominal pain, sore throat, and pruritus, persisted for more than 6 months after vaccination.

A 41-year-old woman developed persistent fatigue, post-exertional malaise, orthostatic dizziness, poor concentration, sleep disturbance, and cervical lymphadenopathy after her first BNT162b2 vaccination and was diagnosed with ME/CFS according to the Fukuda, Canadian Consensus, and IOM criteria after excluding other underlying disorders.
In the post-vaccination ME/CFS case, general fatigue gradually improved with treatment using ascorbic acid, ubidecarenone (coenzyme Q10), ramelteon, and antiemetic medication.

A 33-year-old man developed uveitis, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and biopsy-confirmed noncaseating granulomas (sarcoidosis) after his second BNT162b2 vaccination, and improved clinically with topical betamethasone and tapering oral prednisolone.

An 84-year-old woman developed fever and headache after her third COVID-19 vaccination (mRNA-1273), with CSF pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose and negative bacterial cultures, diagnosed as vaccine-associated aseptic meningitis, which resolved rapidly with high-dose steroid therapy.

A 74-year-old man developed longitudinal myelitis with urinary retention and bilateral lower-limb paralysis after mRNA-1273 vaccination, tested positive for serum anti-aquaporin-4 antibody, and was diagnosed with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder; neurological symptoms gradually improved after plasma exchange, steroid pulse therapy, and IVIG, though immunosuppressive therapy was continued.

A 48-year-old man developed bilateral hip and limb pain with movement limitation and MRI evidence of hip tendon adhesion inflammation ten days after his third mRNA-1273 vaccination, diagnosed as idiopathic tendon adhesions and treated with tapering prednisolone.

An 81-year-old man developed severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count 4000/µL) with mucosal and subcutaneous hemorrhage two days after his first COVID-19 vaccine dose, with positive platelet-associated IgG supporting a diagnosis of idiopathic thrombocytopenia, and recovered after platelet transfusion, prednisolone, and immunoglobulin therapy.
A meta-analysis estimated the pooled global prevalence of ME/CFS at 0.89% across multiple studies.
ME/CFS prevalence estimates are higher in women (1.36%) than in men (0.86%).
ME/CFS prevalence estimates are higher in adults (0.65%) than in children and adolescents (0.55%).
ME/CFS prevalence estimates differ by study setting, higher in community-based studies (0.76%) than in primary care studies (0.63%).

Among 222 ME/CFS patients enrolled in the UK ME/CFS Biobank, prevalence of 47 assessed symptoms (excluding fatigue, at 100%) ranged from 33.9% for palpitations to 98.7% for unrefreshing sleep, with an average prevalence of 72.0%.

Three large systematic reviews of long COVID prevalence reported individual prevalence estimates for only 23, 18, and 14 of the 47 UKMEB-related symptoms respectively, and none reported data on post-exertional malaise.
Two large surveys reported that post-exertional malaise prevalence exceeded 80% in long COVID patients.
One systematic review suggested that 45% of long COVID cases had ME/CFS, but this paper argues that review incorrectly equated persistent fatigue with an ME/CFS diagnosis.

In one long COVID study, 43% of participants met the 2015 IOM criteria for ME/CFS, including some individuals with a BMI of 45 kg/m2, raising concern that comorbid conditions may inflate ME/CFS prevalence estimates.

Highly prevalent ME/CFS-related symptoms among UKMEB patients — unrefreshing sleep (98.7%), sensitivity to light or noise (77.7%), tender lymph nodes (75.5%), and heat/cold intolerance (74.6%) — were not reported by long COVID systematic reviews.
A two-year disease duration in ME/CFS may reflect transition from an early to an established disease stage.
Long COVID symptom duration can reach up to 3 years in some patients.
Network stakeholders reported that severely affected Long COVID patients within the network commonly presented with post-exertional malaise as a defining symptom.
Stakeholders noted that some severely affected Long COVID patients in the network used non-established therapies such as apheresis.
Severely affected Long COVID patients in the network experienced social difficulties, including unemployment due to sickness.
Network stakeholders repeatedly discussed the psychological dimension of Long COVID, including overlap with psychosomatic illness and patient concerns about being 'psychologized.'
Ambulatory health care stakeholders reported that caring for Long COVID patients within the network required a high time commitment.

SWOT participants in both networks identified potential transferability of the multidisciplinary Long COVID network care model to other post-infectious diseases such as ME/CFS as a strategic opportunity.
Participants identified a risk that Long COVID network activity could result in insufficient attention to ME/CFS and post-COVID-19 vaccination syndrome.

The Rhein-Neckar network treated approximately 250 Long COVID patients between January and October 2022, while the Ludwigsburg network's four participating general practices treated approximately 40 patients between January and March 2023, of which 15 were referred from other general practices.
The Functional Limitation Index (FLI), a novel composite physiological parameter, was significantly higher in confirmed CFS patients than in those without a confirmed diagnosis (CFS-).
The FLI showed strong diagnostic discrimination for CFS, outperforming all other spirometric/ergospirometric variables tested.
A dichotomic FLI cutoff of 1.66 was identified as optimal for distinguishing CFS patients, with good sensitivity and specificity.

Across 11 RCTs (960 CFS patients), traditional Chinese mind-body exercise (TCME; Qigong/Tai Chi) probably produced a large reduction in post-intervention fatigue severity compared with passive control.
In 4 studies (441 participants) using Qigong, TCME probably reduced post-intervention depression compared with passive control.
In the same 4 studies, TCME probably reduced post-intervention anxiety compared with passive control.
In 3 studies (291 participants), TCME using Qigong may improve post-intervention sleep quality compared with passive control.
In 2 studies (110 participants), TCME using Qigong may produce a large improvement in post-intervention mental function/quality of life compared with passive control.
The same 2 studies found TCME did not significantly improve post-intervention physical function compared with passive control.

In 3 trials (233 patients) comparing TCME (Qigong) to active controls (cognitive behavioral therapy, moxibustion, point application), TCME showed little to no difference in post-intervention fatigue severity.
One study (115 participants) reported that TCME significantly improved fatigue compared with passive control on the Chalder Fatigue Scale.
The same study found TCME's effect on sleep quality (PSQI) compared with passive control was not statistically significant.
Two studies (258 participants) reporting outcomes at 12-week follow-up found TCME may result in a large reduction in anxiety compared with passive control.
The same two studies found little to no difference in depression at 12-week follow-up between TCME and passive control.
TCME was generally safe, with one study of 150 participants reporting muscle ache as the most common adverse event, followed by palpitation, giddiness, knee pain, back ache, and dizziness.

The authors hypothesise that TCME may alter activity in the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary and hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axes by increasing parasympathetic nervous system activity, thereby reducing negative emotions in CFS.
Researchers have hypothesised that TCME may induce the release of neurotransmitters (dopamine, serotonin, and adrenaline) in the brain, associated with improvements in anxiety and depression.
Genetic counselors perceived a marked increase in referrals for suspected hEDS to genetics clinics in recent years.
Unlike the other twelve EDS subtypes, hypermobile EDS has no identified molecular cause, though pedigree analysis is most consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.
Genetic testing ordered for suspected hEDS was reported to have very low diagnostic yield, with most results being negative or non-diagnostic.
Genetic counselors reported spending substantially more time on hEDS appointments than typical genetics referrals, including extended pre-visit preparation and two-hour clinic blocks.
Genetic counselors reported feelings of professional burnout, compassion fatigue, and emotional exhaustion related to caring for hEDS patients.

A previously published study found that over 40% of genetic counselors (general population, not specific to hEDS) reported leaving or considering leaving their job due to burnout, cited by the authors as relevant background context.
Implementing stricter referral triage criteria for hEDS was associated with substantially shortened clinic waitlist times.

Genetic counselors identified psychosocial counseling (listening, validating patient experiences, providing emotional support) as their predominant and most professionally rewarding role with hEDS patients.

Many hEDS patients reportedly hold misconceptions that genetic testing can provide an official diagnosis or that genetics specialists are responsible for symptom management, leading to unmet expectations.
Participants reported that hEDS referral frequency was almost as prevalent as other common genetics clinic indications such as autism and developmental delay.

Participants recommended that a multidisciplinary care model (e.g., physical therapy, cardiology, pain management, rheumatology alongside genetics) would better meet the needs of hEDS patients than genetics-led care alone.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV is associated with skin and vascular fragility, and spontaneous arterial rupture is one of its higher-risk complications.
The patient developed a spontaneous breast haematoma associated with a pseudoaneurysm of a branch of the left internal mammary artery.
The patient was treated with a minimally invasive endovascular approach for the breast pseudoaneurysm, which was uneventful and effective.
Six months after the initial event, the patient presented with a similar pseudoaneurysm/haematoma episode on the contralateral breast, without active bleeding, and remained under surveillance.
Although most surveyed providers were aware of EDS, the majority reported low comfort diagnosing, caring for, and managing pediatric patients with the condition.
Many providers reported lacking knowledge of and comfort with the 2017 International Classification Criteria used to diagnose EDS.

A newly proposed pediatric-specific diagnostic framework recommends assessing joint hypermobility in children who have not reached biologic maturity separately from the 2017 adult-oriented EDS criteria.

Providers requested standardized clinical practice guidelines and easy access to diagnostic criteria (e.g., hospital intranet, one-page summaries) to improve comfort with EDS diagnosis and management.

Providers expressed a strong desire for clearer guidance on when and how to refer pediatric EDS patients to subspecialists, particularly rheumatology and genetics, and clarification of their own role relative to specialists.
Providers reported that limited clinical exposure to EDS patients, rather than lack of resources alone, undermined their confidence in managing the condition.
Multidisciplinary care has been recommended for EDS management given the complexity and number of associated comorbidities, though such clinics are not universally available.
Families of EDS patients are reportedly willing to travel for subspecialty or EDS-specific care, but this imposes a significant time and financial burden and is not a sustainable access solution.
The EDS ECHO teleconferencing program (based on Project ECHO principles) is cited as an existing initiative aimed at increasing clinician awareness and ability to assess and manage EDS patients.
Vascular EDS is caused by pathogenic variants in COL3A1, which encodes type III collagen, leading to inherent arterial wall weakness.
Reported operative mortality for vascular complications in VEDS ranges from 7% to 41% across the literature.

A ruptured left common iliac artery dissection causing acute limb ischemia in a VEDS patient was successfully treated with an endovascular Viabahn covered stent placed via open superficial femoral artery exposure using no-touch dissection, proximal felt cuff reinforcement, and a preclose pledgetted suture technique.

In a 15-year multi-institutional retrospective study of 53 VEDS patients with 139 aortic/arterial pathologies, the most commonly affected arteries were mesenteric (31.7%), cerebral vascular (16.5%), iliac (16.5%), and renal (12.2%).
Among 23 iliac arteries with pathology in the cited cohort, isolated iliac disease occurred in 16.9% and iliac disease with concurrent abdominal aortic aneurysm in 15.1%.

A separate 2014 study found that iliac artery aneurysms and dissections occurred independently of abdominal aortic involvement in 22 of 68 individuals with VEDS, and examined correlation between COL3A1 mutation type and clinical phenotype.
Nonoperative management was successful in select VEDS arterial cases, including dissections (n=7) and aneurysms less than 2.5 cm in diameter (n=3).

Percutaneous femoral access with 4F to 7F sheaths was successful in 14 VEDS cases per the cited review, with manual pressure used in seven cases (one hematoma) and closure devices (Angio-Seal, StarClose, Perclose ProGlide) successful in five cases without complications.

In the same patient's prior (2018) endovascular repair of a ruptured right subclavian artery, percutaneous femoral access closed with Angio-Seal resulted in a pseudoaneurysm, which was managed by surgical exposure and successful manual compression without requiring stent placement.

The authors estimated that infants of mothers with maximal hEDS-related bone fragility risk have an infant rib fracture incidence of approximately 4 per 100,000 children, derived from an hEDS incidence of 1 in 5000 and a 19% probability of rib fracture seen in osteogenesis imperfecta infants.

The authors state that infants with genetic causes of bone fragility such as osteogenesis imperfecta and Hypermobility Spectrum/EDS Syndrome frequently have symptoms that are misdiagnosed as physical child abuse.

Osteogenesis imperfecta was estimated to be associated with an infant rib fracture incidence of about 1.3 per 100,000, based on an OI incidence of 1:15,000 and 19% of OI children having rib fractures.

Maternal and fetal vitamin D deficiency was estimated to be the dominant non-abuse cause of infant rib fractures, with an estimated incidence of about 339 per 100,000 children, far exceeding estimated physical-abuse-related incidence.

Prematurity was estimated to be associated with infant rib fracture incidences of about 74 per 100,000 in the Netherlands and 147 per 100,000 in the USA, based on national prematurity rates and a rib fracture rate of about 1.4% in babies born before 37 weeks.

The estimated incidence of infant rib fractures caused by physical child abuse was calculated as less than 1.7 per 100,000 children in the Netherlands and less than 12 per 100,000 in the USA, using national physical abuse prevalence combined with resuscitation-related rib fracture rates.

The authors conclude that non-abuse causes of infant rib fractures are approximately 250 times more frequent than physical-abuse-related rib fractures in the Netherlands and 45 times more frequent in the USA.

The disparity between the Netherlands (250x) and USA (45x) abuse-to-non-abuse ratios is interpreted as evidence that physical abuse is diagnosed about 5.6 times more often in the USA than in the Netherlands for comparable cases.

A systematic literature review (Güvencel's thesis) analyzing rib fractures as a sign of physical child abuse concluded there is insufficient scientific evidence that rib fractures can be caused by abuse or to determine diagnostic accuracy of rib fractures for abuse.

Chronic histiocytic intervillositis with massive perivillous fibrin deposition was estimated to be associated with an infant rib fracture incidence of about 1 per 100,000, based on placental pathology incidence and assumed severity/live-birth fractions.

Birth trauma in heavy-weighing newborns (>4 kg) was estimated to produce a rib fracture incidence of about 0.3 per 100,000 births, based on combined data from several large birth cohorts including a Swedish registry of 1,855,267 infants.

A Swedish population-based registry study identified 63 asymptomatic rib fractures among 1,855,267 infants under 1 year of age, most developing perinatally, illustrating that occult rib fractures are more common than typically assumed.

The review notes that median arcuate ligament syndrome and fibromuscular dysplasia disproportionately affect females, while vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has unique manifestations in female populations.
The review discusses pregnancy-specific considerations for females with each of the three rare vascular conditions, including vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
A new homozygous MRPS2 patient is reported who displays joint hypermobility, a feature not previously described in MRPS2-related disease.
The same MRPS2 patient presents with autistic features, a phenotype not previously reported in association with this gene.
The patient also shows initial microcephaly, another feature not previously documented in MRPS2-related disease.

Prior MRPS2 patients were described with sensorineural hearing impairment, mild developmental delay, hypoglycemia, lactic acidemia and combined oxidative phosphorylation system deficiency, or a milder phenotype in one recent case.
Higher resilience scores were associated with a significantly lower degree of interference of pain in the lives of participants (DIPLP) with fibromyalgia after adjustment for 21 confounders.
Resilience was not significantly associated with average pain scores among people with fibromyalgia.

The protective association between resilience and pain interference (DIPLP) was much stronger among fibromyalgia patients with null-to-mild average pain than among those with moderate-to-severe pain, indicating a significant resilience-by-pain-intensity interaction.
The combined MCAS cohorts confirmed a strong association between MCAS and chemical intolerance (CI), with the large majority of MCAS patients screening positive for CI on the QEESI.
In the original first cohort of 149 MCAS patients, 60% were classified as 'very suggestive' and 37% as 'suggestive' of chemical intolerance by QEESI criteria.
In the new second cohort of 395 MCAS patients, 50% were classified as 'very suggestive' and 46% as 'suggestive' of chemical intolerance by QEESI criteria.
MCAS severity scores correlated moderately with QEESI Chemical Intolerance scale scores.
MCAS severity scores correlated with QEESI Symptom Severity scale scores, more strongly than with the Chemical scale.
Higher MCAS clinical scores predicted greater odds of being classified as 'Very Suggestive' rather than merely 'Suggestive' of chemical intolerance.
In the earlier Miller et al. study, patients in the 2nd quartile of MCAS scores were 2.6 times more likely to have CI compared to the lowest quartile.
In the earlier Miller et al. study, patients in the 3rd quartile of MCAS scores were 6.0 times more likely to have CI compared to the lowest quartile.
In the earlier Miller et al. study, patients in the 4th (highest) quartile of MCAS scores were 6.2 times more likely to have CI compared to the lowest quartile.
Across the 544 MCAS patients, an average of 4.6 ICD-10 diagnoses per patient were recorded, reflecting the multisystem nature of MCAS.
Nine of the fourteen ICD-10 diagnostic categories recorded in MCAS patients directly matched QEESI Symptom scale categories, supporting a shared symptom/mechanism overlap between MCAS and CI.

A high rate (59%) of infection diagnoses, including tick-borne infections, was found among MCAS patients, raising the question of secondary vs. primary MCAS, though clinical history suggested MCAS predated the infections in most cases.
There was substantial overlap between the subpopulation of MCAS patients with proven Borrelia infection and those with proven Bartonella infection, indicating frequent tick-borne coinfection.
The authors suggest that treatment for CI may draw on MCAS-directed therapies such as H1 and H2 histamine receptor antagonists and cromolyn, following trigger identification and avoidance.
Prior genetic association research (Fujimori et al.) found no significant differences in allelic distribution of genetic polymorphisms between individuals with and without chemical intolerance.
No statistically significant differences in age or gender distribution were found between the first and second MCAS patient cohorts.
The half maximal inhibitory concentration of HPE on mast cell viability was determined to be 79.94 ng/mL by CCK-8 assay.
HPE treatment for 16 h dose-dependently suppressed proliferation of C57 and HMC-1 mast cells, while 4 or 8 h treatment had no effect.
HPE treatment for 16 h dose-dependently increased the frequency of apoptotic mast cells in vitro (C57 and HMC-1), with no apoptosis observed at 4 or 8 h.
Intraperitoneal HPE injection for 16 h increased the percentage of apoptotic cKit+FcεRI+ peritoneal mast cells in mice, confirming the in vitro apoptosis finding in vivo.
HPE did not change the total number of peritoneal mast cells during the short treatment period, supporting the validity of using percentage-based apoptosis comparisons.

Pre-treatment with HPE substantially suppressed mast cell degranulation (measured by β-hexosaminidase release) triggered by compound 48/80 or by IgE receptor crosslinking, while HPE alone did not induce degranulation.
HPE pre-treatment decreased C48/80-induced production of IL-4, IL-6, IL-13 and TNF-α by C57 and HMC-1 mast cells, with reductions in IL-4 and TNF-α already evident at the 8 h timepoint.
HPE had no detectable effect on mast cell phagocytosis of OVA antigen, assessed by both flow cytometry and confocal microscopy.
HPE pre-treatment reduced SCF-directed chemotaxis of C57 mast cells at 8 and 16 h, and of HMC-1 cells at 16 h (with an inhibitory trend at 8 h).
Local pre-treatment with HPE for 8 or 16 h suppressed IgE-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis dye extravasation in mouse ear tissue, whereas 4 h pre-treatment had no effect.
Toluidine blue staining of ear tissue showed HPE pre-treatment markedly reduced the proportion of degranulating mast cells at 8 h and 16 h but not at 4 h.
HPE pre-treatment for 8 or 16 h reduced tissue histamine production in the passive cutaneous anaphylaxis ear model, indicating reduced mast cell activation.

HPE induced apoptosis in peritoneal B cells to a lesser extent than in mast cells, but had no apoptotic effect on T cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, or granulocytes, suggesting a degree of cell-type selectivity.
Circulating miR-451a was significantly upregulated in chronic urticaria patients compared to healthy controls.
Circulating miR-9-5p was significantly upregulated in chronic urticaria patients compared to healthy controls.
Circulating miR-150-5p was significantly upregulated in chronic urticaria patients compared to healthy controls.
Circulating miR-296-5p was significantly upregulated in chronic urticaria patients compared to healthy controls.
Circulating miR-182-5p was significantly upregulated in chronic urticaria patients compared to healthy controls.
The authors note that dysregulation of miR-451a is recognized elsewhere as an early biomarker in allergic diseases, contextualizing its upregulation in chronic urticaria.
KEGG pathway and disease ontology functional enrichment analysis showed that the differentially expressed miRNAs are associated with skin diseases and inflammation pathways.

A 39-year-old woman with N-ERD developed a marked asthma exacerbation with severe cough and cyanosis minutes after intravenous hydrocortisone sodium succinate (HCs), requiring adrenaline, oxygen, and theophylline to resolve.
In a single-blind loading study of the index patient, intravenous PSLs 10 mg and MPSLs 20 mg each decreased FEV1 by roughly a third and induced severe coughing and wheezing.
In the same patient, intravenous hydrocortisone sodium phosphate (HCp) up to 100 mg did not decrease FEV1 or induce coughing, unlike succinate esters.
In 11 N-ERD patients, intravenous 100 mg HCs decreased FEV1 by a median of 13.1% (range -8.1% to -35.5%), with 4/11 patients meeting the 20% positive threshold.
In 7 N-ERD patients negative at 100 mg HCs, a subsequent 500 mg HCs dose decreased FEV1 by a median of 31.3% (range 10.1%-51.5%), positive in 5/7 patients, indicating dose-dependent hypersensitivity.
Overall, 9 of 11 (82%) N-ERD patients tested positive for hypersensitivity to intravenous HCs at doses below 500 mg.
MPSLs 80 mg was positive in 5/10 (50%) of tested N-ERD patients and PSLs 20 mg was positive in 1/3 (33%), producing symptoms similar to HCs.
Only 1 of 11 (9%) N-ERD patients had a mild cough with no decrease in lung function on HCp 500 mg provocation, in contrast to succinate esters.

A non-corticosteroid succinate ester drug, chloramphenicol sodium succinate (CPs), induced severe coughing and wheezing with unmeasurable pulmonary function in 6 of 7 (88%) N-ERD patients, supporting that the succinate ester structure itself drives hypersensitivity.
HCs 100-500 mg intravenous provocation was negative in all 7 aspirin-tolerant asthma (ATA) patients, showing that succinate hypersensitivity is specific to N-ERD pathogenesis.
Intradermal skin testing with HCs and MPSLs was positive in only 1 of 5 patients, suggesting the succinate hypersensitivity reaction is not primarily IgE-mediated.
In vitro platelet experiments showed that HCs did not inhibit COX-1, suggesting the succinate hypersensitivity mechanism is independent of COX-1 inhibition.

In a retrospective analysis of N-ERD patients receiving slow (>2 h) intravenous drip infusion, only 2/55 (3.6%) had a mild cough with MPSLs (which resolved after switching to DEXp), while none of 31 patients receiving DEXp had airway side effects, indicating slow infusion and non-succinate steroids are safer.
Hypersensitivity to HCs occurred in a dose-dependent manner, with 36% of subjects positive at 100 mg and an additional 76% of the 100-mg-negative subjects positive at the 500 mg dose.

The authors hypothesize that rapid intravenous succinate ester breakdown produces high local concentrations of succinate that activate mast cells via the succinate receptor SUCNR1, which is abundant on human mast cells, driving the rapid-onset hypersensitivity seen in N-ERD.

Persistent mast cell activation is described as a characteristic pathology of N-ERD even during the stable phase, cited from multiple prior reports, supporting the plausibility of a mast cell-driven mechanism for succinate hypersensitivity.

Aspirin desensitization performed on one N-ERD patient did not eliminate the hypersensitivity to HCs, suggesting the succinate ester hypersensitivity mechanism is distinct from the COX-1-mediated aspirin sensitivity pathway.
Endogenous PPARβ/δ protein levels were decreased in the brain after germinal matrix hemorrhage in neonatal rats.
Endogenous CD300a protein levels were decreased in the brain after germinal matrix hemorrhage in neonatal rats.
Chymase levels increased in the brain after germinal matrix hemorrhage, consistent with mast cell degranulation.
Tryptase levels increased in the brain after germinal matrix hemorrhage, consistent with mast cell degranulation.
IL-17A levels increased in the brain after germinal matrix hemorrhage.
TGF-β1 levels increased in the brain after germinal matrix hemorrhage.
Intranasal administration of the PPARβ/δ agonist GW0742 decreased mast cell degranulation, improved neurological outcomes, and attenuated ventriculomegaly after germinal matrix hemorrhage.
GW0742 treatment increased PPARβ/δ protein expression after GMH.
GW0742 treatment increased CD300a protein expression after GMH.
GW0742 treatment increased phosphorylation of SHP1, a downstream effector of CD300a signaling, after GMH.
GW0742 treatment decreased phosphorylation of Syk, a downstream kinase involved in mast cell activation, after GMH.
GW0742 treatment decreased levels of chymase, tryptase, IL-17A and TGF-β1 after GMH.
GW0742 attenuated ventriculomegaly following GMH.
PPARβ/δ siRNA and CD300a siRNA knockdown abolished the beneficial effects of GW0742 on mast cell inflammation and neurobehavior after GMH.
Rats with oxaliplatin-induced neuropathic pain (model group) showed decreased mechanical paw withdrawal threshold compared to normal rats after modeling.
Serum levels of IL-6, TNF-α, and CXCL12 were increased in the oxaliplatin-induced neuropathic pain model group compared to normal rats.
The number of mast cells in the acupoint skin area was increased in the model group compared to the normal group.
Protein expression of tryptase (TPS), TRPV1, and PAR2 was increased in the skin of the acupoint area in the model group compared with the normal group.
Fire needle treatment and pregabalin both increased the paw withdrawal threshold after intervention compared to the untreated model group.
Fire needle treatment and pregabalin both decreased serum IL-6, TNF-α, and CXCL12 compared to the untreated model group.
Fire needle treatment increased mechanical paw withdrawal threshold compared to the untreated model group.
Fire needle treatment decreased serum IL-6 levels compared to the model group.
Fire needle treatment decreased serum TNF-α levels compared to the model group.
Fire needle treatment decreased serum CXCL12 levels compared to the model group.
Fire needle and pregabalin treatment reduced TRPV1 protein expression in the skin of the acupoint area compared with the model group.
Fire needle and pregabalin treatment reduced PAR2 protein expression in the skin of the acupoint area compared with the model group.
Fire needle and pregabalin treatment reduced tryptase (TPS) protein expression in the skin of the acupoint area compared with the model group, consistent with reduced mast cell activation.
Pregabalin (but not necessarily fire needle) decreased TRPV1 protein expression in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) compared with the model group.
Pregabalin decreased PAR2 protein expression in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) compared with the model group, an effect not attributed to fire needle in this analysis.
Skin biopsy showed reduced sweat gland nerve fiber density in the distal arm and left foot of the patient compared to normal reference ranges.
The patient's IENFD was normal despite a clinical diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy, indicating IENFD alone can miss SFN detectable by sweat gland fiber density.

The patient developed multisystem sensory, pain, and autonomic-type symptoms (numbness, paresthesia, burning, itching, tinnitus, headache, palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue) beginning 74 days after her third BNT162b2 dose.
In a prior series, autonomic testing after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination-associated SFN found POTS in half of the tested patients.
Distal hypohidrosis was found in over half of patients tested for autonomic dysfunction after vaccination-associated SFN in a prior series.
Among 23 patients with new neuropathic symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, most reported autonomic symptoms in addition to universal sensory disturbances.
Just over half of patients with post-vaccination neuropathic symptoms were ultimately diagnosed with definite SFN in a prior case series.
Treatment (steroids/IVIG/PLEX) led to complete or near-complete recovery within two weeks for the majority of treated post-vaccination SFN patients in a prior series.
Untreated (steroid-naive) patients with post-vaccination SFN in a prior series recovered spontaneously and completely within 12 weeks.
IVIG treatment produced complete recovery within two weeks in three patients whose post-vaccination SFN had not resolved spontaneously after 5-9 months.

A study of 27 SARS-CoV-2 vaccinated patients found newly onset immunological disease, including neurosarcoidosis with SFN, in only a minority, supporting that immune-mediated SFN post-vaccination is rare.
In three patients with acute SFN after the Astra Zeneca vaccine, IENFD in the lower leg was reduced in all three, and neuropathic pain persisted in two of them.
Plasma exchange (5 cycles) improved sensory disturbances and tinnitus in a male patient with post-vaccination paresthesia, POTS, and tinnitus.
In another post-vaccination SFN case, skin biopsies showed loss of PGP-9.5 labelled nerve fibers in the foot and over the ischial tuberosity, and the patient improved significantly with gabapentin.

Despite a 74-day latency between the third BNT162b2 dose and symptom onset, the authors attributed the patient's SFN to the vaccine because secondary causes were excluded and family/personal history for primary (genetic) SFN was negative.
The authors propose that post-SARS-CoV-2-vaccination SFN most likely arises from a vaccine-induced immune cross-reaction against components of small nerve fibers.
The Body Scan device showed a sensitivity of 0.91 and specificity of 0.97 for detecting at least moderate sudomotor dysfunction (ESC<70 μS) as defined by the reference Sudoscan device.
The Body Scan device showed a sensitivity of 0.91 and specificity of 0.99 for detecting severe sudomotor dysfunction (ESC<50 μS) as defined by the reference Sudoscan device.
Bland-Altman analysis showed excellent agreement between the Body Scan and Sudoscan ESC measurements, with a small positive bias of 1.5 μS and narrow limits of agreement.
ESC values measured with the Body Scan device did not differ significantly by study center or by the presence versus absence of diabetes.
ESC values measured with the Body Scan device were lower in Asian and Sub-Saharan African patients compared with other ethnic groups.
ESC values measured with the Body Scan device were lower in patients with foot injury than in those without foot injury.
Repeated ESC measurements with the Body Scan device showed no significant effect of measurement repetition but a highly significant effect of subject, indicating good repeatability.
The intra-sample repeatability variability of ESC measures was similar between the Body Scan (SD=2.0) and Sudoscan (SD=2.3) devices, consistent with prior published Sudoscan repeatability data.
No adverse effects were observed with either the Body Scan or the Sudoscan device during testing.

HESC showed the same correlation pattern as FESC, being negatively associated with A and E/e' and positively associated with e'.
After adjusting for confounding factors, binary logistic regression showed that ESC was independently associated with impaired LV diastolic function in persons with T2DM.

Substance P immunoreactive neuron density was highest in the inner submucosal plexus compared to the outer submucosal plexus and myenteric plexus in both ascending and descending colon.

Substance P-immunoreactive neurons made up almost a third of all HuCD-immunoreactive neurons in the inner submucosal plexus, but a smaller proportion (19-22%) in the outer submucosal plexus and (13-17%) in the myenteric plexus.

A substantial population of neurons co-expressing substance P and choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) was densest in the inner submucosal plexus, less abundant in the outer submucosal plexus, and least abundant in the myenteric plexus.

The vast majority of substance P-immunoreactive neurons also expressed ChAT, ranging from 62–66% in the myenteric plexus, 74–76% in the inner submucosal plexus, and 71–85% in the outer submucosal plexus.

Neurons co-expressing substance P and neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) were sparse, representing less than 10% of the total HuCD-IR neuronal population, with the highest density in the inner submucosal plexus and lowest in the myenteric plexus.

A small subset of enteric neurons co-expressed substance P, ChAT, and nNOS, with the highest density found in the inner submucosal plexus and lowest in the myenteric plexus, representing a minority (10-36%) of the total substance P-positive population depending on plexus and colonic region.

Unlike a prior study reporting no substance P-IR neurons lacking ChAT, this study identified some substance P-IR neurons that did not co-express ChAT, indicating a discrete non-cholinergic SP neuronal subpopulation.

The percentage of SP-IR neurons found in the outer submucosal plexus in this adult porcine study (19-22%) differed from the lower percentage (11.9%) reported previously in piglets, a discrepancy attributed to differences in animal age and ganglion sampling.

taVNS was reported to attenuate inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) symptoms in children.
Transcutaneous electrical acustimulation (TEAS) ameliorated symptoms of GERD, functional dyspepsia, IBS, and constipation.
Stimulation of the ST36 acupoint improved multiple GI symptoms including abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, gas, bloating, and nausea.
Electroacupuncture at ST36 significantly decreased visceral pain and colonic 5-HT3 receptor levels in an animal model.

Both taVNS and needle-based VNS decreased TNF-α and IL-6 levels in IBS patients and in a rodent TNBS-induced colitis model.

The Folin-Ciocalteu (FC) protocol and the Kolopp-Sarda et al. protocol for cryoglobulin detection showed only moderate agreement (86.0%, Cohen's kappa 0.483).
Cryoglobulin concentrations measured by the FC and Kolopp-Sarda protocols showed a moderately positive correlation in doubly positive samples.
Type II cryoglobulins were found at significantly higher median serum concentrations than type III cryoglobulins.
Patients with type II cryoglobulins had higher rheumatoid factor and lower serum C4 concentrations compared to patients with type III cryoglobulins, with no difference in C3c.

Type II cryoglobulin-positive patients with detectable rheumatoid factor activity in the cryoprecipitate had significantly higher cryoglobulin concentrations and higher serum RF than those without RF activity.
In type III cryoglobulinemia, cryoglobulin concentrations did not differ between patients with and without RF activity, though serum RF levels did differ.
Serum C4 concentration was the strongest predictor of cryoglobulinemia in a CHAID decision tree model, with lower C4 associated with higher probability of a positive cryoglobulin result.

Within the intermediate C4 range in the CHAID model, RF status further stratified cryoglobulinemia risk, with RF-positive patients having a higher rate of positive cryoglobulin results than RF-negative patients.
The overall CHAID decision tree model had 82.9% accuracy for predicting cryoglobulinemia, correctly classifying 97.5% of negative cases but only 30.4% of positive cases.
Among 258 rheumatology patients tested, 21.7% (56/258) were positive for cryoglobulins using the Kolopp-Sarda protocol, with 37.5% classified as type II and 62.5% as type III.
RF activity was detected in only a minority of cryoglobulin-positive samples overall, more frequently in type II than type III cryoglobulins.

In silico docking analysis showed that sesamin exhibited strong binding affinity toward SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) compared to controls.

Phosphoproteomic analysis identified 622 downregulated and 683 upregulated phosphopeptides in the right ventricle of MCT-induced PAH rats relative to controls.
Western blotting confirmed upregulation of Ncam1 in the right ventricle of both MCT-induced and hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension rat models.
Western blotting confirmed downregulation of Nqo2 in the right ventricle of both MCT-induced and hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension rat models.
Western blotting confirmed downregulation of Tmod4 in the right ventricle of both MCT-induced and hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension rat models.
qRT-PCR validated altered expression levels of the top 20 significantly changed proteins, including Nppa, Ltbp2, periostin, Ccn2, Ncam1, Nqo2, and Tmod4, in the PAH rat right ventricle.

Quinone reductase 2 (Nqo2) protein was downregulated in right ventricular tissue of monocrotaline-induced PAH rats, confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting in both MCT- and hypoxia-induced PH models.
Tropomodulin 4 (Tmod4) protein was downregulated in right ventricular tissue of monocrotaline-induced PAH rats, confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting in both MCT- and hypoxia-induced PH models.
Phosphoproteomic analysis identified 622 downregulated and 683 upregulated phosphopeptides in the right ventricle of MCT-induced PAH rats compared to controls.
Pathway enrichment of the altered right ventricular proteome in PAH rats implicated vesicle-mediated transport, actin cytoskeleton organization, the TCA cycle, and respiratory electron transport.

Pathway enrichment of the altered right ventricular phosphoproteome in PAH rats implicated diabetic cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and cardiac muscle contraction pathways.

In healthy participants, myofascial induction OMM produced statistically significant improvements in state anxiety, heart rate, and systolic blood pressure compared to a no-intervention control, but no significant difference in diastolic blood pressure, temperature, or state depression.

In healthy females, a single OMM session produced statistically significant improvement in anxiety and global self-perception scores versus a restful-state control, with no significant difference in body satisfaction.
OMM did not significantly improve stress or depressive symptoms versus non-directed OMM or no treatment, though directed OMM significantly improved sleep on the Epworth Sleepiness Test.

Both sham OMM and cranial OMM produced statistically significant increases in salivary alpha-amylase (a marker of autonomic nervous system activity) relative to a no-intervention control, with no difference between OMM and sham.
In fibromyalgia patients, 23 weeks of OMM treatment showed no statistically significant difference in depression scores compared to control groups.
In 201 spinal pain patients followed for six months, cranial OMM led to statistically significant improvement in the general mental health domain of the SF-12 compared to treatment-as-usual.
In 30 IBS patients, both OMM and sham OMM groups showed improvement in secondary anxiety and depression self-reports, with no statistically significant difference between the two arms.
In a pre-post study of 42 whiplash injury patients, OMM was associated with statistically significant improvement in the mental health domain of the SF-36.

In 120 fibromyalgia patients, adding cervical OMM to a multimodal program produced no significant difference in anxiety, depression, or sleep quality at 12 weeks, but did produce statistically significant improvement in each of these measures at one year.

In a four-week RCT of tension headache sufferers, anxiety and depression scores improved in all four groups (three OMM techniques plus control) but with no statistically significant difference between OMM groups and controls.

In an open-label study of MS patients, the group receiving OMM experienced statistically significant improvements in depression, fatigue, and quality of life scores compared to a group receiving MS education alone.
In 66 chronic low back pain patients, diaphragmatic OMM produced significant improvement in anxiety and depression scores (HADS) versus sham OMM.

In MS patients undergoing rehabilitation, adding OMM sessions was associated with a statistically significant reduction in Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores compared to standard rehabilitation alone.

In 28 chronic pain patients after breast cancer surgery, OMM plus usual care produced statistically significant improvement in depression scores versus usual care alone, though pain scores did not differ.
In 75 chronic neck pain patients, OMM produced statistically significant improvement in the anxiety and depression scales of the PROMIS-29 compared to a waiting-list control.

In women with depression treated with Paxil and psychotherapy, adding OMM produced a statistically significant decrease in Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale scores compared to Paxil and psychotherapy alone.

In children with ADHD, OMM did not significantly improve the primary outcome (accuracy and rapidity on a cancellation test) on univariate analysis, but showed statistically significant improvement on multivariate linear regression.
In an open-label, non-randomized trial, 26 patients meeting criteria for generalized anxiety disorder had clinically significant reduction in anxiety symptoms after five OMM sessions.
In an RCT of patients with clinical anxiety, four sessions of myofascial release OMM produced a substantial reduction in anxiety compared to sham treatment.

Across the 11 studies examining OMM's indirect effect on psychiatric symptoms via treatment of comorbid medical conditions (fibromyalgia, chronic pain, MS, headaches, whiplash, IBS), six of the 11 studies showed a statistically significant improvement in psychiatric outcomes with OMM relative to control.

Overall, the review concluded there is insufficient evidence to recommend OMM for direct treatment of psychiatric symptoms, given limitations of publication bias, low study rigor, small sample sizes, and heterogeneous outcome measures across the 19 included studies.

Patients with IBS scored lower than healthy controls on all resilience measures, including the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale, Brief Resilience Scale, and a relative resilience index derived from SF-12 mental component and Adverse Childhood Experiences scores.

Across all three resilience-related resting-state connectivity signatures, patients with IBS showed reduced connectivity that largely involved the central autonomic network compared with healthy controls.
Men with IBS showed lower CDRISC resilience scores than women with IBS.
Men with IBS showed greater reductions in CDRISC-related resting-state connectivity than women with IBS, and this greater reduction was associated with worse symptom severity.
About one quarter of long COVID patients had low vitamin D (25-OH D3 ≤50 nmol/L), with most being insufficient rather than frankly deficient.
Male long COVID patients had higher odds of having low vitamin D compared with females.
Younger age was associated with higher odds of low vitamin D among long COVID patients.
Patients with low vitamin D had lower odds of having comorbidity (Charlson Comorbidity Index ≥1) than those with normal vitamin D.
No significant difference in low vitamin D odds was found between the ethnically non-western European sub-cohort and the ethnically Danish sub-cohort.
No significant association was found between vitamin D status and BMI category (≥25 vs <25).
No significant difference in vitamin D status was found by smoking status or alcohol consumption after Bonferroni correction.

The prevalence of the most commonly reported long COVID symptoms (disturbed sleep, physical fatigue, concentration difficulties, dyspnea, headaches) did not differ between low and normal vitamin D groups.
Low vitamin D was associated with lower odds of reporting long-term memory problems compared to normal vitamin D, though this did not survive Bonferroni correction.
Sore throat was less frequently reported in the low vitamin D group than the normal vitamin D group, but the association did not survive Bonferroni correction.
Nausea was less frequently reported in the low vitamin D group, but this did not survive Bonferroni correction.
Abdominal pain was less frequently reported in the low vitamin D group, but this did not survive Bonferroni correction.
No significant differences were found in organ-specific symptom scores or overall symptom/health scores between low and normal vitamin D groups.
The Post-COVID Questionnaire Symptom (PCQ) score did not differ significantly between low and normal vitamin D groups, before or after adjustment.

Season of symptom onset modified the effect of low vitamin D on functional status: patients with winter symptom onset and low vitamin D had increased likelihood of severe post-COVID functional impairment.
Season of symptom onset also interacted with vitamin D status for the SCL depression variable, with winter onset and low vitamin D associated with worse depression scores.
The PCQ score showed no significant interaction with season of symptom onset for vitamin D status.
No significant differences in vitamin D-health variable associations were found across ethnic subgroups (non-western European immigrants, western European immigrants, ethnic Danes).
No significant differences in health scores were found when comparing frank vitamin D deficiency (n=15) to normal vitamin D status.
The long COVID cohort had a higher prevalence of low vitamin D (26% low, i.e., 74% sufficient) than estimates for the general Danish population (~86% sufficient based on prior Danish cohort data).
Overall, the study found no association between low vitamin D status and more severe long COVID symptoms in patients referred to a Post-COVID Clinic.
ME/CFS imposes a substantial economic burden on the United States, estimated at $18-51 billion annually.
Principal component analysis of PBMC proteomes showed sufficient differences to separate long COVID patients from healthy controls along principal component 3.
Of 3131 quantified PBMC proteins, 162 were differentially regulated in LC patients versus healthy controls, with 79 down-regulated and 83 up-regulated.
The Reactome 'Immune System' pathway was significantly enriched among the differentially regulated proteins in LC patients, containing 37 of the 162 proteins.
The more specific Reactome pathway 'Cytokine Signaling in Immune system' was enriched among LC differentially regulated proteins, including several highly connected hub proteins.

The Reactome 'SARS-CoV Infections' pathway was strongly enriched among the LC differentially regulated proteins, suggesting persistence of virus-response-related protein changes a year post-infection.

STRING network analysis identified 16 highly connected hub proteins (≥10 first-level interactions) within the LC differentially regulated protein set, indicating strong functional interconnectivity of immune-related proteins.
A distinct cluster of LC differentially regulated proteins was enriched for gene expression and RNA splicing/spliceosome functions.
A separate cluster of LC differentially regulated proteins was enriched for gene expression and RNA Polymerase II transcription functions.

Re-analysis of a prior ME/CFS PBMC proteome dataset under the same statistical thresholds identified 346 differentially regulated proteins, roughly twice as many as in the LC dataset, with 153 up- and 193 down-regulated.
Twenty-two Reactome pathways and five KEGG pathways were commonly enriched in both the LC and ME/CFS differentially regulated protein sets.
Among proteins quantified in both datasets, nine proteins were up-regulated and six were down-regulated in the same direction in both LC and ME/CFS patients.
HLA-B was significantly down-regulated in both LC (sixfold) and ME/CFS (1.7-fold) patients, suggesting altered T-cell recognition and reduced NK cell inhibitory signaling in both conditions.
HLA-E showed opposite directions of regulation between the two post-viral conditions: down-regulated in ME/CFS but up-regulated in LC.
CD4 was up-regulated in both LC and ME/CFS datasets and was one of the most highly connected hub proteins in the network analysis.
CD5, which inhibits T-cell receptor mediated signaling and regulates T-cell/B-cell interactions, was up-regulated in both LC and ME/CFS datasets.
CD84, which enhances T cell and NK cell activation and cytokine release, was down-regulated in both LC and ME/CFS datasets.
CD300LF, an inhibitory receptor of myeloid cells, was down-regulated in both LC and ME/CFS datasets.
S100A4, a calcium-binding protein expressed in CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells, was up-regulated almost 4-fold in LC patients but down-regulated 1.5-fold in ME/CFS patients.
The glial maturation factors GMFB and GMFG, associated with neuroinflammation and immune cell chemotaxis, were up-regulated ~2-fold in LC but down-regulated 2-4 fold in ME/CFS.

Searching the LC differentially regulated proteins against the MitoCarta3.0 database identified 21 of the 162 proteins as mitochondria-associated, involved in metabolism, translation, dynamics and oxidative phosphorylation.

Mitochondrial proteins were significantly over-represented among the up-regulated proteins in LC patients, unlikely to have occurred by chance, whereas mitochondrial proteins among down-regulated proteins showed no such enrichment.

Peroxiredoxin-2 (PRDX2), a mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme that reduces reactive oxygen species by hydrolysing H2O2, was up-regulated in both LC and ME/CFS, suggesting increased ROS generation in immune cells of both conditions.
PSMB9 (proteasome subunit beta type-9), linked to autoinflammation and immunodeficiency and previously reported as increased in COVID-19 patients, was up-regulated in both the LC and ME/CFS datasets.
C16orf54, a transmembrane protein suggested to regulate cellular energy homeostasis, was highly up-regulated in both the LC and ME/CFS study groups.

After Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate adjustment, only nine of the 162 nominally significant differentially regulated proteins remained significant, indicating a high false-negative rate given the small sample size and biological variability.
PRDX2, a mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme that detoxifies H2O2, was upregulated in both the LC and ME/CFS PBMC proteomes, suggesting increased reactive oxygen species generation in both conditions.
PSMB9, linked to autoinflammation and immunodeficiency and previously reported increased in COVID-19 patients, was upregulated in both the LC and ME/CFS datasets.
HLA-B, a Class I HLA protein, was downregulated in both LC (6-fold) and ME/CFS (1.7-fold), suggesting altered T cell recognition and reduced inhibitory signalling in NK cells in both disorders.

HLA-E, a non-classical Class I HLA molecule that engages CD94 on NK cells, was downregulated in ME/CFS (1.6-fold) but upregulated in LC (1.7-fold), showing opposite regulation between the two conditions.
HLA-DRB1 (Class II) was differentially regulated only in the LC dataset, whereas HLA-A, HLA-DQB1 and HLA-DPB1 were differentially regulated only in the ME/CFS dataset.
CD5, which regulates T cell/B cell interactions and inhibits T cell receptor-mediated signalling, was upregulated in both the LC and ME/CFS datasets.
CD84, which enhances T cell and NK cell activation and cytokine activity, was downregulated in both the LC and ME/CFS datasets.
CD300LF, an inhibitory receptor of myeloid cells, was downregulated in both the LC and ME/CFS datasets.

S100A4, a Ca2+-binding protein expressed in CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells, was upregulated almost fourfold in LC but downregulated 1.5-fold in ME/CFS, showing opposite regulation between the two conditions.
Glia maturation factor beta (GMFB), a growth/differentiation factor for glia and neurons implicated in neuroinflammation, was upregulated almost twofold in LC but downregulated 2-4 fold in ME/CFS.
Glia maturation factor gamma (GMFG), a cytokine-responsive protein in inflammatory cells that regulates neutrophil and lymphocyte chemotaxis, was upregulated in LC but downregulated in ME/CFS.
C16orf54, a transmembrane protein thought to regulate cellular energy supply homeostasis, was highly upregulated in both the LC and ME/CFS study groups.

Among the 83 upregulated proteins in LC, 16 were mitochondrial (per MitoCarta3.0), a statistically significant enrichment (binomial p=0.018) unlikely to occur by chance, and confirmed by STRING enrichment of mitochondrial cellular component terms.
The 5 downregulated mitochondrial proteins among the 79 downregulated LC proteins showed no significant enrichment (binomial p=0.94), indicating this subset could occur by chance.

The ME/CFS dataset contained 54 differentially regulated mitochondrial proteins, with 14 forming a distinct STRING cluster, whereas the 21 mitochondrial proteins in the LC dataset did not form a cluster of ≥10 proteins, suggesting a less pronounced mitochondrial protein network at the 1-year LC timepoint compared with 16-year ME/CFS.

Of 35 ME/CFS-differentially-regulated mitochondrial proteins also detected in the LC spectral library, 17 showed very similar fold changes in both datasets, even though only some reached statistical significance in the smaller LC cohort, with others trending toward significance.

A separate cited cohort study found IL-1β, IL-6 and TNFα were elevated in COVID-19 patients who did not recover from their viral infection, suggesting these cytokines may play a significant role in progression to long COVID.

A large LC cohort analysis defined four clinical phenotypes: a chronic fatigue-like condition (42%), a respiratory syndrome (~23%), a chronic pain syndrome (22%), and a neurosensorial syndrome (~11%).
A cited study reported that LC patients have reduced CD4+ and CD8+ effector memory T cells compared with controls.

A cited multi-omics and serology study comparing LC patients to those who recovered found systemic inflammation and immune dysregulation, concluding that normal crosstalk between the humoral and cellular arms of adaptive immunity had broken down in LC patients.

In a cited longitudinal ME/CFS relapse-recovery study, molecular changes occurred during a relapse but were restored to pre-relapse levels upon recovery, demonstrating within-patient reversibility of molecular dysregulation.

A random forest classifier trained on 20 biomarker candidate metabolites and validated with 1000-iteration bootstrapping achieved the best overall diagnostic performance for distinguishing ME/CFS patients from healthy controls.

Random forest feature selection identified oleoylcholine, cortisone, 3-hydroxydecanoate, and C-glycosyltryptophan as the metabolites most relevant for distinguishing ME/CFS patients from healthy controls.
SHAP analysis of the RFC model ranked oleoylcholine, phenyllactate, octanoylcarnitine, hydroxyasparagine, and piperine as the most important metabolite biomarkers contributing to ME/CFS prediction.
Lower plasma levels of oleoylcholine were associated with a positive SHAP contribution toward increased ME/CFS risk classification.
Lower plasma levels of phenyllactate (PLA) were associated with a positive SHAP contribution toward increased ME/CFS risk classification.
Higher plasma levels of hydroxyasparagine, p-cresol glucuronide, and C-glycosyltryptophan were associated with increased ME/CFS risk classification in the SHAP analysis.
A prior study (Germain et al.) found that acylcholines, part of fatty acid metabolism within lipid metabolism, were consistently reduced in two independent ME/CFS patient cohorts.

A prior metabolomics study (Nagy-Szakal et al.) reported higher plasma ceramide levels and variation in carnitine, choline, and complex lipid metabolites in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, with a plasma metabolomics prediction model reaching AUC 0.836.

A prior comprehensive metabolomics study (Naviaux et al.) identified twenty metabolic pathways as abnormal in ME/CFS patients, including sphingolipid, phospholipid, purine, cholesterol, microbiota, pyrroline-5-carboxylate, riboflavin, branched-chain amino acid, peroxisomal, and mitochondrial pathways, with 94% diagnostic accuracy.
Predictive models trained on the 20 biomarker candidate metabolites showed improved performance across all evaluation metrics compared with models trained on the full original 768-metabolite dataset.
Using the full original metabolite set with an 80–20 split, the gradient boosting classifier achieved the lowest performance among all models tested.
Using the full original metabolite set with bootstrap validation, logistic regression achieved the best performance among models trained without feature selection.
SHAP analysis identified indolelactate as the least significant of the analyzed metabolite features contributing to ME/CFS classification.
Nine of ten patients with post-COVID ME/CFS had orthostatic intolerance, and five of ten met diagnostic criteria for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (PoTS).
All ten patients had significant fatigue as measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) or Chalder Fatigue Scale (CFQ).
All ten patients had positive post-exertional malaise (PEM) on the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire-PEM with a duration of at least 24 hours.
Daily functioning measured by the Bell Score ranged from 20-60% (median 30%) across the ten patients, indicating marked functional impairment.
The SF-36 physical component summary score was markedly lower in ME/CFS patients than in the German age-matched norm population.
The SF-36 mental health component summary score in ME/CFS patients did not significantly differ from the German norm population.

Compared to adolescents/young adults with moderate to severe depression, ME/CFS patients scored significantly lower on SF-36 physical functioning, role physical, bodily pain, vitality, and social functioning.
ME/CFS patients scored significantly higher (better) on SF-36 role emotional and mental health domains than a comparator cohort of adolescents/young adults with moderate to severe depression.
General health scores on the SF-36 did not significantly differ between ME/CFS patients and the depression comparator cohort.
All ten patients fulfilled at least one ME/CFS case definition assessed by the MBSQ, with variable concordance across the CCC, IOM, PCD-J, and CDW-R criteria sets.

The most common ME/CFS symptoms among the ten patients were fatigue, daily-life limitations, PEM, and neurocognitive manifestations (all 10/10), followed by unrefreshing sleep (9/10) and dizziness (6/10).

Pre-existing medical conditions were present in 9/10 patients, most commonly bronchial asthma (4/10), followed by hypothyroidism, allergies, Graves' disease, attention deficit disorder, migraine, prior meningitis, and Alport syndrome.
Cardiac MRI in one hospitalized adult patient showed findings indicating prior perimyocarditis in the context of COVID-19.
Two of ten patients demonstrated bronchial hyper-responsiveness on pulmonary function testing, one of whom had pre-existing asthma.
Cranial MRI and EEG were mostly normal in this cohort, with only one stable benign CNS lesion and one transient theta wave slowing identified.

The MBSQs were used to diagnose ME/CFS in ten post-COVID-19 patients aged 11-25, representing the first reported use of a structured, age-adapted case-definition tool for ME/CFS in patients ≤18 years with post-COVID-19 condition.
Participants reported that a strained doctor-patient relationship, misdiagnoses, and incorrect treatments led to significant deterioration in their health status and quality of life.
Some patients reported suicide as a considered last mental option to escape the precarious situation created by poor doctor-patient relationships and lack of medical support.
As a consequence of negative experiences with physicians, some participants avoided discussing ME/CFS-related issues, sought medical care only in emergencies, or avoided contacting doctors entirely.
Several immune, neuroendocrine, pain, post-exertional malaise, and COVID-19 CDC domain symptoms significantly decreased from the time of acute infection to current reporting among youth with PASC.
Fatigue remained at a high level over time in youth with PASC, along with several symptoms within the sleep and post-exertional malaise domains.
Youth with ME/CFS reported overall worse symptomatology than youth with PASC, particularly in the neurocognitive domain.
Reanalysis identified 1256 differentially methylated positions in peripheral blood of FM patients versus controls, most of which (74.8%) were hypomethylated.
In CFS T CD3+ cells, 510 DMPs were identified versus controls, predominantly hypermethylated (78.8%).
In CFS PBMCs, 1751 DMPs were identified versus controls, roughly balanced between hypo- and hypermethylation.
Despite overall small methylation differences (5-10%), unsupervised hierarchical clustering based on identified DMPs clearly separated patients from controls in all three cohorts.

Methylation changes identified with the updated pipeline overlapped only minimally with those reported in the original publications of the same datasets (16.55% for FM, 10.1% for CFS T CD3+, 1.01% for CFS PBMC).
Across all three cohorts, DMPs were consistently enriched in transcription-factor binding sites, open chromatin, and enhancer regions, and depleted in gene promoters and CpG islands.

The GO molecular function term 'calcium ion binding' was the only term common to gene sets annotated to methylation changes in all three FM/CFS datasets, implicating voltage-gated calcium channel biology in pain physiology.
The GO cellular component term 'intrinsic component of plasma membrane' was common to gene sets annotated to methylation changes across all three FM/CFS datasets.

GO biological process terms related to cell adhesion, including homophilic cell adhesion via plasma membrane adhesion molecules, were consistently the top enriched terms across all three FM/CFS methylation datasets.

A binding motif for microRNA-448 (ATATGCA_MIR448) was among the mature-RNA target motifs consistently associated with methylation signatures across all three FM/CFS datasets; prior rodent work links miR-448 upregulation to neuropathic pain via SIRT1/cytokine pathways.

A shared binding motif for microRNA-133A/133B was consistently associated with FM/CFS methylation signatures across all three datasets; these microRNAs have been separately linked to pain modulation and cardiac ischemia in other disease contexts.

A microRNA-518C binding motif was among the three motifs commonly associated with methylation signatures across all FM/CFS datasets, though this specific microRNA has not previously been linked to pain.

The CpG site cg08155325, located in the first intron of protocadherin gamma (PCDHG) family genes, showed uniform methylation changes across all three FM and CFS datasets, implicating neural adhesion and synaptogenesis pathways.

The CpG site cg22838050, located within an EGR1 transcription factor binding site near enhancers of MED16 and CFD, showed uniform methylation changes across FM and CFS datasets, implicating inflammation and pain-related gene regulation.

The CpG site cg02454025, in the TSS200 of C1orf127 and overlapping RARA::RXRG transcription factor binding sites, showed uniform methylation changes across FM and CFS datasets, with RARA and RXRG previously implicated in nociceptor-enriched gene expression.

The CpG site cg19643109, localized in an IRF3 transcription factor binding site, showed uniform methylation changes across FM and CFS datasets; IRF3 inhibition has been linked to reduced visceral pain in rats, a symptom frequently reported in both conditions.

Genes annotated to CFS-associated methylation changes (both T CD3+ and PBMC datasets) were preferentially expressed in pain-perception-related brain structures including amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, cerebellum, and nucleus accumbens; the same tissue-enrichment analysis was not significant for FM.

Differentially methylated probes were identified within the BDNF gene in this reanalysis, consistent with a prior gene-centric study reporting BDNF hypermethylation in patients with CFS and comorbid fibromyalgia.

Among 54 patients making track 2 MAID requests in the first 6 months after Canada's expanded eligibility law, 8 patients (14.8%) had myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome as a qualifying complex chronic condition.
Chronic pain syndromes were the most common diagnosis among patients making track 2 MAID requests, affecting 28 of 54 patients (51.9%).
Providers reported that concurrent mental illness complicated the assessment in 37 of 54 (68.5%) of track 2 MAID requests.
Providers felt that in 19 of 54 (35.2%) track 2 cases, patients had not been offered all appropriate and available treatments prior to requesting MAID.
Providers reported difficulty finding suitable treatments for patients in 9 of 54 (16.7%) track 2 cases and difficulty finding experts to assist with assessments in 8 of 54 (14.8%) cases.

Providers' experiences with track 2 (non-terminal) MAID requesters differed from those with track 1 (terminal) requesters, as track 1 patients usually had end-stage malignancy or organ failure and rarely unmet health care needs, whereas track 2 patients frequently had unmet needs and comorbid mental illness.
Providers reported experiencing moral distress while trying to balance respecting patients' autonomy/rights with concerns about patients' best interests during track 2 MAID assessments.
Track 2 MAID assessments differed from track 1 assessments in that most track 1 patients have end-stage malignancy or organ failure and rarely have unmet health care needs, unlike track 2 patients.
Providers were often uncertain whether track 2 patients had seriously considered available treatments before pursuing MAID, beyond simply whether treatments had been offered.
ME symptoms increasingly restrict social lives, producing a phenomenon the authors term 'necessitated social isolation'.
The combined experience of stigma and having a contested illness leads to social withdrawal and rejection, generating a sense of loneliness described as 'compelled loneliness'.
As ME worsens, participants experience a self-reinforcing cycle in which social isolation and loneliness reproduce one another.
Loneliness in the context of ME is shaped by three situational themes: spatial and temporal restrictedness, communicative alienation, and discreditation.
The stigma associated with ME being a contested illness exacerbates the loneliness experienced by patients.

A cited study found that the FA value of the right arcuate fasciculus was significantly increased in right-handed patients with chronic fatigue syndrome, with the authors proposing CFS as the cause and suggesting this structural change could serve as a diagnostic biomarker.

A cited study found that toddlers with autism spectrum disorder had significantly lower FA values in the left arcuate fasciculus compared with normal individuals, suggesting a link to impaired early speaking ability.

Hierarchical cluster analysis of 40 threat items sorted by patients with RMD/CSS yielded an eight-cluster taxonomy of threats to physical symptoms: environmental stimuli, physical symptoms, food and drugs, inactivity, demands, effort, invalidation, and emotional stress.

Hierarchical cluster analysis of 40 soother items sorted by patients with RMD/CSS yielded a ten-cluster taxonomy of soothing influences on physical symptoms: social emotional support, rest and balance, pleasant surroundings, illness understanding, positive mindset and autonomy, spirituality, leisure activity, wellness, treatment and care, and nutrition and treats.
The card-sorting sample was overwhelmingly female (97.4%), consistent with the known greater female prevalence in central sensitivity syndromes and most rheumatic/musculoskeletal diseases.
Somatic symptom severity (PHQ-15) was medium or high in the majority of card-sorting participants (38.3% medium, 36.5% high), with only 21.7% scoring low and 0.9% minimal.

Prior theory proposes that an imbalance in affect-regulation systems—characterized by a hyperactive threat system and a hypoactive soothing system—may act as a diathesis and maintenance factor for physical symptoms in fibromyalgia.

Threat clusters such as 'demands' (e.g., perfectionism) and 'emotional stress', and soothing clusters such as 'social emotional support' and 'positive mindset', have been previously linked to symptom severity across a variety of chronic illnesses beyond RMD/CSS.

Most card-sorting participants had co-occurring diagnoses, with 85.2% having at least one central sensitivity syndrome and 46.1% reporting at least one rheumatic/musculoskeletal disease other than fibromyalgia.
In six breast cancer patients with musculoskeletal pain from aromatase inhibitor treatment, oxygen-ozone major autohemotherapy reduced pain scores by at least 66%, from a mean NRS of 9.43 to 2.36.
Fatigue, measured with the Fatigue Scoring Scale, was reduced by 66.26% in all six breast cancer patients following oxygen-ozone major autohemotherapy.

The paper reports on dermatologic comorbidities associated with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome as reported by both physicians and patients, but no specific quantitative findings are available from the title alone.

In Kalisch et al.'s online Positive Psychology Intervention RCT, pain disability showed only a small post-intervention improvement that was not maintained, with follow-up scores worse than baseline across all groups.
Patients who self-selected their own positive psychology topics showed significantly higher positive affect post-intervention that was maintained at 1-month follow-up.
No significant improvements in negative affect were found across the three study groups (assigned, self-select, waiting list) at any timepoint.
Patients in the self-selected topic group reported significantly higher satisfaction with life post-intervention, maintained at 1-month follow-up.
The positive psychology intervention did not significantly reduce self-rated fatigue at 1-month follow-up.
The majority of patients (76.6%) reported being satisfied or very satisfied with the online positive psychology intervention, with less than 5% dissatisfied.
The Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation Treatment (physical therapy plus EXP therapy) reduced pain intensity in adolescents with G-HSD/hEDS by 63%.
The Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation Treatment significantly reduced disability scores on the Functional Disability Inventory in adolescents with G-HSD/hEDS.
The Intensive Interdisciplinary Pain Management Programme significantly improved functioning across most Bath Adolescent Pain Questionnaire subscales, except developmental and family functioning.
In the Intensive Interdisciplinary Pain Management Programme, 36.7% of adolescents showed clinically significant pain reduction, but 30% were reliably worse and 33.3% showed no change.

Parents of adolescents in the Intensive Interdisciplinary Pain Management Programme reported reduced depression, anxiety, catastrophising, self-blame, leisure impairment and parental behaviour impact, though partner relationship and parental strain changes were not significant.
The cognitive behavioural Pain Management Programme did not produce a significant long-term reduction in pain intensity at 5-month follow-up in adults.
The Pain Management Programme significantly improved pain self-efficacy by 27% post-intervention, sustained at 5-month follow-up.
The Pain Management Programme significantly reduced pain catastrophising by 31.8% in adults, sustained at 5-month follow-up.
The Pain Management Programme significantly reduced depression scores in adults by 15.2%, sustained at 5-month follow-up.
The Pain Management Programme significantly reduced anxiety scores in adults by 15.1%, sustained at 5-month follow-up.

The Therapeutic Patient Education Programme (PrEduSED) did not significantly improve pain coping strategies (distraction, reinterpretation, ignorance, dramatisation, prayer) at 6-month follow-up in adults.
PrEduSED did not significantly improve anxiety or depression (HADS) at 6-month follow-up despite high baseline scores.
PrEduSED did not significantly improve physical or mental functioning (SF-12) at 6-month follow-up in adults.
PrEduSED showed no significant improvement in fatigue impact subscales (cognitive, physical, social) at 6-month follow-up, with only a borderline change in the relationship subscale.
The overall burden reported by relatives of PrEduSED patients (Zarit Scale) did not significantly change, with most relatives reporting light or no burden.
The neurocognitive behavioural Rehabilitation for Pain Management Programme significantly reduced pain-related fear of movement in patients with chronic low back pain and hypermobility.
The Rehabilitation for Pain Management Programme significantly reduced fatigue severity pre- to post-intervention.
The Rehabilitation for Pain Management Programme significantly reduced disability scores (Oswestry Disability Index) pre- to post-intervention.

Across the six included studies, interventions combining psychological input with physical therapy in multidisciplinary programmes were the most effective at reducing both psychological (fear, catastrophising) and physical (functioning, disability) impacts of pain, compared to an isolated positive psychology intervention or a short inpatient education programme.
