In the multidisciplinary rehabilitation treatment study, family functioning on the Bath Adolescent Pain Questionnaire unexpectedly improved for adolescents with EDS but not for those with joint hypermobility syndrome (JHS).
In the Positive Psychology Intervention RCT, patient-rated fatigue showed only a small, non-significant improvement at 1-month follow-up.

The Therapeutic Patient Education Programme did not significantly improve fatigue impact across cognitive, physical, or social subscales at 6-month follow-up, with only the relationship subscale approaching significance.

The Intensive Interdisciplinary Pain Management Programme significantly reduced parental depression, anxiety, child-related catastrophising, and self-blame/helplessness, but did not significantly change partner relationship or parental strain.
The Therapeutic Patient Education Programme did not significantly change the overall caregiver burden score (Zarit Scale) among relatives of patients, most of whom reported light or no burden.

Most patients in the Positive Psychology Intervention RCT were satisfied or very satisfied with the intervention, with no significant difference in satisfaction between the assigned-topic and self-selected-topic groups.
Among the ten positive psychology topics offered, 'spot the positives' was rated most enjoyable and 'hope quest' least, and patients who self-selected topics most often chose 'self-compassion'.
The cohort of 97 adults with suspected EDS/G-HSD had a median Beighton score of 3 (mean 3.6, range 0-8), with 46 individuals scoring 4 or more.

Manual annotation of joint keypoints by two independent researchers showed high inter-rater reliability (ICC >0.9) across all assessed joints except the knee, which showed moderate-to-strong agreement (ICC=0.823).
Among open-source pose-estimation libraries, Detectron showed the strongest correlation between video-derived elbow extension angles and goniometer measurements.
MoveNet-Thunder achieved the strongest correlation with goniometer measurements for knee extension angle among open-source libraries.
MoveNet-Thunder achieved the strongest correlation with goniometer measurements for shoulder flexion angle among open-source libraries.
Angles for the ankle and fifth finger movements calculated from open-source pose-estimation libraries were not consistently significantly correlated with goniometer measurements.
The Detectron library failed to produce sufficiently confident keypoint predictions for the knee movement in a large fraction of videos, successfully analyzing only 111 of 191 available videos.

A domain-specific fine-tuned MobileNet-v2 model (trained via DeepLabCut on hand keypoints of this cohort) showed strong correlation between video-derived fifth finger extension angles and goniometer measurements, outperforming general-purpose open-source libraries.

Manually annotated ankle dorsiflexion angles from video were only very weakly correlated with goniometer measurements, suggesting the video framing did not adequately capture the movement plane assessed clinically.

Manually annotated fifth finger extension angles from video showed a moderate-to-strong correlation with goniometer measurements, indicating the video framing was adequate for this movement under ideal annotation conditions.

Angles calculated from pose-tracked keypoints were significantly correlated with those calculated from manually annotated keypoints for the elbow, knee, and shoulder, with the top-performing library per joint reaching rho=0.904 (elbow, Detectron), 0.739 (knee, Detectron), and 0.893 (shoulder, MoveNet-Thunder).

The study's correlations between OpenPose-derived and manually annotated angles were consistent with a prior study by Fan, Gu et al. reporting moderate Pearson correlations for elbow extension and shoulder flexion.

Although OpenPose-derived ankle angles moderately correlated with manually annotated angles, this did not translate into correlation with goniometer measurements, indicating a video framing/plane-of-movement problem rather than a pose-estimation accuracy problem for the ankle.

For the fifth finger movement, only MediaPipe-Hands and AlphaPose showed a significant but weak correlation with manual annotations (combining both sides), while all other open-source library correlations were non-significant.
The authors note that, unlike most EDS subtypes, hypermobile EDS lacks an identified genetic cause.
The estimated prevalence of EDS in the general population is approximately 194.2 cases per 100,000 individuals.
The patient with hypermobile EDS presented with aortic valve regurgitation and an aortic bulb aneurysm measuring approximately 5 cm in axial diameter.

The patient exhibited severe rotational scoliosis of the thoraco-lumbar spine with deepened thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis, along with rib deformation and chest wall abnormalities, consistent with connective tissue fragility in EDS.
Coronary CT angiography revealed absence of the left main coronary artery and absence of right coronary artery dominance in this EDS patient.
The left circumflex artery had an ectopic origin from the right sinus of Valsalva with a retroaortic proximal course, an unusual coronary anomaly found in this EDS patient.

A coronary-pulmonary arterial fistula was visualized, originating from the right sinus of Valsalva (~0.3 cm diameter vessel) and dividing into multiple aneurysmally dilated, tortuous fistula vessels communicating with the main pulmonary artery.
Imaging revealed the presence of an additional right pulmonary vein as a further vascular anomaly in this EDS patient.
CCTA also revealed calcifications within the aortic valve of this EDS patient.
The authors state that one prior published paper mentions a patient with coexistent EDS and coronary-pulmonary arterial fistula, indicating this co-occurrence is exceedingly rare.

Vascular EDS, caused by COL3A1 mutations affecting collagen type III production, carries the highest risk of aortic dissection among EDS subtypes, with nearly 80% of affected individuals experiencing vascular complications by age 40.

Aortic dissection in vascular EDS does not show significant gender bias and often manifests in the second or third decade of life, being more aggressive regarding vascular complications than other EDS subtypes.

In vascular EDS, structurally impaired collagen type III (from COL3A1 mutations) weakens the vascular wall, increasing susceptibility to spontaneous rupture including aortic dissection, and increased shear stress from turbulent blood flow further contributes to aneurysm/dissection development.
Classical EDS presents with joint hypermobility, skin hyperelasticity, and easy bruising, and is associated with mutations in COL5A1 and COL5A2, which encode collagen type V.
Kyphoscoliotic EDS, featuring severe muscle hypotonia, joint laxity, and progressive scoliosis, is linked to mutations in the PLOD1 and FKBP14 genes involved in collagen processing.
Arthrochalasia EDS, involving severe joint hypermobility and congenital hip dislocation, arises from mutations in COL1A1 and COL1A2, which encode collagen type I.

Hypermobile EDS lacks a well-defined genetic marker, making clinical assessment and symptomatology crucial for diagnosis, with prominent features of joint hypermobility, chronic joint pain, and skin hyperextensibility.
EDS collectively is estimated to affect approximately 1 in 5000 to 20,000 individuals depending on subtype.

In Marfan syndrome, the lifetime risk of aortic dissection ranges from 5% to 30%, with highest risk in the third and fourth decades of life, and is heightened in individuals with specific FBN1 mutations.

Mutant fibrillin-1 in Marfan syndrome sequesters excessive TGFβ, leading to dysregulated TGFβ signaling that impairs smooth muscle cell function and ECM production, weakening the aortic wall and predisposing to aneurysm and dissection.

Antihypertensive medications such as beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) and calcium channel blockers (e.g., verapamil) are commonly used to reduce force on the weakened aortic wall and mitigate further dissection risk in connective tissue disorder patients.

Musculoskeletal manifestations, including joint hypermobility, joint dislocations, and chronic joint pain, are hallmark features across different EDS subtypes and are managed with physical therapy and joint protection strategies to improve quality of life.
Monoallelic (dominant) mutations in TNXB are established as a cause of hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The CAH-X CH1 chimera is characterized by a 120bp deletion in TNXB exon 35 (Del120bp), causing haploinsufficiency of TNX.
The CAH-X CH2 chimera is defined by the TNXB variant c.12174C>G (p.Cys4058Trp) in exon 40, producing a structural change poorly tolerated due to a dominant negative effect.
The CAH-X CH3 chimera is defined by a cluster of TNXB variants (p.Arg4073His in exon 41, p.Asp4172Asn and p.Ser4175Asn in exon 43).
Among 186 CAH patients selected for risk of TNXB involvement, 78 (41.9%) were carriers of one or several CAH-X chimeras.
The CH1 chimera was the most frequent CAH-X chimera, found in 46 of 186 patients (24.7%).
The CH2 chimera was found in 24 of 186 patients (12.9%).
The CH3 chimera was the least frequent, found in 8 of 186 patients (4.3%).
Clinical manifestations consistent with EDS-like connective tissue disorder were observed in 70% (7/10) of CAH-X carriers who underwent clinical evaluation, most frequently musculoskeletal disorders.
The frequency of CAH-X alleles reported by Gao et al. and Marino et al. was substantially higher than in the Spanish cohort, a difference reaching statistical significance.
Two patients homozygous for classic-form CAH-X were identified in the cohort, one with CH1/CH1 and one with CH2/CH2 genotypes; more severe forms appear associated with biallelic CAH-X.

The frequency of CYP21A2 alleles containing deletions/conversions (potentially involving TNXB) varies by CAH clinical form: 25% in classic (CL) forms, 5% in nonclassic (NC) forms, and 1% in functional hyperandrogenism (FH) carriers, in the Spanish population.
MLPA gene-dosage screening for CYP21A2/TNXB detects only the CH1 chimera and misses CH2 and CH3, which may cause more severe CAH-X forms, requiring additional sequencing-based screening.
Familial segregation analysis confirmed that 21 CAH-unaffected relatives were carriers of CAH-X chimeric alleles.
Fibromyalgia was significantly more common as a comorbidity in patients with difficult-to-treat axial spondyloarthritis compared to non-difficult-to-treat patients.
Peripheral joint involvement was more prevalent among difficult-to-treat axSpA patients than non-difficult-to-treat patients.
Baseline disease activity measured by BASDAI was higher in difficult-to-treat axSpA patients compared to non-difficult-to-treat patients.
Baseline CRP levels were higher in the very difficult-to-treat axSpA subgroup compared to non-difficult-to-treat patients.
Inflammatory bowel disease prevalence was markedly higher in the very difficult-to-treat axSpA subgroup than in non-difficult-to-treat patients.
None of the patients meeting the stricter very difficult-to-treat axSpA criteria had fibromyalgia, suggesting fibromyalgia comorbidity may be independent of this more stringent subgroup.
The FM group showed a higher peak P50 amplitude to electrocutaneous stimulation than the control group, indicating early somatosensory cortical hyperexcitability.
Across all participants, P50 amplitude correlated positively with the PCA-derived 'FM profile' factor reflecting pain, catastrophizing, anxiety, depression, and ADHD symptoms.
Among FM participants, P50 amplitude showed a marginal positive correlation with self-reported functional impact scores on the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire-Revised.

Overall N100 amplitude to innocuous tones did not differ between FM and controls, but the FMO subgroup (FM not on GABA-mimetic medications) showed a larger N100 than both controls and the FMG subgroup.

FM participants taking GABA-mimetic medications (gabapentin, pregabalin, or fluoxetine; FMG subgroup) showed N100 amplitudes not different from healthy controls, suggesting normalization of auditory cortical excitability.
Overall phasic SCR to electrocutaneous stimulation did not differ between FM and controls, but the FMO subgroup showed larger SCR amplitudes than both controls and the FMG subgroup.
SCR amplitude correlated positively with the FM profile factor across all participants.
Tonic SCL was higher in the FMO subgroup than in controls, with no overall FM vs control difference and no difference between FMG and controls.
Tonic SCL correlated positively with the FM profile factor and with tone-evoked anticipatory anxiety ratings.
FM participants rated the electrocutaneous stimulation as more uncomfortable/painful than controls.
FM participants rated innocuous tones as more anxiety-provoking (anticipatory anxiety) than controls, and this anxiety correlated with the FM profile factor.

Overall ECS current threshold selected did not differ between FM and controls, though the FMO subgroup showed a nonsignificant trend toward reaching an uncomfortable level at a lower current than controls.
A PCA-derived composite 'FM profile' factor (loading tender points, pain, catastrophizing, pain anxiety, pain management, ADHD, depression, and anxiety scores) was much higher in FM than controls.
FM participants had a higher body mass index than controls, consistent with prior reports.
FM participants reported markedly higher depression symptom scores (PHQ-9) than controls.
FM participants reported markedly higher anxiety symptom scores (GAD-7) than controls.
FM participants reported higher adult ADHD self-report symptom scores than controls.
P50 peak latency tended to be shorter in controls than in the FMO subgroup, a marginal difference not seen with the FMG subgroup.

A long-trace-interval classical conditioning paradigm pairing tones (CS) with electrocutaneous shock (UCS) failed to produce contingency awareness in the majority of participants, with no difference between FM and control groups.
Prior studies found FM patients had lower levels of PGC-1α and TFAM mitochondrial proteins, while CFS patients showed no significant change in these markers.
Antioxidant enzyme activity (SOD1, catalase, NADPH) is reduced in FM patients and this reduction correlates with pain and fatigue severity.
Altindag and Celik reported lower total antioxidant capacity (TAC) among FM patients compared to individuals without FM.
Multiple studies have shown decreased levels of CoQ10, an enzyme relevant to mitochondrial function, in FM patients.
Mitochondrial imbalance in FM is reflected by increased expression of autophagic genes and elimination of damaged mitochondria.
Mitochondria-derived ROS activate NF-κB signaling, leading to upregulation of inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and TNF-α, consistent with the low-grade inflammation profile linked to FM.
FM patients show higher plasma levels of IL-6 and IL-8 compared to healthy individuals.
Ramírez-Tejero et al. identified 33 differentially expressed proteins in FM patients versus controls, most linked to inflammatory processes.
Wåhlén et al. found differences in inflammatory, metabolic, and immune proteins in FM patients that correlated with patients' pain perception and psychological distress.

Han et al. found 22 differentially expressed proteins in FM patients compared to pain-free controls, mainly related to blood coagulation, immune response and extracellular matrix-receptor interactions.

Secondary hyperalgesia in FM is proposed to be driven by activation of NMDA receptors in the spinal dorsal horn and periaqueductal gray, leading to central sensitization and prolonged synaptic activity.
FM patients show higher levels of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate and lower levels of inhibitory neurotransmitters serotonin and norepinephrine.

Clos-García et al. found FM patients had decreased healthy-microbiome-associated bacterial strains involved in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production and depletion of Firmicutes, alongside disrupted glutamate and serine levels.
Reduced bacterial diversity was found in FM patients, with a specific decrease in Bifidobacterium and Eubacterium genera.

Albayrak et al. found a statistically significant increase in Bacteroidia and Bifidobacterium and a decrease in Firmicutes in FM patients, with non-significant differences in Enterobacter, Streptococcus and Lactobacillus.

A systematic review found Bacteroides spp. positively correlated with FIQ total symptom score and 2016 ACR diagnostic criteria, with increased Parabacteroides merdae and a non-significant trend toward increased Akkermansia muciniphila.

A separate study reported that following a Khorasan wheat diet led to improvements in various FM symptoms accompanied by alterations in certain gut bacteria, with positive correlations among Actinobacteria, Verrucomicrobiae, Saccharibacteria, Bacteroidales and FM symptom questionnaire scores.
Prior testing of olive-oil-based nutritional intervention in FM patients showed beneficial effects on oxidative DNA damage and antioxidant levels.
The authors' own prior research demonstrated increased oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in FM patients, motivating the current biomarker panel design.

In the discussion, the authors state several studies have reported an increase in TAC among FM patients, indicating higher oxidative stress, which conflicts with the earlier introduction statement citing the same reference for lower TAC.
Among 703 patients evaluated for suspected mast cell disorders, 31 (4.4%) were confirmed to have idiopathic mast cell activation syndrome (iMCAS).
Three patients in the cohort were identified as having hereditary alpha-tryptasemia based on baseline serum tryptase levels above 8 ng/mL.
Mucocutaneous symptoms (urticaria or angioedema) were the most common presentation during episodes in iMCAS patients but were significantly less prevalent among patients with clonal MCAS.
Patients with iMCAS experienced a significantly longer diagnostic delay than patients with clonal MCAS.
CCL2 was identified via LASSO, random forest, SVM-RFE and MCC algorithms as a shared immune-related biomarker for heart failure and IBD, being downregulated in HF but upregulated in IBD.
CXCR2 was identified as a shared immune-related biomarker upregulated in both HF and IBD with high diagnostic accuracy in validation cohorts.
S100A9 was identified as a shared immune-related biomarker upregulated in both HF and IBD, with prior literature supporting its role as a potential IBD biomarker and cardiac fibrosis modulator.
CCL2 expression was positively correlated with activated mast cell infiltration in both heart failure and inflammatory bowel disease samples.
S100A9 expression positively correlated with both activated neutrophils and activated mast cells in HF samples, and with neutrophils and activated mast cells in IBD samples.
CXCR2 expression was strongly positively correlated with neutrophil infiltration in both HF and IBD samples.

Immune cell infiltration analysis via CIBERSORT showed neutrophils and M0 macrophages were significantly elevated in both HF and IBD, while M2 macrophages were significantly reduced in both diseases compared to controls.

144 overlapping differentially expressed genes between HF and IBD were significantly enriched in immune response, inflammatory response, chemokine activity, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, chemokine signaling and TNF signaling pathways.

Four machine learning feature-selection methods (LASSO, random forest, SVM-RFE, and cytoHubba MCC) converged on five shared candidate genes (CCL2, CXCR2, PPBP, S100A9, CDH1) from 34 immune-related genes common to HF and IBD.
Levagen+ (PEA) supplementation did not significantly reduce total rTNSS allergy symptom scores compared to placebo at baseline or at any point during the 14-day treatment period.
In a subgroup of participants with baseline weekly rTNSS scores above 4 (n=79), Levagen+ produced a significantly greater reduction in nasal symptom scores than placebo by week 2 of treatment.

Total Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ) scores improved significantly from baseline in both the Levagen+ and placebo groups, with no significant between-group difference at week 2.
Plasma histamine concentration significantly decreased in the Levagen+ group while it increased in the placebo group, with a significant between-group difference after two weeks.
Plasma IL-4 significantly decreased from baseline in both the Levagen+ and placebo groups.
Plasma IL-10 significantly decreased from baseline in the Levagen+ group only, with no significant change in the placebo group.
Plasma IL-8 significantly decreased from baseline in the Levagen+ group only, with no significant change in the placebo group.
Plasma TNF-α significantly decreased from baseline in the Levagen+ group only, with no significant change in the placebo group.
Three adverse events (bloating, diarrhoea, and mild chest pain) were reported, all in the placebo group, with none reported in the Levagen+ group.
TYMP mRNA and protein expression levels were elevated in ccRCC tissue and were associated with worse patient prognosis.
TYMP mRNA expression increased with higher clinical stage of ccRCC.
TYMP protein expression, assessed via the Human Protein Atlas, was higher in renal cancer tissue than in normal renal tissue.
PCR analysis of 20 patient tissue samples confirmed TYMP mRNA was significantly higher in ccRCC tissue than in matched paracancerous tissue.
TYMP expression was significantly higher in 786-O renal carcinoma cells than in HK-2 normal renal tubular epithelial cells.
siRNA knockdown of TYMP in 786-O cells significantly reduced their proliferation ability, as measured by CCK-8 assay.
TYMP knockdown in 786-O cells significantly increased the apoptosis rate as measured by flow cytometry.
TYMP knockdown significantly reduced migration ability of renal cancer cells, as shown by wound healing assay.
TYMP expression positively correlated with PD-1 (PDCD1) and CTLA4 expression, with both immune checkpoint genes elevated in the high-TYMP expression subgroup.

TYMP-associated differential genes were functionally enriched in cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, PD-L1 expression/PD-1 checkpoint pathway, viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor, and T-cell receptor signaling pathway.

GSEA showed genes associated with high vs low TYMP expression were enriched in immune-related pathways (interferon alpha response, interferon gamma response, allograft rejection, inflammatory response) and other signaling pathways (IL6/JAK/STAT3, P53, IL2/STAT5).

Infiltration levels of Macrophage M2, CD8 T cells, Macrophage M0, Macrophage M1, gamma delta T cells, T follicular helper cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), and resting NK cells were elevated in ccRCC tumor tissue compared to normal tissue.

Infiltration levels of resting CD4 memory T cells, mast cells, activated myeloid dendritic cells, eosinophils, naive B cells, activated mast cells, monocytes, and plasma B cells were decreased in ccRCC tumor tissue compared to normal tissue.

Higher activated mast cell infiltration was associated with a more favorable prognosis, whereas higher infiltration of B cell memory, activated CD4 memory T cells, T follicular helper cells, Tregs, activated NK cells, and Macrophage M0 was associated with worse prognosis in ccRCC patients.
In the high TYMP expression group, infiltration levels of B cell memory, activated NK cells, T follicular helper cells, and Tregs were increased compared to the low TYMP expression group.
In the high TYMP expression group, activated mast cell infiltration was decreased compared to the low TYMP expression group, and TYMP expression was negatively correlated with mast cell activation.
A prognostic nomogram combining TYMP expression with clinical features (age, gender, pathologic stage) accurately predicted 1-, 3-, and 5-year overall survival in ccRCC patients.

Pan-cancer analysis showed TYMP was elevated across multiple tumor types (BLCA, BRCA, CESC, CHOL, ESCA, GBM, HNSC, KIRC, KIRP, LIHC, LUAD, LUSC, READ, STAD, UCEC) except pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD).
TYMP expression was associated with negative prognosis in ACC, KIRC, LGG, LUSC, THYM, and UVM, but favorable prognosis in MESO and SKCM.
Differential expression analysis between high- and low-TYMP ccRCC groups identified 55 upregulated genes, including immune-related genes PDCD1, LAG3, CXCL9, CXCL13, and CCL5.
TLSWE-8510 dose-dependently inhibited release of β-hexosaminidase from IgE/BSA-stimulated bone marrow-derived cultured mast cells.
TLSWE-8510 dose-dependently inhibited histamine release from IgE/BSA-stimulated bone marrow-derived cultured mast cells.
TLSWE-8510 reduced surface expression of the high-affinity IgE receptor FcεRI on mast cells and decreased IgE binding to FcεRI.
TLSWE-8510 dose-dependently downregulated IL-1β mRNA expression and production in IgE/BSA-stimulated mast cells.

TLSWE-8510 dose-dependently downregulated mRNA expression and production of allergy-related cytokines IL-1β, IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-13, TNF-α, and IFN-γ in IgE/BSA-stimulated bone marrow-derived cultured mast cells.
TLSWE-8510 downregulated production of the chemokines TARC and RANTES in IgE/BSA-stimulated bone marrow-derived cultured mast cells.
TLSWE-8510 regulated (reduced) phosphorylation of NF-κB in IgE/BSA-stimulated bone marrow-derived cultured mast cells, contributing to suppression of allergic mediator production.

TLSWE-8510 suppressed the Syk-LAT-ERK-Gab2 signaling cascade activated downstream of the high-affinity IgE receptor in IgE/BSA-stimulated mast cells, contributing to reduced allergic cytokine/chemokine production.
In vivo, TLSWE-8510 treatment dose-dependently decreased the IgE/BSA-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) reaction in the ears of BALB/c mice.

Psychophysical and electrophysiological responses to intra-epidermal electric stimulation, analyzed with a Naïve Bayes classifier, could identify diabetic small-fiber neuropathy patients with performance matching or exceeding current diagnostic methods.
The patient was found to carry the pathogenic variant c.466G>A p.(A156T) in the GLA gene, confirming a diagnosis of classic Fabry disease.
Skin biopsy confirmed the presence of small fiber neuropathy in the patient.
After 1 year of enzyme replacement therapy with algasidase-beta, the patient's renal involvement improved, with reduced proteinuria and improved creatinine clearance.
Enzyme replacement therapy normalized the patient's hypertrophic interventricular septum thickness after 1 year of treatment.

Despite ERT and olmesartan, and subsequent trials of gabapentin, pregabalin, and palmitoylethanolamide over several months, the patient's severe burning extremity pain persisted with no positive effect.

Oral medical cannabis (THC 8%/CBD 12%, later increased to 500 mg/day) improved the patient's neuropathic pain as measured by the Brief Pain Inventory, with benefit reported after 1 month and maintained after 1 year without significant side effects.
The main benefit of cannabis treatment was on nocturnal pain interference, allowing the patient to sleep through the night, while daytime pain relief was less pronounced.
Cannabis treatment had no effect on acute Fabry pain crises triggered by stress, exercise, or ambient temperature changes, and the BPI 'worst pain' score remained unmodified.

A role of the endocannabinoid system in the pathophysiology of small fiber neuropathy has been described, with endocannabinoid receptors present throughout the nervous system modulating nociceptive transmission.

The patient's mother, carrying the same GLA variant, had cornea verticillata and cardiomyopathy but no acroparesthesiae, illustrating phenotypic variability in neuropathic pain expression among carriers.

The patient's brother, carrying the same GLA variant, had angiokeratomas, proteinuria, chronic diarrhea, hyperhidrosis, and burning extremity pain only during fever episodes, a milder pain phenotype than the index patient.
Neuropathic pain has been reported to affect up to 81.4% of classical male Fabry patients and 65.3% of females, with a mean pain onset of 14.8 years in men and 19.8 years in women.
Known TRPV1 sensitizers (forskolin, IL-1β, GDNF, PGE2) significantly increased capsaicin-evoked calcium responses in DRG neurons after a 10-minute pre-incubation, validating the sensitization assay.

A 24-hour exposure screen of 480 bioactive compounds identified three proteasome inhibitors (MG-132, Z-Leu3-VS, gliotoxin) that sensitized TRPV1 in primary DRG neurons without directly activating the neurons.
Bortezomib produced a concentration-dependent long-term sensitization of TRPV1 in DRG neurons, confirmed both in the primary FLIPR-based screen and by Fura-2 ratiometric calcium imaging.
Bortezomib pre-treatment increased the proportion of DRG neurons activated faster by a sub-saturating capsaicin dose (30 nM), though the final proportion of activated neurons was unchanged.
The overall calcium response to a saturating dose of capsaicin (1 µM) was similar between bortezomib- and vehicle-treated neurons, indicating no change in total TRPV1-responsive population.
TRPV1 sensitization by bortezomib increased progressively with pre-incubation duration across 1, 6, 24, 48, and 72 hours, with maximal effect at 48 hours but detectable effects as early as 1 hour.
Bortezomib did not change TRPV1 transcript levels, arguing against increased channel expression as the mechanism of sensitization.
Voltage-clamp recordings showed that capsaicin-evoked current density was 84% higher in DRG neurons pretreated with bortezomib compared to naïve neurons.
Bortezomib did not alter resting membrane potential, action potential threshold current, or ramp-evoked firing rate in DRG neurons, indicating no general increase in neuronal excitability.
Bortezomib caused a dose-dependent decrease in DRG neurite outgrowth starting at 3 nM (maximal at 30 nM), with reduced neurite length, branch number, process number, and increased neuronal death.
DRG neurons from TRPV1 knockout mice were protected from bortezomib-induced neurite outgrowth loss and neuronal death, unlike wild-type neurons.
In vivo, bortezomib treatment significantly reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) in wild-type mouse skin compared to vehicle.
TdTomato reporter labeling in TRPV1-cre mice showed that TRPV1-lineage fibers, particularly superficial non-vertical axons, were preferentially lost after bortezomib treatment.

Bortezomib-treated mice showed a shifted, broader thermal preference toward colder temperatures and failed to settle into a narrow preferred zone, indicating impaired innocuous sensory discrimination.

Avoidance of noxious heat (>40°C) was transiently impaired one week after cessation of bortezomib treatment, returning to normal one week later, suggesting partial nerve regrowth or sensitization of remaining terminals.
TRPV1 knockout mice were protected in vivo from bortezomib-induced IENFD reduction and thermal preference deficits, indicating TRPV1 is required for bortezomib neurotoxicity.
The paper cites that bortezomib-induced peripheral neuropathy occurs in 30-50% of treated patients, a clinical background statistic supporting the relevance of the TRPV1 sensitization mechanism.
The paper cites prior literature estimating that 40-86% of sarcoidosis patients experience symptoms related to small fiber neuropathy.
Among 117 participants, 26% of sarcoidosis patients had established SFN, 15% had probable SFN, 42% had no clinical signs of SFN, and 17% were healthy controls.
The SFN Screening List (SFNSL) score was significantly higher in patients with established SFN compared with probable SFN, no SFN, and healthy controls.
Corneal nerve fiber length (CNFL) and nerve fiber area (NFA) were not reduced in sarcoidosis patients with established SFN compared with sarcoidosis patients without SFN or healthy controls.

ACCMetrics-derived CNFL and corneal NFA were significantly higher in sarcoidosis patients with SFN symptoms and clinical signs but fewer than two abnormal thermal threshold testing parameters (probable SFN) than in patients with established SFN.
CNFL values calculated by manual (CCMetrics), semiautomatic (NeuronJ), and fully automatic (ACCMetrics) analysis methods correlated well with each other in the sarcoidosis cohort.
NFA calculated with the NFA FIJI macro correlated with NFA calculated by ACCMetrics, though the correlation was weaker than the CNFL method comparisons.
Fully automatic (ACCMetrics) analysis slightly underestimated CNFL compared with manual (CCMetrics) and semiautomatic (NeuronJ) analysis, consistent with prior research.

The quadratic (exponential) relationship between NFA and CNFL previously described by Brines et al. was reproducible using ACCMetrics CNFL and NFA FIJI data, though shifted toward higher values in this sarcoidosis cohort.

For CCMetrics and NeuronJ, the relationship between CNFL and NFA followed a root/decelerating curve rather than the exponential relationship previously reported, indicating the published formula is not generalizable across all software programs.

Corneal NFA did not differentiate sarcoidosis patients with SFN from those without SFN, contradicting the hypothesis that NFA increases diagnostic sensitivity for SFN by detecting early nerve swelling.

In a meta-analysis of 26 studies screening 10,080 patients, the pooled prevalence of Fabry disease in patients with left ventricular hypertrophy/hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was 1.2% using ACMG variant classification criteria.
In a meta-analysis of 38 studies screening 62,050 patients, the pooled prevalence of Fabry disease in patients with end-stage renal disease/chronic kidney disease was 0.3% using ACMG criteria.
In a meta-analysis of 25 studies screening 15,295 patients, the pooled prevalence of Fabry disease in stroke patients was 0.7% using ACMG criteria.
In a meta-analysis of 3 studies screening 1033 patients, the pooled prevalence of Fabry disease in patients with cardiac conduction disturbance requiring pacemaker was 0.7% using ACMG criteria.
The pooled prevalence of Fabry disease among patients screened for small-fiber neuropathy was 1.0% using ACMG criteria for GLA variant pathogenicity.
Newborn screening studies showed a pooled Fabry disease prevalence of 0.01% using ACMG criteria for GLA variant pathogenicity.

The estimated prevalence of Fabry disease differed depending on whether GLA variants were classified using ACMG criteria or the ClinVar database, with most discrepant cases carrying one of the variants p.A143T, p.D313Y, or p.E66Q.
Luteolin treatment reduced excessive colonic motility in water avoidance stress (WAS) rats.
Luteolin lowered reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels in the WAS rat model.
Luteolin increased Nrf2 protein expression levels and promoted its nuclear translocation.
Luteolin increased heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) protein expression levels, downstream of Nrf2 activation.
In intestinal epithelial cells, luteolin markedly reduced hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-induced oxidative damage.
Overall, luteolin is proposed to protect against excessive intestinal motility and diarrhea by regulating the Nrf2 signaling pathway, thereby reducing colonic oxidative stress damage.
High-fat diet alone increased heart rate and impaired parasympathetic autonomic tone in mice.
Nicotine vapor exposure increased sympathetic vascular tone, shown by a greater blood pressure drop in response to ganglionic blockade.
Neither nicotine nor high-fat diet alone or in combination significantly altered overall blood pressure levels.
Nicotine exposure disrupted circadian blood pressure regulation, producing reduced nocturnal BP dipping.
Combined nicotine and high-fat diet exposure caused left ventricular diastolic dysfunction with increased LV end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), an effect not seen with either exposure alone.
Combined exposure to nicotine and HFD increased inhibitory phosphorylation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) and worsened endothelium-dependent vasodilation impairment.
A small cohort of female mice with combined nicotine and HFD exposure showed similarly increased LVEDP, indicating both sexes are susceptible to this combined cardiovascular harm.
L-NAME-induced hypertensive mice showed increased intraocular pressure compared to normotensive controls.
Hypertensive mice showed reduced fluorescein signal on fundus fluorescein angiography compared to normotensive mice, indicating retinal vascular alteration.

Fibrosis-related parameters including matrix metalloproteinases, tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases, connective tissue growth factor, and TGF-beta family members were altered in the retina and choroid of hypertensive mice.

Dietary supplementation with ACE (wild olive/acebuche) oil prevented hypertension-induced increases in intraocular pressure and retinal alterations, with better outcomes than reference extra virgin olive oil (EVOO).
Dietary supplementation with reference extra virgin olive oil (EVOO) also reduced hypertension-related IOP elevation and retinal fibrotic changes, though less effectively than ACE oil.
qPCR on 3 dpf larvae showed decreased dspa and dspb mRNA expression in respective mutants, likely via nonsense-mediated decay.
Western blot in -ab larvae showed all Desmoplakin isoforms present but reduced by about 60% relative to WT.
In homozygous single mutants lacking the mutated isoform, the non-mutated Dsp paralog protein was also reduced, suggesting Dspa/Dspb interdependence.
Approximately 30% of -ab and -aa mutant embryos showed visible cardiovascular alterations at 3 dpf compared to WT.
Heart size analysis showed significant cardiac dilation in all Dsp mutant embryos compared to WT.
Heart rate monitoring detected substantial bradycardia in all Dsp mutant genotypes at 5 and 7 dpf, with the -ab line showing the earliest onset (3 dpf).
All Dsp mutant genotypes showed significantly decreased survival to juvenile stages compared to WT.
qPCR showed downregulation of Wnt/β-catenin pathway members ccnd1 and myca in 3 dpf Dsp mutant larvae.
General whole-body upregulation of Hippo/YAP-TAZ signalling members ccn2a (in -aa) and ccn2b (in all mutant lines) was detected in larval Dsp mutants.
A Hippo/YAP-TAZ transgenic reporter showed comparable whole-body activation but a cardiac-specific reduction of signal in -ab mutants.
TGF-β signalling members smad2 and smad3 showed a downregulation trend in all larval Dsp mutant genotypes.
Using a myocardial-specific transgene, -ab mutant embryos showed increased total area of both atrium and ventricle, indicating cardiac chamber dilation.

Functional imaging showed increased atrial ejection fraction/heartbeats but diminished ventricular ejection fraction, contractility and heartbeats in -ab mutants, suggesting atrial compensation for ventricular dysfunction.
-ab mutants showed reduced blood flow without gross morphological vascular tree defects.
Immunostaining for the leucocyte marker L-plastin revealed a two-fold increase in positive cells in 3-dpf mutant hearts, indicating cardiac inflammation.
A three-fold increase in L-plastin positive cells was detected at the skin level in -ab mutants, a Desmoplakin-rich tissue, compared to WT.
Birefringence analysis showed no difference in skeletal muscle fibre organization between WT and -ab larvae at 5 dpf.
-ab larvae showed normal light-response but a significant reduction in total distance swum, indicating impaired motor performance despite preserved sensory perception.
A physical training protocol (denser swimming medium, 3-13 dpf) increased mortality in trained versus untrained larvae, with Dsp mutants under exercise showing the highest mortality.
Adult (1-year-old) -ab mutant hearts showed Wnt/β-catenin pathway downregulation, mirroring larval findings.
Adult -ab mutant hearts showed downregulation of both Hippo/YAP-TAZ and TGF-β signalling pathway members.
1-year-old -ab mutant ventricles showed significant dilation compared to WT.
TEM analysis of 3- and 6-mpf mutant hearts revealed pale, disorganized and delocalized desmosomes with increased extracellular space distance, significant at 6 mpf.

At 6 mpf, mutant hearts showed cardiomyocyte rarefaction, myocardial thinning, trabecular disorganization, abnormal ventricular shape, vessel dilation and adipocyte accumulation in the myocardium, without fibrosis.
Unlike human AC, fibrotic substitution of the myocardium was not observed in Dsp mutant zebrafish hearts.

A 3-month training protocol (3-6 mpf) exacerbated cardiac histopathology in -ab mutants (trabecular disorganization, vessel dilation, adipocytes) without affecting WT hearts, resembling the phenotype of untrained 9-mpf mutants.
Doubling the duration of the training protocol did not further worsen the cardiac condition compared to WT, suggesting a ceiling effect or regenerative compensation.
Transmission electron microscopy of 3- and 6-month-old -ab mutant zebrafish hearts revealed pale, disorganized and delocalized desmosomes compared to wild-type.
The extracellular space distance between desmosomes was significantly increased in 6-month-old -ab mutant zebrafish hearts compared to wild-type, though not significant at 3 months.

Histological analysis of 6-month-old -ab mutant hearts showed cardiomyocyte rarefaction, thinning of the myocardial layer, trabecular disorganization, abnormal ventricular shape, vessel dilation, and intramyocardial adipose accumulation, without fibrosis.

Physical training from 3 to 6 mpf worsened cardiac histopathology in -ab mutants (more disorganized trabeculae, vessel dilation, adipocytes) while wild-type hearts showed no change; doubling training duration did not further worsen the phenotype.

At 9 mpf, -ab mutant hearts showed further worsening compared to 6 mpf, with a more altered ventricular shape, thickened myocardial layer (suggestive of compensatory hypertrophy), and more dilated vessels with more intrusive adipose infiltration.

The paper cites prior evidence from a DSP mouse model showing that Wnt/β-catenin regulators AKT1 and GSK3-β are dysregulated after physical exercise, supporting a cross-species role of Wnt/β-catenin modulation in AC.
Vascular morphology appeared grossly normal in -ab mutants but blood flow was reduced compared to controls.
L-plastin positive inflammatory cells were increased three-fold in -ab mutants at the skin level, a desmoplakin-rich tissue, compared to wild-type.

Trained -ab mutants treated with SB216763 during physical training showed the highest survival rate (53%) among trained groups, exceeding even trained wild-type fish, with a mortality decrease more than two-fold compared to untreated trained mutants.
Treatment with the Wnt inhibitor XAV939 did not significantly change the bradycardic phenotype in -ab mutants, unlike SB216763 which partially rescued it.
The dspa mutant allele sa13356 carries a nonsense point mutation in exon 23 (Chr2: g.2324300C>T) generating a premature stop codon p.Gln960Ter.
A CRISPR-Cas9-generated dspb mutant line (allele ia303) carries a 13-nucleotide deletion (Chr20: g.52912248_52912260del) in exon 3.
Epithelialization, indicated by cytokeratin expression, began on day 3 and connective tissue maturation was more pronounced in the i-PRF-treated mucosal wounds compared to saline-treated wounds.
Protein-level release of VEGF, EGF, TGF-β, PDGF, and FGF was higher in the i-PRF-treated buccal mucosa than in the saline-treated side over a 14-day period.
TGF-β gene expression showed a statistically significant change at 14 days after i-PRF injection compared to saline control.
VEGF gene expression showed a statistically significant change at 21 days after i-PRF injection compared to saline control.
Overall, autologous i-PRF application was suggested to enhance oral mucosal wound healing by increasing growth factor release for up to 21 days.
Point shear wave elastography showed significantly higher shear wave velocity in the myofascial trigger point (MTrP) muscle than in control muscle, indicating increased tissue stiffness.
Masson staining showed increased collagen fibre deposition and collagen volume fraction in MTrP muscle compared with control muscle, suggesting a fibrotic process.
TGF-β1 protein expression, measured by immunohistochemistry and Western blot, was significantly higher in MTrP muscle than in control muscle.
Phosphorylated Smad2/3 protein expression was significantly higher in MTrP muscle than in control muscle, consistent with activation of TGF-β1 downstream signalling.
In the MTrPs group, collagen volume fraction was positively correlated with shear wave velocity.
Collagen volume fraction was positively correlated with TGF-β1 expression in the MTrPs group.
No significant correlation was found between collagen volume fraction and p-Smad2/3 expression in the MTrPs group.
No significant correlation was observed between shear wave velocity and rat body weight or paw withdrawal threshold.
Transmission electron microscopy showed a decreased number of mitochondria with blurred double-membrane structure and fractured/deformed cristae in the MTrPs group compared with controls.
Sarcomeres were shorter and Z-lines were twisted/broken in the MTrPs group compared with the control group.

Histological (H&E) examination showed muscle cell disarrangement, fibrous connective tissue hyperplasia, neovascularization, and inflammatory cell infiltration in the MTrPs group, while control muscle showed normal architecture.
MTrPs model rats showed slower weight gain than control rats, with a significant difference emerging from the second week of modelling and persisting (though narrowing) through the rest period.

MTrPs rats showed a gradually decreasing paw withdrawal threshold (indicating mechanical hyperalgesia/allodynia) that became significantly different from controls beginning at week 4 and persisted to the end of the experiment.

Electromyography revealed spontaneous electrical activity (fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves, increased endplate spines) in MTrP muscle that was absent (only a horizontal baseline) in control muscle.

Overnight heart-rate-derived low-frequency aperiodic activity showed a pink-noise structure in healthy controls but a white-noise structure in most idiopathic gastroparesis patients, suggesting altered autonomic regulation of the sleep cycle in gastroparesis.

Strain elastography (tissue stiffness) of the dominant trapezius muscle was significantly positively associated with the pressure pain threshold at that same tender point in women with fibromyalgia, after adjusting for age, menopause status, and BMI.

Strain elastography showed no significant association with pressure pain threshold at any of the other 12 tender points assessed (occiput, low cervical, supraspinatus, paraspinous, lateral pectoral, second rib, lateral and medial epicondyle, gluteus, greater trochanter, knee, anterior tibial, and non-dominant trapezius) in women with fibromyalgia.

Aged dogs, but not young dogs, showed abnormal giant, swollen NADPH-diaphorase-positive neuronal processes in the sacral spinal cord dorsal horn and dorsal gray commissure, newly termed 'megaloneurites'.
Megaloneurites were selectively restricted to the sacral spinal cord segments (S1-S3) and were not found in adjacent lumbar, coccygeal, thoracic, or cervical segments.
NADPH-diaphorase-positive megaloneurites co-localized with VIP immunoreactivity but not with GFAP, NeuN, or CGRP, suggesting a parasympathetic/autonomic fiber origin.
Aged dogs showed a significant decrease in the number of neurons and a dramatic reduction in neurite processes in the sacral dorsal horn, as shown by NeuN, MAP2, and CGRP immunofluorescence.
Iba1 immunofluorescence, a marker of microglia, was significantly up-regulated in the sacral spinal cord of aged dogs compared with young dogs.
In the superficial dorsal horn of aged dogs, fibrous astrocytes with elongated processes decreased while protoplasmic astrocytes with thicker, more branched processes increased.
Megaloneurite fibers in aged dogs were significantly thicker in average diameter than normal fibers in aged dogs and than NADPH-d-positive fibers in young dogs.
Megaloneurite terminal branches had a significantly thinner diameter than the megaloneurite trunk itself, showing a 49% diameter reduction rate at branch points.
Individual or clustered megaloneurites in the dorsal gray commissure were spaced at regular intervals of approximately 186.6 μm apart along the rostro-caudal axis.

A novel age-related NADPH-diaphorase-positive abnormality, termed neuritic hypertrophy, was found around the central canal of the coccygeal spinal cord only in aged dogs, and was absent in young dogs.
Punctate NADPH-diaphorase activity in the white matter of the sacral and coccygeal spinal cord, resembling megaloneurites, was markedly higher in aged dogs than in young dogs.

No NADPH-diaphorase-positive megaloneurite-like abnormalities were observed in the gracile nucleus, cuneate nucleus, or the ventral posterolateral thalamic nucleus of aged dogs, unlike the sacral spinal cord.

The number of NADPH-diaphorase-positive neurons was significantly reduced with aging in the dorsal horn, ventral horn, and around the central canal at all spinal levels, but this reduction was not seen in the intermediolateral cell column (IML, sympathetic preganglionic neurons) of the thoracic segment.

The number of large, lightly-stained motoneurons in the ventral horn was significantly increased in the thoracic and lumbar spinal cords of aged dogs compared with young dogs, with no significant change in the cervical or sacral cord.
Just over half (51%) of the 338 responding German inpatient medical rehabilitation facilities reported treating patients with long COVID.
The cumulative number of rehabilitants with long COVID treated across the surveyed facilities up to the time of the survey was 11,948.
Rehabilitation facilities that treated long COVID patients in pneumology departments were more likely to report a lack of treatment capacity.
Capacity bottlenecks in rehabilitation facilities were related to the proportion of long COVID rehabilitants relative to all rehabilitants in the department.
There was substantial heterogeneity across facilities in the treatment concept used for long COVID and in how patients were allocated to specific departments.
Healthcare workers with long COVID reported a mean of 9.5 symptoms, most commonly fatigue, brain fog, breathlessness, sleep disturbance and heart palpitations.
Long COVID symptoms adversely affected day-to-day activities in over 90% of participants, with about half reporting activities were limited a lot.
SF-12 physical and mental component scores among healthcare workers with long COVID were lower than general population averages.
Self-rated health on the EQ-5D-5L VAS averaged 61.5 and the health utility index averaged 0.66, indicating reduced health-related quality of life.
Just over a quarter of participants reported moderate to severe psychological stress on the PHQ-4.
Healthcare workers with long COVID had a mean PROMIS fatigue T-score of 62.6, substantially higher than the standardized US population mean of 50.
Almost two-thirds of participants had taken sick leave and nearly half had been issued a medical certificate because of long COVID symptoms.
Nearly a fifth of surveyed healthcare workers were unable to work at all at the time of the survey because of long COVID.
Among those still working, a third had changed work duties and 17% had reduced their contracted hours because of long COVID.
One in ten participants were considering leaving NHS employment within the next year due to long COVID, with nearly a quarter unsure.
Less than half of participants were satisfied with the support received from their NHS employer regarding their long COVID symptoms.
Qualitative interviews indicated that symptom improvement was often linked to workplace adjustments such as phased return, role/responsibility changes, altered hours, and location flexibility.
Returning to work too soon was described as detrimental, often exacerbating long COVID symptoms and necessitating further time off.

Interview participants reported that GPs and other healthcare professionals often attributed their long COVID symptoms to mental rather than physical causes, which frustrated patients who felt physical causes were overlooked.
Occupational Health services were described as having mixed effectiveness, with personnel seen as well-meaning but often unable to provide adequate advice, referrals or workplace adjustments.

Healthcare workers used self-management strategies including rest, pacing, planning and prioritizing to cope with long COVID symptoms while continuing to work, generally prioritizing work over other activities.
Most staff off-work due to long COVID continued to receive full salary through the UK Government long COVID special leave fund, though with uncertainty about its duration.
GPs, unlike other NHS staff, were not afforded the same financial protections for long COVID absence due to their independent contractor employment status.
Faecal VLP DNA yield was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in same-household healthy controls despite similar VLP particle counts.
The number of virus-like particles per gram of faeces did not differ between ME/CFS patients and household controls.

In the VLP-enriched dataset, 37 viral clusters were composed uniquely of ME/CFS-associated viruses compared with only 10 uniquely SHHC-associated clusters, with 147 shared clusters common to both groups.
In the whole-metagenome sequencing (WMS) dataset, 17 viral clusters were uniquely ME/CFS-associated and 10 were SHHC-associated, with 93 shared communal clusters.
Beta diversity analysis of intestinal DNA phages showed no clustering by ME/CFS disease status, with viral composition similar between household-matched ME/CFS and SHHC samples.
Bacterial beta diversity (Jaccard distance, genus level) showed no overall difference between ME/CFS and SHHC groups, though household-matched pairs shared similar compositions.
No significant differences in relative abundance (CLR) of the 12 most abundant bacterial genera were found between ME/CFS and SHHC groups.
Bacterial alpha diversity (observed richness, Chao1, Shannon index) did not differ between ME/CFS and SHHC samples, though a high intraclass correlation was seen within household-matched pairs.

A power calculation indicated at least 15 household-matched pairs would be needed to detect a 10-fold abundance difference in bacterial genera, and over 100 pairs to detect 90% of genera with a true two-fold change, at 90% power.

The bacterial genus Anaerotruncus (from the VLP-derived dataset) was uniquely predicted as a host for ME/CFS-unique viruses, with no interactions with SHHC-unique or communal viruses, consistent with previously reported increased Anaerotruncus abundance in ME/CFS faecal metagenomes.

Eleven bacterial genera shared between the VLP and WMS datasets (QAMI01, Erysipelatoclostridium, Lacticaseibacillus, Firm-11, Christensenella, Eubacterium, Anaerobutyricum, Anaerostipes, Acutalibacter, Veillonella and Salmonella) were predicted as potential hosts for ME/CFS-unique viruses.
Among 94 VLP-derived bacterial hosts, 37 genera including Clostridium_J, Clostridium_AP and Anaerotruncus were predicted to be associated with ME/CFS-unique viruses.
In the WMS dataset, only six bacterial genera (Bacteroides_G, Campylobacter_D, HGM12998, Pseudoflavonifractor, Oxalobacter and Klebsiella) were potentially associated with ME/CFS-unique viruses.

Rare unique human-associated eukaryotic viruses, including HHV-6A, papillomaviruses, coronavirus NL63 and adenovirus 54, were detected only in ME/CFS-derived faecal samples, though overall eukaryotic viral reads were extremely sparse.
Among nine severely affected ME/CFS patients in this cohort, four had a self-reported gastrointestinal disorder.

Putative integrated proviruses (prophages) were more numerous in the whole-metagenome sequencing (WMS) high-quality vOTUs than in the VLP-enriched high-quality vOTUs, reflecting differences in viral lifecycle capture by each method.

Alpha diversity of the intestinal DNA virome (Shannon index) was significantly higher in whole-metagenome sequencing (WMS)-derived datasets than in VLP-enriched datasets, independent of disease status.

Post-exertional malaise in ME/CFS patients is associated with exacerbations of fatigue, cognitive difficulties, sleep problems, neuromuscular complaints, bodily heaviness, and flu-like symptoms affecting daily functioning.
Higher levels of PEM are associated with more symptoms, greater psychological distress, and increased social burden in ME/CFS patients.
Factor analysis of symptoms and triggers in 704 respondents showed PEM is composed of two distinct constructs: generalized fatigue and muscle-specific fatigue.
Onset and duration of PEM vary widely, with delayed onset ranging from 1 hour to a week and duration lasting from 1 day to several months.
A meta-analysis of 15 studies found patients with ME/CFS perceived exercise as more effortful (higher ratings of perceived exertion) than healthy controls, even after controlling for confounders.

In a well-controlled study matching patients and controls for physical fitness, most cardiometabolic differences between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls disappeared, including in cardiometabolic responses to exercise.
Despite fitness matching, ME/CFS patients still reported higher perceived exertion and showed lower respiration frequency with higher tidal volume compared with controls.

A meta-analysis found that exercise triggered a larger increase in post-exercise fatigue among ME/CFS patients compared with controls, with the largest group differences seen at 4 hours or later after exercise.
Following two exercise bouts separated by 24 hours, ME/CFS patients reported fatigue peaking approximately 2 days after the last exercise bout, whereas healthy controls showed no exacerbation.
Approximately 60%-65% of ME/CFS patients showed increased fatigue one week after exercise.
A 2022 meta-analysis found exercise triggered higher pain intensity in patients with fibromyalgia or ME/CFS compared with healthy controls, with largest differences 1-3 days post-exercise.
Patients' self-assessed recovery time after a second day of exercise ranged from 6 to 12 days in two studies.

A meta-analysis of 5 studies (98 patients, 51 controls) using repeated CPETs found ME/CFS patients had a larger decline in oxygen consumption on the second exercise day and a reduced workload at the onset of hyperventilation compared with controls.
ME/CFS patients showed a reduced workload for the onset of blood lactate accumulation on the second day of repeated exercise testing, consistent with earlier onset of anaerobic metabolism.

A meta-analysis of heart rate parameters found ME/CFS patients had deviations suggestive of reduced vagal (parasympathetic) and increased sympathetic modulation of heart rate in relation to exercise and other triggers.

A study measuring heart rate parameters before, during, and after exercise found diminished cardiac parasympathetic and sympathetic activation during rest and exercise, and reduced parasympathetic reactivation after exercise, in ME/CFS patients compared with controls.
Blood samples taken during exercise showed decreased adrenaline levels in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, though levels did not differ before exercise or 30 minutes after.
Altered exercise responses reported in long COVID patients may be attributable to deconditioning, and a brief report suggests these altered responses may normalize within 2 years.
PEM-like symptoms are not unique to ME/CFS and occur with relatively high prevalence in other chronic conditions such as multiple sclerosis and long COVID.
In 71 ME/CFS patients retested after worsening symptoms, the percentage reduction in cerebral blood flow during tilt testing increased from 19% at the first visit to 31% at follow-up.
Among the 71 patients who worsened, ICC disease severity distribution (mild/moderate/severe) shifted from 51/45/4% at visit-1 to 1/72/27% at follow-up.
In 39 patients with stable disease, both ICC severity distribution and %CBF reduction were unchanged between visit-1 and follow-up.
In combined data from two previously published cohorts (n=219), %CBF reduction during tilt testing increased with disease severity: 25% in mild, 29% in moderate, and 33% in severe ME/CFS.

The authors conclude that disease severity and %CBF reduction during tilt testing are highly associated, and propose a causal relationship in which a larger CBF reduction leads to worsening ME/CFS symptoms.
Individuals with long COVID had a higher prevalence of CPTSD (33%) than healthy controls (0%).
Individuals with ME/CFS had a higher prevalence of CPTSD (20%) than healthy controls (0%).
Individuals with long COVID had a higher prevalence of PTSD (5%) than both ME/CFS (0%) and healthy controls (0%).
Individuals with long COVID had greater scores than controls across all PTSD symptom clusters.
Individuals with long COVID had greater DSO (disturbances in self-organization) scores than controls.
Individuals with ME/CFS had greater DSO scores than controls.
Both the long COVID and ME/CFS groups differed from healthy controls in overall PTSD/CPTSD symptom scores.
German treatment-case data show ME/CFS prevalence rose from about 0.42-0.48% pre-pandemic to 0.6% (601 per 100,000) in 2021, one year after the COVID-19 pandemic began.
Women are affected by ME/CFS more than twice as often as men, consistent with a cited US prevalence study.

Roughly a quarter of the 544 patients reported having had ME/CFS for 6-10 years, 5% for 31 to ≥40 years, and 37.5% received their diagnosis more than 5 years after symptom onset, with 11 participants diagnosed 31-40+ years after onset.
Nearly 80% of respondents reported having received one or more misdiagnoses during the course of their illness, with women reporting this more often than men.
Among the 434 patients who reported a misdiagnosis, depression was by far the most frequently named specific misdiagnosis, cited by 36.6%.
Patients frequently reported that their symptoms were incorrectly framed as generically 'psychological' (16.6%) or 'psychosomatic' (12.9%) rather than being given a specific psychiatric label.
Men reported being misdiagnosed with adjustment disorder considerably more often than women.

More than half of participants explicitly complained about their treating physicians' lack of expertise in ME/CFS, and an even larger proportion reported that physicians incorrectly assumed a psychological cause for their symptoms.
Roughly a quarter of people with ME/CFS are unable to leave their homes and two-thirds are unable to work, reflecting the severe functional impairment associated with the disease.

Patients reported that despite describing classic post-exertional malaise (PEM) to numerous specialists over years, physicians frequently failed to derive a suspected ME/CFS diagnosis from this hallmark symptom.

Patients repeatedly cited the absence of an exclusive, routinely measurable physiological biomarker for ME/CFS as a core reason their symptoms were not believed and were instead attributed to psychiatric causes.

ME/CFS most often follows an infectious illness and is characterized by dysregulation of the nervous and immune systems along with problems in cellular energy metabolism and ion transport.

In a review of 630 molecularly confirmed vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome patients, 70% were diagnosed only after a major complication, with an average diagnosis age of 30 years.

Skin fibroblast collagen electrophoresis and transmission electron microscopy frequently give false-negative results in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with 29% of genetically confirmed patients and 83% of clinically diagnosed patients showing normal TEM.

Molecular genetic testing of COL3A1 has an approximately 96% mutation detection rate for deleterious variants causing vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, supporting its use as the primary diagnostic method over fibroblast-based testing.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has an estimated minimum prevalence of 1 in 200,000 in the general population.

Only two prior case reports describe thrombosis in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, one with multiple arterial and venous thrombi and another with a deep vein thrombosis attributable to pseudoaneurysm compression, unlike the present unexplained case.

Surgery in individuals with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is generally discouraged unless absolutely necessary due to generalised tissue fragility and increased complication risk, as illustrated by this patient's fatal outcome following elective cholecystectomy.

The vast majority (90%) of patients with symptomatic Tarlov perineurial cysts are women.
Connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which weaken connective tissue, confer considerable risk for developing Tarlov perineurial cysts.
Symptomatic Tarlov cysts most commonly cause sacropelvic dermatomal neuropathic pain along with bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction due to sensory and autonomic sacral nerve root involvement.
Large Tarlov cysts routinely cause muscle atrophy and weakness by compressing the ventral motor nerve roots, and multiple or multiroot compression can produce cauda equina syndromes.

Across 31 case series, open surgical procedures for Tarlov cysts had smaller sample sizes but somewhat better outcomes with longer follow-up, at the cost of slightly higher procedural risks compared with percutaneous interventions.

Cyst-wrapping surgery appeared to provide the best long-term outcomes among treatments by permanently reducing cyst size and reconstructing the nerve root sleeve, which may curtail ongoing axonal injury and death and promote axonal regeneration to improve sacral somatic and autonomic nerve function.

Controls showed significant hypoalgesia after the mental stressor, but this stress-induced pain reduction was absent in the knee OA and FM groups.

Pain severity/interference (BPI), depression/anxiety/stress (DASS-21), and pain catastrophising (PCS) were all significantly higher in both the knee OA and fibromyalgia groups compared to pain-free controls.
Both the knee OA and fibromyalgia groups had significantly higher BMI than controls.
Positive affect positively mediated the effect of openness to experience on pain acceptance in women with fibromyalgia.
The strength of the association between openness to experience and positive affect increased at medium and high levels of preference for mood management (hedonic) goals.
Pooled meta-analysis of 15 blood-based studies showed significantly higher circulating BDNF levels in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls, with high heterogeneity.
In subgroup analysis, serum-measured BDNF was significantly higher in FM patients than controls, with very high heterogeneity.
Plasma-measured BDNF was significantly higher in FM patients than controls with no observed heterogeneity in this subgroup.
In female-only subgroup analysis across 10 studies, peripheral BDNF was significantly higher in female FM patients than female healthy controls, despite high heterogeneity.
Meta-analysis of BDNF rs6265 Val/Met genotype found no significant difference in carrier rates between FM patients and healthy controls, despite a higher proportion of Val carriers in FM patients.
A single study measuring cerebrospinal fluid BDNF found markedly higher levels in primary FM patients compared to healthy controls.
None of the studies assessing correlation between BDNF levels and age in FM patients found a significant relationship.
Iannuccelli et al. found that male FM patients had significantly lower serum BDNF levels than female FM patients.

Bidari et al. found an inverse relationship between serum BDNF level and quality-of-life scale scores (VAS pain and Polysymptomatic Distress Scale) in FM patients, while other studies found no significant correlation between BDNF and pain/symptom measures.

Fawzy et al. found a positive correlation between mean serum BDNF and grade of depression, whereas Laske et al. found no significant difference in BDNF between FM patients with and without recurrent major depression.
Polli et al. showed via repeated-measure regression that serum BDNF significantly predicts chronic fatigue syndrome symptom scores and widespread hyperalgesia in FM patients.
Nugraha et al. reported that serum BDNF significantly increased with depression level (HADS) in FM patients, but was not correlated with anxiety scores.
A one-month course of duloxetine significantly reduced serum BDNF levels in FM patients, even after adjusting for depression, pain, and disease severity.

Cardinal et al. found serum BDNF positively correlated with analgesic and anticonvulsant use but negatively correlated with SSRI use in FM patients, while Deitos et al. found a negative correlation between serum BDNF and weekly analgesic use.
Haas et al. found no significant differences in plasma BDNF levels between FM patients on no antidepressants, analgesic-dose antidepressants, or therapeutic-dose antidepressants.

A resistance exercise trial in FM patients found no significant change in BDNF levels before versus after the intervention, despite significant improvements in pain, catastrophizing, and fatigue scores.
In women with FM undergoing aquatic physical therapy, BDNF pre-intervention values showed a significant reduction from session 1 to session 10.
Deitos et al. found that cortical silent period after pregabalin use was positively associated with pre-treatment BDNF level, though there was no interaction between pregabalin use and BDNF levels.
Park et al. reported that the BDNF rs11030104 GG genotype was a protective factor against fibromyalgia.

Thermal therapy (mud-bath or balneotherapy) reduced BDNF concentration alongside pain reduction and improved FIRQ and SF-36 scores in FM patients, without changing oxytocin, ATP, or serotonin transporter levels.
Gentle touch therapy in FM patients resulted in pain reduction associated with decreased BDNF levels.
Patients with bladder pain syndrome/interstitial cystitis frequently have comorbid fibromyalgia, which complicates clinical management.
Patients with bladder pain syndrome/interstitial cystitis frequently have comorbid irritable bowel syndrome, adding to management complexity.

High-affinity mast-cell-bound IgE can be cross-linked by trace amounts of allergen, activating mast cells and causing anaphylaxis, whereas low-affinity IgE is not efficiently cross-linked and can prevent anaphylaxis.
Serum levels of high-affinity, but not low-affinity, IgE correlate with allergic symptoms such as eczema, allergic asthma and anaphylaxis.

IgE has a short serum half-life of approximately 3 days and IgE-expressing B cells show high apoptosis rates and little proliferation, explaining its low serum abundance relative to other antibody isotypes.
The FcεRI receptor binds the Fc region of IgE with a very high affinity of 10^10 M−1, arming mast cells and basophils with antigen-specific receptors.

In murine models, IgG1, IgG2a and IgG2b can promote anaphylaxis via activation of activating Fcγ receptors FcγRI, FcγRIII and FcγRIV, though this requires much higher antigen doses than IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.
IgG-dependent allergic reactions are mediated by secretion of platelet-activating factor from neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages and basophils.
Increasing levels of allergen-specific IgG are associated with natural resolution of food allergies.

Serum IgG4 rises in patients undergoing allergen immunotherapy and is associated with increased clinical tolerance, while depleting IgG4 from peanut-tolerant patients' serum promotes stronger mast cell degranulation.
IgG blocks IgE-mediated allergic reactions through allergen neutralization (competing with IgE for allergen binding) and through FcγRIIb-mediated inhibitory signaling on mast cells/basophils.

IgG4's unique blocking properties are due to its ability to undergo Fab arm exchange, enabling bispecific antigen recognition that prevents immune complex formation, and IgG4 cannot activate complement C1q.

In a murine model of oral immunotherapy, mucosal IgA binds allergens and prevents them from crossing the epithelial barrier, thereby preventing mast cell and basophil degranulation in an allergen-specific manner.

The authors' own work found that non-sialylated IgE antibodies have greater potential to activate mast cells and basophils, contrasting with another study that associated high IgE galactosylation/sialylation with allergic severity.

Tfh13 cells, which produce IL-13, IL-5 and some IL-21, are required for generation of high-affinity, anaphylactic IgE within germinal centers; genetically modified mice lacking Tfh13 cells show only very low levels of high-affinity IgE.

In a murine food allergy model, approximately 5% of IgE clones with substantial clonal expansion (>50 copies/clone) showed no signs of hypermutation even after repeated, long-lasting allergen challenge, indicating a persistent low-affinity extrafollicular IgE response.
Forced IgE BCR signaling induces apoptosis independent of antigenic stimulation, and primary IgE+ cells show a higher apoptosis rate than IgG1+ cells.

A separate study could not confirm that IgE BCR signaling directly promotes apoptosis, instead finding that it supports antigen-independent terminal differentiation into plasma cells via Syk, CD19, BLNK, Btk and IRF4.

Whole-genome CRISPR screening comparing IgE+ and IgG1+ murine B cells showed that IgE+ B cells and plasma cells exhibit chronic calcium signaling leading to BCL2L11-dependent apoptosis, distinct from IgG+ cells.

In a murine egg allergy model, IgE-to-IgG ratios are controlled at the level of single B cell clones: most clones show high IgG1-to-IgE ratios, but a considerable subset shows more than 5-fold more IgE than IgG1, related to differential BCR signaling strength.
Monoclonal IgG against the cat allergen Fel d1 has been shown to reduce allergic symptoms in both mice and patients.
Mouse IgG can reduce airway hypersensitivity through interaction with the inhibitory receptor FcγRIIb on dendritic cells.
Very early exposure to egg and peanut allergens, between 4 and 11 months of age, can enhance allergenic tolerance and decrease the risk of developing food allergy.
There is a higher prevalence of food allergies in women than men after adolescence.
In body fluids, IgG antibodies are present at levels typically exceeding IgE by approximately 100-fold or more.
IL-6/IL-23-dependent IL-17A+ Tfh17 cells within the germinal center induce a program of low IgG Fc sialylation in B cells.

A 61-year-old woman with wasp-sting anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest had a markedly elevated acute tryptase (>200 ng/mL) versus baseline (20 ng/mL), a positive KIT D816V mutation, and aberrant CD2/CD25/CD30-positive mast cells, leading to a diagnosis of indolent systemic mastocytosis.

A 66-year-old woman with wasp-venom anaphylaxis had an acute tryptase of 38 ng/mL and baseline of 12 ng/mL, tested positive for KIT D816V, and had CD25-expressing aberrant mast cells, resulting in a diagnosis of indolent systemic mastocytosis.

A 32-year-old man with an atypical neurologic presentation of anaphylaxis after an insect sting had an acute tryptase of 909 ng/mL versus baseline 8.3 ng/mL, with a low-burden KIT D816V mutation (0.02% in blood and marrow), leading to a diagnosis of monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome (MMAS).

A 43-year-old woman with ~50 episodes of mast cell mediator-related symptoms, predominantly during menses, had acute tryptase levels (14 and 12 ng/mL) significantly higher than her baseline (2.5–3.5 ng/mL) during two anaphylactic episodes, with negative KIT D816V and non-clonal bone marrow, yielding a diagnosis of idiopathic MCAS.
Prophylactic H1-antihistamine treatment with desloratadine 5 mg three times daily for 3 years was associated with cessation of anaphylactic episodes in a patient with idiopathic MCAS.

A 60-year-old woman with severe nitrofurantoin-induced anaphylaxis had an elevated baseline tryptase (19.1 ng/mL) explained by an increased TPSAB1 alpha-tryptase copy number (3 alpha, 2 beta), identifying hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT) rather than clonal mast cell disease.

A 49-year-old man with recurrent idiopathic angioedema had a slightly elevated baseline tryptase (14 ng/mL) attributed to an increased TPSAB1 alpha copy number, leading to a diagnosis of HαT, with partial improvement of angioedema episodes on antihistamine prophylaxis.

A 60-year-old man on hemodialysis with end-stage renal failure had elevated but stable tryptase (aST 15.3 ng/mL, bST 14.7 ng/mL) that did not meet criteria for mast cell activation, with normal TPSAB1 copy number ruling out HαT, and the elevation was attributed to renal failure.
The consensus formula, defined as an acute tryptase increase to at least 1.2 times baseline plus 2 ng/mL, is used to document mast cell activation and is considered the current gold standard.
A baseline serum tryptase above 20 ng/mL fulfills a minor diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis.

Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, caused by increased TPSAB1 alpha-tryptase copy number, is the most common cause of elevated baseline tryptase, accounting for about 91% of cases, followed by chronic renal failure (7%) and hematologic malignancies/mastocytosis (1%), and is present in up to 6% of the general population.

An acute-to-baseline tryptase ratio above 1.685 has been proposed to increase diagnostic specificity for mast cell activation in patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis and/or hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, who can show baseline variability without true MCAS.
The severity and magnitude of hypotension during anaphylaxis correlates with the height of tryptase elevation.

In patients with systemic mastocytosis, tryptase level does not correlate with symptom severity, but it does correlate with overall disease severity, serving as a B-finding when above 200 ng/mL (adjusted for TPSAB1 status).
Patients with systemic mastocytosis who experience anaphylaxis appear to have lower baseline tryptase levels than SM patients without anaphylaxis, though this finding has some conflicting reports.
Diamine oxidase increases significantly during anaphylaxis and has a longer half-life than tryptase, suggesting it may be a useful additional biomarker for mast cell activation.
A reported case of Gaucher disease type 1 had an elevated tryptase level (up to 80 ng/mL) that improved after initiation of enzyme replacement therapy.
Elevated stem cell factor in chronic kidney disease is proposed to induce mast cell hyperplasia and thereby raise baseline tryptase, since tryptase itself is not renally cleared.

There is consensus that hereditary alpha-tryptasemia is a risk modifier for severe anaphylaxis, though a recent study found no difference in HαT prevalence between patients with and without anaphylaxis in the setting of underlying systemic mastocytosis, and further conflicting studies exist.
A rise of approximately 1.3-fold in leukotriene E4, 2,3-dinor-11b-prostaglandin F2a, and n-methylhistamine has been proposed as an additional sign of mast cell activation.
