The REMA score, incorporating baseline tryptase cut-offs and KIT D816V status, is the most commonly used and validated tool to predict underlying clonal mast cell disease in patients with severe anaphylaxis, originally developed for Hymenoptera venom allergy and later extended to other triggers.
Compound 5 at 320 µM inhibited compound 48/80-induced release of β-hexosaminidase from mast cells without cytotoxicity.
Compound 9 at 160 and 320 µM inhibited compound 48/80-induced release of β-hexosaminidase from mast cells without cytotoxicity.
Compound 5 inhibited calcium ionophore A23187-induced β-hexosaminidase release from mast cells across a dose range (40-320 µM) without affecting cell viability.
The mast cell-stabilizing potency of compounds 5 and 9 exceeded that of the reference drug sodium cromoglycate at equivalent concentrations.
Biochemical inhibition of mast cell degranulation by compounds 5 and 9 was corroborated by morphological analysis using light and transmission electron microscopy.
Plasma H3Cit-DNA levels, a marker of neutrophil extracellular trap release, did not differ between systemic mastocytosis patients and healthy controls.
A strong trend towards correlation between leukocyte, eosinophil, and neutrophil counts and H3Cit-DNA levels was observed in advanced systemic mastocytosis but not in indolent disease.
H3Cit-DNA levels did not correlate with SM disease burden, tryptase levels, history of anaphylaxis, or presence of cutaneous mastocytosis, indicating no general increase in NET release in SM.
H3Cit-DNA levels and leukocyte counts were elevated in a subgroup of SM patients showing aberrant mast cell CD2 expression, an association flagged as warranting further investigation.
Among patients with abnormal skin biopsies, reduced pin sharpness at the toes was the most prevalent examination abnormality, found in 71.7% of these patients.
A MAGNET total score threshold of 14 best predicted abnormal skin-biopsy results among symptomatic patients versus healthy controls, with an accuracy of 0.74.
A MAGNET score cut-off of 30 maximized predictive accuracy (0.60) for abnormal autonomic function testing results, indicating weaker performance than for skin biopsy prediction.

Among patients with any abnormal neuropathy-test results, MAGNET showed strong discriminative performance for identifying a diagnostic result, with AUCs of 0.87-0.89, accuracy 0.80-0.89, and Youden's index 0.62.
MAGNET demonstrated excellent inter-rater reliability, test-retest reliability, and convergent validity with the Utah Early Neuropathy Scale, ranging from 91.3% to 95.6%.
Sensory symptoms suggestive of small fiber neuropathy were reported in 32.2% of ALS patients and became more frequent with advancing King's clinical stage.
Sensory nerve conduction study abnormalities were found in 24% of ALS patients and became more common with increasing clinical stage.
Amplitude of the sensory and motor ulnar nerve potentials progressively decreased from King's stage 1 to stage 4.
Skin biopsy showed a significant loss of intraepidermal nerve fiber (IENF) density in ALS patients compared with healthy controls.
Skin biopsy showed a significant loss of Meissner corpuscle (MC) density in ALS patients compared with healthy controls.
Meissner corpuscle density progressively decreased across ALS clinical stages.
Meissner corpuscle density progressively decreased across increasing ALS King's clinical stages.
Intraepidermal nerve fibre density progressively increased across ALS clinical stages.
A longitudinal follow-up study with repeat thigh skin biopsies at 6 and 12 months confirmed the progressive increase in intraepidermal nerve fibre density over time.
Meissner corpuscle density in the skin was inversely correlated with serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels in ALS patients.
Low Meissner corpuscle density was associated with poorer survival prognosis in ALS patients.
Higher serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels were associated with poorer survival prognosis in ALS patients.
Higher serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels were associated with poorer prognosis in ALS patients.
An increase in IENF density over the longitudinal follow-up period was associated with a poorer prognosis in ALS.
Overall, peripheral sensory nerve involvement in ALS worsens in parallel with motor disability, and skin innervation changes may serve as a prognostic biomarker of disease activity.
CARD9 shows markedly stronger auto-inhibition than the other CARD-CC family members, exhibiting very low spontaneous activity when overexpressed in HEK293T cells.
CARD10 (CARMA3) and CARD14 (CARMA2) show poor auto-inhibition relative to CARD9, which hampers characterization of upstream activators or activating mutations in overexpression studies.
Grafting CARD11 (CARMA1) domains onto the CARD9 backbone did not further reduce CARD11 activity compared with its native context.

The chimeric CARD9 backbone approach was validated using several known disease-associated mutations from CARD10 and CARD14, and further screening identified previously unknown activating natural variants in human CARD9 and CARD10.
Using Genebass exome-based disease association statistics, activated (gain-of-function) alleles of CARD9 were found to correlate with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
Activated CARD9 alleles were also found to correlate with constipation in the Genebass exome association dataset.
Exome-based disease association analysis (Genebass) showed that activating CARD9 alleles correlate with irritable bowel syndrome.
Genebass exome association statistics indicate that activating CARD9 alleles correlate with constipation.
Genebass exome association statistics indicate that activating CARD9 alleles correlate with osteoarthritis.
Genebass exome association statistics indicate that activating CARD9 alleles correlate with fibromyalgia.
Genebass exome association statistics indicate that activating CARD9 alleles correlate with insomnia.
Exome-based association analysis in Genebass showed that activated CARD9 alleles correlate with depression as a comorbid condition.
A cited meta-analysis found that acupuncture was more effective than pharmaceutical drugs at improving gastrointestinal symptoms and quality of life in patients with IBS.
A cited meta-analysis found that acupuncture considerably improved depression and anxiety in IBS patients compared to conventional oral Western medicine.
A meta-analysis by Deare et al established the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for fibromyalgia and found it may reduce depressive symptoms in fibromyalgia patients.

An updated individual patient data meta-analysis by Vickers AJ concluded acupuncture is an effective treatment for chronic pain with enduring treatment effects, with inter-trial variance mainly driven by differences in control-group treatment rather than acupuncture technique.

An animal study cited in this bibliometric analysis found that electroacupuncture alleviates anxiety-like behaviors induced by chronic neuropathic pain via regulation of different dopamine receptors in the basolateral amygdala.
Fibromyalgia affects 2-3% of the general population, while depression occurs in 20-80% of individuals with fibromyalgia.
Chronic pain is commonly comorbid with depression or anxiety, with rates reported between 50% and 60%.
Patients with IBS commonly experience severe psychosocial difficulties, with anxiety and depression as particularly common comorbidities.
In this sample of women with fibromyalgia, 65.21% were identified as at risk for dysphagia using the EAT-10 screening tool.
41.30% of women with fibromyalgia had alterations in swallowing-related quality of life as measured by the SWAL-QOL questionnaire.
EAT-10 dysphagia risk scores correlated positively with orofacial pain measures including orofacial VAS and CF-PDI subscales in women with fibromyalgia.
Swallowing-related quality of life (SWAL-QOL) scores correlated negatively with orofacial pain measures including orofacial VAS and CF-PDI subscales in women with fibromyalgia.
Women with fibromyalgia at risk of dysphagia (by both EAT-10 and V-VST) had significantly higher orofacial VAS and CF-PDI scores than those not at risk.
The ELiA dsDNA fluoroenzyme immunoassay showed high specificity (0.97) but relatively low sensitivity (0.38) for detecting SLE in a prospective single-center cohort.
The anti-dsDNA-NcX ELISA showed high specificity (0.90) and moderate sensitivity (0.51), outperforming ELiA dsDNA in sensitivity for SLE detection.
Anti-dsDNA concentrations measured by ELiA dsDNA showed a mild-to-moderate negative correlation with complement C4 levels when SLE and control patients were analyzed together.

Anti-dsDNA concentrations measured by the anti-dsDNA-NcX ELISA showed a significant positive correlation with CRP concentrations when SLE and control groups were combined, with a similar non-significant trend within the SLE group alone.

Patients with proteinuria showed higher dsDNA concentrations in both assays, and patients with hematuria showed higher ELiA dsDNA concentrations, but neither association reached statistical significance.

Direct comparison of ELiA dsDNA and anti-dsDNA-NcX ELISA titers across all samples initially showed no significant correlation, but became a statistically significant moderate positive correlation after removal of a single outlier patient with strongly positive anti-nucleosome antibodies.
Medication regimen explained only a small proportion of variance in dsDNA antibody concentrations for both assays.
Exposure-based CBT (Exp-CBT) and traditional CBT (T-CBT) did not differ significantly in reduction of overall fibromyalgia severity from pretreatment to posttreatment.
Higher baseline physical activity predicted a larger reduction in fibromyalgia severity in T-CBT but not in Exp-CBT, in an exploratory moderator analysis.
T-CBT produced a significantly larger reduction in depressive symptoms than Exp-CBT at posttreatment.
Exp-CBT produced a significantly larger reduction in disability than T-CBT at posttreatment.
The advantage of Exp-CBT over T-CBT on disability was slightly larger at 12-month follow-up than at posttreatment.
The initial between-group advantage of T-CBT on depression was no longer statistically significant at 12-month follow-up.
Exp-CBT and T-CBT did not differ significantly in their effects on pain intensity, fatigue, general anxiety, pain catastrophizing, or quality of life.
Similar proportions of participants achieved minimal clinically important improvement in fibromyalgia severity with Exp-CBT and T-CBT.
Rates of minimally clinically important deterioration did not differ significantly between Exp-CBT and T-CBT, though numerically higher in Exp-CBT.
Reported adverse events did not differ significantly in frequency between Exp-CBT and T-CBT, and no serious adverse events were attributed to treatment.
Participant-rated treatment credibility/expectancy of improvement was similar between Exp-CBT and T-CBT.
Participant satisfaction with treatment did not differ significantly between Exp-CBT and T-CBT.
Participants in Exp-CBT were more likely to decrease or discontinue pain medication than participants in T-CBT, despite identifying less with the Exp-CBT treatment model.
The relative efficacy of Exp-CBT vs T-CBT was not moderated by baseline age, education, years with diagnosis, symptom severity, pain intensity, avoidance behaviors, or pain catastrophizing.
The within-group effect of Exp-CBT on fibromyalgia severity in this trial was smaller than that observed in a previous RCT of the same protocol against waitlist control.

A prior RCT of the same Exp-CBT protocol produced moderate to large effects on fibromyalgia severity, fatigue, disability, and quality of life compared with a waitlist control, including an unusually large effect on pain intensity.
Meta-analytic evidence shows traditional CBT produces only small between-group effects on pain, disability, and negative mood compared with rudimentary control conditions.

Daily oral gavage of CFGS water extract or ethanol extract at 50 or 250 mg/kg significantly reduced allergic diarrhea severity scores compared to vehicle-treated (VH) OVA-sensitized mice at the 3rd and 4th challenges.

The villus height/crypt depth ratio, an index of intestinal health, significantly increased with 250 mg/kg water extract or ethanol extract treatment compared to VH controls, indicating protection against allergic enteritis-induced villus damage.
Duodenal mast cell infiltration, markedly increased in vehicle-treated allergic mice, was infrequent in mice treated with either CFGS extract.

Mice in the WEH, EEL, and EEH groups showed statistically reduced OVA-specific IgE levels compared to VH controls, indicating suppression of allergen-specific IgE production by higher-dose CFGS extracts.
Total serum IgG concentrations showed no significant differences between any of the six groups, suggesting CFGS extracts had limited impact on general humoral immunity.

Vehicle-treated OVA-allergic mice (VH) exhibited elevated IFN-γ, IL-4, and IL-10 secretion from OVA-stimulated splenocytes and reduced TGF-β production compared to naive (NA) mice, suggesting food allergy induction impairs immune tolerance.
Treatment with water extract and ethanol extract, especially at 250 mg/kg, significantly down-regulated IL-4 production from OVA-stimulated splenocytes compared to VH controls.

Treatment with water extract and ethanol extract at 250 mg/kg significantly up-regulated IL-10 and TGF-β production from OVA-stimulated splenocytes, suggesting restoration of Treg-mediated immune tolerance.
Water extract treatment at 250 mg/kg obviously enhanced IFN-γ production, unlike the ethanol extract, suggesting distinct mechanisms of action between the two extracts.
Treatment with water extract and ethanol extract reduced Faith's phylogenetic diversity (alpha diversity) of fecal microbiota compared to NA and VH groups.
Extract-treated groups exhibited higher unweighted UniFrac beta diversity values than NA and VH groups, indicating a shift in microbial community structure with treatment.
The VH (allergic, vehicle-treated) group displayed reduced relative abundance of Lactobacillaceae in fecal microbiota compared to other groups.
CFGS water extract treatment increased the relative abundance of Ligilactobacillus, Lactobacillus, L. johnsonii, and L. murinus in fecal microbiota compared to VH controls.

CFGS ethanol extract treatment increased relative abundance of Duncaniella, Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, Lacrimispora, D. dobosii, L. johnsonii, B. acidifaciens, and L. saccharolytica; B. acidifaciens is noted for alleviating allergic inflammation by inhibiting FcεRI expression on mast cells.
Having had COVID-19 (vs. not) was significantly associated with higher fatigue scores in the mixed-sex sample, but this did not hold when stratified by sex or after multiple-testing correction.
Greater self-reported COVID-19 severity was significantly associated with worse physical health scores in the whole cohort and in both men and women separately.
COVID-19 severity significantly worsened mental health, fatigue, and reaction time in the whole cohort and in women, but not in men.

Symptom trajectories after COVID-19 followed a non-monotonic pattern, improving over the first ~2 years post-infection and then worsening again, most clearly for fatigue but also for mental health and error rate.
Men who had COVID-19 reported orthopedic disorders more frequently than uninfected men, and this remained significant after correction for multiple testing.
Women who had COVID-19 reported a higher prevalence of metabolic diseases than uninfected women, significant after correction for multiple testing.
Women who had COVID-19 rated their physical health as worse compared to peers than uninfected women, a difference that survived multiple-testing correction.
In men, COVID-19 severity correlated strongly with the frequency of metabolic disorders.
In men, COVID-19 severity correlated with the frequency of common infectious diseases, a proxy for immune deficiency.
In men, the frequency of skin problems decreased with longer time elapsed since COVID-19 infection.
Current momentary tiredness correlated with COVID-19 severity across the cohort, being stronger in women than men.
In men, having had COVID-19 was most strongly associated with fatigue after a long train journey.
Fatigue after returning from work/school increased with time elapsed since COVID-19 infection, significantly in the whole cohort and in women.
Fatigue after a long train journey increased with time elapsed since COVID-19 infection, significantly in women.
No significant association was found between memory test performance (free recall and recognition) and COVID-19 exposure, severity, or time since infection, in the whole sample or in either sex.
Women who had contracted COVID-19 took noticeably longer to read test instructions (a covert processing-speed measure) than uninfected women; no such effect was seen in men.
Women with more severe COVID-19 showed faster (improved) reaction times on the Stroop test, an effect not seen on the simpler Choice reaction-time test or in men.
Women who had recovered from COVID-19 scored higher on a 12-item intelligence test than uninfected women.
Among female students, older age was correlated with a significantly more severe reported course of COVID-19, despite the narrow age range studied.
Female students reported a more severe course of COVID-19 than male students.

In women, COVID-19 severity was strongly correlated with the incidence of common infectious diseases and frequency of antibiotic use, proxies for immune deficiency, as well as with GP visits, skin and neurological disease frequency, anxiety, depression and other mental health issues.
A significant, replicated reduction in cerebral blood flow is among the most important organic abnormalities documented in ME/CFS.
Endothelial dysfunction is described as a replicated organic abnormality in ME/CFS.
A reduction in systemic oxygen supply is reported as a replicated organic abnormality in ME/CFS.
Reduced peak oxygen consumption is cited as a replicated organic abnormality in ME/CFS.
Increased ventricular lactate levels are reported as a replicated organic abnormality in ME/CFS.
Hypometabolism is described as a replicated organic abnormality in ME/CFS.
Increased levels of autoantibodies against G-protein-coupled receptors are reported as a replicated organic abnormality in ME/CFS.
Many organic abnormalities in ME/CFS correlate with symptom severity, suggesting a relevant role in disease pathophysiology rather than a psychosomatic origin.
In a prospective study, premorbid psychological factors did not predict which individuals went on to develop ME/CFS.
90% of ME/CFS patients report being told at least once by health professionals that their symptoms are psychosomatic before receiving an ME/CFS diagnosis.

During a second cardiopulmonary exercise test 24 hours after the first (2-day CPET), the anaerobic threshold and maximal oxygen capacity of ME/CFS patients dropped significantly, unlike in healthy controls.
Moore et al. found that ME/CFS patients need on average two weeks to recover from a 2-day CPET, compared to only two days for sedentary controls.
Studies using exercise testing found changes in gene expression after exercise in patients with ME/CFS.
ME/CFS patients showed a lack of reduction of arterial stiffness after exercise, possibly indicating impaired vasodilation.
Ghali et al. found that elevated resting-state lactate levels correlate with more severe post-exertional malaise episodes in ME/CFS.
Van Campen et al. showed that decreased cerebral blood flow in the upright position in ME/CFS is independent of physical fitness, contradicting the deconditioning hypothesis.
Patient surveys show that activity-enhancing therapies like Graded Exercise Therapy (GET) worsen the disease state in a large proportion of ME/CFS patients.

The PACE trial reported only minor improvements in ME/CFS from activity-enhancing therapies (GET/CBT), and its methodology was rated low or very low quality by the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.
Psychosomatic attributions of ME/CFS symptoms by physicians, family, or acquaintances are associated with higher perceived stigma and lower life and relationship satisfaction in patients.

A systematic review by Muller et al. found that a clear majority of primary studies on causal factors of ME/CFS (1979-2019) investigated organic factors, while only around 20% investigated psychological factors.
A content analysis of 241 American newspaper articles (1987-2013) found 65% portrayed ME/CFS etiology as organic, 22% as both organic and psychogenic, and only 3% as strictly psychogenic.
Expert-led webinars educating physicians about ME/CFS reduced the number of incorrect psychosomatic attributions made by physicians on a subsequent knowledge test.
In a prospective study, ME/CFS patients were no more likely to have a history of mental illness prior to disease onset than the average population.
Heart rate variability profiles can differentiate ME/CFS from depression, unlike some overlapping organic abnormalities such as endothelial dysfunction.
Endothelial dysfunction, one of the organic abnormalities seen in ME/CFS, is also present in depression, complicating differential diagnosis.

Joint hyperflexibility, measured by modified Beighton score, did not differ significantly between students who developed ME/CFS after infectious mononucleosis and recovered controls, indicating no association between joint hyperflexibility and ME/CFS development.
Female participants had significantly higher joint hyperflexibility (Beighton) scores than male participants, independent of ME/CFS status.
The review notes that fewer than 5% of ME/CFS patients return to their pre-morbid activity levels under current symptom-management-focused treatment guidelines.

Random forest analysis identified the antibody against EBV peptide EBNA6_0066 as the single most important feature (mean Gini importance 0.36) for discriminating the full ME/CFS cohort from healthy controls, with EBNA proteins dominating the top-ranked antibodies.

A super learner classifier combining anti-EBV IgG antibody responses achieved 85% accuracy in the training set with only two antibodies but failed to generalize, reaching only about 50-64% accuracy in the independent test set when comparing the whole ME/CFS cohort to healthy controls.

In ME/CFS patients with non-infectious or unknown disease triggers, antibodies against EBNA1_0595, EBNA1_0530, and EBNA6_0400 were the most important features, and a three-antibody classifier reached 94% accuracy in training but only 78% in the test set, below the 85% diagnostic target.

In ME/CFS patients who reported an infectious disease trigger, a super learner classifier based on 26 anti-EBV IgG antibodies spanning nine EBV proteins achieved 99% accuracy in training and 90% in the test set, exceeding the 85% target, with 100% sensitivity and 80% specificity.
Twenty-two of the twenty-six selected anti-EBV IgG antibodies had increased levels in ME/CFS patients with an infectious disease trigger compared to healthy controls.

IgG antibody levels against the EBNA1_430 peptide, which shows potential molecular mimicry with human Anoctamin-2, were similar between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls and ranked very low (1866th) in predictive importance for the whole cohort.

Across the 26 selected antibodies, there was no significant correlation between an antibody's importance for ME/CFS prediction and the maximal sequence-alignment score of its associated EBV peptide against human RefSeq reference proteins.
The lack of correlation between antibody importance and peptide-human protein alignment score was replicated using the RefSeq non-redundant protein database.

The EBNA6_0070 EBV peptide showed the highest sequence-alignment score (32.9) among the 26 selected peptides, aligning with human Homeobox-9A (HOXA9) and adrenergic receptor alpha-1B (ADRA1B), though this antibody was not among the top predictors of ME/CFS status.

The EBNA6_0488 EBV peptide had the second-highest sequence homology among the 26 selected antibodies, showing extensive similarity to the human proteins CTCF and AEBP1, which the authors speculate could link cross-reactive antibodies to altered gene regulation and inflammation in ME/CFS.

In one prior large-scale EBV antibody screening study, levels of the same 26 antibodies identified here were not significantly different between multiple sclerosis patients and healthy donors, supporting specificity of this signature to ME/CFS.

A different, larger multiple sclerosis study found that antibodies against six of the same EBV peptides were significantly elevated in MS patients, indicating overlap between the ME/CFS EBV antibody signature and MS.

Immunoadsorption, an apheresis procedure removing plasma antibodies, has previously been used successfully in a small cohort of ME/CFS patients with an infectious disease trigger and elevated adrenergic receptor autoantibodies.
Initial small clinical trials of rituximab in ME/CFS were promising, but these results were not replicated when the trial was scaled to a larger ME/CFS cohort.
Cyclophosphamide, an immunosuppressive drug acting on T and B cells, was previously tested with promising results in ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS patients from Italy showed a higher frequency of the TNF promoter variant rs1800629:G>A, associated with elevated TNF-alpha, but this association was not replicated in a German ME/CFS cohort.

Immunoadsorption, a plasma-based antibody-removal procedure, has previously been used successfully in a small cohort of ME/CFS patients with an infectious disease trigger who had elevated autoantibodies against adrenergic receptors.
Immunoadsorption was also recently tested in long-COVID ME/CFS patients with similarly successful outcomes as in classical infection-triggered ME/CFS.
Initial clinical trials of rituximab (anti-CD20 antibody) in ME/CFS were promising, but similar benefit was not observed when the trial was scaled to a larger ME/CFS cohort.
Cyclophosphamide, an immunosuppressive drug acting on T and B cells, has previously shown promising results when tested in ME/CFS patients.
Italian ME/CFS patients showed a higher frequency of the TNFα-elevating rs1800629:G>A allele variant, but this finding was not replicated in a German ME/CFS cohort.
CD40 ligand (CD40L) levels were reported to be significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients with shorter disease duration.
A follow-up study found elevated expression of VPACR2 (the VIP receptor) on immune cells in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
The frequency of regulatory Foxp3+CD4+ T cells was increased in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls in a prior study.

Antibodies against endogenous and microbial HSP65 peptides were at similar levels in ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, except for a higher seroprevalence to a Chlamydia pneumoniae-derived HSP65 peptide in ME/CFS patients.
A systematic review found that 20-25% of studies reported elevated TNFα and IL1β levels in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, but no meta-analysis was performed to confirm this.
Mutations in the AEBP1 gene are implicated in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and EDS hypermobility type is a recognized comorbidity that can co-occur with ME/CFS diagnosis.
Genome-wide association studies of ME/CFS have not reported any genetic markers located in the AEBP1 gene.
One prior study identified more than 12,000 CpG sites with altered DNA methylation levels in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Proportions of regulatory NK cells (cluster 15) were elevated in ME/CFS patients relative to controls at both baseline and post-exercise.
The proportion of γδ T cells was modestly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls at both baseline and post-exercise timepoints.
Effector/memory CD8+ T cell proportions showed a marginal decrease in ME/CFS patients compared to controls at both timepoints.

CD4+ T cells (naive and effector/memory), monocytes (classical, nonclassical, intermediate), and cytotoxic NK cells showed the strongest transcriptome dysregulation between ME/CFS patients and controls among all PBMC clusters.
Expression of ribosomal protein genes and core translational machinery was downregulated across multiple immune cell types in ME/CFS at both baseline and post-exercise.
Gene sets associated with chemokine signaling, cell migration, and activation were expressed at elevated levels in classical monocytes from ME/CFS patients.
Genes associated with interferon gamma (IFN-γ) signaling were suppressed in classical monocytes from ME/CFS patients.
Genes associated with the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 were activated in classical monocytes from ME/CFS patients, suggesting conflicting inflammatory and anti-inflammatory inputs.
CCL4, a monocyte chemoattractant, was upregulated in classical monocytes of ME/CFS patients regardless of exercise challenge (BL and PC).
CX3CR1, a marker of classical-to-nonclassical monocyte differentiation and tissue repair, was upregulated in ME/CFS classical monocytes.
SELPLG and ITGAL, genes involved in leukocyte tissue recruitment, were upregulated in ME/CFS classical monocytes.
CXCR4, a receptor regulating monocyte-macrophage differentiation, was downregulated at baseline in ME/CFS classical monocytes, and this was confirmed in an independent RNA-seq cohort.
Post-exercise, both inflammatory receptor genes (TNFRSF1A, TLR4, TLR5) and the anti-inflammatory receptor gene IL10RB were upregulated in ME/CFS classical monocytes.

CSF2 (granulocyte-monocyte colony-stimulating factor), an important monocyte differentiation cytokine, was upregulated in classical monocytes of ME/CFS patients by RNA-seq, consistent with prior reports of elevated CSF2 in plasma and extracellular vesicles correlating with disease burden.
Chemokines CCL20, CCL5, and CCL3, important for monocyte recruitment, were also upregulated in ME/CFS classical monocytes by RNA-seq.

Proteomic analysis of classical monocytes confirmed upregulation of proteins involved in iron metabolism (FTL1), monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation (CNN2, SERPINA1, DCTN1, NUDT21, PLD3), immune cell recruitment (ALDH3B1), activation (HVCN1, NCF1, PPIA), and platelet activation (STXBP5) in ME/CFS classical monocytes.
Proteins involved in translation (RTRAF, RPS2), mitochondrial function (HADHB), and cell-to-cell interaction (JUP, TPD52L2) were downregulated in ME/CFS classical monocytes at the protein level.

Positive unlabeled machine learning revealed that ME/CFS patients possess a heterogeneous classical monocyte population, with only a subset of cells classified as 'diseased' (pD) while the remainder resemble control cells (pN).
The percentage of classical monocytes classified as 'diseased' correlated with patients' Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI-20) fatigue score.
The fraction of diseased classical monocytes also correlated with general health scores, SF-36 Physical Component Summary scores, and PEM severity, in both female and male samples.

In a paired intraindividual analysis, CCL4 showed the strongest upregulation in predicted-diseased (pD) monocytes compared to predicted-normal (pN) monocytes within the same ME/CFS individuals, with the effect more prominent in female than male patients.

TMEM176B, involved in maintaining the immature (anti-inflammatory) state of dendritic cells, was downregulated in predicted-diseased monocytes compared to predicted-normal monocytes in both cases and controls.

GIMAP7 and TRIM7 were upregulated in pD cells (potentially promoting cell survival and inflammation), while OLR1, G0S2, ATF3, and RGCC were downregulated in pD cells, reflecting a complex mixed inflammatory signaling environment.
CellChat analysis of intercellular communication suggested that monocyte signaling to certain T and NK cells, as well as monocyte-monocyte signaling, is elevated in ME/CFS compared to controls.
Increased predicted ligand-receptor signaling from classical monocytes to platelets in the CCL pathway was identified in ME/CFS patients, driven by elevated CCL3/CCL5 expression in monocytes.
At baseline, ME/CFS patients showed reduced expression of platelet-function-related gene sets in the platelet cluster compared to controls, but this difference was not significant post-exercise.

Following the strenuous exercise challenge (CPET), platelet transcriptomes in ME/CFS patients shifted toward a normal (control-like) profile for platelet-function genes, indicating a marked change in circulating platelets associated with PEM.

Platelets in ME/CFS patients showed increased detection of ribosomal protein/translation machinery transcripts at baseline, consistent with an older platelet population, with this signal absent post-exercise.

RNA-seq of platelet-derived plasma particles from an independent small cohort validated the scRNA-seq findings: platelet-function genes were downregulated at baseline in ME/CFS, shifted toward normal post-exercise, and translation-related transcripts were elevated at baseline relative to post-exercise.

Flow cytometry quantification of major subsets of monocytes and T cells showed no substantial proportion differences between ME/CFS patients and controls, corroborating the scRNA-seq cluster proportion analysis.
In the independent RNA-seq cohort, classical monocytes from ME/CFS patients showed upregulation of CCL3 and CCL5 transcripts, chemokines important for monocyte recruitment, in addition to CCL20.

CSF2 (GM-CSF), a key monocyte differentiation cytokine, was upregulated in classical monocytes from ME/CFS patients by RNA-seq, consistent with prior reports of its elevation in plasma and extracellular vesicles correlating with disease burden.
Proteomic analysis of classical monocytes showed upregulation of FTL1, an iron-metabolism protein that controls Fe2+ levels during inflammation, in ME/CFS cases.
Proteins regulating monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation (CNN2, SERPINA1, DCTN1, NUDT21, PLD3) were upregulated in the classical monocyte proteome of ME/CFS cases.
STXBP5, a protein correlated with platelet activation, was upregulated in the classical monocyte proteome of ME/CFS patients, suggesting a link between monocyte and platelet activation states.

Proteins involved in translation (RTRAF, RPS2), mitochondrial function (HADHB), and cell-cell interaction (JUP, TPD52L2) were downregulated in the classical monocyte proteome of ME/CFS cases, with RTRAF remaining significant after removing an outlier sample.

TMEM176B, which maintains dendritic cell immaturity and an anti-inflammatory state, was downregulated in predicted-diseased classical monocytes compared to predicted-normal monocytes in ME/CFS patients and controls.

GIMAP7 and TRIM7, genes potentially contributing to suppression of apoptosis and promotion of inflammation respectively, were upregulated in predicted-diseased classical monocytes compared to predicted-normal monocytes in ME/CFS patients.

ATF3, a regulator of IFN responses able to suppress CCL4 expression in animal models, was downregulated in predicted-diseased classical monocytes compared to predicted-normal monocytes in ME/CFS patients.

The IFN-γ pathway was upregulated in predicted-normal (pN) monocytes relative to predicted-diseased (pD) monocytes within ME/CFS patients, suggesting reduced interferon-gamma signaling specifically in the diseased monocyte subset.

CellChat analysis identified 782 upregulated and 1,046 downregulated ligand-receptor pairs when comparing ME/CFS patient and control cell-cell communication networks across all pairwise cell-type combinations.

Increased CellChat-predicted signaling from classical monocytes to platelets in ME/CFS patients was driven by elevated CCL3/CCL5 expression in monocytes, implicating monocyte-platelet crosstalk in the inflammatory state.

Flow cytometry confirmed no substantial differences in proportions of major monocyte and T lymphocyte subsets between ME/CFS patients and controls, consistent with scRNA-seq cluster proportion analyses.

Sex was found to be the largest source of variation in the PBMC single-cell dataset, complicating pseudobulk differential expression analysis and motivating sex-stratified analyses throughout the study.
Interindividual variation in classical monocyte gene expression profiles was higher among ME/CFS cases than among controls, consistent with disease heterogeneity.

The proportion of predicted-diseased classical monocytes per individual correlated with SF-36 Physical Component Summary score, general health score, and PEM severity, in addition to MFI-20 fatigue score, with similar trends observed in male samples.

Isolated plasma particles used for platelet transcriptome validation were confirmed by flow cytometry to be positive for the platelet marker CD41 and negative for leukocyte marker CD45 and erythrocyte marker CD235a.

Prior studies found aberrant platelet activation and fibrin amyloid microclots in ME/CFS and long COVID, though microclot load was reported to be smaller in ME/CFS than in long COVID, and one prior study found no platelet alterations in ME/CFS, illustrating conflicting evidence in the field.

Prior literature cited indicates that CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in ME/CFS exhibit reduced glycolysis and that NK cells have impaired cytotoxic activity, findings the authors relate to the translational repression they observed across immune cell types.
Prior to culture, the frequency of CD24-positive B cells was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls, confirming previous peripheral blood findings.

During in vitro culture, the percentage of CD24-positive B cells remained elevated for longer in ME/CFS cultures than in healthy control cultures, indicating delayed loss of CD24 with cell cycle entry.

During in vitro culture, the frequency and mean fluorescence intensity of CD38-positive B cells were significantly increased in ME/CFS cultures compared with healthy controls, particularly during peak proliferation.
The frequency of CD73-positive B cells was significantly higher in ME/CFS cultures than in healthy controls during in vitro stimulation, though CD73 expression (MFI) did not differ.
CD39 surface expression on B cells did not differ between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls during in vitro culture.

Relative mitochondrial mass (MitoTracker Red MFI) of B cells over sequential cycles of proliferation was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls, in most TD-stimulated cycles and all TLR9D-stimulated cultures.

The proportion of viable CD24-positive B cells correlated strongly with glucose consumption and lactate production during culture in both ME/CFS and healthy control B cells, with no difference between groups in this relationship.
Fold changes in live cell, dead cell, debris, and total culture mass over time did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and healthy control B cell cultures.

During the proliferative phase, culture media from ME/CFS B cells showed a significant decrease in amino acid (particularly essential amino acid) levels that was not observed in proliferating healthy control cultures, suggesting increased amino acid utilization for energy production.
Lactate concentration in the media of proliferating ME/CFS B cell cultures was significantly elevated compared with proliferating healthy control cultures, suggesting heightened glycolysis in ME/CFS.
CD38 was significantly elevated on live ME/CFS B cells but showed a reduced fold change on dying ME/CFS B cells, suggesting CD38 may be linked to B cell survival advantage in ME/CFS.
The proportion of live B cell mass in ME/CFS cultures decreased less rapidly over time than in healthy control cultures.
ME/CFS patients in this cohort reported a median symptom severity of 7.3 for fatigue, 4.3 for cognitive impairment, and 4.0 for pain on visual analogue scales at time of blood sampling.
More than half of the CFS patients (56.6%) had an abnormal P50 sensory gating ratio exceeding the 50% threshold established as normal in healthy populations.

Clinician-rated scales (HAMA, HAMD) indicated high rates of anxiety (69.5%) and depression (79%) in CFS patients, whereas the self-report SCL-90-R found that 69.5% of a subset showed no significant mental health problems, indicating discordance between assessment methods.
No significant difference in P50 sensory gating ratio was found across age, sex, HAMD, SCL-90, or anxiety/depression subgroups when grouped using the stricter 7/7 cutoff.
Using the 14/20 HAMA/HAMD threshold, the P50 sensory gating ratio significantly differed between patients with no anxiety (NA) and those with obvious anxiety (TMBOA).
Using the 14/20 threshold, the P50 sensory gating ratio significantly differed between patients with no anxiety or depression (NAOD) and those with both anxiety and depression (AAD).

Somatization scores on both the HAMA and HAMD were significantly correlated with the P50 sensory gating ratio in the overall CFS sample, with associations also seen in specific anxiety/depression subgroups.
Among the general CFS population, sense of despair, hostility, and paranoid ideation subscale scores were significantly correlated with the P50 sensory gating ratio.
In binary logistic regression across all scale items, only the hopelessness item on the HAMD emerged as a significant risk factor for an abnormal P50 sensory gating ratio.

Binary logistic regression showed that, under the 14/20 threshold, the only-anxiety (OA) and anxiety-and-depression (AAD) subgroups significantly influenced the P50 sensory gating ratio compared with other groups.

The proportion of CFS patients classified as having an abnormal P50 sensory gating ratio rose from 17.3% (using the strict 7/7 no-anxiety/depression threshold) to 43.4% (using the more lenient 14/20 threshold), paralleling worsening anxiety/depression symptom severity.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha are highlighted as contributing to neuronal dysfunction and death in COVID-19 neuroinflammation.
Approximately half of patients recovering from COVID-19 were reported to develop Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome.
Imaging studies of long COVID showed hypometabolism in brain regions including olfactory bulbs, limbic/paralimbic domains, brainstem, and cerebellum.
Ninety imaging and neuropathological studies of COVID-19 showed evidence of white matter, brainstem, frontotemporal, and oculofrontal lesions.
NF-kB, MAPK, AP-1, and interferon regulatory factors are described as the main pathways involved in microglia activation underlying COVID-19 neuroinflammation.
Repeated cold stress (RCS) markedly reduced hind paw mechanical withdrawal thresholds in mice, indicating persistent mechanical allodynia lasting until day 17 after RCS loading.

RCS induced progressive accumulation of activated (Iba1-positive) microglia in the dorsal and ventral horns of the lumbar spinal cord, increasing with duration of stress exposure and normalizing when pain behavior resolved.
Despite spinal microglial activation, RCS did not increase peripheral blood markers of inflammation or muscle damage (C-reactive protein and creatine kinase).

RCS did not significantly change mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, or TNF-α in hind paw skin or intrinsic foot muscle, indicating a non-inflammatory local muscle/skin response.
ATF3, a marker of neuronal hyperactivation/injury, was progressively induced in DRG neurons over the course of RCS, rising from 3.2% on day 1 to 21.5% on day 7.
A subset of ChAT-positive motor neurons in the dorsal ventral horn expressed ATF3 beginning on RCS day 5, later than DRG onset, and these neurons were surrounded by activated microglia.
In Atf3:BAC transgenic reporter mice, the proportion of DRG neurons expressing ATF3 and GFP markedly increased after RCS, with high concordance between the two markers.
ChAT-positive motor neurons in the ventral horn showed a large increase in ATF3 and GFP expression after RCS, indicating motor neuron hyperactivation.

Among sensory neuron subtype markers, GFP-positive (hyperactivated) DRG neurons after RCS most frequently co-expressed the proprioceptor markers TrkC and VGluT1, identifying proprioceptors as the predominant neuron type activated.

Retrograde tracing from hindlimb muscles showed that ATF3/GFP-positive spinal motor neurons activated by RCS project specifically to the intrinsic muscles of the foot (IMF), identifying the muscle target of the hyperactivated reflex arc.

GFP labeling (indicating hyperactivation) was observed in VGluT1-positive proprioceptive fibers of muscle spindles and in axons innervating neuromuscular junctions of the IMF after RCS, but never in control mice.

Microglial accumulation spatially co-localized with the trajectory of GFP-positive (hyperactivated) fibers along the spinal reflex arc, with both GFP area and microglia number significantly increased in all measured regions after RCS.
Oral administration of the CSF1R inhibitor PLX3397 (pexidartinib) eliminated spinal microglia and significantly suppressed RCS-induced microglial accumulation in all measured spinal cord regions.
Microglial depletion by PLX3397 increased the mechanical withdrawal threshold (reduced pain behavior) after RCS, demonstrating that microglial suppression alleviates RCS-induced chronic pain.

In a supplementary experiment, female mice showed altered pain behavior and altered microglial/ATF3 activation patterns in response to RCS compared with males, motivating the use of male mice for the main study to avoid estrous-cycle confounds.

The authors propose that proprioceptor hyperactivation leading to spinal microglial activation is a common mechanism of chronic pain shared between this fibromyalgia (RCS) mouse model and a previously described ME/CFS mouse model, despite different stress-loading paradigms.
Several studies found that people with fibromyalgia consume fewer calories and lower amounts of carbohydrates, protein, lipids, and several micronutrients compared with healthy controls.

FM patients showed altered food-group intake, with lower consumption of dairy, bread, whole-grain cereals, fresh fruit, and fish, but higher intake of cured meat and sweetened beverages than healthy controls.
A higher percentage of dietary protein intake was associated with a higher pain threshold in fibromyalgia patients.
In a CFS cohort study, 95% of participants had poor fiber intake and 70% had an unhealthy fat intake.
Elimination diets for glutamate, aspartame, and histamine did not improve FM symptoms, although sample sizes were small and the diets led to weight loss and improved digestive symptoms.

A three-month anti-inflammatory diet combined with a low-FODMAP first month and subsequent food reintroduction improved functionality, pain, sleep quality (PSQI), and quality of life in FM patients, though inflammatory markers did not change.
A four-week low-FODMAP weight-loss diet reduced BMI, weight, waist circumference, pain, and FM severity, but had no impact on body composition.
A lacto-ovo vegetarian diet combined with core stabilization exercises improved muscle mass and reduced body fat and pain in women with FM.
A Mediterranean diet enriched with walnuts showed beneficial effects on fatigue, anxiety, depression, and eating disorders in women with FM.

A 12-week program of 800 kcal low-calorie diets improved FM symptoms at three weeks but produced no significant weight loss, and the authors questioned the safety of this restrictive approach and did not recommend it.

Ferritin, vitamin B12, and vitamin D levels were negatively correlated with the number of tender points, and ferritin and vitamin B12 were identified as independent risk factors potentially involved in FM etiopathogenesis.
Vitamin B12 deficiency (below 350-400 ng/dL) was observed in 42.4% of FM patients, who presented greater fatigue and memory loss than patients with higher levels.

FM patients had lower vitamin D levels than healthy controls, which has been linked to fatigue, widespread muscle pain, weakness, and higher pain sensitivity; vitamin D deficiency was also associated with elevated serum IL-6 and IL-8, which correlate with greater FM impact.

Patients with FM had significantly lower plasma concentrations of the branched-chain amino acids valine, leucine, and isoleucine, and of phenylalanine, than normal controls, likely due to lower dietary protein intake.
A subgroup of FM patients presented altered tryptophan metabolism suggesting a tryptophan deficiency, potentially associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis.

In FM patients, plasma lipid peroxidation, protein carbonyls, nitric oxide, copper, manganese, and aluminum were significantly elevated while magnesium and zinc were significantly reduced; oxidative stress markers, FIQR, and tender points positively associated with Cu, aluminum, and Mn, and negatively with Zn and Mg.

In an analytical observational study, mean serum 25-OH vitamin D levels were moderately to severely suboptimal in 60.1% of CFS participants not taking supplements, with lower levels in winter/spring than summer/autumn.

A significant reduction was shown in the CFS cohort for the n-3 to n-6 PUFA ratio and the EPA to arachidonic acid ratio, with severity of CFS symptoms positively related to certain n-6/n-9 PUFAs and negatively related to the n-3/n-6 ratio.

Pimentel et al. (2004) found that 100% of their FM study group presented small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), with pain severity correlating with hydrogen breath test level; eradicating SIBO led to notable clinical improvement.

Alterations in bile acid-metabolizing gut bacteria in women with FM were accompanied by marked depletion of serum secondary bile acid α-muricholic acid, which was highly correlated with symptom severity including pain intensity and fatigue.

One study found that FM microbiome diversity and stool propionate were reduced, whereas a separate study found neither microbiome composition nor alpha/beta diversity differed from healthy controls, suggesting a limited or inconsistent role of gut microbiome in FM pathophysiology.

Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Eubacterium rectale, health-promoting butyrate-producing gut bacteria, were found in reduced quantities in persons with ME/CFS, with reduced F. prausnitzii abundance inversely associated with fatigue severity.

Short-term CFS patients showed significant microbial dysbiosis, while long-term patients had largely resolved dysbiosis but showed metabolic aberrations including reduced microbial butyrate biosynthesis and reduced plasma butyrate, bile acids, and benzoate.

High-dose vitamin D supplementation improved short-term musculoskeletal pain and long-term functional capacity in young people and improved musculoskeletal pain and long-term quality of life in elderly subjects, though another study found no difference in pain after 12 weeks of supplementation.

Ferric carboxymaltose supplementation yielded greater improvements after 42 days in functionality (FIQR), Brief Pain Inventory score, fatigue visual numeric scale score, and iron indices in iron-deficient FM patients.
Daily sublingual vitamin B12 significantly improved functionality (FIQR scores across all domains) and anxiety scores in people with FM.
Daily oral magnesium chloride supplementation improved mild/moderate stress and reduced pain in FM patients.

High-dose vitamin D supplementation improved short-term musculoskeletal pain and long-term functional capacity in young people with FM, and improved pain and long-term quality of life in elderly patients.
One study found no differences in pain following 12 weeks of vitamin D supplementation in FM.

A review concluded vitamin D supplementation has beneficial effects and reduces pain in patients with an established vitamin D deficiency and FM/widespread chronic pain, but also improved physical function, emotional role, social function, and general health without affecting pain VAS or depression scores in another study.
Ferric carboxymaltose supplementation for 42 days improved functionality, pain, fatigue, and iron indices in iron-deficient FM patients.
Daily sublingual vitamin B12 significantly improved functionality (FIQR scores) in all domains and anxiety scores in people with FM.

Frequent high-concentrate vitamin B12 injections combined with daily oral folic acid may raise blood saturations enough to relieve symptoms in a subgroup of FM and/or CFS patients, though this may interact with drugs requiring demethylation such as opioids.
Magnesium intake was inversely correlated with C-reactive protein levels in the FM group.
Daily oral magnesium chloride supplementation improved mild/moderate stress and reduced pain in FM patients, though larger clinical trials are needed.

In a small preliminary study, probiotic supplementation significantly improved sleep quality, depression, anxiety, and pain scores in FM patients, while prebiotic supplementation significantly improved pain scores and sleep quality.

Symbiotic nutritional supplementation improved dysregulated immune-neuroendocrine interaction and reduced perceived stress, anxiety, and depression, and improved quality of life in women with FM, particularly those without prior CFS diagnosis.
Multispecies probiotic supplementation improved impulsivity and decision-making in persons with FM.

Coenzyme Q10 supplementation improves clinical parameters including pain, fatigue, depression, and quality of life scores in FM, related to its role in mitochondrial bioenergetics and antioxidant activity.

A review found melatonin supplementation showed positive results in FM, osteoarthritis, and osteoporosis/osteopenia, but not in rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, and was well tolerated with mild side effects.

An orally administered amino acid-based supplement (L-lysine, L-arginine, oxo-proline, N-acetyl-l-cysteine, L-glutamine, and Schizonepeta tenuifolia) over 24 weeks showed sustained augmentation of IGF-1, which could improve stress-related weight gain and lower-than-normal hGH levels in FM.

Supplementing ongoing pregabalin and duloxetine treatment with palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) and acetyl-L-carnitine (ALC) for 24 weeks improved widespread pain index (WPI) and FIQR scores in FM patients.
Oral CoQ10 plus NADH supplementation for 8 weeks improved fatigue and biochemical parameters in CFS patients.
D-ribose and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation led to positive outcomes for CFS symptom relief.

Multivitamin and mineral supplementation in CFS patients improved superoxide dismutase antioxidant enzyme activity and various fatigue and quality-of-life measures including sleep disorder, autonomic symptoms, headaches, physical function, pain, and mental health.
Magnesium supplementation improved fatigue at six months of treatment in CFS but showed no significant relationship at two years of treatment.

A small cohort study of probiotic supplementation in CFS reported subjective improvement and improved neurocognitive function measures post-trial, but found no significant changes in fatigue or physical activity scores, and no major changes in gastrointestinal microflora.
A randomized clinical trial detected a decrease in systemic inflammatory markers such as CRP and TNF-alpha in FM/CFS patients after oral intake of Bifidobacterium infantis.
A non-controlled pilot study with 13 ME/CFS patients showed improvements in well-being and oxidative and inflammatory parameters after probiotic intake.

In mice models, Astragalus polysaccharide (APS) regulated gut microbiota abundance, increased SCFA and anti-inflammatory bacteria production, reversed abnormal Nrf2 and NF-κB expression in the brain, and alleviated reduction in cecal SCFAs associated with CFS.

A significant correlation was observed between total BRIAN questionnaire scores (measuring circadian rhythm disruption) and higher pain levels, worse functionality, greater depression, and worse sleep quality in FM.

FM patients showed disrupted circadian variations of melatonin, cytokines, and serotonin, with lower nighttime melatonin secretion and elevated evening serum cortisol and cytokine levels compared to healthy subjects.
Night-shift work is associated with increased pain perception and disruption of circadian rhythms due to nocturnal light exposure.
A meta-analysis showed that night-shift work is associated with suppression of melatonin production, especially among fixed night-shift workers.

Using actigraphy data and machine learning, chronic pain predictions were more accurate using rest-activity rhythm features than sleep or activity features, with intraday variability being the most predictive feature.

FM pain, like postoperative pain, trigeminal neuralgia, and migraines, showed a circadian pattern with higher pain scores in the morning, while other pain types such as temporomandibular joint pain and cluster headaches increased throughout the day; arthritis and cancer pain showed no circadian rhythmicity, and rhythm of pain was not altered by analgesics.

One study found both bright and dim morning light treatment over four weeks achieved significant and similar improvement in pain intensity, pain interference, physical function, depressive symptoms, and sleep disturbance in FM, comparable to physical exercise treatment, with minimal side effects.

CFS patients showed lower amplitude and stability of daily activity rhythm measured by actigraph, lower nocturnal distal skin temperature in winter, and absence of the post-lunch dip in activity and skin temperature peak seen in controls, suggesting altered circadian temperature regulation and vasodilator responses.

In CFS patients, circadian rhythm and hemodynamic measures assessed via orthostatic testing and skin temperature/vascular endothelium analysis were associated with endothelial biomarker levels (ET-1 and VCAM-1), suggesting dysautonomia and vascular tone abnormalities.
A meta-analysis found sleep is altered in CFS, with changes differing between adolescents and adults, suggesting sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system alterations in ME/CFS.

F. prausnitzii and E. rectale, health-promoting butyrate-producing gut bacteria, were found in reduced quantities in persons with ME/CFS, with a deficient microbial capacity for butyrate synthesis confirmed, and F. prausnitzii abundance was inversely associated with fatigue severity.
FM patients secreted less melatonin during nighttime hours than healthy controls, which may contribute to impaired sleep, daytime fatigue, and altered pain perception.
Evening serum cortisol and cytokine levels were found to be elevated in FM patients compared to controls.
A meta-analysis found that night-shift work suppresses melatonin production, particularly among fixed night-shift workers, linking circadian disruption to increased pain perception.
Machine-learning analysis of actigraphy data showed that rest-activity rhythm features (especially intraday variability) predicted chronic pain more accurately than sleep or activity features alone.

FM pain, like postoperative pain, trigeminal neuralgia, and migraine, follows a circadian pattern with higher pain scores in the morning, whereas conditions like arthritis and cancer pain show no circadian rhythmicity.

A trial of one hour of daily bright morning light versus dim morning light over four weeks in FM patients showed similar, significant improvements in pain, physical function, depression, and sleep disturbance in both groups, with minimal side effects.
The amplitude and stability of daily activity rhythms, measured by actigraphy, were lower in CFS patients than in controls.

Distal skin temperature showed lower nocturnal values in CFS patients than controls during winter, and CFS patients lacked the normal post-lunch dip in activity and skin temperature peak seen in controls.
CFS patients showed circadian rhythm and hemodynamic modifications associated with endothelial biomarkers ET-1 and VCAM-1, implicating dysautonomia and vascular tone abnormalities.
A meta-analysis found altered sleep in CFS, with differences between adolescents and adults, suggesting both sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system alterations in ME/CFS.
Oral CoQ10 plus NADH supplementation for 8 weeks improved fatigue and biochemical parameters in CFS patients.
Multivitamin and mineral supplementation in CFS patients improved superoxide dismutase (SOD) antioxidant activity along with multiple fatigue and quality-of-life measures.
Magnesium supplementation improved fatigue in CFS at six months but showed no significant relationship with fatigue after two years of treatment.
D-ribose and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation resulted in positive outcomes for CFS symptom relief.
A small probiotic cohort study in CFS reported subjective and neurocognitive improvements but no significant changes in fatigue, physical activity, or gastrointestinal microflora.
A randomized clinical trial found that oral intake of Bifidobacterium infantis decreased systemic inflammatory markers CRP and TNF-α in FM/CFS patients.
A non-controlled pilot study of 13 ME/CFS patients showed improvements in well-being and oxidative/inflammatory parameters after probiotic intake.

In a mouse model, Astragalus polysaccharide regulated gut microbiota, increased SCFA-producing anti-inflammatory bacteria, reversed abnormal Nrf2/NF-κB expression in the brain-gut axis, and alleviated CFS-associated reductions in cecal SCFAs.
Butyrate-producing gut bacteria Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Eubacterium rectale were reduced in ME/CFS patients, with reduced F. prausnitzii abundance inversely associated with fatigue severity.

In IBS patients, fecal microbiota transplantation increased specific bacteria (e.g., Alistipes, F. prausnitzii, Prevotella) inversely correlated with IBS symptoms and fatigue, while decreasing Streptococcus thermophilus and Coprobacillus cateniformis correlated with symptom and fatigue severity.

CFS patients showed distinct microbial and metabolomic dysbiosis by illness duration: short-term patients had significant microbial dysbiosis, while long-term patients had largely resolved microbial dysbiosis but retained metabolic aberrations including reduced microbial butyrate biosynthesis and reduced plasma butyrate, bile acids, and benzoate.

A 24-week amino acid-based supplement (L-lysine, L-arginine, oxo-proline, N-acetyl-L-cysteine, L-glutamine, Schizonepeta tenuifolia) produced sustained augmentation of IGF-1 in FM patients, potentially improving stress-related weight gain and low hGH levels.
Adding palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) and acetyl-L-carnitine (ALC) to ongoing pregabalin and duloxetine treatment for 24 weeks improved widespread pain index and FIQR scores in FM patients.

A review of melatonin supplementation in rheumatological diseases found positive results in FM, osteoarthritis, and osteoporosis/osteopenia, but not in rheumatoid arthritis or lupus, with mild, well-tolerated side effects.
FM patients show a reduction in muscle function (dynapenia) without an accompanying loss of muscle mass.
Obese FM patients had higher IL-6 concentrations, decreased blood flow, and increased pyruvate compared to non-obese FM patients, with inflammatory proteins correlated with sedentary behavior.
FM status and depressive symptoms are associated with BMI and physical performance in mid to late life.
Gut microbiome diversity was lower in FM patients than controls, with reduced stool propionate levels potentially linked to decreased abundance of propionate-producing bacteria.
One study found no significant difference in fecal microbiome composition or diversity between FM patients and healthy controls, suggesting a limited role of gut microbiome in FM pathophysiology.

Serum α-muricholic acid, a secondary bile acid, was markedly depleted in women with FM and highly correlated with symptom severity including pain intensity and fatigue, potentially secondary to gut microbiome alterations.
Higher circadian rhythm disruption scores on the BRIAN questionnaire correlated with greater pain, worse functionality, greater depression, and worse sleep quality in fibromyalgia patients.
Fibromyalgia patients showed lower nocturnal melatonin secretion than healthy subjects, potentially contributing to impaired sleep, daytime fatigue, and altered pain perception.
Fibromyalgia patients showed elevated evening serum cortisol levels together with higher cytokine levels.
Night-shift work is associated with increased pain perception.
A meta-analysis found that night-shift work is associated with suppression of melatonin production, especially among fixed night-shift workers.
A review emphasized the clinical relevance of the insomnia–pain–anxiety pathological cycle in fibromyalgia and recommended developing patient programs focused mainly on improving sleep quality.

Machine learning analysis of actigraphy data showed that rest-activity rhythm features predicted chronic pain more accurately than sleep or activity features, with intraday variability of rest-activity rhythm being the most predictive feature.

Fibromyalgia pain, along with postoperative pain, trigeminal neuralgia, and migraine, showed higher pain scores in the morning, while temporomandibular joint pain, neuropathic pain, labor pain, biliary colic, and cluster headaches increased throughout the day peaking in the evening or night; arthritis and cancer pain showed no circadian rhythmicity.
The circadian rhythm of pain was not found to be altered in patients taking analgesics.

In a four-week trial, one daily hour of bright morning light therapy and a dim morning light comparison condition produced similar significant improvements in pain intensity, pain interference, physical function, depressive symptoms, and sleep disturbance in fibromyalgia patients, with minimal side effects.
Night fasting, a reduced daytime eating window, and consuming two to three meals earlier in the day including breakfast contribute to regulating circadian clocks.
Autonomic dysfunction is well documented in CFS, but little is known about its relationship with circadian rhythms and endothelial dysfunction.
The amplitude and stability of daily activity rhythm, measured by actigraphy, were lower in CFS patients than in healthy controls.

Distal skin temperature showed lower nocturnal values in CFS patients than controls during winter, and CFS patients lacked the post-lunch activity dip and distal skin temperature peak seen in controls.

In CFS patients, an orthostatic test revealed modifications in circadian rhythm and hemodynamic measures that were associated with the endothelial biomarkers ET-1 and VCAM-1, suggesting dysautonomia and vascular tone abnormalities.
A meta-analysis found that sleep is altered in CFS, with changes differing between adolescents and adults, suggesting alterations in sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system activity in ME/CFS.
CBT significantly reduced fatigue compared with control conditions at post-treatment across 11 studies.
The fatigue-reducing effect of CBT was maintained at long-term follow-up (13-48 weeks) across 7 studies.
Beyond one year, individual studies found no significant CBT effect on fatigue severity relative to comparators at 2- and 3.5-year follow-ups.
CBT significantly reduced depression symptoms compared with control conditions at post-treatment with a small to moderate effect.
CBT significantly reduced anxiety symptoms compared with control conditions at post-treatment with a small to moderate effect.
CBT significantly improved perceived health status (including functional disability/quality of life) compared with control conditions at post-treatment with a small effect.
At long-term follow-up, CBT's effects on depression and perceived health status were no longer significant, while the effect on anxiety remained a significant small effect.
Beyond one year, perceived health status effects in two individual studies were not statistically significant.
About 22% of participants in CBT groups did not complete all mandatory treatment sessions.
Using each study's own drop-out definition, the overall weighted drop-out rate in CBT groups was 15%.
On average, participants who started CBT completed 84% of the treatment modules.
About 7% of participants allocated to CBT refused to start the intervention.
The relative risk of non-completion did not differ significantly between CBT and control groups, though the confidence interval was very wide.
Participants in CBT groups were more than twice as likely to drop out compared with control groups.
CBT's effect on fatigue was larger when compared with inactive (wait-list) control groups than with non-specific (TAU/placebo) control groups.
Higher CBT treatment dosage (total contact time) was associated with greater reduction in fatigue, accounting for nearly all between-study heterogeneity.
A greater number of CBT sessions was associated with greater improvement in perceived health status.

Higher baseline fatigue severity was associated with greater rates of non-completion and drop-out from CBT, with each one-point rise in fatigue score associated with a 0.1 increase in non-completion proportion.
Aerobic and strength training programs have shown benefit for adults living with long COVID.
Breathing pattern disorder is described as common among adults with long COVID and requires treatment consideration before or alongside rehabilitation.

Postexertional malaise is an important consideration in long COVID rehabilitation, with chronic fatigue syndrome literature supporting individualized exercise programs and caution for those with adverse reactions to activity/exercise.
After five omalizumab injections, the patient's chronic systemic pain decreased from a pre-treatment VAS of 10/10 to a consistent post-treatment VAS of 6–7/10.

The hEDS patient had multiple comorbid conditions including CRPS, chronic idiopathic urticaria, hereditary alpha tryptasemia, gastroparesis, small fiber neuropathy, MCAS, POTS, depression, and fibromyalgia.

The authors describe mast cells as contributing to pain via secretion of proinflammatory mediators (e.g., histamine) that induce peripheral sensitization, potentially underlying systemic pain in hEDS/MCAS.

The patient had genetically confirmed hereditary alpha tryptasemia, which contributed to her clinical picture alongside chronic idiopathic urticaria and MCAS, informing the decision to initiate omalizumab.
A 23-year-old woman with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presented with chronic pain and fainting spells (syncope), illustrating characteristic clinical features of the disorder.
The authors note that diagnosis of hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome can often take years, reflecting poor recognition and difficulty coordinating comprehensive care for these patients.
The title indicates a case report describing a novel/off-label use of telitacicept as a treatment approach in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, but no further detail is available from title alone.
Most participants in this qualitative study of EDS patients reported that their general function declined over time, primarily due to chronic pain.
Participants described pain as manifesting largely through joint-related events such as spontaneous dislocations and subluxations affecting multiple joints including hips, larynx, and neck.
Participants commonly experienced multiple overlapping conditions such as psoriatic arthritis and osteoarthritis alongside EDS, making it difficult to attribute joint pain to a single cause.
The study found no differences in symptom experience or trajectory across the different EDS diagnostic subtypes (hypermobile, classical, vascular, not specified).
Many participants described their symptom trajectory as fluctuating, using metaphors like a 'roller coaster' or cycles of decline and reprieve rather than a steady decline.

Participants reported that alternative/complementary therapies (e.g., acupuncture, chiropractic, meditation, mindfulness, medical marijuana) were perceived as more effective for symptom management than prescribed medications and elective surgery.
Participants reported undergoing multiple surgeries (up to 26 in one individual), predominantly neurosurgery and orthopedic surgery, but none provided evidence that these surgeries were successful.
Most participants did not view a physician as their central source of care and lacked access to an integrated system of care, instead navigating fragmented care with multiple individual specialists.

Participants demonstrated resilience and self-management strategies such as home accommodations (stair lifts, single-story housing), assistive devices (braces, splints, TENS units), diet/exercise modification, and social/family support to cope with declining function.

Unlike prior qualitative EDS studies, participants in this cohort did not report feeling that their condition was poorly understood or dismissed by healthcare professionals, likely because they had been long engaged with EDS research and knowledgeable practitioners.
Unlike some prior qualitative studies, most participants in this cohort continued to work despite significant disability, having adapted and negotiated their work environment.
Widespread pain in EDS has previously been associated with central sensitization, and fatigue, depression, and anxiety may intensify pain in EDS patients.

At 1-year follow-up, high-load shoulder strengthening exercise (HEAVY) was not superior to low-load exercise (LIGHT) for self-reported shoulder function measured by WOSI-total score change from baseline.
Both HEAVY and LIGHT groups showed clinically meaningful within-group improvement in WOSI-total score from baseline to 1 year.
HEAVY showed a greater improvement than LIGHT in the WOSI 'emotions' subdomain at 1 year.
A greater proportion of HEAVY participants reported an important improvement in Global Perceived Effect for the emotions subdomain compared to LIGHT.
A greater proportion of HEAVY participants reported an important improvement in Global Perceived Effect for the lifestyle subdomain compared to LIGHT.
A similar proportion of participants achieved a clinically important improvement in WOSI-total score in HEAVY versus LIGHT at 1 year.
In the per-protocol analysis, HEAVY showed a larger but statistically non-significant improvement compared with LIGHT in WOSI-total score.
HEAVY and LIGHT groups were comparable in healthcare utilisation, subsequent shoulder injuries/dislocations, painkiller consumption and adverse events at 1-year follow-up.
A larger proportion of LIGHT participants continued shoulder-specific exercise after the intervention period compared with HEAVY participants.
Self-efficacy data did not show a greater improvement in the HEAVY group compared with LIGHT.
The majority of patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD) experience shoulder symptoms such as pain and/or instability.

In the primary 16-week trial (prior report), a supervised, progressive high-load shoulder strengthening programme resulted in greater self-reported improvements in shoulder function than less supervised, less progressive low-load exercise.
Intermittent cold stress (ICS) transiently elevated plasma corticosterone at post-stress days 1–2, which normalized by day 3–12.
Constant cold stress (CCS), unlike ICS, produced no change in plasma corticosterone levels between post-stress days 1 and 12.
ICS induced long-lasting mechanical hyperalgesia/allodynia in the hind paw starting at post-stress day 1 and persisting to at least day 13.
In contrast to ICS, hyperalgesia induced by constant cold stress (CCS) resolved by post-stress day 5.
ICS decreased the femoral muscle mechanical pain threshold at post-stress day 5, indicating widespread (generalized) pain beyond the paw.
Thermal hyperalgesia following ICS was long-lasting, persisting until at least post-stress day 17.

ICS produced allodynia specific to Aδ- and Aβ-fiber electrical stimulation, lowering thresholds substantially, while C-fiber thresholds were unaffected, suggesting a specific rather than global small-fiber deficit.

Orchiectomy (removal of androgen source) significantly decreased ICS-induced mechanical hyperalgesia in male mice, whereas ovariectomy had no effect in females, implicating androgens in maintaining hyperalgesia.
In LPAR1-knockout mice, ICS-induced thermal hyperalgesia was completely absent, with no difference from wild-type basal pain thresholds, indicating LPAR1 is required for hyperalgesia development.

Systemic and intracerebroventricular morphine lost analgesic efficacy in ICS-treated mice, whereas intrathecal morphine retained significant analgesia, suggesting a brain-specific loss of opioid analgesia.
ICS abolished the morphine-induced increase in spinal cord serotonin turnover (5-HIAA/5-HT), consistent with a disrupted descending inhibitory system underlying loss of morphine analgesia.

Intrathecal SNRIs/tricyclic-type antidepressants (milnacipran, amitriptyline, mianserin, paroxetine) all produced potent anti-hyperalgesia in the ICS model, with milnacipran the most potent at the lowest dose.

Repeated mirtazapine treatment (1 mg/kg i.p. every other day from P5-P13) gradually and completely reversed ICS-induced hyperalgesia to control levels, with the effect persisting at least until P17, suggesting erasure of 'pain memory'.

Among 16 pain-related brain regions, only the habenula showed increased ADRA2A (adrenergic α2a receptor) transcription after ICS, and habenular siRNA knockdown of ADRA2A reversed hyperalgesia, implicating this receptor in the region as necessary for hyperalgesia maintenance.

Gabapentin dose-dependently reversed ICS-induced hyperalgesia at doses (1-3 mg/kg i.p.) much lower than those needed in the partial sciatic nerve ligation neuropathic pain model (30 mg/kg), and was effective centrally (i.c.v.) where the neuropathic pain model was not.

Repeated intracerebroventricular pregabalin (post-ICS at P5, 8, and 11) reversed nociceptive thresholds to control levels by P14, with the effect persisting to at least P20, indicating reversible erasure of established pain memory.

Co-administration of systemic pregabalin with the P-glycoprotein inhibitor valspodar (both i.p., every other day P5-P11) reversed the pain threshold to normal by P13, sustained to at least P19, offering a less invasive route to a similar radical effect as central pregabalin.
Pilocarpine's anti-hyperalgesia action in the ICS model was abolished by the muscarinic antagonist pirenzepine, showing that brain muscarinic receptor activation mediates the analgesic effect.

Repeated low-dose donepezil (10 μg/kg i.p., daily P5-P10) reversed ICS-induced hyperalgesia to normal thresholds, with the effect persisting to at least P18, via brain muscarinic receptor activation, suggesting erasure of pain memory.

Only intermittent psychological stress (IPS) produced persistent hyperalgesia (still present at day 8); repeated psychological stress (RPS) without the intermittent/unpredictable component did not, suggesting unpredictability drives chronicity.

IPS-treated mice showed significantly increased acetic-acid-induced writhing behavior, indicating increased sensitivity to chemical/visceral-somatic pain stimuli, supporting a generalized pain phenotype (IPGP).
IPS-treated mice showed no increased sensitivity in an intra-colonic capsaicin visceral pain test, indicating IPGP affects somatic but not visceral pain pathways.
