In the IPS model, orchiectomized male mice showed progressive recovery of pain threshold (complete abolition of hyperalgesia by P15), whereas ovariectomized female mice showed no change, again implicating androgens in maintaining hyperalgesia.

IPS-induced thermal hyperalgesia was lost in LPAR1-knockout mice, and repeated treatment with the LPAR1 antagonist AM966 abolished established hyperalgesia, confirming LPAR1's role in the psychological-stress pain model.

The spinal cord norepinephrine turnover rate (MHPG/NE) was significantly decreased in IPS-treated mice compared to controls, consistent with impaired descending noradrenergic pain inhibition, and mirroring reports of decreased spinal monoamines in FM patients.

The NSAID diclofenac showed no anti-hyperalgesia effect in the IPGP model, despite being effective in an inflammatory (Freund's complete adjuvant) pain model, mirroring the clinical observation that FM patients report no pain relief from NSAIDs.

Pregabalin dose-dependently produced anti-hyperalgesia in the IPGP model but not in control mice, with a markedly longer duration of action via the intracerebroventricular route than the intrathecal route.
Serum IL-1R antibody and IL-8 levels were reported to be significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls.
Salivary chemokines and interleukins, including IL-8, have been proposed as potential biomarkers for diagnosing fibromyalgia.
Passive transfer of IgG from fibromyalgia patients into mice reproduced several symptoms observed in FM patients, suggesting an autoantibody-mediated mechanism.
IgM from patients with complex regional pain syndrome produced pain in mice, analogous to the IgG findings in FM, supporting antibody-mediated pain mechanisms.

NK cell cytotoxicity is reported to be negatively correlated with chronic pain conditions, being increased by acute stress/pain but inhibited by chronic pain or chronic stress hormones via the HPA axis.

LPAR1 is expressed on NK cells and lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) decreases NK cell cytotoxicity and induces interferon-γ secretion, though whether this modulates chronic pain via NK cell activity remains unclear.

In the AcGP (repeated acid saline-induced generalized pain) model, intracerebroventricular injection of the microglia inhibitor minocycline abolished chronic hyperalgesia, implicating brain microglial mechanisms.

Microinjection of the MAPK inhibitor U0126 or PKC activator phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate into the anterior paraventricular thalamus completely reversed hyperalgesia in the AcGP model, implicating thalamic signaling in central pain maintenance.

In the ICGP model, Neurometer testing showed hyperalgesia from Aδ-fiber stimulation but no significant change with C-fiber stimulation, suggesting the model does not fully replicate a combined Aδ/C small fiber neuropathy pattern seen clinically.

Loss of morphine analgesia in the ICGP model was recovered in NR2A-knockout mice, by intracerebroventricular NR2A antagonist, or by micro-injection of NR2A-specific siRNA into the periaqueductal gray, implicating an anti-opioid NMDA receptor mechanism in the periaqueductal gray.

The authors note that analgesia induced by mild swim stress was lost in β-endorphin-knockout mice, supporting the hypothesis that endogenous opioid release drives loss of morphine analgesia in the ICGP model via an anti-opioid tolerance mechanism.

Hyperalgesia in the ICGP model, assessed via thermal, mechanical, electrical, and deep muscle pressure stimuli, was not affected in μ-opioid receptor-knockout mice, indicating endogenous opioid receptor function is not required for generalized hyperalgesia itself.

Diclofenac (10 mg/kg i.p.), a representative NSAID, showed no anti-hyperalgesia effect in the IPGP model at P5, despite being effective in a Freund's complete adjuvant inflammatory pain model, consistent with the clinical lack of NSAID efficacy in FM.

Duloxetine (30 mg/kg i.p.) produced significant anti-hyperalgesia in the IPGP model but not in control mice, and intrathecal duloxetine (1 μg) was effective while intracerebroventricular duloxetine (3 μg) was not, mirroring findings in the ICGP model.

In the IPS model, spinal cord norepinephrine turnover rate (MHPG/NE ratio) was significantly decreased compared with control mice, while turnover rates of serotonin and dopamine were not significantly changed.
TMD patients in the high pain-disability group reported significantly greater jaw functional limitation (JFLS-20) than those with low disability.
Current pain intensity measured by the McGill Pain Questionnaire (MPQ) was significantly higher in the high pain-disability TMD group.
Initial pain intensity on a 0-10 numeric rating scale was significantly higher in the high disability group.
Self-reported physical activity level measured by the IPAQ did not differ significantly between low and high TMD disability groups.
Objectively measured moderate-intensity physical activity (actigraphy) was significantly higher in the high disability TMD group than the low disability group.
Objectively measured vigorous-intensity physical activity was significantly higher in the high disability TMD group than the low disability group.
Total moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) was significantly higher in the high disability TMD group.
Time spent in light-intensity physical activity was lower in the high disability group but the difference was not statistically significant.
Actigraphy-measured sleep indices (total sleep time, sleep efficiency, WASO, fragmentation) showed no significant differences between low and high disability TMD groups.
The proportion of patients meeting 2016 ACR fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria (based on Symptom Severity scale and Widespread Pain Index) was significantly higher in the high TMD disability group.
Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) scores did not differ significantly between low and high TMD disability groups.
Systemic inflammatory hematologic indices (PLR, NLR, dNLR, SII, ESR, hs-CRP) trended higher and LMR trended lower in the high disability group, but none reached statistical significance.
In multivariable logistic regression, less time spent in light-intensity physical activity was significantly associated with high TMD pain-disability.
Mucosal ridging was inversely associated with high TMD pain-disability in the logistic regression model.
Higher depressive symptom scores (PHQ-9) were significantly associated with high TMD pain-disability in the logistic regression model.
Pain on mouth opening was significantly associated with high TMD pain-disability in the logistic regression model.
The combined logistic regression model (light PA time, age, mucosal ridging, GAD-7, PHQ-9, pain on mouth opening) classified TMD disability level with 84.5% accuracy.
Time spent in vigorous physical activity showed significant predictive power for high TMD pain-disability, with a cutoff of 2.5 minutes/week yielding an AUC of 0.643.
Other physical activity metrics (average kcals/day, METs, step counts, light PA, moderate PA, MVPA) did not show statistically significant predictive power for TMD disability level by ROC analysis.
Tyrosine-kinase inhibitors targeting wild-type and mutated KIT can efficiently deplete mast cells.
Avapritinib and midostaurin can temper IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation.
Avapritinib has been approved by the FDA for treatment of indolent systemic mastocytosis.
The anti-Siglec-8 antibody lirentelimab showed promising results in indolent systemic mastocytosis.
MCAS is described as a heterogeneous disorder requiring a personalized therapeutic approach, with anaphylaxis not yet formally captured as an outcome in prospective TKI trials.

MCAS diagnosis requires fulfillment of three criteria: symptoms in ≥2 organ systems, a validated transient increase in a mast cell activation marker during the episode, and symptom response to MC mediator-targeting drugs.
Serum tryptase rises acutely during systemic mast cell activation events, peaking about 1 hour after onset and declining with a half-life of about 2 hours.
To confirm MCAS, the event-related tryptase must exceed the patient's baseline tryptase by a validated formula (sBT × 1.2 + 2 ng/mL).
Genetically determined normal baseline serum tryptase is generally considered to be under 8 ng/mL.
Urinary histamine metabolites, mainly N-methyl histamine, correlate with mast cell burden and activation but are less MC-specific than tryptase.
Urinary levels of the PGD2 metabolite 9α-11β-PGF2 are elevated during anaphylaxis and in systemic mastocytosis patients compared with healthy controls.
Urinary LTE4 is higher in anaphylaxis patients who develop severe hypotension and in systemic mastocytosis patients.
There is no scientific evidence supporting chromogranin A as a biomarker of mast cell activation, and reported data show no elevation in mastocytosis patients.
A reported rise in plasma heparin activity after venous occlusion in patients with MC activation symptoms is not sufficiently validated as a biomarker for MC activation.
Anaphylaxis incidence estimates differ by region, with US studies reporting up to 40-50 per 100,000 person-years versus 1.5-7.9 per 100,000 person-years in Europe.
Food-induced anaphylaxis is the most common cause of anaphylaxis in children, accounting for 80-92% of cases.
Mastocytosis is a rare disease with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 10,000 persons in recent studies.
More than 85% of systemic mastocytosis patients have the indolent subtype (ISM) with a good prognosis, while the remaining ~15% have advanced, more aggressive SM variants with poor prognosis.

Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT), caused by extra copies of the alpha-tryptase gene TPSAB1, is found in about 6% of the general population and is usually asymptomatic, but carriers tend to have elevated baseline tryptase.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia is associated with an increased prevalence of systemic mastocytosis and an increased risk of severe mediator-related symptoms and MCAS in those with SM.
In a study of 703 adult patients referred for suspected mast cell disorders, the overall prevalence of idiopathic MCAS was 4.4%, rising to 27% among patients with unprovoked anaphylaxis.
In the same 703-patient cohort referred for suspected mast cell disorders, 35% of patients had experienced at least one episode of anaphylaxis.
An activating KIT D816V mutation in bone marrow, blood, or other extracutaneous organs is a minor WHO diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis and monoclonal MCAS.
The diagnostic delay for idiopathic MCAS is estimated to be approximately 4 years, based on the authors' personal experience.
Acute episodes of any MCAS variant should be promptly treated with intramuscular epinephrine.
Allergen immunotherapy is recommended for MCAS patients with documented Hymenoptera venom allergy, with life-long immunotherapy standard in patients with mixed (combined) MCAS.
Serum tryptase rise from an individual's baseline during a symptomatic episode is currently the most accepted objective biomarker of mast cell activation.
Urine N-methylhistamine is discussed as an emerging non-invasive biomarker with utility for diagnosing mast cell activation syndrome.
Urine leukotriene E4 (a cysteinyl leukotriene) is reviewed as a candidate non-invasive urine biomarker for identifying mast cell activation.
Urine 2,3-dinor-11beta-prostaglandin F2 alpha, a prostaglandin metabolite, is reviewed as a candidate non-invasive urine biomarker for mast cell activation.
Urine mast cell mediator testing is proposed as a non-invasive, at-home-collectable complement to serum tryptase, which can be difficult to obtain via venipuncture during symptomatic episodes.
Melatonin was reported to inhibit mast cell activation, suggesting a possible therapeutic role in inflammatory conditions.
Mast cells maintain and amplify baseline type 2 inflammation in the upper and lower airway in AERD.
Mast cells are prominently involved in the hypersensitivity reaction to COX-1 inhibition that defines AERD.
The authors identify further dissection of COX-1-mediated mast cell activation mechanisms as a key next step for understanding NSAID-induced hypersensitivity and AERD pathophysiology.
Baseline serum tryptase was significantly higher in pre-school children (0-6 yr) than in school-age children (6-16 yr) among uncomplicated anaesthesia controls.
Intraoperative serum tryptase measured 60-90 min after induction of uncomplicated anaesthesia was significantly lower than baseline serum tryptase in control children, across all age groups.
In control children with available infusion rate data, higher intravenous fluid infusion rates correlated with a greater decrease in intraoperative tryptase concentration.
Median baseline serum tryptase in children was significantly higher than in a previously published cohort of adult controls.

In the previously published cohort of 75 adult controls undergoing uncomplicated general anaesthesia, intraoperative tryptase was lower than but did not significantly differ from baseline tryptase, contrasting with the significant decrease seen in the paediatric cohort.
Baseline serum tryptase was significantly higher in paediatric perioperative hypersensitivity patients than in uncomplicated anaesthesia control children.
In paediatric POH patients, acute serum tryptase was significantly higher than baseline serum tryptase, consistent with mast cell degranulation during hypersensitivity reactions.
The current 2012 consensus formula (aST > 1.2×bST + 2) for mast cell activation had poor sensitivity (31.91%) but high specificity (99%) when applied to the paediatric POH cohort.
Adjusting the consensus formula to account for the median intraoperative tryptase decrease (aST > 1.2×bST + 1.59) increased sensitivity to 35.1% in paediatric POH without reducing specificity.

A newly derived paediatric formula (aST>bST+0.71) had significantly higher sensitivity than the current consensus formula for detecting mast cell activation in paediatric POH, with a modest reduction in specificity.

Both the consensus formula and the new formula showed markedly higher sensitivity in POH patients where a culprit drug was identified compared with those without an identified culprit, suggesting an IgE-mediated mechanism improves tryptase-based detection.
Both the consensus formula and new formula showed higher sensitivity in grade 3-4 (severe anaphylaxis) reactions compared with grade 1-2 reactions in paediatric POH.
ROC analysis identified an optimal ΔT% cut-off of 15.9% (Youden index) to distinguish paediatric POH patients from controls, with cross-validated sensitivity 56.6% and specificity 86.4%.

ROC analysis identified an optimal absolute ΔT cut-off of 0.71 μg/L (Youden index) to distinguish paediatric POH patients from controls, with cross-validated sensitivity 53.3% and specificity 93.3%, forming the basis of the proposed new paediatric formula.

Roughly one-third of paediatric POH patients showed a decrease rather than an increase in serum tryptase during their reaction, likely reflecting fluid resuscitation given as anaphylaxis treatment lowering the acute sample value.

One control child undergoing uncomplicated anaesthesia met the current consensus formula criteria for mast cell activation despite showing no clinical signs or symptoms, representing a false-positive result.
Patients with ixekizumab treatment-associated urticaria (ITAUR) had a higher proportion of mast cells in resolved psoriasis skin compared with patients without urticaria (NUR).
The proportion of IL-17A-positive mast cells in resolved skin was inversely correlated with the duration of psoriasis remission after ixekizumab discontinuation.
Patients who developed urticaria during ixekizumab treatment (ITAUR) experienced earlier psoriasis relapse after treatment withdrawal than those without urticaria (NUR).
In psoriasis-like mouse models, activation versus inactivation of mast cells altered disease patterns, supporting a mechanistic role for mast cells in psoriasis relapse.

Clonal mast cells in mastocytosis most frequently carry the KIT D816V mutation, which is now targeted by tyrosine kinase inhibitors aimed at modifying disease course and controlling mast cell activation symptoms.
In a retrospective study of 388 mastocytosis patients, 11.3% reported an adverse NSAID reaction, the majority (89%) limited to the skin, with only 2.8% having confirmed NSAID-induced anaphylaxis.

A Spanish cohort of 681 cutaneous and systemic mastocytosis patients found that the large majority tolerated NSAIDs (87% of adults, 91% of children), suggesting the true prevalence of NSAID hypersensitivity is lower than previously assumed.

A double-blind, placebo-controlled aspirin challenge study (n=50) found 98% tolerance, and a related retrospective chart review (n=191) found 95.9% tolerance, confirming high overall tolerability of aspirin in mastocytosis patients.

Female sex, advanced age, prior drug-induced anaphylaxis, higher baseline tryptase, and multilineage KIT D816V involvement were identified as risk factors for a higher probability of NSAID hypersensitivity reactions in mastocytosis.
In a cohort of 239 mastocytosis patients, 14.2% had an allergic reaction to antibiotics, with 0.8% presenting anaphylaxis, and beta-lactams accounted for 63% of triggering agents.
In a cohort of 133 children with cutaneous mastocytosis, 4.5% (6/133) had a reaction to beta-lactam antibiotics.

One report found that 54.5% of patients reactive to quinolones had specific IgE to the drug, but subsequent studies failed to confirm this IgE mechanism and instead implicated non-IgE pathways such as MRGPRX2.
MRGPRX2, a G-protein coupled receptor on cutaneous mast cells that mediates non-IgE drug-induced activation, has increased expression in patients with urticaria and cutaneous mastocytosis.

A case report of a 46-year-old woman with systemic mastocytosis (no cutaneous involvement) who had two anaphylactic episodes to ciprofloxacin and three severe reactions to Hymenoptera venom, with negative skin testing to both, supports MRGPRX2-mediated non-IgE reactions as the underlying mechanism.

In a study of 72 adults and children with mastocytosis receiving 137 vaccines, vaccines were well tolerated, with no adverse events in adults (0/57) and adverse events in 7/80 pediatric vaccinations, and no anaphylaxis reported.
Of the adverse vaccine events reported in mastocytosis patients, 57% were related to the hexavalent (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, poliovirus, H. influenzae type b, hepatitis B) vaccine.

With antihistamine premedication, only 2 of 73 (2.3%) mastocytosis patients developed symptoms following Pfizer mRNA COVID-19 vaccination, a rate comparable to 2% in atopic patients without a mast cell disorder.

In the largest study of COVID-19 vaccination in mastocytosis (323 patients, 666 vaccinations), 6% of vaccinations resulted in adverse events (mostly cutaneous), and the anaphylaxis rate was higher than in the general population, prompting recommendations for premedication and extended observation.

An Italian study comparing vaccination safety between children with mastocytosis and their unaffected siblings found a higher vaccine reaction rate in the mastocytosis group (4 per 634 vaccines) than the general population rate (2.3 per 10,000 doses), though reactions were mild and transient.
An NIH retrospective chart review of 94 children with mastocytosis who received 2136 vaccines found that 4% had urticaria, anaphylaxis, or exacerbated skin lesions.

In a retrospective study of 501 mastocytosis patients, 2% of adults had a drug hypersensitivity reaction and 0.4% experienced anaphylaxis to perioperative anesthesia; in the pediatric counterpart, 4% had a hypersensitivity reaction and 2% had anaphylaxis.

Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (atracurium, rapacuronium, mivacurium) are associated with higher drug hypersensitivity reactions in mastocytosis, thought to be mediated via concentration-dependent MRGPRX2 activation, and are not recommended perioperatively.
Unlike non-depolarizing NMBAs, succinylcholine does not interact with MRGPRX2 and is considered safe for use in mastocytosis patients.

Natural opiates (morphine, codeine, meperidine/pethidine, buprenorphine) cause dose-dependent mast cell degranulation, whereas synthetic piperidine-derived opiates (fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil) show low mast cell activation and little tryptase/histamine release, making them safer for mastocytosis patients.
In a study of 120 anaphylaxis patients, radiocontrast media was identified as the trigger in only 2 cases, suggesting RCM is a relatively infrequent anaphylaxis trigger.
In a study of 220 patients with radiocontrast media hypersensitivity, no patients were found to have an underlying clonal mast cell disorder.

Anaphylaxis to Hymenoptera venom occurs in 20-30% of mastocytosis patients compared to only 0.3-8.9% in the general population, making it the most common cause of anaphylaxis in clonal mast cell disorders.

A subset of male patients with isolated bone marrow mastocytosis (no cutaneous lesions, low baseline tryptase) are often at the highest risk for severe Hymenoptera venom anaphylaxis, frequently presenting with cardiovascular collapse without urticaria.

A retrospective study of 501 mastocytosis patients found that 2% of adults had a drug hypersensitivity reaction to general anesthesia (0.4% anaphylaxis), while 4% of pediatric patients developed a hypersensitivity reaction (2% anaphylaxis).
A smaller pediatric study (n=22) found approximately 9% of children with mastocytosis had a drug hypersensitivity reaction to general anesthesia.

Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents such as atracurium, rapacuronium, and mivacurium are associated with higher drug hypersensitivity reactions in mastocytosis patients, likely mediated via concentration-dependent MRGPRX2 activation, and are not recommended perioperatively.
Unlike non-depolarizing NMBAs, succinylcholine does not interact with MRGPRX2 and is considered safe for use in patients with mastocytosis.
Sugammadex can safely be used to reverse neuromuscular blockade in patients with systemic mastocytosis.

Natural opiates including morphine, codeine, meperidine/pethidine, and buprenorphine can cause dose-dependent mast cell degranulation, while synthetic opiates generally do not elicit similar histamine and tryptase release.

Piperidine-derived opiates (fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil, naloxone) show a low degree of mast cell activation with little release of tryptase and histamine, making them safer options for mastocytosis patients.

Other synthetic opiates including oxycodone, hydromorphone, and tramadol show a similarly low histamine response in vivo, though no studies have specifically compared natural versus synthetic opiate reaction rates in mastocytosis.

In a REMA network retrospective study, of 45 pregnant patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis, 35 received epidural or local anesthesia and only 5 displayed symptoms of mast cell mediator release, limited to pruritus, erythema, and flushing.
A retrospective study comparing local anesthetic allergy in ISM patients found that only 5 of 252 patients had a history of local anesthetic allergy, to either lidocaine or mepivacaine.
Brockow et al. reported that radiocontrast media was a trigger in 2 of 120 reported anaphylaxis reactions in patients with mast cell disorders.
In a study of 220 patients with radiocontrast media hypersensitivity, none were found to have an underlying clonal mast cell disorder.

Anaphylaxis following Hymenoptera sting occurs in 20-30% of mastocytosis patients compared to 0.3-8.9% of the general population, making it the most common cause of anaphylaxis in patients with clonal mast cell disorders.

A subset of male patients with isolated bone marrow mastocytosis, characterized by absence of cutaneous lesions and low baseline tryptase, are often at the highest risk for severe Hymenoptera venom anaphylaxis.
More than 20% of mastocytosis patients report side effects from venom immunotherapy (VIT), particularly during the build-up phase.
Omalizumab premedication has been shown to reduce the severity of adverse reactions to venom immunotherapy in mastocytosis patients.

A 6-hour ultrarush venom desensitization protocol using 12 incremental injections with omalizumab premedication was developed for high-risk mastocytosis patients such as beekeepers and golfers, achieving maintenance doses within approximately 6 hours.
Two case reports described fatal Hymenoptera stings in mastocytosis patients who had previously been on venom immunotherapy but discontinued it, underscoring the lifesaving nature of continued VIT.

Matito et al. reported that among 45 pregnancies in 30 women with mastocytosis, 37 involved epidural, local, or general anesthesia exposure, with mast cell activation symptoms occurring in 5/37 (13%) cases and no anaphylaxis, suggesting pregnancy does not increase mast cell activation risk.

Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, caused by extra copies of the alpha tryptase gene, has an estimated prevalence of 5-7% in the general population but is markedly higher (12-18%) among patients with systemic mastocytosis.
Individuals with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia are at higher risk for grade III/IV anaphylaxis, particularly involving cardiovascular compromise, as reported in several unselected cohorts.

The specific risk of drug allergy conferred by hereditary alpha-tryptasemia has not been determined, and TPSAB1 gene duplication testing in systemic mastocytosis patients with severe anaphylaxis may help address risk from venom, food, and drug exposures.

The authors note that higher expression of MRGPRX2 receptors on skin mast cells combined with TPSAB1 gene duplication (found more frequently in mastocytosis with high tryptase levels) may together contribute to the increased frequency of drug adverse reactions observed in clonal mast cell disorders.
Self-assembled PPSU nanoparticles enable controlled multicomponent adsorption of enzymes and antibodies while preserving their bioactivity.

Simulations show that hydrophobic patches on protein surfaces trigger a site-specific dipole relaxation of PPSU assemblies, allowing non-covalent anchoring of proteins without disrupting their hydrogen bonding or structure.

PPSU nanoparticles displaying an optimized ratio of co-adsorbed anti-Siglec-6 and anti-FcεRIα antibodies effectively inhibited mast cell activation and degranulation and prevented anaphylaxis in a humanized mouse model.
A nanotherapy employing multiple mast-cell-targeted antibodies for preventing anaphylaxis was demonstrated as a proof of concept in a humanized mouse model.
In the Greek district of Achaia, 52 Kounis syndrome cases over 4 years yielded an estimated annual incidence of 4.33 per 100,000 inhabitants.
In a prospective ED study of 138,911 admissions, KS incidence was 19.4 per 100,000 of all admissions and 3.4% of allergy-presenting patients.
Between 2010 and 2014, 51 KS cases were reported to the International Pharmacovigilance Agency, with nearly half occurring in 2014.

A Swiss Canton retrospective study found anaphylaxis with circulatory symptoms occurred in 246 episodes among 226 individuals over 3 years, at an incidence of 7.9-9.6 per 100,000/year, with a case-fatality rate of 0.0001% (3 deaths).
Mast cell activation causes degranulation of vasoactive mediators (histamine, tryptase, chymase, cathepsin-D, heparin, proteoglycans, cytokines) released into circulation, causing vasoconstriction.
Histamine induces coronary vasoconstriction and platelet activation, leading to coronary thrombosis during allergic reactions.
Tryptase contributes to activation of the coagulation cascade, promoting both thrombosis and fibrinolysis.
Tryptase- and chymase-activated metalloproteinases drive collagen degradation, destabilizing pre-existing atherosclerotic plaques and promoting their erosion and rupture.

Kounis syndrome is classified into three types: Type I (vasospastic allergic angina/MINOCA in non-atherosclerotic coronaries), Type II (allergic acute MI in patients with pre-existing coronary atherosclerosis), and Type III (stent thrombosis [IIIa] or restenosis [IIIb] with eosinophils/mast cells on histology).
Symptom onset after allergen exposure occurs within an hour in 80% of KS cases, while 9.2% present later than 6 hours after exposure.
In KS, chest pain occurs in 60% and hypotension in 75% of patients, with dermatological (70%), respiratory (30%), and gastrointestinal (20%) manifestations also common.
A serum tryptase concentration above 11.4 ng/mL indicates anaphylaxis with 73% sensitivity and 98% specificity in clinical practice.
Troponin I levels are higher in patients with anaphylaxis, angioedema, or urticaria compared with healthy patients or those with milder allergic reactions.
The most common ECG finding in KS is ST-segment elevation in the anterior and inferior leads, related to vasospasm of the right coronary artery, the most frequently involved vessel.
Postmortem peripheral blood tryptase levels of 10 µg/L or greater have 86% sensitivity and 88% specificity for diagnosing anaphylactic death.
Two forensic studies proposed alternative femoral blood tryptase cutoffs of ≥53.8 µg/L and ≥45 µg/L for diagnosing anaphylactic death, differing from the original threshold.

Central blood (aortic) tryptase threshold for postmortem anaphylaxis diagnosis is suggested at 110 µg/L, higher than peripheral cutoffs, due to artifactual increases from resuscitation trauma such as chest compressions.
Serum tryptase is a stable enzyme detectable up to 6 days after death, making it a useful postmortem biomarker despite degradation over the postmortem interval.
Histamine remains in circulation for only about 8 minutes after an allergic event, requiring immediate blood sampling after chest pain onset for accurate measurement.
High numbers of mast cells are found in coronary artery walls in KS coronary spasm cases, particularly concentrated in the tunica adventitia.
The largest concentrations of mast cells are found in atherosclerotic and hemorrhagic plaques.
Del Duca et al. identified anti-chymase positive mast cells in perivascular spaces in postmortem cardiac tissue samples, supporting chymase as an additional mast cell marker for KS diagnosis.
Anti-CD117 immunohistochemistry, targeting the cKIT receptor tyrosine kinase required for mast cell maturation, can be used to detect activated tissue mast cells in myocardium and coronary arteries.
Increased carboxypeptidase A, a mast-cell-secreted enzyme, has been found in both postmortem serum and pericardial fluid of individuals who died from anaphylaxis.

Increased postmortem tryptase levels are not specific to anaphylaxis and have also been reported in non-anaphylactic deaths such as sudden infant death syndrome, heroin overdose, trauma, and asphyxia, limiting diagnostic specificity.

Postmortem serum IgE measurement provides only approximate diagnostic data due to its short half-life and the lack of an established cutoff distinguishing anaphylaxis from other allergic diseases like asthma.

Super-resolution array tomography (srAT) revealed intraepidermal nerve fibers (IENF) ensheathed within keratinocytes in the basal and upper epidermal layers of skin biopsies from all three healthy subjects examined.

3D reconstruction of a representative traced nerve fiber showed that while most of the fiber grew closely between keratinocytes, a substantial portion tunneled directly through one basal keratinocyte.

Cx43 plaques identified by srAT were mostly located at keratinocyte-keratinocyte junctions, but distinct plaques were also found in direct proximity to single IENF passing between keratinocytes in native human skin.

Expansion microscopy (ExM) in diagnostic paraformaldehyde-fixed skin punch biopsy sections confirmed that IENF, traced via PGP9.5 and actin labeling, were ensheathed by keratinocytes over several micrometers.
Immunolabeling against TRPV1 to discriminate IENF subtypes did not yield IENF-specific co-localization even after expansion microscopy.

The fiber ensheathment ratio (PGP9.5-positive pixels without WGA membrane co-localization) did not differ significantly between skin sections from SFN patients and healthy controls, though variance was higher in the SFN group.
The Cx43-IENF contact ratio (PGP9.5/Cx43-WGA double-positive pixels) did not differ significantly between SFN patients and healthy controls.

A fully human co-culture system of iPSC-derived sensory neurons and primary keratinocytes was established, in which neurites actively grew toward keratinocytes and formed contacts within a few days after barrier removal.
Lattice-SIM super-resolution microscopy of the fully human co-culture revealed neurite ensheathment by keratinocytes, recapitulating the native in vivo neuro-cutaneous unit phenotype in vitro.

In the co-culture, non-ensheathed neurites frequently passed in close proximity over keratinocytes, and Cx43 plaques were found at these passing sites, distributed across several individual keratinocytes.

Distinct additional contact morphologies between neurites and keratinocytes were observed in co-culture, including gutter-like structures, neurites merging into/enwrapped by the keratinocyte membrane, and bouton-like contacts.

Synaptophysin (SYP) was distributed throughout the cytoplasm of iPSC-derived sensory neurons, but only weak, sparse SYP labeling not associated with contact sites was seen in keratinocytes, with no specific SYP-positive clusters at keratinocyte-neurite contacts.

Calcium imaging of the human co-culture showed spontaneous Ca2+ activity in both keratinocytes and neurites (4/7 wells), with keratinocyte Ca2+ rises preceding neurite Ca2+ peaks in three wells with neurites contacting keratinocytes, suggesting functional coupling between the two cell types.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density in rat foot pads was not significantly altered by any of four gadolinium-based contrast agents compared with saline at 5 days or 5 weeks post-injection.
Skin gadolinium concentrations were substantially higher after the linear agent gadodiamide than after macrocyclic agents at both 5 days and 5 weeks post-injection.

Macrocyclic GBCAs (gadoteridol, gadobutrol, gadoterate) were efficiently cleared from rat skin between 5 days and 5 weeks, with reductions of 95-96%, and were confirmed to remain as intact chelate found in sweat glands.

The spatial distribution of gadolinium in rat skin did not visually overlap with the distribution of intraepidermal nerve fibers, arguing against a direct anatomical link between gadolinium deposition and nerve fiber damage.
Immunohistochemical staining showed overexpression of SLC39A7 in the skin of systemic sclerosis (SSc) patients compared to controls.
Both SLC39A7 mRNA and protein levels were significantly upregulated in dermal fibroblasts from SSc patients compared to healthy controls, as measured by qPCR and western blot.
shRNA-mediated knockdown of SLC39A7 in SSc dermal fibroblasts suppressed production of type 1 collagen, implicating SLC39A7 in fibrosis pathogenesis via the TGF-β/SMAD pathway.

Knocking down NCoR1 with siRNA reduced iNOS levels in LPS-stimulated BV2 microglial cells.

NCoR1 siRNA knockdown reduced phosphorylated-JNK levels in LPS-stimulated BV2 microglial cells.
