After radiofrequency application, women with fibromyalgia showed significantly lower electrical pain threshold values compared with healthy controls.
Electrical pain intensity was significantly higher in the FM group compared to healthy controls following radiofrequency application.
Within the FM group, electrical pain threshold significantly decreased from pre- to post-radiofrequency application.
Within the FM group, electrical pain intensity score significantly decreased from pre- to post-radiofrequency application.

Significant group differences in pressure pain thresholds between FM and healthy women were found at multiple musculoskeletal sites (occiput, trapezius, epicondyle, gluteus, knee, second metacarpal, and anterior tibial) after RF application.
In the control group, PPTs significantly decreased after RF at the occiput, epicondyle, knee, and second metacarpal sites.
In the FM group, PPTs significantly decreased at the supraspinatus and non-dominant anterior tibial sites but significantly increased at the dominant gluteus site after RF.
Core body temperature measures (tympanic and axillary) showed significant group differences between FM and control women following RF application.
In healthy controls, both core body (tympanic) temperature and axillary temperature significantly decreased after RF application, consistent with normal heat-induced vasoconstriction.
Peripheral temperature at the dorsal centre of the hands was significantly higher in the FM group than in healthy controls after RF application.
At palmar sites, peripheral temperature was significantly lower in healthy controls than in FM patients at the thumb fingertip, index fingertip, and thenar eminence following RF.
Peripheral temperature at the palm centre was significantly higher in the FM group compared to healthy controls after RF application.
In the FM group, temperature significantly increased pre- to post-RF at the dorsal centre, palm centre, and hypothenar eminence of the hands.
In the healthy control group, temperature significantly decreased pre- to post-RF at the dorsal index fingertip, palm thumb fingertip, palm centre, and thenar eminence.
Postn mRNA expression was significantly higher in mdx mouse diaphragm compared to wildtype at all measured ages, with the largest increase (over 50-fold) seen at 5 months.
Tgf-β1 mRNA was significantly higher in mdx diaphragm compared to wildtype at 3, 8 and 12 months of age, with expression elevated to a similar level across timepoints.
Ctgf mRNA showed a disease-progression pattern of upregulation, becoming significantly higher in mdx compared to wildtype diaphragm at 8 and 12 months, reaching almost a 5-fold increase.
Col1α1 mRNA was significantly higher in mdx diaphragm than in wildtype at all four ages studied (3, 5, 8 and 12 months).
Within the mdx mouse group, Col1α1 mRNA expression declined with age, being significantly lower at 12 months compared to 3 months, suggesting a disease-progression downregulation.
Within mdx mice, Ctgf mRNA expression increased with disease progression, being significantly higher at 8 and 12 months compared to 3 months.
Periostin protein was significantly higher in mdx diaphragm compared to wildtype at 3, 5 and 8 months of age, assessed by Western blot.
Tgf-β1 protein was consistently more highly expressed in mdx diaphragm compared to wildtype, reaching statistical significance at 8 and 12 months of age.
Immunofluorescence staining showed significantly increased periostin-positive area in 5-month-old mdx diaphragm compared to wildtype, exceeding a 30-fold increase.
Sirius red staining showed fibrotic area in 5-month-old mdx diaphragm was over four times higher than in wildtype, confirming increased collagen I/III deposition and fibrosis at this timepoint.

The authors propose that periostin upregulation precedes Tgf-β1 upregulation in the dystrophic diaphragm, suggesting periostin may act upstream of Tgf-β1 in the fibrotic cascade of dystrophic muscle, though the study design cannot confirm sequential order.
Gut transit was significantly slower after stroke, with barium sulfate traveling a shorter distance through the small intestine of poststroke mice than sham-operated mice.
Gastric BaSO4 levels 15 minutes after gavage were similar between sham and poststroke mice, indicating delayed gastric emptying does not drive poststroke gut dysmotility.
Poststroke mice showed significantly higher BaSO4 accumulation in the middle small-intestinal segment (segment 2), indicating delayed transit through this region.
There was significantly less BaSO4 and fewer fecal pellets in the colon of poststroke mice compared with sham-operated mice, indicating delayed passage from small to large intestine.

Proinflammatory gene expression (Il1b, Tnf, Ccl2, Ccl12, Cox2) in the ileal muscularis externa was significantly decreased after stroke compared with sham, arguing against a local inflammatory driver of dysmotility.
Anti-inflammatory gene expression (Arg1, Cd163, Il10, Chil3, Tgfb) in the ileal muscularis externa did not differ between sham and poststroke mice.
The number of CD45+CD11b+F4/80+CD11c−MHCII+ muscularis macrophages in the ileum was significantly increased 24 hours after stroke compared with sham.
Ileal monocyte numbers showed a non-significant trend toward elevation after stroke, with high interanimal variability.
A higher proportion of infiltrating CX3CR1-intermediate monocyte-derived macrophages was found in the ileal muscle layer after stroke.

The proportion of long-term tissue-resident CX3CR1-high macrophages was unchanged between sham and poststroke mice, indicating the increased macrophage pool derives from infiltration rather than self-renewal.

Stroke caused significantly fewer CX3CR1+ muscularis macrophages located near myenteric ganglia (ROI 1), while macrophage numbers in the perimeter (ROI 2) were unchanged, indicating redistribution away from ganglia.
Muscularis macrophages near myenteric ganglia showed hyperramified morphology (increased branches, junctions, end-point/junction voxels, triple points) after stroke.

RNA sequencing of ileal muscularis macrophages identified 14 differentially expressed genes after stroke, with the majority (10/14) downregulated ~2-fold or more, enriched for MHC class II antigen processing/presentation pathways.
MHC II protein expression on ileal muscularis macrophages was significantly reduced after stroke, suggesting a less activated macrophage phenotype.
Csf1 gene expression in the ileal muscle layer was slightly but significantly reduced after stroke.

Csf1r, Bmp2, and Bmp2r mRNA and BMP2 protein levels in the small intestinal muscle layer were unchanged after stroke, suggesting the CSF1-BMP2 neuroimmune axis is not a major driver of poststroke gut dysmotility.
Myenteric ganglion size and PGP9.5+ area were unchanged 24 hours after stroke, indicating gross neuronal architecture is preserved.
Myenteric tyrosine hydroxylase expression, a surrogate marker of catecholamine activity, was unaltered after stroke.
Myenteric ChAT expression was equivalent between sham and poststroke mice at 24 hours.
Myenteric neurons showed significantly decreased nNOS expression 24 hours after stroke, implicating impaired inhibitory (relaxation-promoting) neurotransmission.

Electrical field stimulation of ex vivo ileal tissue elicited larger-amplitude and longer-duration neurogenic contractions in poststroke tissue compared with sham, consistent with impaired inhibitory neuromuscular signaling.
The NOS inhibitor L-NAME significantly reduced spontaneous contraction frequency in poststroke ileal tissue more than in sham tissue, consistent with reduced NO bioavailability after stroke.
Chemical sympathectomy with 6-hydroxydopamine before stroke protected against the poststroke loss of myenteric nNOS expression.
Chemical sympathectomy with 6-OHDA before stroke preserved gut transit distance and prevented the abnormal BaSO4 accumulation pattern otherwise seen after stroke.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia is an autosomal dominant genetic predisposition causing high-normal or pathologically elevated basal serum tryptase concentrations.
The prevalence of HAT is reported as 5%-6% in the United Kingdom and France, whereas its prevalence in Germany is unknown.
HAT is very common among patients in medical centers with basal serum tryptase values of 8 µg/L or above, found in 64%-74% of such patients.
Exhaustion is reported in 85% of symptomatic HAT patients, making it the most common neuropsychiatric symptom described.
Depressive episodes occur in 59% of symptomatic HAT patients.
Sleep disturbances occur in 69% of symptomatic HAT patients.
Memory impairment occurs in 59%-68% of symptomatic HAT patients.
Nausea is reported in about 51% of symptomatic patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia according to the reviewed literature.
Reflux is reported in 49%-77% of symptomatic HAT patients across reviewed studies.
Flushing occurs in about 47% of symptomatic HAT patients as a typical mast cell-mediated symptom.
Itch is reported in about 69% and urticaria in about 37% of symptomatic HAT patients.
Anaphylaxis is reported in 14-28% of symptomatic HAT patients and is often triggered by insect toxins or unknown triggers.
Cardiovascular manifestations including hypotonia, dizziness, and tachycardia are reported in about 34% of symptomatic HAT patients.
Joint hypermobility is reported in about 28% of symptomatic HAT patients.
HAT is more common among patients with systemic mastocytosis (12-21%) than in the general population.
Therapeutic options for symptomatic HAT include antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, or anti-IgE antibodies.
Diagnosis of HAT can be strongly suspected through history-taking and basal serum tryptase measurement, then confirmed by molecular genetic testing.
Brief Smell Identification Test scores did not significantly differ from pre-SGB to post-SGB1 or post-SGB2 in the overall, unilateral, or bilateral cohorts.
Parosmia severity scores significantly improved from before SGB to after the first and second treatments in the overall cohort.
Parosmia severity did not significantly differ between the first and second SGB treatments, suggesting no additive improvement from a second procedure.
The number of parosmia triggers decreased significantly after SGB in the overall, unilateral, and bilateral cohorts.
Quality of life measures related to food enjoyment, meal preparation, and socialization improved after SGB across all cohorts.
At interview, self-reported comorbidities among the 41 long COVID patients included hypertension (44%), arthritis (39%), asthma (24%), diabetes (22%) and mood disorders (17%).
Prior literature cited in the paper reports that female sex, older age, and having more than five symptoms during acute infection are risk factors for developing long COVID-19.
Immune profiling cited from prior literature identified elevated humoral responses against SARS-CoV-2 as a feature of long COVID-19.
Immune profiling cited from prior literature reported decreased cortisol levels as a feature of long COVID-19.
The reported prevalence of long COVID-19 varies widely across sources and populations, ranging from 8% to 57%.
A cited study found an elevated risk of hospitalisation and death over 2 years of follow-up among patients who had been hospitalised during acute COVID-19.
Long COVID-19 is estimated to cost around US$2.6 trillion in the USA when accounting for reduced quality-adjusted life expectancy.

The authors note that persistence of long COVID-19 symptoms for 12 weeks or more has been reported to be higher in females than males, consistent with the predominantly female composition of their own sample.
A cited community-based study (>600,000 individuals) found that an Asian population had a lower risk of persistent COVID-19 symptoms compared with a White population.

Other cited studies reported that Black/Afro-Caribbean and other minority ethnic groups (Native American, Middle Eastern, Polynesian) had a higher risk of long COVID-19 compared with a White population.
Cited neurorehabilitation programmes for long COVID-19 patients improved working memory, verbal fluency, and anxious-depressive symptomatology.
Patients described neurocognitive symptoms (e.g., brain fog, memory problems) as particularly pertinent and reported some persisting for several months.
Fatigue was reported by patients as highly variable in severity and course, with some describing improvement and others persistent, fluctuating fatigue.
Loss of smell and taste was a commonly reported symptom, but severity varied widely, from total loss to altered senses.

Saturation analysis of the 41 total symptoms found that 93% were identified in the first 24 interviews, with only two new subdomains (fine motor skill challenges and stiffness) emerging in the remaining 9 interviews.
All 22 unique impact subdomains were identified within the first three groups of interviews, with no new impacts emerging in the final 16 interviews, indicating saturation was achieved for impacts.
Clinicians identified fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain/discomfort, cough, and loss of smell and taste as the most common symptoms of long COVID-19 in their patients.
Clinicians reported that cognitive impairment frequently accompanied both common and less common symptoms, alongside mental health issues such as depression, anxiety and feeling vulnerable.

A latent variable for pre-existing health conditions (cardiovascular disease, immunological disorders, hypertension) derived via item response theory was significantly associated with greater COVID-19 severity in the structural equation model.
COVID-19 severity was significantly associated with post-COVID neuropsychiatric symptoms (post-COVID-NPS), even after adjusting for age, sex, and pre-COVID neuropsychiatric conditions.
Female sex was more strongly associated with post-COVID neuropsychiatric symptoms than male sex in the structural equation model.
Pre-existing neuropsychiatric conditions including neuroticism, cognitive impairment, psychosis, and addiction were significantly associated with post-COVID neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Pre-existing cognitive impairment was significantly associated with increased severity of acute COVID-19 infection.

Factor analysis of post-COVID neuropsychiatric symptoms identified pain, fatigue syndrome, autonomic dysfunction, cardiovascular disorders, and neurological symptoms as the highest-loading symptom clusters, explaining 47% of variance.

Cardiovascular disease, immunological disorders, and high blood pressure showed the highest item loadings on the pre-health conditions latent factor, while pre-existing neurological disease loaded very low, likely due to small representation in the sample.
Age, treated as a confounder, was not directly associated with COVID-19 severity or post-COVID neuropsychiatric consequences in this study's model.
Hospitalized COVID-19 convalescent patients showed higher somatomorphic symptomatology and autonomic dysfunction compared with healthy (PCR-negative) hospitalized controls.

Healthy PCR-negative controls who were hospitalized and isolated also experienced some neuropsychiatric symptoms such as anxiety and depression, attributed to isolation and quarantine rather than SARS-CoV-2 infection itself.

Young women who had been long-term bedridden with ME/CFS in childhood or adolescence described their experience through four major storylines involving ambivalence toward others' presence, feeling on the edge of life, and an overwhelming sense of an endless, dark isolation.

Looking back from a state of full or partial recovery, participants recast painful memories of being bedridden and alone, suggesting that retrospective narrative framing shapes how the illness experience is understood and communicated.
Random forest machine learning models using the DSQ-SF accurately classified adults with Long COVID, ME/CFS, and healthy controls with high sensitivity and specificity.
The study identified specific DSQ-SF symptom items that best distinguish Long COVID from ME/CFS.
PoTS was a highly prevalent comorbidity, present in 21 of 23 (83%) tested patients in this EBV-triggered ME/CFS cohort.
Allergies were a common comorbidity, reported in 12 of 23 (48%) patients in the ME/CFS cohort.
Adults had significantly higher (worse) fatigue scores than adolescents on the Chalder Fatigue Scale at baseline.
Adults reported significantly lower health-related quality of life (PedsQL) than adolescents at baseline.
Elevated antinuclear antibodies were detected in 56% of the ME/CFS cohort, exceeding expectations for this age group.
ANA titers were significantly higher in adults than in adolescents, though not correlated with disease severity, functional status, sex, or connective tissue disease signs.
Elevated IgE levels were found in about a third of patients, though prior studies found no clear association with ME/CFS.
Low vitamin D levels were prevalent in the cohort but did not appear directly linked to fatigue severity based on other ME/CFS cohort data.
EBV DNA was detected in peripheral blood cells and throat washes of a subset of patients but was not correlated with disease severity or physical functioning.
Detection of anti-EBV-VCA IgM did not significantly correlate with disease severity or physical function scores.
No evidence of primary immunodeficiency was found based on total immunoglobulin levels and peripheral blood lymphocyte phenotypes.
Only adolescents achieved partial remission at 12 months, significantly associated with shorter illness duration, lower baseline fatigue, and higher baseline HRQoL.
Greater fatigue severity was strongly correlated with lower health-related quality of life across the whole cohort.
Fatigue and functional impairment (Bell Score) were significantly correlated in adolescents but not in adults.
Adolescents had significantly better (lower impairment) Bell Scores than adults at all three visits over 12 months.

Overall symptom number, severity, and frequency in the cohort did not significantly change between the first visit and 6/12-month follow-ups, though adolescents' school functioning subscale of PedsQL significantly improved.
Over 12 months, adults showed a moderate worsening in fatigue (CFQ) while adolescents showed a moderate improvement.
Adults reported symptoms occurring at least frequently significantly more often than adolescents, nearly double the frequency.
ME/CFS diagnostic criteria fulfillment fluctuated over time, with some patients losing and later regaining criteria positivity, reflecting a relapsing-remitting disease course.
Herpes simplex virus coinfection was not significantly more frequent in adults compared to adolescents.
The article argues that ME/CFS and Long COVID are biomedical, multisystem physiologic diseases rather than psychologically mediated conditions caused by deconditioning or fear avoidance.
The paper proposes that mental health practitioners can apply three decades of ME/CFS research and clinical experience to inform treatment and support frameworks for patients with Long COVID.
A large pediatric meta-analysis reported a PASC prevalence of 25% among children and adolescents.
An umbrella review found the prevalence of PCC in initially non-hospitalized children to be 2.0-3.5%.
Infection with a pre-omicron SARS-CoV-2 variant was associated with a two- to fourfold higher risk of developing PASC compared with later variants.
COVID-19 vaccination was shown to reduce the risk of developing PASC, with the magnitude depending on the triggering virus variant.
Higher age, female sex, and pre-existing health issues were suggested as risk factors for PASC in the pediatric population.

Among 110 pediatric patients with suspected PASC seen at a specialized outpatient clinic, only 29% received a final PASC diagnosis, 47% were diagnosed with alternative somatic/mental diseases, and 23% remained unclarified.
In a study of 1560 Dresden schoolchildren, rates of concentration problems, listlessness, fatigue, and mood swings (40-80%) were similar regardless of detectable anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody status.
The LongCOVIDKidsDK study found comparable rates of PCC-like symptoms in adolescents with (46%) and without (41%) a prior positive SARS-CoV-2 test.
In the CLoCk study, 24.5% of SARS-CoV-2 test-positive versus 17.8% of test-negative children and adolescents had PCC-like symptoms at 6 months.

The DePaul Symptom Questionnaire (DSQ) for post-exertional malaise correctly categorized adult ME/CFS patients 81.7% of the time, while misclassifying multiple sclerosis and post-polio syndrome patients as ME/CFS only 16.6% of the time.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy was shown to improve neurocognitive function in a phase II RCT for post-COVID-19 condition.
Combined SPECT/CT and cardiopulmonary exercise testing suggested pulmonary circulation dysfunction in a 13-year-old child with PASC.
Low-field-strength MRI showed persistent pulmonary dysfunction in both pediatric patients who had recovered from COVID-19 and those with PASC.
ME/CFS has been documented as a severe subtype of post-COVID-19 condition in adults and, recently, in pediatric PCC patients younger than 18 years.
Racine et al. reported an almost twofold increase in the global prevalence of depressive and anxiety symptoms among children and adolescents during the pandemic compared to before.
A German survey reported a 38% increase in general school absenteeism compared to pre-pandemic years.
School absenteeism in Belgian secondary education increased by 56% between the 2020/2021 and 2021/2022 school years.
Pre-pandemic, ME/CFS was identified as the most common cause of long-term school absence in children and adolescents.

Postural tachycardia syndrome (PoTS) in pediatric long COVID patients is diagnostically defined by a sustained heart rate ≥120 bpm and/or a sustained heart rate increase ≥40 bpm within 10 minutes of standing compared to supine, for individuals ≤19 years.
Depletion of pathogenic autoantibodies via plasma exchange, immunoadsorption, or infusion of the aptamer BC007 is being investigated as a treatment approach for PCC.
EBV is described as a prominent infectious trigger of post-acute infection syndromes, including ME/CFS, in adolescents and children.

Several pathogenic mechanisms have been proposed for PASC and other post-acute infection syndromes, including viral persistence, virus-induced tissue damage, endothelial dysfunction, coagulopathy, autonomic dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and autoimmunity.

Global plasma metabolomic profiling showed that long COVID (LC) patients with ME/CFS had a distinct metabolome compared with healthy controls (HC) and recovered (R) individuals, with the recovered group falling intermediate between LC and HC.
Plasma sarcosine levels were significantly reduced in LC patients compared with both healthy controls and recovered individuals.
Plasma serine concentrations were significantly reduced in LC patients relative to HC and R groups.
Plasma arginine was significantly lower in LC patients versus healthy controls, consistent with prior reports in acute COVID-19.
Plasma kynurenine was significantly elevated in LC patients compared with healthy controls, consistent with enhanced tryptophan-kynurenine pathway activity reported in COVID-19.
Plasma serotonin levels were significantly increased in LC patients compared with healthy controls, potentially contributing to gastrointestinal symptoms.
Plasma xanthine was significantly elevated in LC patients versus healthy controls, linked to purinergic system dysregulation and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Plasma glutamine and ornithine levels were reduced in LC patients, suggesting disturbed amino acid and nitrogen metabolism similar to that reported in idiopathic CFS.

Recovered (R) individuals who had no clinical symptoms still showed metabolomic alterations across 15 pathways compared with healthy controls, including increased glutamate, 4-aminobutanoate, carnosine, thymine, porphobilinogen, homogentisate, and 4-guanidinobutanoate, and reduced glutamine, asparagine, putrescine, serotonin, kynurenine, and other metabolites.
Plasma IL-1α, IL-6, TNF-α, IP-10, CRP, and SAA were significantly elevated in LC patients compared with recovered and healthy control groups.
Plasma IL-13 and IL-1β concentrations showed no significant differences between LC, recovered, and healthy control groups.
Soluble Flt-1 (VEGFR1) was significantly elevated in LC patients compared with healthy controls, though not significantly different from the recovered group.
Soluble CD14, a monocyte activation marker, was significantly elevated in the plasma of LC patients compared with both healthy control and recovered groups, indicating residual immune activation.

Anti-calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) autoantibodies were detected at significant levels in LC patients, suggesting an autoimmune component potentially linked to prior hypocalcemia/hypoparathyroidism in COVID-19.
Soluble/shed CaSR was elevated in acute COVID-19 patients but not in LC patients, indicating a transient rather than persistent alteration.
Plasma ATP levels were substantially reduced in LC patients compared with both recovered and healthy control groups, suggesting impaired mitochondrial bioenergetics.
Plasma ATP levels were significantly reduced in acute hospitalized COVID-19 patients compared with healthy controls and recovered individuals.
Lower plasma sarcosine concentrations correlated inversely with worse cognitive failure and depression scores in LC patients.
Lower plasma serine levels were associated with higher anxiety and depression scores in LC patients.
Plasma serotonin, tryptophan, aspartate, and kynurenine levels showed no association with cognitive function, anxiety, chronic pain, or depression symptom scores in LC patients.

No significant alteration was found in taurine and hypotaurine metabolism in LC patients compared with the recovered group, contradicting a prior report of altered taurine pathway in long COVID at 6 months.
TCA cycle intermediate metabolites (fumarate, succinate, malate) showed no significant differences between study groups, despite reduced plasma ATP.
Patients with post-COVID-19 condition who received low-dose naltrexone had a significantly higher relative hazard of symptom improvement compared with those receiving physical therapy alone.
Amitriptyline use was associated with improvement in fatigue but not in pain among post-COVID-19 condition patients.
All 16 participants with complex chronic conditions who requested medical assistance in dying described long-lasting suffering unresponsive to a range of medical treatments.
Many participants stated that MAID approval provided or would provide validation of their illness and a sense of control, particularly if their condition became unbearable.
Participants sharply distinguished MAID from suicide, preferring MAID because it offered greater certainty and caused less emotional pain to others.

A heterozygous nonsense mutation c.430C>T (p.Q105*) in COL3A1 was identified in a patient with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and PBMCs from this patient were reprogrammed into an induced pluripotent stem cell line.
The generated vEDS patient-derived iPSC line shows high expression of pluripotency markers, trilineage differentiation capacity, and a normal karyotype.
Across the 12 included studies, the prevalence of temporomandibular disorders (TMD) in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome patients ranged from 26.6% to 100%.

Bech et al. found higher prevalence of myalgia, myofascial pain, arthralgia, TMD-attributed headache, disc displacement, and degenerative joint disease in genetically confirmed hEDS patients compared to controls.
Patients with vascular EDS (vEDS) showed a markedly higher prevalence of TMD compared to controls (82% vs 24%).

Castori et al. reported a 57.1% prevalence of TMD among hEDS patients diagnosed via Villefranche and Brighton criteria, with disc disorders (disc displacement with/without reduction and joint hypermobility) being most common.

Generalized joint hypermobility, present in 2-57% of the population with female predilection, is a known risk factor for diffuse musculoskeletal pain, which likely underlies TMD susceptibility in EDS.
Arthralgia related to TMD was reported in 4 of the 12 included studies, with prevalence ranging from 23.1% to 59% among EDS patients assessed via RDC/TMD and DC/TMD criteria.
Myofascial/muscular TMD disorders were reported in 5 of the included studies, with prevalence between 12% and 49% among EDS patients.
In one Hagberg et al. study, roughly half of 44 individuals with EDS presented masticatory muscle pain.
A second Hagberg et al. study similarly found that 49% of EDS patients manifested masticatory muscle pain.
De Coster et al. reported 100% pain symptomatology in EDS cases, with 38% having myofascial pain and 21%/51% having unilateral/bilateral arthralgia.
Di Giacomo et al. found similarly high rates, with 93% of patients showing myofascial pain and 70% showing arthralgia.
Imaging (2D radiography) showed premature remodeling of the temporomandibular joint surface in 43% of vEDS patients versus 4.3% of controls.
Bech et al. reported that hEDS patients had a greater proportion of subcortical sclerosis on cone-beam imaging compared to controls.

In a case series using MRI, Wilkes classification staging showed the highest prevalence of stage III disc displacement (anterior displacement with significant anatomical deformation) among EDS patients.

Because the TMJ's fibrocartilaginous structures, supporting ligaments, disc, and retrodiscal tissue are composed of collagen, altered collagen synthesis in EDS subtypes may lead to TMJ joint pathology.
hEDS patients are frequently misdiagnosed with fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, or depression due to the diversity of signs/symptoms and psychosocial impact.
Genetic testing identified a pathological mutation in the COL3A1 gene, confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
A sneeze precipitated sudden severe pain and active bleeding from the proximal right subclavian artery in a pediatric vEDS patient, forming a mediastinal hematoma.
Joint hypermobility of the wrist and fingers and a tendency for easy bruising were observed as clinical signs suggestive of connective tissue disease in this vEDS patient.
The mortality rate for vascular complications in vEDS ranges from 20% to 40%, with a mortality rate as high as 68% specifically for aortic lesions.

Celiprolol, a partial β2-agonist and β1-blocker, has been shown to enhance collagen production, maintain collagen fiber continuity in arterial walls, and decrease mechanical stress from pulsation, thereby preventing vascular complications in vEDS.

In vEDS, a 'remote vascular catastrophe' can occur, involving a fatal vascular event at a site distant from the original lesion following endovascular treatment or surgery, which was deemed the cause of this patient's fatal aortic rupture.
Approximately 25% of vEDS patients develop serious complications such as ruptured arteries by age 20, and over 80% experience such complications by age 40, with a median age of death of 48 years.
Compared to other types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, skin and joint symptoms are mild in vEDS, making clinical diagnosis in childhood more difficult.
Patients with FMS had a significantly younger age at symptom onset than patients with SFN.
Time until diagnosis was roughly three times longer for patients with FMS than for patients with SFN.
Among SFN patients, etiology was potentially genetic in 20.8%, metabolic in 32.1%, autoimmune in 11.3%, and idiopathic in 35.9%.
Burning and stabbing pain descriptors were significantly more frequent in SFN than in FMS.
Pain localization differed by diagnosis, with widespread pain predominant in FMS and acral (distal) pain predominant in SFN.
FMS patients reported a higher number of pain-aggravating factors than SFN patients.
NPSI pressure and evoked pain scores and GCPS pain intensity were the questionnaire measures that best discriminated FMS from SFN, being higher in FMS.
FMS patients spontaneously reported a greater number of additional symptoms than SFN patients.
Tingling, numbness, and touch hypersensitivity were significantly more frequent in SFN than in FMS.
Fatigue, apathy, cognitive impairment, attention problems, and depressed mood were all significantly more frequent in FMS than in SFN.
Patients with FMS more frequently reported gastrointestinal, urogenital, and sleep symptoms than patients with SFN.
Mental disorders and chronic pain were more prevalent in the family history of FMS patients compared with SFN patients.
Patients with SFN had a higher prevalence of neurological disease in family history compared with FMS patients.
FMS patients had lower HbA1c levels than SFN patients, and diabetes-range HbA1c was found only in the SFN cohort.
SFN patients showed higher post-load glucose levels on oGTT than FMS patients, indicating a higher prevalence of impaired glucose metabolism in SFN.
FMS patients underwent more pharmacological, procedural, and nonpharmacological treatment attempts than SFN patients, including more frequent psychotherapy use.
Reduction of proximal intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) was twice as frequent in FMS as in SFN, while distal IENFD did not differ between groups.
Reduced distal IENFD compared to laboratory normative values was not significantly different in frequency between FMS and SFN.

Small fiber impairment on quantitative sensory testing (QST) versus normative values was significantly more frequent in SFN than FMS, with intergroup differences in cold/mechanical/pressure thresholds.
Corneal nerve fiber density (NFD) and length (NFL) on corneal confocal microscopy did not differ between FMS and SFN or versus normative values.
Corneal nerve branch density (NBD) was pathologically reduced more often in SFN than FMS patients.
Prolonged N1 and P1 latencies of pain-related evoked potentials (PREP), reflecting A-delta axonopathy, were markedly more frequent in SFN than FMS.
Pain-related evoked potential peak-to-peak amplitude (PPA) was pathologically reduced more often in FMS than SFN.
In the neurological examination, over half of SFN patients showed sensory abnormalities (thermal hypoesthesia or allodynia) indicating peripheral deafferentation.

In a subgroup analysis restricted to disease duration ≤5 years, pain intensity without analgesic treatment and the number of analgesics used were comparable between FMS and SFN, whereas distal skin innervation was higher in FMS than SFN.
Fibromyalgia affects approximately 2% to 8% of the general population, with a higher prevalence in women than men.
A study of FM patients found that following a plant-based diet improved cholesterol, peroxidase, and fibrinogen levels, body weight, and pain at rest compared with an omnivorous diet.
FM patients who consumed extra-virgin olive oil for three weeks had a strong improvement in FM symptoms, attributed to antioxidant phenolic compounds protecting against oxidative damage.
Increased consumption of ancient grains, including Khorasan wheat, resulted in significant improvement in FM symptoms.
FM patients following a low-FODMAP diet for one month experienced alleviation of FM symptoms.

Plasma nitric oxide and lipid peroxidation levels were significantly elevated and positively correlated with FM severity, while antioxidant enzymes (catalase, superoxide dismutase) were significantly lower and negatively correlated with severity.
Reduced levels of CoQ10 have been identified in FM patients, and CoQ10-deficient patients treated with supplementation showed a significant reduction in symptoms.
A double-blinded RCT in pregabalin-treated FM patients found CoQ10 supplementation successfully reduced pain, anxiety, oxidative stress, and inflammation while increasing antioxidant levels.
A clinical study examining alpha-lipoic acid treatment for FM found no statistically significant treatment outcomes.
A study found significant positive effects of ozone therapy on FM symptoms with no reported side effects.
Butyrate-producing bacteria such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, known for anti-nociceptive/anti-inflammatory effects and gut barrier support, are depleted in FM patients.
Levels of Bacteroides uniformis and Prevotella copri, commonly elevated in inflammatory arthritis, were found elevated in FM patients.

Coprococcus comes, an anti-inflammatory gut bacterial species, was found depleted in patients with chronic widespread pain, with a high-fat diet proposed to mediate this depletion and resultant low-grade inflammation.
Probiotics did not significantly improve depressive or anxiety symptoms in FM patients but were found to reduce impulsive decision-making.
A follow-up study found that multi-probiotic supplementation improved attention with reduced errors but did not influence memory in FM patients.
Magnesium citrate combined with amitriptyline supplementation alleviated the majority of symptoms associated with FM.
Many FM patients exhibit symptoms of magnesium deficiency, including reduced inspiratory muscle strength, with recent findings showing declined intracellular magnesium content.
A contradictory review concluded that magnesium supplementation makes little to no difference in pain or depressive symptoms in FM patients.
Iron supplementation showed promising benefits, alleviating many hematological symptoms of FM in one study.
A double-blinded RCT found that FM patients supplementing with creatine had improved muscle strength but no significant changes in other FM symptoms.
In a study of 20 FM patients with non-celiac gluten sensitivity, a gluten-free diet led to remission of FM pain criteria, return to work and normal life, and cessation of opioid use.

Multiple studies found that vitamin D deficiency contributes to FM symptoms, with some reporting a significant correlation between lower vitamin D levels and pain intensity, while other studies found no such correlation.

Vitamin D supplementation to levels greater than 30 ng/mL has been recommended as safe and cost-effective, with significant therapeutic benefit in reducing pain, though some studies found no symptom improvement despite supplementation.
Leptin levels may be increased in FM patients, and increased BMI is associated with higher leptin levels and increased pain sensitivity via IL-6 production and macrophage activation.
Weight loss in obese FM patients led to significant improvements in depression, sleep quality, tender-point count, and quality of life, and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and CRP.
CBT for FM resulted in lasting improvements in pain-related behaviors, self-confidence, and wellness/physical practices, with results most prominent in juvenile FM patients.
A Cochrane systematic review meta-analysis concluded that acupuncture is significant in reducing pain and improving quality of life in FM patients compared with sham acupuncture.

FM patients show abnormal alpha rhythms and decreased slow-wave sleep, suggesting wakefulness during non-REM sleep, which is postulated to be pathogenic and exacerbates fatigue, tenderness, and myalgia.
LLLT, an FDA-approved non-invasive treatment, improved pain severity, anxiety, depression, fatigue, stiffness, and tender-point count in FM patients, particularly those unable to exercise regularly.

Low-intensity physical exercise, such as combined endurance and coordination training, improved pain in FM patients by shifting from sympathetic to parasympathetic activity and regulating hippocampal metabolites.

Anti-inflammatory diets may alleviate fatigue in FM patients but do not always decrease inflammatory load, suggesting fatigue is part of a larger multi-factorial syndrome rather than solely driven by inflammation.
Approximately 4.7% of the world's population is affected by fibromyalgia, which presents with generalized pain, hypersensitivity, and a range of physical and psychological symptoms.
Fibromyalgia patients show quantitative imbalances in intestinal microbiota composition, described as dysbiosis, compared with the non-FM state.
Bacterial metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids, show differential relative abundance in fibromyalgia patients compared to non-FM controls.
Bacterial metabolites, particularly lipopolysaccharides, show differential relative abundance in fibromyalgia patients compared to non-FM controls.
The gut microbiota is proposed to indirectly influence host neurotransmitter mechanisms in fibromyalgia via the serotonin precursor pathway.
The gut microbiota is proposed to indirectly influence host neurotransmitter mechanisms in fibromyalgia via glutamate.
The gut microbiota is proposed to indirectly influence host neurotransmitter mechanisms in fibromyalgia via gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
ALE meta-analysis of fMRI studies found that the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) was less active in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy individuals.
The insula (Ins) showed abnormally reduced activation in fibromyalgia patients relative to healthy controls in the ALE meta-analysis.
Pain severity in fibromyalgia patients was negatively correlated with insula activation.
Migraine has an established relationship with irritable bowel syndrome as a comorbid visceral pain condition.
Migraine is comorbid with endometriosis, a visceral pain condition, though the underlying mechanisms are not well established.
Migraine is comorbid with dysmenorrhoea as a visceral pain condition.
Migraine is comorbid with temporomandibular dysfunction, a nonvisceral chronic pain condition.
Migraine is comorbid with fibromyalgia as a nonvisceral chronic pain condition, and this comorbidity worsens migraine-related disability.
Migraine is comorbid with lower back pain as a nonvisceral chronic pain condition.

The authors propose that progression and chronification of migraine is associated with peripheral and central sensitization, which may predispose patients to other chronic pain comorbidities, while mechanisms of each comorbid condition may in turn promote further migraine attacks in a bidirectional relationship.

Upregulation of EPAC1 expression is commonly linked to hypersensitivity of nociceptive neurons and hyperalgesia across multiple pain models including CFA, chronic constriction injury, and diabetic neuropathy.
Modulation of persistent postoperative pain in rats occurs via the EPAC1/PKC-betaII pathway in a postoperative tonic pain model.
Propofol co-regulates the spinal GluN2B-p38MAPK-EPAC1 pathway together with EPAC1 to alleviate postoperative pain in animal models compared to isoflurane.
Chronic pain caused by diabetes was significantly alleviated in rats by reducing EPAC1 expression and subsequently activating GRK2.
EPAC1 knockout mice were protected from paclitaxel-induced mechanical allodynia, and pretreatment with the EPAC inhibitor ESI-09 strongly inhibited mechanical allodynia in both male and female mice.
Paclitaxel caused sustained astrocyte activation and GFAP overexpression in spinal cord, which was normalized by ESI-09 but not observed in EPAC1-deficient mice.

The PDE3 inhibitor cilostazol increased intracellular cAMP and MBP expression while decreasing p75 expression, promoting Schwann cell differentiation and restraining paclitaxel-induced CIPN via cAMP/EPAC signaling, an effect blocked by ESI-09.

EPAC1-related PKC signaling activated by the PGE2 receptor enhances nociceptor hypersensitivity in DRG, and EPAC1 enhances capsaicin-induced CGRP secretion and TRPV1-mediated pain and ionic current in mouse and rat DRG neurons.
In a GDNF-induced mouse model of acute pain, inhibiting EPAC1 or increasing GRK2 protein prevented the transition from acute to chronic pain.
The NPY-Y1R axis inhibits PKA and EPAC1/2, maintaining pain relief and having an endogenous inhibitory effect on latent sensitization in a persistent pain mouse model.
The NMDAR-AC1-EPAC1/2 pathway drives inflammation-induced latent sensitization in spinal dorsal horn without gender difference, unlike the NMDAR-AC1-PKA pathway which is only active in males.
EPAC is involved in epinephrine-induced PKCε-mediated hyperalgesia through PLC/PLD-mediated translocation and activation of PKCε, specific to small-diameter IB4(+) injury-inducing neurons in rats.
Pretreatment with ESI-09 reduced chronic morphine-induced P2X3 receptor expression and PKCε phosphorylation, showing anti-nociceptive tolerance effects against morphine in rats.

In a chronic postoperative pain model established by plantar incision, p38MAPK-driven increase in neuronal EPAC1 expression is a key component of long-term nociceptive hypersensitivity, and both ESI-09 and the p38 MAPK inhibitor FR167653 shortened mechanical hypersensitivity duration.
GRK2 mediates phosphorylation of Ser-108 on EPAC1, regulating EPAC1 activity, and imbalance between EPAC1 and GRK2 is closely related to prolonged hyperalgesia in a mouse CFA model.

EPAC1 knockout mice showed significant relief from abnormal pain compared to wild-type mice in an L5 spinal nerve ligation model, and the EPAC agonist 8-pCPT enhances Piezo2-mediated mechanical transduction in low-threshold mechanosensitive neurons, promoting abnormal pain.

Blocking EPAC1 reversed chronic postsurgical pain induced by the SMIR model in rats by inhibiting overexpression of Cav-1, which is normally upregulated in the spinal cord after nerve injury and promotes mechanical hyperalgesia.

In a db/db mouse model of type 2 diabetes, intrathecal administration of TRPA1, AC1, and EPAC1/2 inhibitors reversed methylglyoxal-induced mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity, identifying the spinal TRPA1-AC1-EPAC cascade in diabetic neuropathic pain.

Macrophages and endothelial cells are functionally coupled through EPAC1-P120 in rat postoperative chronic pain models, potentially remodeling nociceptors and marking the transition from acute to chronic postsurgical pain.
Valproate reduced somatic hyperalgesia induced by orofacial inflammation combined with stress in a rat model of TMD/FMS comorbidity.
Valproate treatment down-regulated IL-6 expression in the L4-L5 spinal dorsal horn following orofacial inflammation combined with stress.
Intrathecal administration of recombinant rat IL-6, either as a single dose or over 5 consecutive days, blocked the anti-nociceptive effect of valproate.
Orofacial inflammation combined with stress increased the ratio of phosphorylated STAT1 to total STAT1 in the spinal cord.
Valproate down-regulated the p-STAT1/STAT1 ratio without affecting total STAT1 expression.
Neither STAT3 expression nor the p-STAT3/STAT3 ratio were affected by orofacial inflammation combined with stress or by valproate treatment.
Intrathecal administration of exogenous IL-6 up-regulated the p-STAT1/STAT1 ratio in the spinal cord, supporting IL-6-driven STAT1 activation as the mechanism of hyperalgesia.
The incidence of diagnosed hypertension did not differ significantly across healthy controls, positive controls (fibromyalgia/CFS/IBS), and UCPPS patients.
A composite measure of self-reported hypertension diagnosis and/or antihypertensive medication use was significantly higher in UCPPS patients than in positive and healthy controls.
ARB use was significantly greater among UCPPS patients compared to healthy and positive controls.
Rates of ACE-inhibitor use were similar between UCPPS and control groups.
Overall, a diagnosis of hypertension was not significantly associated with symptom severity across multiple validated UCPPS measures.
Among IC/BPS patients specifically, those diagnosed with hypertension had significantly worse ICSI, AUA-SI, and BPI pain severity scores than normotensive IC/BPS patients.
Age-matched UCPPS patients diagnosed with hypertension but not on antihypertensive medication (n=7) had significantly higher symptom severity across multiple measures than those on treatment.
No difference in UCPPS symptom severity was observed based on whether patients used ACE-i/ARB versus other classes of antihypertensive medication.
Among CP/CPPS patients specifically, there were no significant differences in pain-related outcomes based on hypertension diagnosis.

A cited prior study found CP/CPPS patients had lower corticosterone and aldosterone but higher progesterone than controls, and that within CP/CPPS patients, higher aldosterone levels correlated with worse NIH-CPSI pain and total scores.
The authors note that UCPPS symptomatology overlaps with and may be comorbid with other painful conditions including irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia syndrome, and inflammatory bowel disease.
An event-related increase in serum tryptase to at least 120% of the individual's own baseline plus 2 ng/mL is the qualifying diagnostic criterion for severe systemic mast cell activation and MCAS.

Hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HαT), caused by two or more extra copies of the TPSAB1 gene encoding alpha tryptase, leads to elevated basal serum tryptase levels, with each additional gene copy raising tryptase by 7–15 ng/mL and multiple copies raising levels up to 100 ng/mL.

HαT itself, and persistently elevated basal tryptase in HαT or systemic mastocytosis, cannot be used as a biomarker of anaphylaxis or MCAS, but instead reflects increased basal secretion or total mast cell burden.
The normal basal serum tryptase level in healthy Caucasian adults ranges from 0–15 ng/mL overall, or approximately 0–11.4 ng/mL when HαT carriers are excluded.

Basal serum tryptase is elevated in myeloid malignancies including myelodysplastic syndromes, myeloproliferative neoplasms, chronic myeloid leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, MDS/MPN overlap disorders, and mast cell neoplasms such as systemic mastocytosis, as well as in eosinophilic neoplasms with PDGFR fusion genes.

The highest basal tryptase levels (over 1000 ng/mL) occur in patients with smoldering or advanced systemic mastocytosis, including mast cell leukemia, and some AML patients, especially core binding factor AML.
Reduced renal function in chronic kidney disease can elevate basal serum tryptase levels.

Histamine, PGD2, and their urinary metabolites can serve as markers of mast cell activation, but are less specific than tryptase since they are also produced by other cell types (e.g., basophils, platelets) and are elevated in less severe, non-MC-specific reactive conditions.

During an anaphylactic reaction, serum tryptase rises substantially over the individual's baseline and then returns to baseline over several hours, providing a diagnostic testing window recommended up to 4 hours post-event, with baseline best re-measured 24–48 hours after symptom resolution.

The 120%+2 ng/mL tryptase formula has been clinically validated in patients with systemic mastocytosis, reliably distinguishing anaphylactic (MCAS) events from less severe mast cell activation regardless of SM variant, comorbidities, or basal tryptase level.
The 120%+2 ng/mL formula has also been validated as a robust criterion for confirming perioperative anaphylaxis and anaphylaxis in children presenting to the emergency department.

In patients with local mast cell activation or less severe mediator-induced symptoms, such as pollen or food allergies, tryptase levels often remain below the 120%+2 ng/mL threshold even when symptoms are clinically relevant.

MCAS diagnosis requires three criteria: recurrent episodic systemic symptoms involving two or more organ systems that are induced by mast cell mediators, an event-related tryptase increase of at least 120% of baseline plus 2 ng/mL, and a documented response to drugs targeting mast cell mediators or activation.
MCAS is subdivided into primary (clonal, KIT-mutated mast cell disease), secondary (underlying allergic/reactive disorder), and idiopathic (no identifiable trigger or clonal disease) variants.
PAMP protein expression was significantly increased in lesional skin of prurigo nodularis (PN) patients with severe itching compared with healthy control skin.
The number of MRGPRX2-expressing mast cells was significantly increased in lesional PN skin compared with healthy control skin.
Unlike PN, atopic dermatitis (AD) lesional skin with severe itching did not show a significant increase in PAMP expression or MRGPRX2+ mast cell numbers compared with healthy skin.
Mrgprb2 mRNA expression was significantly higher in mouse peritoneal mast cells (PMC) than in bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMC).
PAMP9-20 induced dose-dependent release of β-hexosaminidase and histamine from mouse peritoneal mast cells after 30 minutes of stimulation.

PAMP9-20 activated PMC to express the degranulation marker CD107a in a dose-dependent manner, with peak expression at 1 minute, sustained through 8-15 minutes, and decline by 30 minutes post-stimulation.
PAMP9-20 significantly increased mRNA expression of Ccl2, Ccl3, Ccl4, Tnf, and Csf2 in PMC after 30 minutes at 100 μM, while Mrgprb2 mRNA itself was unchanged.
PAMP9-20 significantly increased secretion of CCL2, TNF-α, and GM-CSF proteins into PMC supernatant after 24 hours of stimulation with 100 μM.
siRNA knockdown of Mrgprb2 significantly reduced the proportion of CD107a+ PMC, β-hexosaminidase, and histamine release induced by PAMP9-20 compared with control siRNA.
siRNA knockdown of Mrgprb2 significantly reduced PAMP9-20-induced mRNA expression of Ccl2, Ccl3, Ccl4, Tnf, and Csf2 and reduced secreted CCL2, TNF-α, and GM-CSF in mast cells.

Mrgprb2 knockdown did not alter IgE-FcεRI-mediated mast cell degranulation (CD107a, β-hexosaminidase, histamine) or cytokine release (CCL2, TNF-α, GM-CSF) induced by anti-DNP-IgE/DNP-HSA, indicating the MRGPRX2/Mrgprb2 pathway is independent of classic IgE signaling.
The authors' previous transcriptomic study found that ADM was significantly increased in prurigo-like lesions compared with eczematous lesions, consistent with the current protein-level findings.
Treatment of mast cells with recombinant S100A4 protein induced mast cell activation and release of inflammatory mediators.
S100A4 stimulation altered molecules involved in lipid metabolism and glycolysis in mast cells over time.
S100A4 stimulation resulted in cellular oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in mast cells.
S100A4-induced alterations in the RAGE/Src/JAK2/STAT3/PPAR-γ and NF-κB signaling pathways were partially reversed by the PPAR-γ agonist ROSI or the RAGE inhibitor FPS-ZM1.
Patients with allergic asthma who had elevated serum S100A4 levels showed a trend of metabolic alterations.
Serum S100A4 was positively correlated with serum IgE, suggesting an indirect association between S100A4 and asthma.
tmSCF nanodisc treatment significantly increased vessel grid intersection counts in the ischemic thigh at the study endpoint compared to alginate-only control.
When vascularity of the ischemic thigh was ratioed to the contralateral control limb at week 10, tmSCF nanodisc-treated rabbits showed significantly improved recovery compared to alginate control.
Vascularity of the ischemic thigh at week 10 ratioed to pre-surgery baseline was significantly increased in the tmSCF nanodisc group compared to control.
Tortuous (corkscrew-like) new vessel formation, indicative of angiogenesis, was significantly increased in the ischemic thigh of the tmSCF nanodisc group compared to control.
Vessel counts in the ischemic calf and foot were significantly higher in the tmSCF nanodisc group than in the alginate control group.
The ratio of vascular count in the ischemic calf/foot to the contralateral control limb at week 10 was significantly higher in the tmSCF nanodisc group.
The ratio of vessel counts at week 10 versus pre-surgery baseline further demonstrated the effectiveness of tmSCF nanodisc treatment in improving vascularity.
PECAM immunostaining showed significantly more small and large vessels in tmSCF nanodisc-treated ischemic muscle compared to control, indicating induction of both angiogenesis and arteriogenesis.
Histological (H&E) analysis of thigh and calf muscle showed no signs of inflammation, edema, or immune cell infiltration associated with mast cell activation in tmSCF nanodisc-treated tissue.
No difference in blood pressure or body temperature was observed between tmSCF nanodisc and control groups during injection, indicating absence of systemic mast cell activation/anaphylactic response.

The amino acid sequence of stem cell factor is highly conserved among mammals, with 86% similarity between human and rabbit SCF, supporting the translational relevance of rabbit mast cell responses to SCF for predicting human outcomes.
The double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge (DBPCFC) remains the gold standard test for diagnosing food allergy despite risks of severe reactions.
The filaggrin (FLG) gene and HLA are among the most repeatedly implicated genetic factors associated with food allergy.
Pollen-food allergy syndrome (PFAS) is accompanied by concomitant allergic rhinitis in 20-40% of patients.
Nearly one quarter (23.1%) of adult patients reporting an asthma attack within the past year also reported at least one food allergy symptom.

In a prospective study, patients with chronic (persistent) milk protein allergy had significantly higher IgE levels against peptides containing informative epitopes than those who had outgrown their milk allergy, supporting use of these epitopes as a biomarker of chronic allergy.

EDN, released from activated eosinophils, can be measured in stool, urine, serum, or plasma to help diagnose immediate food allergy reactions, distinguish FA from food intolerance, and monitor elimination diet effectiveness.
In Song et al.'s DBPCFC study of 67 pediatric patients, results of the basophil activation test (BAT) correlated with symptom severity, unlike other diagnostic methods tested.

In Wai et al.'s study of 35 subjects (15 shrimp-allergic, 20 tolerant), BAT with shrimp allergen extract was significantly more effective than skin prick test and specific IgE determinations at distinguishing allergic from tolerant subjects.

In the mast cell activation test, allergen stimulation of passively sensitized cultured mast cells produced a dose-dependent increase in CD63 and CD107a expression, and mast cell degranulation was confirmed via allergen-dependent PGD2 release.

In a mouse model, intranasal (vs oral) challenge with peanut protein extract produced significant increases in IL-4, IL-17, IFN, and CCL-11 levels, along with neutrophilia and higher MAC-1 levels not seen with oral challenge.

Among 142 subjects undergoing oral food challenge, 29 patients showed an upper respiratory (nasal) allergic response within 3 hours after challenge, and another 38 patients showed such a response within 6-24 hours.

In Clark et al.'s study of 24 egg-allergic children, oral provocation produced a 0.8°C increase in nasal area temperature (measured by thermography) beginning 20 minutes and persisting until 60 minutes after challenge, with high diagnostic accuracy, and antihistamines normalized the temperature and reduced complaints.

Nasal provocation test with food allergens showed positive results in 11.1% (2/18) of sensitized-non-allergic subjects versus 90% (18/20) of sensitized-allergic subjects, with only one symptomatic (local reaction) subject in the negative control group.

Case reports describe patients who continued to have local allergic reactions (LAR) from sublingual immunotherapy tablets (SLIT-T) despite pretreatment with another second-generation antihistamine, but whose reactions remitted or resolved faster when rupatadine was used instead.

Unpublished clinical case notifications indicate that off-label premedication with rupatadine reduced the number and intensity of adverse effects during oral immunotherapy for paediatric food allergy and facilitated reintroduction of small amounts of food.
Clinical trials across multiple European sites showed that a 4-week course of rupatadine significantly reduced ocular itching in addition to nasal symptoms in patients with rhinitis.

A pooled analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials found that 50% symptom responder rates in chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) were higher with rupatadine 10 mg and 20 mg than with placebo after 4 weeks of treatment.
The same pooled analysis found that a ≥75% reduction in weekly urticaria activity score occurred in more rupatadine-treated CSU patients than placebo-treated patients at both dose levels.

Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies showed that off-label doses of rupatadine 20 mg and 40 mg (2–4x approved dose) reduced cold-induced symptoms and lowered the critical temperature threshold in patients with cold urticaria.

A long-term, 1-year prospective clinical study found that continuous treatment with 20 mg rupatadine provided good control of disease symptoms in cold urticaria patients, in contrast with other sgAHs that only had short-term (2–4 week) outcome data.

A couple of recent studies reported that serum PAF levels may be a significant predictor of poor response to off-label, high-dose second-generation antihistamine treatment in chronic urticaria patients.

Intradermal injection of PAF has been shown to induce wheal and flare skin reactions that are independent of histamine release and mast cell degranulation, implicating a distinct PAF-mediated pathway in chronic urticaria.

PAF and its receptor mRNA are expressed throughout ocular tissues (cornea, iris, ciliary body, retinal ganglion cells, microglia, choroidal vessels) and PAF is released into the tear film upon conjunctival allergen provocation, contributing to eosinophil accumulation, vascular permeability, oedema and itching in allergic conjunctivitis.

In a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study with standardized skin challenge, 20 mg rupatadine produced clear improvement in Darier's sign and significantly reduced skin reaction severity, flushing, tachycardia, and headache in patients with mast cell activation disorders, though not gastrointestinal symptoms.
In vitro studies have demonstrated that rupatadine has a unique capacity, attributable to its dual H1/PAF receptor antagonism, to block the effects of mast cell mediator secretion.
A double-blind, placebo-controlled study showed that rupatadine 10 mg is effective in reducing itching and wheals associated with mosquito bite allergy.

A prospective clinical trial in Japan evaluated rupatadine at 10 mg and 20 mg for itchy skin diseases, and both doses are now authorized for this indication in Japan, unlike in most Western countries where sgAHs are used off-label for pruritus.
Clonal mast cell disease is defined by the presence of a somatic, activating mutation in the KIT gene in mast cells.
Analytical determination of tryptase levels is highlighted as one of the biological parameters suggestive of underlying mast cell clonality.
Bone marrow biopsy remains the gold standard for definitive diagnosis of mast cell clonality, while clinical predictive scores may help avoid unnecessary biopsies.
Umbilical skin shows greater cumulative drug penetration and faster penetration rates than non-umbilical skin, a phenomenon termed umbilical pro-permeability.

Umbilical pro-permeability is attributed to a thinner stratum corneum, altered stratum corneum lipid composition and keratin structure, and lower levels of intercellular tight junction proteins in the viable epidermis and dermis of umbilical skin.
Umbilical paste therapy enhances transdermal drug delivery and absorption by activating mast cells to stimulate local blood flow in the umbilical skin.
Skin temperature modulation and levels of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P did not significantly affect umbilical pro-permeability.
The special transdermal permeability of drugs through umbilical skin is influenced by drug molecular weight, logP value, hydrogen bond forming ability, and molecular volume.
GPR35 was found to be expressed in mature peritoneal mast cells but not in immature bone marrow-derived cultured mast cells or the rat mast cell line.
Disodium cromoglycate (DSCG) and other known and newly designed GPR35 agonists suppressed IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation.
Antigen-induced degranulation was significantly downmodulated in a mast cell line stably expressing GPR35 compared to cells lacking GPR35 expression.
The GPR35 agonist zaprinast induced a transient activation of RhoA along with a transient decrease in filamentous actin content.

GPR35 agonists suppressed passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) responses in wild-type mice, but this suppressive effect was abrogated in GPR35 knockout mice, demonstrating that GPR35 is required for the antiallergic effect.
The overall study concludes that GPR35 prevents IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and represents the primary molecular target of clinically used mast cell stabilizers such as DSCG.

Ileal mast cell numbers showed a non-significant tendency to increase (30%) at 12 hours of heat stress compared to thermoneutral controls.
Colon mast cell numbers did not differ significantly between environmental or therapeutic treatment groups overall.
A post hoc analysis suggested a non-significant tendency for reduced colon mast cell numbers (43%) in ketotifen-treated pigs after 12 hours of heat stress compared to heat-stressed controls.
Intestinal MPO-positive area (a neutrophil infiltration marker) did not differ across environmental or therapeutic treatments in jejunum, ileum, or colon.
Colon MPO area tended to be increased in heat-stressed control pigs compared to thermoneutral controls.
Circulating plasma histamine concentrations were unaffected by heat stress or ketotifen treatment.
Circulating cortisol doubled at 2 hours of heat stress relative to thermoneutral controls, then gradually returned to and fell below baseline levels by 12 hours.
Ketotifen treatment did not alter circulating cortisol levels compared to saline-treated controls.
Plasma CRF concentrations consistently decreased with increasing duration of heat stress exposure relative to thermoneutral controls.
Overall circulating white blood cell counts did not differ by treatment, but ketotifen-treated heat-stressed pigs had reduced leukocyte counts relative to thermoneutral controls across time points.
Circulating lymphocyte counts were reduced in ketotifen-treated heat-stressed pigs compared to both thermoneutral and heat-stress control pigs.
Circulating monocytes were reduced in heat-stressed pigs compared to thermoneutral controls, regardless of therapeutic treatment.
Circulating eosinophils were reduced in heat-stressed pigs relative to thermoneutral controls, though levels returned to thermoneutral levels by 12 hours.
Circulating basophils decreased over time in ketotifen-treated heat-stressed pigs relative to both thermoneutral and heat-stress control pigs.
Circulating IL-1β tended to be decreased in both saline- and ketotifen-treated heat-stressed pigs relative to thermoneutral controls.
Circulating IL-6 was significantly decreased in heat-stress control pigs and tended to be decreased in ketotifen-treated heat-stressed pigs compared to thermoneutral controls.
Ketotifen administration had no therapeutic effect on any of the circulating cytokines measured (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10).

Contrary to expectations, ketotifen did not alter circulating histamine levels or intestinal mast cell numbers, indicating limited therapeutic effect on mast cell activation markers during heat stress.
Plasma NEFA concentrations were increased two-fold in ketotifen-treated heat-stressed pigs relative to thermoneutral and heat-stress control pigs, with the effect most evident at 6 and 12 hours.

Blood ionized calcium decreased in heat-stressed pigs relative to thermoneutral controls, with the lowest levels observed at 6 hours of heat stress, consistent with hypocalcemia associated with immune activation.

A prior systematic review (Kitselaar et al.) reported that high neuroticism and low self-discipline predicted onset of functional somatic symptoms, irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome, stress predicted onset of irritable bowel syndrome and chronic back pain, and negative life events (especially childhood adversities) predicted onset of a range of functional somatic disorders.

The current study's findings partly diverge from the Dutch LifeLines cohort study, which found negative life events predicted irritable bowel syndrome and chronic fatigue syndrome but not fibromyalgia, and neuroticism predicted fibromyalgia but not chronic fatigue syndrome, whereas the present study found ALEs predicted chronic widespread pain and chronic fatigue, and neuroticism predicted chronic fatigue.
Other population-based studies cited in the discussion have shown childhood trauma to predict irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, chronic back pain and chronic fatigue syndrome.
Mutations in the FBN1 gene cause Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder with skeletal, ocular and cardiovascular manifestations.
Genetic knockout of FBN1 in mice (Fbn1-/-) causes death shortly after birth due to aortic aneurysm formation and rupture, indicating FBN1 is required for postnatal vascular maturation.
Reduction or loss of FBN1 due to gene mutations paradoxically activates TGF-β signaling, contributing to progression of fibrillinopathies such as Marfan syndrome.

Missense mutations are the most prevalent FBN1 mutation type, and approximately 73.1% of all missense mutations occur in the calcium-binding EGF-like (cbEGF) domain, most involving cysteine substitutions.

Mutations near the RGD integrin-binding site in the TB4 domain of FBN1 cause stiff skin syndrome, characterized by excessive microfibril deposition and skin fibrosis without the classic Marfan features.

Missense mutations located downstream of TB4 and in the heparin-binding TB5 domain of FBN1 cause Weill-Marchesani syndrome, geleophysic dysplasia, and acromelic dysplasias, which present with a phenotype opposite to Marfan syndrome (short stature, short limbs, stiff joints).

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, losartan lowered blood pressure in individuals with Marfan syndrome but did not reduce aortic dilatation, in contrast to findings in mouse models.
Compared to atenolol, losartan did not yield significant differences in aortic root and ascending aortic diameters over a 3-year follow-up in Marfan syndrome patients.

Genetic inhibition of TGF-β signaling in postnatal smooth muscle cells of Fbn1C1039G/+ mice aggravates rather than alleviates thoracic aortic aneurysm, suggesting TGF-β may have a protective role whose mechanism remains unclear.

AT1 receptor antagonism restores heart size and function in FBN1-deficient (Marfan syndrome) mouse hearts, which show dilated cardiomyopathy driven by aberrant AT1R/β1-integrin mechanosensor signaling.
Serum FBN1 level is elevated in chronic kidney disease and correlates inversely with eGFR and positively with serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and cystatin C.

FBN1 forms a fibrogenic niche in chronic kidney disease that triggers endothelial cell apoptosis via the integrin αvβ6/TGF-β1/Smad3 signaling pathway, and FBN1 depletion improves renal fibrotic lesions and vascular rarefaction in a mouse CKD model.
FBN1 mRNA is upregulated in adipose tissue of obese women, correlating with increased adipocyte size.

Rapamycin-mediated mTOR inhibition ameliorates the osteopenia phenotype in Fbn1+/- systemic sclerosis mice, implicating FBN1-regulated IL4Rα/mTOR signaling in osteogenic/adipogenic lineage selection of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells.

Deletion of FBN1 in mouse bone marrow causes significant hematopoietic abnormalities, with depletion of hematopoietic stem cells and increased erythropoiesis, reflecting differential regulation of TGF-β signaling in hematopoietic versus erythroid niches.
In vitro exposure of intestinal epithelial cells to gliadin triggers zonulin release, an effect exaggerated in amplitude and duration in celiac disease tissue compared with healthy controls.
Celiac disease is diagnosed 1.5-2 times more frequently in women than men.

Celiac disease frequently co-occurs with other autoimmune and neurological conditions including dermatitis herpetiformis, type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, selective IgA deficiency, alopecia areata, Addison's disease, Sjögren's syndrome, and neurological disorders such as cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy and epilepsy.
Several studies demonstrated a higher prevalence of celiac disease among women with unexplained infertility.
Adherence to a rigorous gluten-free diet appears to improve fertility rates in celiac women, although larger, higher-quality studies are needed.
Celiac women are at higher risk of osteoporosis due to nutrient malabsorption and indirect hormonal effects, but a gluten-free diet alone effectively improves bone mineral density.
10-19% of celiac disease patients present persistent symptoms despite following a gluten-free diet, mainly due to unintentional cross-contamination.
In a study by Carroccio et al., NCGWS patients had significantly lower bone mineral density than IBS controls at the lumbar spine and femoral neck, with CD patients showing the lowest BMD overall.

Mansueto et al. found a higher incidence of autoimmune disorders in NCGWS patients (25%) compared to IBS patients and healthy controls, positively associated with female sex, older age at diagnosis, duodenal lymphocytosis, and eosinophilic infiltration.
Over 70% of NCGWS patients in the Mansueto et al. cohort tested positive for serum antinuclear antibodies.
In a UK comparative study, 20% of patients with self-reported NCGWS fulfilled IBS Rome III diagnostic criteria, indicating frequent co-occurrence of the two conditions.
About half of NCGWS patients test positive for IgG antigliadin antibodies, which disappear quickly after starting a gluten-free diet.
Rodrigo et al. found a slight but significant improvement in fibromyalgia and IBS symptoms following a gluten-free diet in a subgroup of patients with duodenal intraepithelial lymphocytosis.
Slim et al. found no difference between a gluten-free diet and a hypocaloric diet in improving gastrointestinal symptoms in fibromyalgia patients, though both were well tolerated.

A meta-analysis of four studies found that a gluten-free diet in patients with chronic autoimmune thyroiditis decreased TgAb and TPOAb levels and produced a statistically significant improvement in TSH and free T4.
Krysiak et al. (2019) reported a significant reduction in anti-TPO and anti-TG antibodies after 6 months of gluten-free diet in CAT patients, with no effect on TSH or free thyroid hormones.
Pobłocki et al. found amelioration of TSH and ft4 only after logarithmic transformation following 12 months of gluten-free diet in CAT patients, and concluded a GFD cannot be recommended for CAT.

Krysiak et al. (2022) found no changes in TSH, ft3, or ft4 with gluten-free diet plus vitamin D in women with CAT and NCGWS; only the group on a gluten-containing diet plus vitamin D showed decreased anti-TPO and anti-TG, suggesting the GFD may blunt vitamin D's beneficial effect.

In a cross-sectional survey of 4078 women with endometriosis, 17% reported autoimmune disease and 1.2% reported celiac disease, while 66.4% changed dietary habits after diagnosis and 15% adopted a gluten-free diet.

In a retrospective study of 207 women with endometriosis following a gluten-free diet for 12 months, 75% reported a statistically significant reduction in painful symptoms and improvement across all quality-of-life domains.

Gluten-free products are often richer in saturated fat, sugar, and salt and lower in protein, fiber, and vitamins, and a gluten-free diet has been associated with increased risk of micronutrient deficiency, hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia, and coronary artery disease.
In a cross-sectional survey of 4078 women with endometriosis, 17% self-reported an autoimmune disease and 1.2% reported celiac disease.
Among endometriosis patients surveyed, two-thirds had changed their dietary habits after diagnosis, with a gluten-free diet being the most commonly chosen modification.

In a retrospective study of 207 women with endometriosis following a gluten-free diet for 12 months, three-quarters reported significant improvement in pelvic pain and all quality-of-life domains improved.

A gluten-free diet reduces gut bacterial richness and probiotic species such as Bifidobacteria while favoring opportunistic pathogens like Enterobacteriaceae and E. coli, especially in healthy subjects.
Women with endometriosis show increased rates of depression and anxiety related to chronic pain, correlating with worse health-related quality of life.

There was a small positive association between triglycerides and pure chronic widespread pain.

The long-read sequencing-based CACAH approach showed 100% concordance with the traditional MLPA plus Sanger sequencing method in detecting SNV/indel variants in exons and exon-intron boundaries of CAH-related genes.
CACAH can directly determine the cis-trans relationship of variants without needing to analyze parental genotypes, which reduces the time to diagnosis.
CACAH was able to distinguish different CYP21A1P/CYP21A2 and TNXA/TNXB chimeric alleles that are difficult to resolve with traditional MLPA/Sanger methods.
CACAH detected additional CYP21A2 variants (c.-121C>T, c.*13G>A, c.*52C>T, c.*440C>T, c.*443T>C) that were not identified by the traditional MLPA plus Sanger sequencing approach.
CACAH additionally detected the TNXB variants c.12463+2T>C and c.12204+5G>A, which were missed by the traditional method.
CACAH detected additional TNXB splice-region variants (c.12463+2T>C and c.12204+5G>A) that were not identified by the traditional MLPA plus Sanger sequencing method.
In two newborns, CACAH identified the TNXB variant c.11435_11524+30del occurring alone rather than as part of the TNXA/TNXB-CH-1 chimera, which the authors suggest might arise via gene conversion.

The authors conclude that the CACAH long-read sequencing approach offers substantial advantages over traditional MLPA plus Sanger sequencing for the genetic diagnosis and screening of neonatal congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

MCPIP1 protein levels were induced in LX-2 human hepatic stellate cells upon activation with TGF-β, in parallel with induction of activation markers TGFB1, COL1A1, ACTA2, CCN2, and α-SMA.
Silencing MCPIP1 (shRNA) in LX-2 cells enhanced TGF-β-induced HSC activation, increasing α-SMA, ACTA2, TGFB1, CCN2, and COL1A1 expression compared with control shRNA cells.

Overexpression of wild-type MCPIP1 reduced α-SMA, ACTA2, COL1A1, and TGFB1 in TGF-β-stimulated LX-2 cells, whereas the catalytically inactive D141N mutant had no effect, showing MCPIP1 RNase activity is required to inhibit HSC activation.

MCPIP1D141N-Fc protein-RNA immunoprecipitation showed enrichment of TGFB1 mRNA, and in silico folding identified three stem-loop structures with YRY motifs in TGFB1 mRNA, indicating TGFB1 transcript is a direct MCPIP1 RNase target.

Hepatocytes (but not cholangiocytes) from Mcpip1fl/flAlbCre mice co-cultured with wild-type HSCs induced HSC activation markers (Acta2, Col1a1, Ccn2), and hepatocyte Ccn2 (Ctgf) expression was increased in the Mcpip1-knockout hepatocytes, indicating paracrine activation via hepatocyte-derived Ctgf.

siRNA silencing of Ccn2 in Mcpip1fl/flAlbCre hepatocytes reduced HSC activation markers Acta2 and Col1a1 compared with control siRNA, and abolished the difference in HSC activation between Mcpip1fl/fl and Mcpip1fl/flAlbCre hepatocyte co-cultures, confirming Ctgf mediates paracrine HSC activation.
