After correcting for multiple comparisons, COVID-19 case status was not significantly associated with DBSI-RF (a putative marker of neuroinflammatory cellularity) in any of the 40 gray matter or 20 white matter regions examined.
At uncorrected significance thresholds, COVID-19 positive participants showed the strongest nominal increase in DBSI-RF in the right rostral anterior cingulate cortex.

COVID-19 positive participants showed nominally higher DBSI-RF in the right amygdala, caudate, caudal anterior cingulate cortex, lateral orbitofrontal cortex, and fusiform gyrus compared to controls, though these did not survive FDR correction.

COVID-19 positive participants showed nominally lower DBSI-RF in the left caudal middle frontal gyrus, superior parietal lobule, and postcentral gyrus compared to controls, indicating inconsistent directionality of effects across regions.

COVID-19 positive participants showed nominally higher DBSI-RF in the temporal portion of the left superior longitudinal fasciculus, a white matter tract implicated in language, attention, memory, and emotion.

COVID-19 positive status was significantly associated with increased DBSI-HF (a putative marker of vasogenic edema/neuroinflammation) in the left pre- and postcentral gyri and right caudal middle frontal gyrus after FDR correction for multiple testing.

COVID-19 positive participants showed additional nominally significant (uncorrected) increases in DBSI-HF across bilateral superior frontal gyrus, bilateral pars triangularis, and the right cingulum bundle among other regions.
Sensitivity analyses excluding the 13 hospitalized COVID-19 cases showed negligible change in results, indicating that the null DBSI-RF findings were not driven by symptom severity.

After restricting to COVID-19 cases tested within 60 or 90 days of the second scan, elevated DBSI-HF findings observed in the full sample were no longer significant after correction, though nominal associations persisted in some regions such as left pars triangularis and right cuneus/rostral ACC.

Whole-brain voxel-wise permutation testing with threshold-free cluster enhancement found no significant clusters of difference between COVID-19 positive and negative participants for either DBSI-RF or DBSI-HF.
PI-ME/CFS participants showed reduced 24-hour heart rate variability time-domain indices (SDNNi, rMSSD, pNN50) compared with healthy volunteers, indicating decreased parasympathetic tone.
PI-ME/CFS participants had decreased high-frequency and low-frequency HRV power along with altered nonlinear Poincaré-plot measures, further supporting autonomic imbalance.
PI-ME/CFS participants showed increased daytime heart rate and a diminished nighttime heart rate drop, suggesting increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic activity.
PI-ME/CFS participants had a decreased baroslope and longer blood pressure recovery time after the Valsalva maneuver, reflecting impaired baroreflex-cardiovagal function.
Head-up tilt table testing for up to 40 minutes showed no group differences in orthostatic hypotension, excessive orthostatic tachycardia, or tilt-related symptoms.
In an effort-based decision-making task (EEfRT), healthy volunteers chose the harder task more often than PI-ME/CFS participants, indicating reduced effort preference in ME/CFS.
PI-ME/CFS participants showed a decline in button-pressing speed over time during the EEfRT task, consistent with pacing behavior to limit exertion.

Grip strength time-to-failure at 50% maximal voluntary contraction was significantly shorter in PI-ME/CFS participants despite no difference in maximum grip strength, and correlated with effort preference only in PI-ME/CFS.

Repetitive grip testing revealed a rapid decline in force and fewer non-fatigued blocks with a decreased Dimitrov index slope in PI-ME/CFS, but these remained constant in HVs, suggesting the decline was not due to peripheral/neuromuscular fatigue.

Motor evoked potential amplitudes via TMS decreased over the grip task in HVs (consistent with post-exercise depression) but increased in PI-ME/CFS participants, indicating the motor cortex remained excitable and suggesting reduced motor engagement rather than peripheral fatigue.

fMRI during repetitive grip tasks showed that BOLD signal decreased across blocks bilaterally in the temporo-parietal junction, superior parietal lobule, and right temporal gyrus in PI-ME/CFS, in contrast to increased activation in HVs.

During CPET, PI-ME/CFS participants had lower peak VO2, peak power, peak heart rate, and peak respiratory rate compared to HVs, despite achieving similar peak respiratory exchange ratios, indicating a genuine reduction in cardiorespiratory fitness rather than reduced effort.

Chronotropic incompetence during CPET was significantly more frequent in PI-ME/CFS participants than HVs, with a lower heart rate response slope, indicating autonomic contribution to exercise intolerance.
Anaerobic threshold occurred at lower VO2 levels in PI-ME/CFS participants, correlating with muscle fiber type ratio, suggesting concomitant muscular deconditioning.
Salivary cortisol was significantly lower in PI-ME/CFS participants one hour after CPET, though resting cortisol at other time points did not differ.
At-home actigraphy showed PI-ME/CFS participants had lower step counts and total activity due to less moderate-intensity activity per day than HVs.

PI-ME/CFS participants reported significantly more subjective cognitive complaints than HVs across all five measured domains, but this was not accompanied by objective differences on 15 neuropsychological performance tests.
Cerebrospinal fluid levels of DOPA, DOPAC, and DHPG were significantly decreased in PI-ME/CFS participants compared to HVs, suggesting decreased central catecholamine biosynthesis.

CSF norepinephrine correlated with both grip time-to-failure and effort preference in PI-ME/CFS participants, and CSF dopamine correlated with time to failure, indicating catecholamine involvement in motor/behavioral performance specific to PI-ME/CFS.

Cerebrospinal fluid metabolomics revealed decreased glutamate, dopamine 3-O-sulfate, butyrate, polyamine, and TCA cycle pathway metabolites in PI-ME/CFS, with tryptophan metabolites among the top significant differentially expressed metabolites after correction for multiple comparisons.

Sex-stratified CSF metabolomics showed threonine and glutamine decreased in males and several tryptophan metabolites decreased in females, suggesting reduced serotonin signaling specifically in female PI-ME/CFS participants, independent of SSRI/SNRI use.
PI-ME/CFS participants had an increase in naïve B-cells and a decrease in switched memory B-cells in blood compared to HVs.
PD-1+ CD8 T-cells, a marker of T-cell exhaustion/activation, were elevated in the cerebrospinal fluid of PI-ME/CFS participants but not in blood, and PD-1+ CD4 T-cells did not differ.
CD226+ CD8 T-cells were decreased in blood of PI-ME/CFS participants, with no change in CD244 or TIGIT expression.

When stratified by sex, male PI-ME/CFS participants had increased CXCR5 expression on CD8 T-cells in CSF, while female PI-ME/CFS participants had increased naive CD8 T-cells in blood, indicating sex-specific immune cell alterations.

PBMC gene expression analysis found 614 differentially expressed genes distinguishing PI-ME/CFS from HV, with substantial sex-based clustering; only 34 of the sex-separated DE genes (<5%) overlapped between male and female cohorts, indicating largely distinct male and female pathophysiology.

Male PI-ME/CFS PBMC DE genes were enriched in ubiquitin, IL-10, T-cell, and NF-kB pathways with upregulation of STAT4-TLR9 interactome genes, while female PI-ME/CFS DE genes were enriched in B-cell proliferation processes with upregulation of B-cell interactome genes, cytokine and lymphocyte proliferation processes.

An independent publicly deposited monocyte RNASeq dataset (GSE130353) confirmed sex-specific gene expression differences in ME/CFS, with only 23 of the DE genes overlapping between 638 male and 420 female DE genes.

In male PI-ME/CFS muscle tissue, differentially expressed genes upregulated were enriched in epigenetic and RNA processing pathways, while downregulated genes were enriched in hexose metabolism and mitochondrial processes.

In female PI-ME/CFS muscle, upregulated genes were enriched in growth hormone receptor signaling and ubiquitin transferase function, while downregulated genes were involved in fatty acid oxidation and mitochondrial processes.

Analysis of a publicly deposited ME/CFS monocyte RNA-seq dataset (GSE130353) confirmed sex-specific differential gene expression, with only 23 of the combined 638 male and 420 female DE genes overlapping between sexes.

Univariate analysis found no statistically significant differences in plasma lipidomic profiles between PI-ME/CFS and healthy volunteers, though multivariate analysis identified several lipids as predictive variables, particularly when stratified by sex.
PI-ME/CFS participants had lower gut microbial alpha diversity (fewer observed taxa) than healthy volunteers, though overall relative abundance distribution (Inverse Simpson Index) did not differ.
Microbial community composition (beta diversity via Bray-Curtis dissimilarity) differed significantly between PI-ME/CFS and healthy volunteer groups.
While overall NK cell frequency did not differ between groups, a subset of PI-ME/CFS participants showed an elevated CD56 bright/dim NK cell ratio in cerebrospinal fluid.
Discovery autoantibody assays did not reveal a consistent pattern of autoimmunity in PI-ME/CFS, with only low-level detectable autoantibodies in one PI-ME/CFS participant and two healthy volunteers.

Resting salivary cortisol did not differ between groups, but PI-ME/CFS participants had significantly lower cortisol one hour after cardiopulmonary exercise testing, suggesting HPA-axis hyporesponsiveness.
Within four years of participation, four of the 17 PI-ME/CFS participants experienced spontaneous full recovery, with no other new medical diagnoses reported.

Female PI-ME/CFS participants showed elevated plasma lymphotoxin α1β2 and plasminogen, and elevated cerebrospinal fluid galectin-10, CCL22 (MDC), and IL-18 receptor accessory protein, proteins linked to NF-kB-mediated proinflammatory activation.
Differentially expressed genes related to the STAT4-TLR9 protein-protein interactome were upregulated in male PI-ME/CFS PBMCs, alongside enrichment in ubiquitin, IL-10, T-cell, and NF-kB pathways.

Univariate analysis of serum and cerebrospinal fluid aptamer (SOMAscan) proteomic data found no FDR-corrected statistically significant differential proteins between PI-ME/CFS and healthy volunteers, though exploratory sex-stratified multivariate analyses suggested candidate predictive aptamers.
Plasma GDF-15 levels, along with NK lytic units and CD16/CD56 ratio, did not differ between PI-ME/CFS and healthy volunteer groups.
Skin biopsy measurements of small nerve fiber density and blood/CSF neuronal injury markers did not differ between PI-ME/CFS and healthy volunteer groups.

Head-up tilt table testing for up to 40 minutes showed no group differences in frequency of orthostatic hypotension, excessive orthostatic tachycardia, or tilt-related symptoms requiring test cessation between PI-ME/CFS and healthy volunteers.
Whole-body composition by DXA and slow-to-fast muscle fiber atrophy (Type2:Type1 fiber Feret diameter ratio) in the vastus lateralis did not differ between PI-ME/CFS and healthy volunteer groups.
VO2 at the anaerobic threshold correlated with the Type2:1 muscle fiber diameter ratio in PI-ME/CFS participants but not in healthy volunteers, suggesting concomitant muscular deconditioning.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly reduced functional connectivity between the cerebellar vermis IX and the pontine nucleus compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients had reduced functional connectivity between cerebellar vermis VI and a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus compared to controls.
Reduced functional connectivity was found between the left cuneiform nucleus and bilateral occipital pole clusters in ME/CFS patients relative to controls.
Reduced functional connectivity was observed between the culmen and left cerebellum lobule VI in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
ME/CFS patients showed stronger functional connectivity between the default mode network's posterior cingulate cortex and the cuneus compared to controls.

ME/CFS patients exhibited stronger functional connectivity between the pontine nucleus and clusters in the left frontal pole and left superior frontal gyrus relative to controls, possibly reflecting hyper-stimulation compensating for diminished frontal function.
In ME/CFS patients, longer duration of illness was positively correlated with functional connectivity between the salience network's anterior cingulate cortex and the right insula.
In ME/CFS patients, functional connectivity between cerebellar vermis VIIIb and left insula was positively correlated with duration of illness.
In ME/CFS patients, functional connectivity between cerebellar vermis VIIIb and left supramarginal gyrus was negatively correlated with duration of illness.
In ME/CFS patients, functional connectivity between vermis X and vermis crus II was negatively correlated with self-reported impaired memory scores.
In ME/CFS patients, functional connectivity between vermis X and vermis VIIb was positively correlated with self-reported impaired memory scores.

In ME/CFS patients, respiratory rate was positively correlated with functional connectivity between the left medulla and the default mode network's right lateral parietal region, consistent with prior findings of increased medullary-DMN connectivity in long COVID.
All ME/CFS volunteers experienced post-exertional malaise (PEM) following CPET, whereas healthy volunteers experienced none or only minor symptoms.
Qualitative interviews (QIs) captured the multidimensional PEM experience and its change over time more effectively than visual analogue scales (VAS).
Physical fatigue VAS failed to detect PEM in 30% (3/10) of ME/CFS volunteers, showing a flat line across timepoints despite QI-confirmed PEM.
The 12-item composite VAS failed to align with QI-rated PEM severity for any of the 10 ME/CFS volunteers.
Correlations between QI-rated PEM and VAS scores at pre-CPET were strong for physical fatigue, mental fatigue, and composite VAS, but weak for muscle ache and headache.
At the time of maximum PEM, correlations between QI severity and all VAS measures (including most-bothersome symptom VAS) became uniformly weak.
Correlations between change in QI PEM severity and change in VAS scores from pre-CPET to peak PEM were weak across the four most bothersome symptoms and the composite VAS.
At the individual level across all timepoints, correlations between VAS and QI severity data were strong (r=0.70-0.96) for 7 of 10 ME/CFS volunteers but weak (r=0.09-0.35) for the remaining 3.
The most bothersome PEM symptom varied among ME/CFS volunteers: physical fatigue (40%), headache (30%), mental fatigue (20%), and muscle ache (10%).
VAS scores among ME/CFS volunteers showed wide variation and evidence of ceiling effects, with several scores sustaining high levels throughout the six timepoints.
Timing of peak PEM varied widely among ME/CFS volunteers, occurring at every measured timepoint after CPET (1, 4, 24, 48, or 72 hours).
At the first study visit, three-quarters of post-COVID-19 patients had moderate-to-high fatigue based on the Fatigue Severity Scale.
The proportion of patients with moderate-to-high fatigue declined from visit 1 (9-month) to visit 2 (~15-month follow-up).
Moderate-to-high fatigue (FSS≥4) was numerically more common in females than males at visit 1, though no formal statistical test of this sex difference was reported.
Post-exertional malaise, defined by the DSQ-2 2/2 threshold, was frequently reported in post-COVID-19 patients at both visits.
Among patients with FSS≥4, the great majority also endorsed fatigue on the DSQ-2, with concordance increasing at the second visit.
Unrefreshing sleep was among the most commonly reported symptoms in post-COVID-19 patients at both visits.
Problems staying asleep were commonly reported in post-COVID-19 patients, decreasing modestly from visit 1 to visit 2.
Shortness of breath prevalence in post-COVID-19 patients declined markedly between visit 1 and visit 2.
Joint pain was one of the most frequently reported symptoms and slightly increased in prevalence from visit 1 to visit 2.

A minority of post-COVID-19 patients met all four ME/CFS case definitions (Fukuda, CCC, ME-ICC, IOM) using DSQ-2 data, while about a third to a fifth met none, with proportions shifting between visits.

When post-COVID-19 patients' symptom profiles were mapped onto a pre-existing ME/CFS symptom-based clustering solution (45 clusters from 337 ME/CFS patients), post-COVID-19 patients fell into 11 of these clusters, indicating partial phenotypic overlap.
Among the two largest symptom-based clusters at visit 1, patients in cluster 19 had significantly higher mean fatigue severity than those in cluster 37.
Symptom-based cluster membership was largely unstable over time, with only about a quarter of patients remaining in the same cluster at both visits.

The largest symptom cluster identified in the reference ME/CFS cohort, characterized by sound sensitivity, sleep problems and post-exertional symptoms, was not represented among post-COVID-19 patients.
Nearly two-thirds of the cohort had at least one pre-existing comorbidity, most commonly cardiovascular disease, asthma, and diabetes.
CD8 T-cells from ME/CFS patients produced significantly less IFNγ than healthy controls after PMA/ionomycin stimulation.
CD8 T-cells from ME/CFS patients produced significantly less TNFα than healthy controls after stimulation.
CD8 T-cells from Long COVID patients produced significantly less IFNγ than healthy controls after stimulation.
CD8 T-cells from Long COVID patients produced significantly less TNFα than healthy controls after stimulation.

ME/CFS and Long COVID patients reported similar severity for fatigue, PEM, sleep problems, headaches, postural hypotension, difficulty concentrating and dysnomia, the core diagnostic features of ME/CFS.
Across all 8 treated patients, mean overall self-reported symptom severity decreased by 54% (4.4 points out of 10) after treatment with the nebulized antioxidant/anti-pathogen agent.
Post-exertional malaise severity scores decreased by a mean of 3.9 points (54%) after treatment with the nebulized agent.
Dysnomia and difficulty concentrating symptom scores decreased substantially (64% and 73.8% respectively) after treatment with the nebulized agent.
Frequency of CD8 T-cells producing IFNγ increased 3.6-fold after treatment with the nebulized agent across 7 evaluable treated patients.
Frequency of CD8 T-cells producing TNFα increased 2.5-fold after treatment with the nebulized agent across 7 evaluable treated patients.
In the detailed ME/CFS case (ME patient 1), CD8 T-cell IFNγ production increased approximately 5-fold from pre- to post-treatment over 15 months.
In the detailed ME/CFS case (ME patient 1), CD8 T-cell TNFα production increased from essentially zero pre-treatment to 10.3±2.3% post-treatment.
In the detailed Long COVID case (LC patient 1), CD8 T-cell IFNγ production increased from essentially none pre-treatment to 12.4±2.5% post-treatment.
In the detailed Long COVID case (LC patient 1), CD8 T-cell TNFα production increased from below detection pre-treatment to 15±6% post-treatment.
Interruption of the nebulized treatment in LC patient 1 was temporally associated with apparent reactivation of EBV, CMV, HHV6 and VZV.
During a treatment interruption, ME patient 1 developed chronic shingles (zoster sine herpete) and cold sores with elevated VZV, HSV1 and EBV antibody titers, consistent with viral reactivation.

Adjunct antiviral (valacyclovir) and spironolactone therapy combined with the nebulized agent was associated with continued improvement in ME patient 1, approaching pre-vaccine baseline symptom severity after 15 months.

In ME patient 1, symptoms severely relapsed (overall severity score of 10/10) following the first dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, representing her fourth severe ME/CFS episode in 47 years.

In LC patient 1, Long COVID symptoms were further aggravated by immune overactivation following the first dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, with extremely dysfunctional CD8 T-cells noted 12 days post-vaccine.
Across the retrospective case series, all 8 treated patients showed a positive symptomatic response with no serious adverse events or laboratory anomalies attributable to the nebulized agent.
Routine CBC, liver, kidney and thyroid function remained within normal limits throughout 15 months of continuous nebulized agent treatment in the two detailed cases.
Fatigue severity measured by multiple validated scales was significantly correlated across instruments, but did not differ by sex, post-COVID period, or age.
Plasma cortisol levels showed a significant negative correlation with fatigue severity scores in fatigue-dominant long-COVID subjects.
Plasma cortisol levels showed a significant positive correlation with quality-of-life scores in fatigue-dominant long-COVID subjects.
The negative correlation between cortisol levels and mKCFQ11 scores was more specific to mental fatigue than physical fatigue, contrasting with patterns seen in other fatigue measurements.
A meta-analysis found that people with CFS had a 1.7-fold higher likelihood of a previous HHV-6 infection compared with healthy controls.
Six systematic reviews reported moderate associations between previous gastrointestinal infection and subsequent development of IBS.
Lactose intolerance, but not lactose maldigestion, was identified as a risk factor for IBS in one high-quality systematic review.
Counts of lactobacillus, bifidobacterium, E. coli, and enterobacter significantly differed between IBS patients and healthy controls, indicating gastrointestinal dysbiosis.
A systematic review found lower vitamin E levels in individuals with CFS or FMS, with no other significant associations between vitamins/minerals and these conditions.
One meta-analysis found that a functional polymorphism in the serotonin transporter gene (SERT-P) was associated with increased risk of IBS.
In contrast to another meta-analysis, a separate review found no association between the SERT-P gene polymorphism and IBS.
Two meta-analyses found low to moderate associations between altered parasympathetic nervous system activity (high-frequency HRV) and both IBS and FMS.
A meta-analysis initially found altered parasympathetic activity/HRV in a mixed group of CFS, FMS, and IBS patients, but this difference disappeared after correction for publication bias.
A weak association was found between hypocortisolism (HPA axis dysfunction) and CFS/ME.
A systematic review found increased levels of various interleukins in FMS patients compared to healthy controls, indicating immune dysregulation.
Conditioned pain modulation was significantly decreased in IBS patients compared to healthy controls.
FMS patients showed a significantly lower nociceptive flexion reflex threshold, a possible biomarker of central sensitization.
FMS patients showed significantly worse postural balance scores across multiple measures compared to healthy controls, with large effect sizes.
A moderate association was found between a history of sexual abuse and a lifetime diagnosis of IBS.
The association between sexual abuse and FMS was only significant in a sensitivity analysis restricted to severe abuse, specifically rape.
Pain catastrophising moderately explained variance in pain intensity and disability in individuals with combined FMS and CFS/ME.
A study found unique family genetic risk score profiles for individual FSS (IBS, CFS, FMS) that differed substantially from those of major depression and rheumatoid arthritis.
A study found that both increased enterochromaffin cell counts and depression were equally important predictors of developing post-infectious IBS.

Numerous somatic symptoms constitute a risk factor for FMS; a subgroup of new-onset FMS patients with few somatic symptoms shows a distinct pattern of risk factors compared with those with many somatic symptoms.
Peak oxygen consumption during cardiopulmonary exercise testing was significantly lower in post-COVID syndrome patients than in healthy controls.
Body fat percentage differed significantly between healthy controls, CFS patients, and PCS patients.
BMI differed significantly between healthy controls, CFS patients, and PCS patients, with PCS patients showing lower BMI.
Muscle mass per kg body weight was lower in PCS patients compared to CFS patients.
High-resolution respirometry revealed lower Complex I activity in muscle of PCS patients compared to age-matched healthy controls.
No significant differences were found between groups in maximal coupled/uncoupled respiration or Complex II and Complex IV activity.
A multivariate analysis (MANOVA) of OXPHOS parameters showed no overall significant difference between healthy controls, CFS, and PCS patients.
Intermyofibrillar mitochondrial cristae score was significantly higher in PCS than in CFS patients.
Subsarcolemmal mitochondrial cristae score was significantly higher in PCS than in CFS patients.
Subsarcolemmal mitochondrial Feret's diameter was significantly larger in PCS than in CFS patients.
Subsarcolemmal mitochondrial perimeter was significantly larger in PCS than in CFS patients.
Total subsarcolemmal mitochondrial area and mitochondrial volume percentage (total and subsarcolemmal) were higher in PCS compared to CFS.
A one-way MANOVA of electron microscopy parameters showed a highly significant overall difference between CFS and PCS patients.
Aside from a positive correlation between subsarcolemmal cristae score and subsarcolemmal mitochondrial form, no other associations between mitochondrial and performance parameters were found.
A prior systematic review and meta-analysis (Lim et al.) found women are 1.5- to 2.0-fold more affected by ME/CFS than men.
A prior study (Kedor et al.) found that half of post-COVID-19 patients met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria six months after infection.
A prior study reported increased complement activation (C1q, C3, C4) in ME/CFS patients, potentially useful for clustering disease severity.

A prior study found fewer capillaries, thicker capillary basement membranes, increased CD169+ macrophages, and elevated complement-related serum proteins in PCS patients, suggesting immune-mediated microvascular changes.
A prior study indicated mitochondrial genes are down-regulated during SARS-CoV-2 infection, offered as a potential explanation for decreased Complex I activity in PCS.
Multiple prior studies found decreased ATP production in PBMCs and skeletal muscle of ME/CFS patients, indicating a metabolic defect and decreased electron transport chain activity.
A contradictory study reported increased, non-mitochondrial ATP production in ME/CFS patients in a similar cohort, conflicting with reports of decreased ATP production.
A prior hypothesis (Booth et al.) proposed a lack of essential substrates and partial blockage of mitochondrial translocator protein sites in ME/CFS patients, potentially reducing energy supply.
All four diagnostic groups (EDS/HSD, fibromyalgia, WAD, spinal) showed reduced pain intensity over time following interdisciplinary pain rehabilitation.
Patients with spinal pain showed a greater reduction in pain intensity over time compared with the EDS/HSD group.
The fibromyalgia group had a higher baseline pain rating than the EDS/HSD group before IPRP.
Pain interference on the MPI decreased over time across the diagnostic groups following IPRP.
At baseline, the spinal pain group reported lower pain interference than the EDS/HSD group.
Patients with spinal pain showed a greater improvement in pain interference than patients with EDS/HSD at endpoint, with a small effect size.
At baseline, the fibromyalgia group had lower mental health scores than the EDS/HSD group.
Vitality (SF-36 VT) scores improved over time across all diagnostic groups following IPRP.
The WAD group had significantly higher baseline vitality scores than the EDS/HSD group.
The spinal pain group had markedly higher baseline vitality scores than the EDS/HSD group, the largest baseline difference observed.
Physical functioning (SF-36 PF) improved over time across all diagnostic groups following IPRP.
The WAD and spinal pain groups both had significantly higher baseline physical functioning scores than the EDS/HSD group.

Patients with spinal pain showed a substantially larger improvement in physical functioning after IPRP than patients with EDS/HSD, a large effect size, though baseline differences complicate interpretation.
Self-rated health perception (EQ-VAS) improved at 1-year follow-up compared with baseline across all diagnostic groups.
The spinal pain group scored significantly higher on baseline self-rated health (EQ-VAS) than the EDS/HSD group.
In a sensitivity analysis, patients with missing follow-up data in the EDS/HSD group showed a different physical functioning trajectory over time compared with the other three diagnostic groups.
A sensitivity analysis found that missing follow-up data patterns differentially affected pain interference trajectories when comparing EDS/HSD with fibromyalgia patients.
Overall, pattern-mixture sensitivity analyses indicated that missing follow-up data did not substantially bias the main study findings.
The EDS/HSD group had a lower 1-year follow-up questionnaire response rate (40%) than the other diagnostic groups (51-55%).
In prior work using the same registry, young age and a long history of pain were identified as characteristic traits distinguishing the EDS/HSD group from other pain groups.
In prior work using the same registry, fibromyalgia patients reported the highest pain intensity levels among the diagnostic groups compared, including EDS/HSD.
In prior work using the same registry, both EDS/HSD and fibromyalgia patients reported lower vitality and physical health than patients with spinal- or neck-related pain.
On Day 2 after eccentric bicep exercise, VAS pain scores were significantly higher in the hypermobile group than the non-hypermobile group with a large effect size.
On Day 4 after eccentric exercise, VAS pain scores remained significantly higher in the hypermobile group compared to the non-hypermobile group with a large effect size.

Arm girth was significantly lower on average in the hypermobile group compared to the non-hypermobile group, though the authors attribute this to a sex imbalance between groups rather than hypermobility itself.
Aside from VAS, no significant differences in DOMS-related measures (McGill Pain Questionnaire, resting arm angle, pressure pain threshold) were found between hypermobile and non-hypermobile groups.

Both hypermobile and non-hypermobile groups showed significant changes over the 5-day period for VAS, McGill, RANG, and PPT, consistent with the expected typical DOMS response to unaccustomed eccentric exercise, independent of hypermobility status.

In a cited study, participants with JHS experienced centralized fatigue following electrically-induced biceps muscle fatigue, while non-hypermobile controls did not, suggesting an altered central fatigue mechanism in JHS.

In a cited study of JHS/EDS patients, no somatosensory nerve damage was found, but persistent nociceptive input from joint abnormalities was proposed to trigger central sensitization in dorsal horn neurons, explaining widespread pain.

A cited study comparing hypermobile EDS subjects to healthy controls confirmed that small fiber peripheral neuropathy and autonomic nervous system dysfunction are common features underlying joint pain and dysfunction in hypermobile EDS.

A cited study found women reported significantly greater DOMS and had significantly greater ACL elasticity after exercise compared to men, suggesting women may need more time for musculoskeletal recovery.
A cited study reported that people with JHS experience higher levels of pain, fatigue, and repeated injury, along with greater anxiety about injury and social acceptance.
A cited prevalence study reported JHS occurs in 12.5% of college-aged students overall, with higher prevalence in women (16.2%) than men (8.7%).
The review states that a true causal association between hEDS/HSD and mast cell activation disorders remains unclear.
Individuals with hEDS/HSD have a high prevalence of nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms.
Patients with hEDS/HSD may be at risk of macro-nutrient and micro-nutrient deficiencies.
Children with HSD/hEDS showed a significantly longer percent stance time during gait compared to typically developing children.
Lower pain interference in relationships with other people was significantly associated with faster gait speed in children with HSD/hEDS.
Greater pain interference during mobility was significantly correlated with greater stride length variability in children with HSD/hEDS.
Greater pain interference during going to school was significantly correlated with greater stride length variability in children with HSD/hEDS.
Greater pain interference during enjoyment of life was significantly associated with greater percent stance time variability in children with HSD/hEDS.
Greater pain catastrophizing was correlated with decreased step width variability in children with HSD/hEDS.
Thirteen adults with HSD or EDS were enrolled within a 4-month period and eight completed the 9-week integrative medicine program, indicating feasibility of recruitment and retention.
Only a minority of participants achieved adequate adherence to the prescribed Mediterranean diet and macronutrient tracking during the intervention.
Overall VAS pain scores did not significantly decrease at 5 or 9 weeks, though the majority of participants reported reduced pain by 9 weeks relative to baseline.
Satisfaction with care significantly improved in half of the measured domains after completion of the integrative medicine intervention.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (VEDS, type IV EDS) results from mutations in COL3A1, causing deficient synthesis and excretion of type III procollagen.
Approximately 17% to 37% of patients with vascular EDS experience iliac artery pathology during their lifetime.

A patient with VEDS and a left common iliac artery aneurysm developed a type II/Ib endoleak years after prior iliac stent placement, which was successfully treated with transgluteal embolization of the internal iliac artery followed by relining of the entire iliac system with an endograft, resulting in no residual endoleak at 1-month follow-up.

The authors note that use of stent grafts in patients with connective tissue disorders is typically not recommended due to mismatch between device radial force and vessel tensile strength, though earlier endovascular experiences in this population had high complication and mortality rates that have since improved with technology.

A heterozygous null COL3A1 variant (c.712C>T, p.Arg238Ter) was identified by NGS and confirmed by Sanger sequencing in a 27-year-old man diagnosed with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome after presenting with renal infarction and multiple arterial dissections.
Cascade genetic screening identified the same COL3A1 null variant in the patient's father, paternal uncle, brother, and sister, all of whom were asymptomatic at the time.

Null variants in COL3A1, comprising about 5% of vEDS-causing mutations, are associated with a milder phenotype including lower penetrance, better survival, and onset approximately 15 years later than other variant types.

COL3A1 null variants tend to produce a phenotype mainly limited to vascular complications, with a lower risk of gastrointestinal and obstetric complications, consistent with the presentation seen in this patient.

The milder phenotype of null COL3A1 variants is proposed to result from haploinsufficiency causing a quantitative ~50% reduction in type III collagen, in contrast to dominant-negative structural defects from other variant types that disrupt triple helix folding.

Imaging revealed a left renal infarct due to left main renal artery occlusion, contour irregularity and an intimal flap in the right main renal artery, dissection flaps in the left common and external iliac arteries, thrombus with stenosis in the right external iliac artery, and stenosis of the proximal celiac trunk, consistent with widespread arterial fragility from vEDS.
The patient was treated with subcutaneous enoxaparin followed by oral dabigatran for management of arterial dissection/thrombus, with a relatively static clinical course on follow-up.

The patient required a combination of four antihypertensive agents (amlodipine, carvedilol, hydralazine, terazosin) for optimal blood pressure control, likely reflecting renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation secondary to renal infarction.

Despite carrying a pathogenic COL3A1 null variant, the patient exhibited only subtle skin laxity, thinness, and translucency confined to the posterior calves, lacking the more marked cutaneous features typically associated with other vEDS variant types.

The same COL3A1 null variant identified in this patient had previously been reported in a different patient with spontaneous coronary artery dissection who did not display other typical vEDS characteristics.
Collagen V expression was reexpressed and upregulated during corneal tissue repair in the Col5a1+/- mouse model of classical EDS.
Corneal wound healing was delayed and impaired in the Col5a1+/- mouse model, resulting in large atrophic corneal scars, mirroring the impaired wound healing seen in classical EDS patients.
In a corneal matrix containing only 50% of normal collagen V content, activation of latent TGF-β was dysregulated.
Corneal myofibroblasts haploinsufficient for collagen V failed to mechanically activate latent TGF-β, unlike normal myofibroblasts.

Second harmonic imaging microscopy revealed a disorganized, undulated, and denser collagen matrix in the healed corneas of Col5a1+/- mice, indicating altered extracellular matrix structure and function.
Patients without osteochondral fracture after patellar dislocation had significantly more joint hypermobility than those with osteochondral fracture.
Absence of joint hypermobility was identified as an independent risk factor for osteochondral fracture occurrence after first-time patellar dislocation on logistic regression analysis.
TT-TG distance was significantly higher in patients with osteochondral fracture compared with those without.
TT-PCL distance was significantly higher in patients with osteochondral fracture compared with those without.
Lateral patellar displacement was significantly higher in patients with osteochondral fracture compared with those without.
The rate of osteochondral fracture after sports-related injuries was significantly higher than after other injury mechanisms, though this was a nonindependent risk factor on regression analysis.
In patients with normal joint mobility (absence of hypermobility), the rate of osteochondral fracture localization in the patella (vs femur) was significantly higher.
Among screened wrists, 64.4% met diagnostic criteria for chronic wrist hypermobility (CWH), and affected participants were mostly asymptomatic females.
Benign joint hypermobility syndrome (BJHS) was identified as an etiologic factor in 37% of CWH cases and was more common in females (30%) than males (8%).
Midcarpal ligamentous instability was the most frequent etiologic factor identified in chronic wrist hypermobility, present in 96.5% of cases.
Scapholunate ligamentous instability was identified as an etiologic factor in 39% of chronic wrist hypermobility cases.

Participants with chronic wrist hypermobility showed statistically significant reductions in wrist joint position sense (proprioception) compared to healthy controls, with moderate-to-high effect size.
Wrist isometric extension strength, measured by hand-held dynamometry, was significantly reduced in the CWH group compared to healthy controls.
Grip strength was significantly reduced in participants with chronic wrist hypermobility compared to healthy controls.
Grip strength was significantly lower in wrists with chronic wrist hypermobility compared to healthy control wrists, with a moderate-to-high effect size.
Wrist function, measured by the patient-rated wrist evaluation, was significantly worse in the chronic wrist hypermobility group compared to healthy controls.
No significant gender differences were found in wrist proprioception or function among participants with chronic wrist hypermobility.
Sleep heart rate on one night significantly predicted next-day pain intensity even after accounting for pain on the previous day.
More frequent use of symptomatic painkillers was associated with higher daily pain intensity, likely reflecting reverse causation (higher pain leading to more medication use).
The predictive effect of sleep heart rate on next-day pain remained significant even after controlling for painkiller use.
There was no significant interaction between sleep heart rate and painkiller use in predicting pain intensity.
Sleep heart rate variability (rMSSD) did not significantly predict next-day pain intensity or interact with pain type, contrasting with prior HRV-chronic pain literature.
Pain type (fibromyalgia vs back pain) did not moderate the association between sleep heart rate and next-day pain, with the HR-pain link found across both groups.
In the preregistered model, sleep HR had a significant main effect on next-day pain, and this effect interacted with study day, growing stronger over the course of the study.
Daytime pain intensity did not significantly predict subsequent night's heart rate or heart rate variability, supporting a directional (HR-to-pain, not pain-to-HR) relationship.
Participants with fibromyalgia and those with chronic back pain did not differ in age, average sleep heart rate, HRV, or number of days with biometric data.

Participants with fibromyalgia reported more years living with chronic pain, higher pain intensity, and greater pain interference than participants with primary back pain, indicating higher overall disease severity.
Within-participant night-to-night reliability of wrist-worn sensor measurements was high for both heart rate and heart rate variability.
The predictive effect of sleep heart rate on next-day pain intensity found in this larger, longer follow-up study was similar in magnitude to that found in the authors' earlier pilot study.
A prior study by the same group found that pro-inflammatory cytokines IL6, IL8, MIP-1α (CCL3), and MIP-1β (CCL4) are consistently under-expressed in FM patients relative to healthy controls.

Prior work cited in the introduction reported elevated platelet counts, RBC counts and fibrinogen levels with decreased prothrombin time in FM, suggesting an enhanced inflammatory tone and cardiovascular thrombosis risk.
Cited prior work reported increased CRP and apolipoprotein B in FM patients, biomarkers linked to cardiovascular events.

Cited microarray work implicated dual TH17 and type I interferon gene signatures in FM, with higher IL-17-producing CD4+ T cells and elevated TGF-beta, IL-6, IL-21, and IL-23 promoting Th17 differentiation.
Cited epigenetic work reported a hypomethylated DNA pattern enriched for stress response and DNA repair genes in FM.
Hierarchical clustering of clinical symptoms alone achieved near-perfect separation of FM patients from controls, with only 5 of 189 subjects misclassified.
Within FM patients, symptom clustering revealed redundant symptom pairs: poor sleep/insomnia with memory impairment, depression with anxiety/nervousness, and body pain with tender points.

Whole-transcriptome RNA-seq of PBMCs identified 1720 differentially expressed genes between the entire FM cohort and controls (1695 protein-coding, 24 lncRNA, 1 miRNA), distributed across subgroups FM1 (914), FM2 (361), and combined FM3/FM4 (402).
In the FM1 transcriptional subgroup (43 patients), the GP6 signaling pathway was found to be upregulated relative to controls.

In the FM1 subgroup, genes involved in Rho GDP-Dissociation Inhibitor (RhoGDI) signaling were downregulated, implicating altered Rho GTPase-mediated cytoskeletal/stress fiber regulation and pain perception in somatosensory neurons.

Interactome analysis of the FM1 subgroup identified a major cluster of 338 co-expressed DEGs enriched for extracellular matrix (ECM) genes linked to connective tissue disorders (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis, wound healing, cytoskeletal organization), consistent with fibrocyte-mediated tissue remodeling.
A minor 24-gene cluster (including coding and lncRNA genes) in the FM1 subgroup interactome was associated with cell cycle regulation and DNA damage checkpoint processes.
GSEA of the FM1 subgroup transcriptome showed the expression pattern most prominently correlated with olfactory receptor activity gene sets.
GSEA using a custom 9-gene extracellular matrix protein set (collagen, fibrinogen, elastin, fibrillin, fibronectin, fibulin, laminin, matrilin, tenascin) showed strong enrichment in the FM1 subgroup.

In the FM2 subgroup (30 patients), IPA identified downregulation of numerous inflammatory/immune pathways including phagosome formation, pyroptosis signaling, TREM1 signaling, neuro-inflammation signaling, Th1 pathway, IL1-mediated inhibition of RXR function, dendritic cell/NK cell crosstalk, toll-like receptor signaling, the inflammasome pathway, and Th2 pathway, indicating a lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio imbalance.

The CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression And Regulation) signaling pathway and LXR/RXR activation pathway were upregulated in the FM2 subgroup, suggesting dysregulated lysosomal biogenesis and nutrient-sensing signaling (via TFEB/mTORC1).

In the FM2 subgroup, genes encoding lysosomal hydrolases/accessory proteins (ASAH1, GAA, GNS, IFI30, PSAP) and lysosomal acidification subunits (ATP6V0B, ATP6V0C, ATP6V0D1, ATP6V1B2) were differentially expressed, indicating dysregulated lysosomal homeostasis.
The autophagy gene GABARAP (GABA type A receptor-associated protein), involved in autophagosome maturation and ER-phagy, was differentially expressed in the FM2 subgroup.
In the combined FM3/FM4 subgroup (17 patients), interferon signaling, death receptor signaling, natural killer cell signaling, and JAK/STAT signaling pathways were upregulated.
In the FM3/FM4 subgroup, the pathway for processing of capped intron-containing pre-mRNA was strongly downregulated, indicating global dysregulation of the transcription machinery.

Overall, whole-transcriptome analysis revealed that FM patients are not a single homogeneous molecular entity but comprise multiple subgroups (FM1, FM2, FM3, FM4) with distinct, non-overlapping gene expression signatures, representing genetic/transcriptional heterogeneity within a single clinical FM diagnosis.
Fibromyalgia patients had significantly slower (prolonged) serial five-choice reaction time compared with matched healthy controls.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgG and IgA antibody assay results were retained as significant predictors of reaction time in the multiple regression model for fibromyalgia patients.
Sensory and affective pain parameters (eight sensory, three affective) were significant predictors of reaction time in the fibromyalgia regression model.
The prevalence of symptoms compatible with fibromyalgia in the general population typically ranges from 2 to 4% across most studies.
A Brazilian study in Montes Claros using the COPCORD questionnaire estimated fibromyalgia prevalence at 2.5%.
Polymorphisms in the COMT gene, along with genes related to neurotransmitter transporters/receptors, have been identified in patients with fibromyalgia, suggesting a genetic predisposition.
Patients with fibromyalgia show hyperexcitability of nociceptive pathways with higher levels of substance P, neural growth factor, and glutamate.
Neural growth factor levels are elevated in fibromyalgia, contributing to nociceptive pathway hyperexcitability.
Glutamate levels are elevated in fibromyalgia, associated with facilitation of painful afferents.
Fibromyalgia patients show dysfunction of descending pain inhibition pathways with lower levels of antinociceptive neurotransmitters including noradrenaline, serotonin, dopamine, and GABA.
Functional MRI studies show greater activation of the somatosensory cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and insula (pain perception areas) in fibromyalgia patients.

Fibromyalgia is associated with changes in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and autonomic nervous system, including sympathetic hyperactivity and increased plasma cortisol levels compared to healthy individuals.
Psychological variables such as depression and anxiety are associated with lower functional capacity and greater perceived severity of fibromyalgia symptoms.
EULAR guidelines strongly recommend regular exercise (aerobics, stretching, muscle strengthening) for fibromyalgia based on meta-analyses showing effects on pain, functionality, and well-being.
Cognitive behavioral therapy is particularly helpful for fibromyalgia patients with mood disorders, aiding coping/self-efficacy and reducing negative beliefs, catastrophizing, and hypervigilance.
EULAR guidelines strongly discourage the use of growth hormones, sodium oxybate, strong opioids, and glucocorticoids in fibromyalgia due to lack of efficacy and high risk of side effects.

Simple analgesics and non-hormonal anti-inflammatory agents are not effective for the central sensitization of fibromyalgia, but may help with specific peripheral pain generators such as tendinitis and bursitis.
Establishing a diagnosis of fibromyalgia has been suggested in some studies to lead to lower resource use and lower overall health care costs.

Fibromyalgia has multiple differential diagnoses that occupational physicians must consider, including autoimmune rheumatic diseases, myopathies, osteoarthritis/myofascial syndrome/soft tissue rheumatism, endocrine disorders, infectious diseases (including chronic viral hepatitis and chronic-phase Chikungunya), and peripheral neuropathies.
Aerobic exercise is recommended as a first-line non-pharmacological treatment for fibromyalgia to improve pain and other symptoms.
Cognitive behavioral therapy is recommended as a first-line non-pharmacological treatment for fibromyalgia to improve pain and other symptoms.
Patient education is recommended as a first-line non-pharmacological treatment for fibromyalgia to improve pain and other symptoms.
Digital health interventions have been studied as an additional approach for managing fibromyalgia.
Noninvasive neuromodulation has been studied as an additional approach for managing fibromyalgia.
Duloxetine is an FDA-approved medication for fibromyalgia that acts through pain modulation.
Milnacipran is an FDA-approved medication for fibromyalgia that acts through pain modulation.
Pregabalin is an FDA-approved medication for fibromyalgia that acts through pain modulation.
Amitriptyline is considered an off-label medication option for fibromyalgia.
Amitriptyline is considered an off-label pharmacological option for managing fibromyalgia symptoms.
Cyclobenzaprine is considered an off-label pharmacological option for managing fibromyalgia symptoms.
Gabapentin is considered an off-label pharmacological option for managing fibromyalgia symptoms.
Naltrexone is considered an off-label pharmacological option for managing fibromyalgia symptoms.
The use of cannabinoids for fibromyalgia remains controversial and requires further research.
Vitamin D supplementation for fibromyalgia remains controversial and requires further research.
Combining old, recent, or reformulated therapies is presented as the most effective overall strategy for managing fibromyalgia symptoms.
Radial shockwave therapy (RSWT) did not significantly change hypermobility scores compared to placebo.
Pain catastrophizing scale scores did not differ significantly between RSWT and placebo groups.
VAS pain scores showed no statistically significant difference between RSWT and placebo groups.
Despite lacking statistical significance, VAS pain score changes in the RSWT group exceeded the minimal clinically important difference, indicating clinically meaningful pain improvement.
Quantitative sensory testing for skin temperature and stimuli showed no significant difference between RSWT and placebo groups.
Pressure pain threshold measured by QST did not differ significantly between RSWT and placebo groups.
Brain fMRI scans showed no changes in cortical thickness following radial shockwave therapy compared to placebo.
Post-treatment surveys indicated that participants experienced improvements in pain and symptoms and reported feeling hope after undergoing the study.
Radial shockwave therapy was implemented safely in fibromyalgia patients with no negative treatment effects reported.
SCD1 was highly expressed in IgE-activated bone marrow-derived mast cells.
SCD1 was also confirmed to be highly expressed in DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells.
SCD1 expression was up-regulated in peripheral blood leukocytes of asthmatic children compared with the reference population studied.
SCD1 expression was positively correlated with adiposity measures — upper arm skinfold thickness, abdominal skinfold thickness, and BMI — in the studied children.
Inhibiting SCD1 expression significantly suppressed degranulation in DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells.
Inhibiting SCD1 expression significantly suppressed lipid mediator production in DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells.
Inhibiting SCD1 expression significantly suppressed the migration ability of DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells.
Mast cells from anaphylaxis patients showed more robust degranulation upon LTP (Pru p 3) challenge than those from sensitized patients.
PGD2 release was more frequent in mast cells from anaphylaxis patients than in sensitized patients following LTP challenge.
IL-8 release from mast cells was more frequent in anaphylaxis patients compared to sensitized patients.
GM-CSF release from mast cells was more frequent in anaphylaxis patients compared to sensitized patients.
TGF-ß secretion from mast cells was more frequent in sensitized patients than in anaphylaxis patients.
CCL2 secretion from mast cells was more frequent in sensitized patients than in anaphylaxis patients.
Anaphylaxis patients had a larger population of TFH13 cells in peripheral blood than sensitized patients.
The distinct mast cell activation profile was determined by the patient's serum used for sensitization rather than the source of the mast cells themselves.
LAD2 mast cells activated with the same patient sera reproduced the distinct activation patterns seen in CD34+-derived mast cells from anaphylactic and sensitized patients.
The presence of TFH13 cells in anaphylaxis patients suggests an essential role for IgE affinity maturation in determining reaction severity.
The distinct mast cell activation profile enables discrimination between patients at risk of anaphylaxis and those who are merely sensitized to LTP-containing foods.

In ischemic stroke and vascular dementia gene expression profiles, GAS2L1 expression showed the strongest positive correlation with macrophage M1 infiltration and the strongest negative correlation with mast cell activation.

PFKFB3 expression showed the strongest positive correlation with macrophage M1 infiltration and the strongest negative correlation with mast cell activation in ischemic stroke and vascular dementia gene expression data.
In the authors' small fiber neuropathy cohort, serum NfL levels correlated negatively with sural sensory nerve action potential amplitude, consistent with findings in other neuropathies.
The authors state that NfL levels in peripheral neuropathies are higher during the acute stage and decline over time, even when axonal damage persists.

The authors note that in the first peripherin study, some multiple sclerosis patients and healthy subjects also showed increased peripherin levels, raising doubts about its specificity as a purely peripheral nervous system marker.
Large reference databases for NfL in adults and children have consistently identified age as the most important confounder of NfL concentration.
Body mass index has only a small effect on NfL concentration compared with age, and is mainly relevant in cohorts including obese patients (BMI >30 kg/m2).

Nerve-root and blood-nerve barrier disruption have been shown in Guillain-Barre syndrome and similar acute neuropathies to be important determinants of serum NfL levels, arguing against NfL being purely a central nervous system marker.
Serum NfL levels did not differ significantly between small fiber neuropathy patients and healthy controls in the referenced study.
In the SFN patient group, serum NfL levels were negatively correlated with sural sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitude, suggesting a link to axonal degeneration.
Serum NfL did not correlate with any parameter of small fiber impairment in the referenced SFN cohort.

The authors propose that peripherin (PRPH), a peripheral nervous system-specific neurofilament protein, may be a better biomarker than NfL for small fiber neuropathy, citing a novel Simoa-based homebrew assay with high sensitivity for quantifying PRPH in blood.
The authors note that body mass index (BMI), along with age, is a potential confounding factor affecting serum NfL levels that was not accounted for in the original Baka et al. analysis.

A heterozygous pathogenic MPZ nonsense variant (c.302G>A, p.Trp101Ter) was identified by NGS panel and confirmed by Sanger sequencing in a patient with predominant painful small-fiber neuropathy attributed to CMT1B.
Skin punch biopsies at the ankle and thigh showed markedly reduced intraepidermal nerve-fiber density, supporting a diagnosis of non-length-dependent small-fiber neuropathy.

Electroneurography demonstrated reduced motor and sensory nerve conduction velocities across multiple nerves with preserved amplitudes, classified as an intermediate demyelinating/axonal pattern typical of adult-onset MPZ-related CMT.
The patient scored 4/10 on the DN4 questionnaire, a result consistent with a diagnosis of neuropathic pain.
The Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory revealed a predominance of paroxysmal and superficial burning pain qualities, with a total score of 24/100.
The patient's Small-Fiber Neuropathy Symptoms Inventory Questionnaire score of 26/39 exceeded the proposed screening cut-off of 6.5, supporting a small-fiber neuropathy diagnosis.
The CMT Neuropathy Score version 2 was 4/36, indicating a mild degree of overall motor/sensory impairment despite significant neuropathic pain.
MLPA analysis showed a normal PMP22 copy number, excluding CMT1A (duplication) as the cause of the patient's neuropathy.

A literature review identified 20 CMT patients with MPZ mutations from 11 families in whom neuropathic pain predominated with absent or mild motor signs, distinct from cases where severe motor impairment or sensory ataxia was the main feature.
Among 20 literature-reported patients with painful MPZ-related neuropathy, electrophysiology was classified as intermediate in 12 (including the present case), demyelinating in 5, and axonal in 2.

The same p.Trp101Ter MPZ mutation had previously been reported in the Ramirez family with neuropathic pain, but in that patient intraepidermal nerve-fiber density was normal, contrasting with the reduced IENFD found in the present case.
The p.Thr124Met MPZ mutation was independently reported in two different families with a painful neuropathy phenotype, indicating recurrence of a specific variant associated with pain.
Most reported patients with a painful MPZ-associated phenotype harbored mutations located in the extracellular domain of the protein, which is generally the domain most frequently affected.

The exception to the extracellular-domain pattern was a family with the MPZ c.700G>T (p.Asp234Tyr) missense mutation, whose proband had clinical features consistent with a superimposed chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP).

The truncating p.Trp101Ter variant is predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay because it introduces a premature termination codon within a small exon (exon 3, 216 bp) more than 55 nucleotides from a splice site, consistent with a haploinsufficiency/loss-of-function mechanism.

Restless legs syndrome co-occurred with neuropathic pain in the present patient and in another MPZ-mutation family, where RLS was proposed as a phenotypic equivalent of neuropathic pain among relatives lacking overt pain.

The patient experienced a painful symptom exacerbation at age 57 after the second dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccine, which the authors suggest may reflect susceptibility to inflammatory/immune triggers, although they note the temporal relationship could be coincidental since pre-existing SFN and pain antedated vaccination.

The authors propose that the painfulness of MPZ-related nerve-fiber changes could be unmasked or amplified by superimposed autoimmune/inflammatory processes, drawing on evidence of secondary autoimmunity and CIDP-like manifestations in P0 knockout mice and on literature cases showing elevated CSF protein and response to immunotherapy.
Just under half of patients with symptoms suggestive of small fiber neuropathy had reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy.
The proportion of patients with reduced IENFD did not significantly differ between females (43.2%) and males (50.9%) when Z-scores were applied.
Mean IENFD was significantly lower in males than in females using raw values, but this sex difference disappeared after adjusting with Z-scores for age and height.
Quantitative sensory testing was abnormal in half of the patients overall, with similar rates in females and males.
The rate of abnormal QST was identical (50%) in patients with low IENFD and in those with normal IENFD, indicating IENFD status did not predict QST abnormality.
Sweat volume measured by QSART at the foot was significantly higher in patients with tinnitus than in healthy controls.
QSART sweat volumes at the arm, proximal leg, and distal leg sites did not differ significantly between patients with tinnitus and healthy controls.
Approximately 52% of patients with tinnitus showed abnormal QSART results based on Korean population reference values, indicating a high prevalence of small fiber dysfunction in this group.
About 11.6% of patients with tinnitus exhibited a length-dependent pattern in QSART, consistent with a distal small fiber neuropathy pattern.
No abnormal results were detected in the sympathetic skin response test among patients with tinnitus.
Only about 4.3% of patients with tinnitus showed abnormal heart rate variability results, indicating parasympathetic dysfunction was uncommon.
About 8.6% of patients with tinnitus showed abnormal Valsalva ratio results.
No association was found between total Tinnitus Handicap Inventory scores and QSART, HRV, or Valsalva ratio results.
There was no association between sweat volumes in QSART and pure tone audiometry results (air conduction threshold) in patients with tinnitus.
In older patients with tinnitus, sweat volume was significantly higher than healthy controls at the feet in both sexes and at the arm in women.
In younger men with tinnitus, foot sweat volume was significantly higher than in healthy controls.
Higher mean heart rate and correspondingly shorter mean NN interval were associated with chronic fatigue in this population sample.
Higher mean heart rate and shorter mean NN interval were associated with chronic widespread pain.
Higher mean heart rate and shorter mean NN interval were associated with irritable bowel, though this association was not significant in women.
Higher mean heart rate and shorter mean NN interval were associated with bodily distress syndrome (BDS), the unifying diagnosis for functional somatic disorders.

Parasympathetically-influenced HRV time-domain parameters (SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50) were slightly but significantly reduced in persons with chronic fatigue, chronic widespread pain (except RMSSD in men), irritable bowel (except women), and BDS.
After correcting SDNN for heart rate (cSDNN), the association with FSD was attenuated but remained significant for chronic fatigue in men, chronic widespread pain, and BDS (single and total).
In pure (non-overlapping) syndrome delimitations, only pure chronic fatigue and pure chronic widespread pain were significantly associated with higher mean HR and lower mean NN.
Men, but not women, with pure chronic fatigue showed significantly reduced SDNN, RMSSD and pNN50.
Persons with pure chronic widespread pain showed lower pNN50 overall, and lower SDNN, cSDNN and RMSSD specifically in women but not men.
Pure irritable bowel (not overlapping with chronic fatigue or chronic widespread pain) was not associated with any time-domain HRV measure.
Frequency-domain total power measures (LFtotal, HFtotal) showed a slight negative association with most FSD delimitations, but few reached statistical significance.
In pure irritable bowel, LFnorm was significantly negatively associated and HFnorm was significantly positively associated, a pattern opposite to the expected sympathetic-predominance direction.
Persons with multi-organ BDS (multi-BDS) showed a positive association with LFnorm and a negative association with HFnorm, consistent with sympathetic predominance.
No association was found between the LF/HF ratio and any of the FSD delimitations examined.
The same pattern of reduced HRV was observed for BDS cases identified through a semistructured clinical diagnostic interview, replicating the questionnaire-based findings.

Adjusting the HRV-FSD associations for self-perceived chronic stress attenuated them only slightly, with most significant associations remaining, indicating chronic stress does not fully explain the HRV-FSD relationship.
Among 6891 participants with valid HRV data, prevalence was 16.9% for BDS total, 9.2% for chronic fatigue, 4.5% for chronic widespread pain, and 3.5% for irritable bowel.

A prior systematic review and meta-analysis of 85 mostly small case-control studies found significantly lower HRV in fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome and IBS patients compared with healthy controls, with the strongest association in fibromyalgia, though publication bias could not be excluded.

In a separate prior analysis (Tak et al), the association between FSD and reduced HRV disappeared after statistical correction for funnel plot asymmetry, suggesting the originally reported association may have reflected publication bias.
Celastrol pre-treatment blocked TGFβ1-induced upregulation of the profibrotic marker CCN2 in human gingival fibroblasts.
Bulk RNAseq showed celastrol impaired TGFβ1-induced upregulation of gene clusters related to extracellular matrix, wound healing, focal adhesion, and cytokine/Wnt signaling in gingival fibroblasts.
RT-PCR confirmed that celastrol antagonized TGFβ1-induced expression of genes anticipated to contribute to fibrotic responses in gingival fibroblasts.
Celastrol reduced proliferation of human gingival fibroblasts.
Celastrol reduced TGFβ1-induced nuclear localization of YAP1 in gingival fibroblasts.
taVNS increased fecal pellet number, fecal water content, and gastrointestinal transit in IBS-C model mice compared with sham electrostimulation.
taVNS significantly decreased the abdominal withdrawal reflex (AWR) score compared with sham-ES, indicating relief of visceral hyperalgesia.
taVNS restored Lactobacillus abundance in the gut microbiota of IBS-C model mice.
taVNS increased Bifidobacterium probiotic abundance at the genus level in IBS-C model mice.
taVNS increased the number of c-kit-positive interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC) in the myenteric plexus region of IBS-C model mice compared with sham-ES.
In IBS patients, the gut microbiota showed higher abundance of the bacterial families Bacteroidales, Lactobacillaceae, and Enterobacteriaceae compared with healthy controls.
IBS patients showed lower levels of Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium, and Clostridiales compared with healthy controls.
Sigmoid colon mucosa-associated bacterial composition differs between IBS patients and healthy controls.

Propionate, a metabolite produced by gut bacteria such as Prevotellaceae, has been linked in prior research to sensorimotor dysfunction, cognitive deficits, social abnormalities, and worsening of autism spectrum disorder symptoms.
Serum TGFβ levels declined with age in healthy children, with lower levels seen at the onset of puberty and adolescence.
No sex-based difference in serum TGFβ level was found among healthy children of any age.
Presence of inflammation (elevated CRP) had no measurable influence on serum TGFβ levels in healthy children.
Impaired kidney function markers (creatinine) had no measurable influence on serum TGFβ levels in healthy children.
Baseline serum TGFβ levels did not differ significantly between untreated pediatric Marfan patients and healthy children.
TGFβ levels did not differ significantly between healthy children and Marfan patients who had aortic root dilatation.
In 11 pediatric Marfan patients, serum TGFβ dropped to its lowest level 6 hours after valsartan administration.
TGFβ levels rose back toward baseline approximately 11.5 hours after valsartan dosing, just before the next dose, with no significant difference from baseline at that timepoint.
At 12-month follow-up, random-time TGFβ measurements in ARB-treated Marfan patients did not show a decrease compared to baseline.
The sinus valsalvae (aortic root) z-score in ARB-treated Marfan patients did not change significantly over the 1-year observation period.
No relevant difference in TGFβ levels was detected between patients with haploinsufficient versus dominant-negative FBN1 variants, either at baseline or after ARB treatment.

A pathogenic FBN1 variant enhances TGFβ activity, and this excess TGFβ activation impairs regeneration of vascular smooth muscle cells such as in the aortic wall, contributing to Marfan syndrome pathology.
A random-effects meta-analysis estimated that IBS is diagnosed in 16% of patients with FND.
A random-effects meta-analysis estimated that fibromyalgia is diagnosed in 10% of patients with FND.
CRPS was diagnosed in an estimated 22% of patients with FND across pooled studies, most commonly among those with fixed dystonia.
Overall, a random-effects model estimated that 55% of patients with FND report chronic pain symptoms.
Chronic pain was more common in patients with functional seizures than in patients with epilepsy attending an epilepsy monitoring unit.
Patients with functional limb weakness reported worse SF-36 bodily pain scores than controls with weakness due to other neurological disorders, over a 14-year case-control study.
Patients with FND and a comorbid chronic pain diagnosis were less likely to show overall clinical improvement at 7-month follow-up than those without a pain diagnosis.
Female patients with FND (including functional seizures) reported pain symptoms more often than male patients across two cohorts.
Physiotherapy, psychotherapy, and rehabilitation programmes generally did not improve pain scores in FND despite improving other quality-of-life measures such as physical and social function.
An interdisciplinary outpatient chronic pain rehabilitation programme improved Pain Disability Index scores in patients with FND and comorbid pain.
Opioid/opiate analgesic use was common among patients with FND, particularly those with functional seizures and functional dystonia.
IBS diagnoses among patients with functional seizures and functional movement disorders varied widely across studies, ranging from 3% to 36%.
Patients with functional seizures more often had more than one comorbid pain diagnosis compared with patients with functional movement disorders.
The review authors conclude chronic pain is at least as common a comorbidity/risk factor overlap in FND as childhood maltreatment, a recognized aetiological risk factor for FND.
At baseline (median 9 months post-infection), 21% of participants had clinically relevant fatigue on the FACIT-Fatigue scale.
At baseline, 23% of participants had cognitive deficits as measured by MoCA, mostly mild severity.
Only 6% of participants suffered from both fatigue and cognitive deficits simultaneously, suggesting the two syndromes affect largely distinct patient groups.
Among patients with baseline fatigue, 46% had recovered by follow-up at a median 26 months post-infection.
Among patients with baseline cognitive deficits, 57% had recovered by follow-up at a median 26 months post-infection.
FACIT-Fatigue scores for patients with baseline fatigue significantly improved from baseline to follow-up with a large effect size.
MoCA scores for patients with baseline cognitive deficits significantly improved from baseline to follow-up with a large effect size.

Pre-infection neuropsychiatric disease, depressive symptoms (PHQ-8), anxiety symptoms (GAD-7), and headache at baseline were significantly associated with non-recovery from fatigue in univariate models.
In multivariable analysis, headache and PHQ-8 (depression) score were independently associated with fatigue non-recovery, in a best-fitting model also including employment status.

Loss of energy (PHQ-8 item 1) at baseline showed a strong association with non-recovery from fatigue, and anticipatory fear (GAD-7 item 7), a non-fatigue-like symptom, was also significantly associated with non-recovery.
Sex, age, education, BMI, and pre-infection cardiovascular disease at baseline showed significant univariate associations with cognitive non-recovery.

In the multivariable model, male sex, older age, and less than 12 years of school education were independently associated with significantly lower odds of cognitive recovery, while no COVID-specific factors were significant predictors.
Reinfection with SARS-CoV-2 between baseline and follow-up had no relevant impact on fatigue recovery.

No COVID-specific factors (e.g., hospitalization, number of acute symptoms) showed significant association with cognitive recovery in the final multivariable model, in contrast to sociodemographic pre-infection factors.
Individuals with long COVID reported significantly lower trait forgiveness of self than those without long COVID.
Individuals with long COVID reported significantly lower trait forgiveness of others than those without long COVID.
Individuals with long COVID reported significantly lower trait forgiveness of situations than those without long COVID.
Among individuals with long COVID, higher forgiveness of self was positively associated with better mental health.
Among individuals with long COVID, forgiveness of self was not significantly associated with physical health.
Among individuals with long COVID, higher forgiveness of situations was positively associated with better mental health.
Among individuals with long COVID, higher trait forgiveness of self was positively associated with better mental health but not physical health.
Forgiveness of self was not significantly associated with physical health among individuals with long COVID.
Among individuals with long COVID, higher trait forgiveness of situations was positively associated with better mental health but not physical health.
Forgiveness of situations was not significantly associated with physical health among individuals with long COVID.
Among individuals with long COVID, higher trait forgiveness of others was negatively associated with physical health.
Among individuals with long COVID, higher trait forgiveness of others was negatively associated with mental health.

Women with ME/CFS reported that COVID-19 lockdown disrupted their established routines, partly due to partners being present more and increased working-from-home, though having partners at home was also experienced as helpful.

Participants believed that pandemic-induced societal changes reduced the perceived difference between their restricted lifestyle and the outside world, which had previously felt prominent before lockdown.

Participants feared that contracting COVID-19 would worsen their ME/CFS, and the lifting of lockdown restrictions was described as an anxiety-provoking period that impacted their symptoms, leading many to continue adhering to guidelines after restrictions eased.
Among 92 children and young people with suspected severe ME/CFS, 33 met criteria for confirmed severe ME/CFS while 59 were classified as probable or possible severe ME/CFS.
For 16 of the possible severe ME/CFS cases, incomplete investigation to exclude alternative diagnoses prevented confirmation of a severe ME/CFS diagnosis.
Only 21 of 33 (64%) confirmed severe ME/CFS cases had been referred to specialist services, indicating poor implementation of NICE referral recommendations.
Management provided to confirmed severe ME/CFS cases varied considerably, with four patients receiving no management at all.
The most frequent management approaches for confirmed severe ME/CFS cases were medication (67%), activity management (61%) and physiotherapy (61%).
Domiciliary assessments and support, and social services referrals were received by only 12% and 6% of confirmed severe cases respectively, suggesting the needs of housebound CYP are poorly met.
ME/CFS is estimated to have a worldwide prevalence of 0.89%.
Long-COVID prevalence has been estimated at approximately 37% at 30 days and 49% at 120 days after acute infection.
About 45% of patients with persistent moderate-to-severe fatigue 6 months after a mostly mild SARS-CoV-2 infection meet Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS.
Autoantibodies against thyroperoxidase (TPO), beta-adrenergic receptors (β2AR), and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (MAR) are frequently detected in ME/CFS patients.
Two studies found that B cell-depleting monoclonal antibody rituximab led to partial or complete remission in 60% of ME/CFS patients.
A trial of the broadly immunosuppressive drug cyclophosphamide showed a beneficial effect in ME/CFS.
Multiple studies support a positive effect of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) on fatigue symptoms and physical functioning, especially in severe ME/CFS.
Autoantibodies against several G-protein-coupled receptors were found in sera of patients with persistent long-COVID symptoms including fatigue.
Central nervous system-reactive autoantibodies were detected in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid of COVID-19 patients with neurologic symptoms.
Early pilot studies on immunoadsorption in ME/CFS patients suggest clinical improvement in some patients.
Bornstein et al. 2022 reported that extracorporeal apheresis significantly reduced β-adrenergic and muscarinic receptor autoantibody levels along with clinical improvement in PACS-CFS patients.
Autoantibodies against GPCRs are found in up to 30% of patients with ME/CFS.
GPCR-directed autoantibodies correlated with symptom severity, including fatigue, vasomotor, and cognitive symptoms, in patients with PACS-CFS.
Autoantibodies targeting brain epitopes were common in post-COVID syndrome patients and strongly associated with pathological cognitive screening test results, particularly when detected in CSF.
