Half of post-COVID syndrome patients with moderate to severe fatigue and exertional intolerance meet Canadian Consensus Criteria 2003 for ME/CFS.
The rate of clinically symptomatic complaints associated with the TheraSorb Ig-omni adsorber was 0.03% after more than 12,000 treatments, indicating a good safety profile.
Allergy-like reactions such as pruritus, red skin, back pain, and asthma occurred in about 1 of every 1000 immunoadsorption treatments.
Prior data show the mean Chalder Fatigue Scale score in a CFS population (24.4, SD 5.8) is substantially higher than in a healthy sample (14.2, SD 4.6).
A systematic review reported that the minimal important difference for global change on the Chalder Fatigue Scale ranges between 2.3 and 3.3 points.

This exploratory, double-blinded, sham-controlled trial hypothesizes that five cycles of immunoadsorption will produce significant clinical improvement in ME/CFS and PACS-CFS patients compared to sham apheresis, but no outcome data are yet reported.
Recent workforce reports cited in this commentary indicate that a majority of nurses and a substantial fraction of doctors plan to leave clinical practice amid pandemic-era burnout and strain.
The authors describe ME/CFS as sharing many clinical features and possibly underlying pathophysiology with more severe long COVID.

The CDC-supported Long COVID & Fatiguing Illnesses Recovery Program (LC&FIRP), using an ECHO case-based tele-mentoring model, has reached thousands of participants across nearly all US states and dozens of countries through monthly learning sessions.

A CDC-commissioned qualitative study of primary care providers participating in the weekly tele-mentoring sessions found increased awareness of long COVID, greater confidence, empathy, patience, and expanded treatment options.
The authors note that although no approved treatments exist for long COVID, symptomatic management strategies developed for ME/CFS can be applied to long COVID patients with overlapping symptoms.
Nearly all post-COVID consultation patients (98.2%) reported fatigue as the cardinal symptom of their complaints.
Over 73% of patients reported subjective limitations in brain functioning (cognitive complaints) alongside fatigue.
Symptom duration averaged 14-15 months and was similar between female and male insured patients.
More than 85% of the total sample met criteria for chronic fatigue based on the Fatigue Scale.
Fatigue severity was associated proportionally with reduced quality of life as measured by the SF-36.
Fatigue severity was proportionally associated with increased anxiety and depression scores on the HADS.
Fatigue severity was proportionally associated with reduced psychological resilience as measured by the RS-13.
Fatigue severity was associated with reduced motor performance, including lower maximum grip strength and reduced endurance capacity.
More than half of post-COVID patients received a suspected psychiatric/mental health diagnosis during the consultation.
Over a third of patients were recommended for further neuropsychological diagnostic assessment.

The authors recommend multimodal, interdisciplinary outpatient rehabilitation oriented toward ME/CFS treatment principles, emphasizing psychoeducational rather than curative approaches plus aftercare strategies for chronic fatigue in post-COVID patients.

A patient with pre-existing fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, and myofascial disorder developed rhabdomyolysis and compartment syndrome after a single electrical muscle stimulation (EMS) training session.
Laboratory testing showed elevated creatine kinase (CK), CK-MB, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), consistent with rhabdomyolysis.
CK and myoglobin levels gradually decreased during hospitalization with intravenous fluid therapy, correlating with symptom improvement.
The patient had mildly elevated troponin on follow-up a week after discharge, which normalized over two weeks and was attributed to a noncardiac cause.

Days after EMS training, the patient developed spreading muscle soreness, significant gluteal swelling, and mild sensory changes/paresthesia in the sciatic nerve distribution, consistent with gluteal compartment syndrome.
Intensive intravenous fluid therapy and sodium bicarbonate supplementation were used to flush out myoglobin and prevent kidney damage in this rhabdomyolysis case.
Prior studies cited indicate that high-frequency EMS training produces more muscle damage than low-frequency EMS training.
Exercise adaptation is reported to reduce muscle damage from EMS/exercise, as evidenced by lower blood CK levels.
The patient's gluteal compartment syndrome was managed conservatively (without surgical fasciotomy) and she had gradual improvement without neurological deficits or sequelae.
The review recommends celiac disease serologic screening in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) among numerous other high-risk conditions.

Celiac disease is a chronic immune-mediated condition triggered by gluten in genetically predisposed individuals and affects approximately 1% of the general population, but is frequently underdiagnosed due to heterogeneous presentation.
CFS model rats had a higher general condition score than control rats, indicating worsened overall status.
In the Morris water maze, CFS model rats showed prolonged escape latency compared with controls, indicating impaired spatial learning.
CFS model rats crossed the original platform location fewer times than controls in the Morris water maze probe trial.
In the open field test, CFS model rats showed increased grid crossings and central area entries relative to controls, indicating altered locomotor/anxiety-like behavior.
CFS model rats had a shortened exhaustive treadmill running time compared with controls, reflecting reduced physical endurance/fatigue.
Electroacupuncture treatment increased hippocampal and serum IL-10 content compared with the untreated CFS model group.
Electroacupuncture treatment decreased hippocampal and serum IL-17 content compared with the untreated CFS model group.
Electroacupuncture treatment decreased hippocampal and serum TGF-β1 content compared with the untreated CFS model group.

Compared with the model group, electroacupuncture-treated rats showed improved general condition score, shortened escape latency, increased original-platform crossings, decreased grid-crossing/central-area entries, and prolonged exhaustive treadmill time.
H.E. staining showed that CFS model rats had fewer hippocampal neurons with disordered arrangement, loose structure, and some missing neuronal nuclei compared to controls.
The degree of hippocampal tissue damage in electroacupuncture-treated rats was milder than that in the untreated model group.
Immunofluorescence intensity of IL-10 in the hippocampus increased after electroacupuncture treatment, while IL-17 and TGF-β1 immunofluorescence intensity decreased, compared with the model group.
Heavy menstrual bleeding is reported to be highly prevalent among adult patients with hypermobile-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, though adolescent-specific data is limited.

The review recommends comprehensive medical and menstrual history, focused physical exam, and baseline laboratory studies to identify anemia or underlying bleeding disorders in adolescents with hypermobile EDS presenting with heavy menstrual bleeding.
The review recommends prompt initiation of treatment to reduce heavy menstrual flow and referral to specialty care to improve quality of life in this adolescent population.
Dysautonomia was the most frequently reported comorbidity among EDS/HSD survey respondents, reported by 78% as formally diagnosed or suspected.
Anxiety was reported by 69% of EDS/HSD respondents as a comorbid diagnosis or suspected condition.
Migraine was reported by 67% of EDS/HSD respondents as a comorbid diagnosis or suspected condition.
MCAS was reported by 66% of EDS/HSD respondents as a comorbid diagnosis or suspected condition.
IBS was reported by 65% of EDS/HSD respondents as a comorbid diagnosis or suspected condition.
Depression was reported by 58% of EDS/HSD respondents as a comorbid diagnosis or suspected condition.
On average, respondents reported 6.6 of 10 surveyed comorbid conditions as either formally diagnosed or suspected, indicating substantial multimorbidity in the EDS/HSD population.
Almost all respondents (94%) reported that their EDS/HSD-related symptoms negatively affected their ability to work, attend school, and/or participate in preferred recreational activities.
Despite most respondents having private insurance, 30% reported spending $10,000 or more in the preceding year on EDS/HSD-related healthcare costs, with 9% spending over $20,000.

Nearly all respondents (95%) reported experiencing medical trauma or medical gaslighting, defined as providers discounting or minimizing symptoms or inappropriately framing them as psychosocial rather than physical.
Over half of respondents (56%) reported that experiences of medical trauma/gaslighting led them to avoid or put off medical care, and an additional 11% avoided seeking care as much as possible.
Nearly half of respondents (49%) were dissatisfied or very dissatisfied with their current local medical support for EDS/HSD, while only 5% were very satisfied.
The majority of respondents (82%) found it somewhat difficult, difficult, or very difficult to access quality care for their EDS/HSD condition.
While 99% of respondents believed provider collaboration was important to their health outcomes, 63% expressed dissatisfaction with the actual collaboration among their past or current providers.

Nearly all respondents (95%) said they would utilize a proposed collaborative EDS/HSD specialty center within the next one to two years, with 82% stating they were 'very likely' to do so, and only 2% unlikely.
55% of respondents reported using complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) or integrative care in the last five years, and 90% said they would likely use such services at a future center.
Physical therapy showed both high past utilization (78%) and high future interest (92%) among EDS/HSD respondents.
68% and 75% of respondents indicated interest in psychiatric and psychological services respectively, supporting inclusion of CBT-based pain management and mental health support in a proposed center.

Respondents expressed much higher future interest in orthopedics, gastroenterology, and neurology specialty care (~90-92%) than their actual past utilization of these specialties (53-68%), indicating an access gap.

Nearly half of respondents (46%) had seen 11 or more medical providers in pursuit of EDS/HSD care, with 28% having accessed 16 or more providers, reflecting a heavy diagnostic and care-seeking burden.

Among survey respondents, 68% reported a formal diagnosis of hEDS or HSD and an additional 20% suspected they had EDS/HSD, with the remainder having a formal or suspected diagnosis of another EDS type.

In a hypermobile woman, left renal vein compression (nutcracker physiology) led to secondary spinal epidural venous congestion, hypothesized to elevate CSF pressure and cause severe early morning wake-up headaches.
Acetazolamide treatment mostly eliminated the patient's wake-up headaches prior to definitive diagnosis and treatment of the underlying venous anomaly.
Lumbar vein coil embolization to relieve spinal epidural venous congestion resulted in cessation of the patient's wake-up headaches.

The authors note that, to date, only women with underlying symptomatic hypermobility appear to develop headache related to nutcracker physiology and spinal epidural venous congestion, suggesting a link between hypermobility (EDS) and this headache mechanism.
A patient with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presented with spontaneous perforation of the sigmoid colon.
The patient was diagnosed with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome via genetic testing revealing missense variants in COL3A1, the gene encoding type III collagen.

The patient presented with spontaneous sigmoid colon perforation with a 2-cm area of wall thinning and 7-mm perforation, associated with thinning of the intrinsic muscular layer, a recognized major criterion of vEDS.

Nine days after sigmoid colon surgery, the patient developed sudden abdominal pain and hypotension due to rupture of a dissecting splenic artery aneurysm at a site distant from the surgical field, despite no aneurysm being present on preoperative CT.

Urgent transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) of the ruptured splenic artery, and subsequently the common hepatic, proper hepatic, and gastroduodenal arteries after dissection spread, successfully controlled hemorrhage and preserved hepatic perfusion via collateral flow, allowing discharge without liver dysfunction or GI ischemia.
Celiprolol, a beta-blocker, is recommended for prevention of arterial complications in vEDS, and was administered to this patient both before and after surgery alongside blood pressure control.
A cited study reported that high pulse pressure (>50 mmHg) may be associated with vascular events in vEDS, suggesting pulse pressure reduction as a treatment goal.
Repeat sigmoid perforation rates of up to 55% have been reported after segmental colon resection in vEDS, informing the surgical decision-making in this case.
Open surgical repair and endovascular treatment of arterial complications in vEDS carry high mortality risks of approximately 30% and 24%, respectively.

A summary of 88 patients with splenic arterial aneurysms in vEDS found that embolization was associated with favorable outcomes, with no periprocedural mortality or access-site complications, whereas open repair of ruptured splenic aneurysm was associated with high morbidity and mortality.
Vascular EDS is associated with reduced life expectancy, with a previously reported median survival of 48 years, mostly due to arterial rupture.
A population study found thoracic aortic disease incidence of 10.4 per 100,000 person-years, with 51% of cases in women who were diagnosed at an older age than men.
Women with type A dissection have higher surgical mortality than men (32% vs 22%), along with more frequent imaging findings suggestive of rupture and in-hospital complications.

In the ROPAC registry of nearly 6,000 pregnant women with cardiovascular disease, 3.3% had thoracic aortic disease, with half diagnosed with Marfan syndrome, 26% BAV, 8% Turner syndrome, and 2% vascular EDS; four dissections occurred (three type A, one type B), three in women with Marfan syndrome, with no maternal or fetal mortality.

In the International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection, pregnancy-related dissections represented 0.3% of all dissections and 1% of dissections in women, with 65% having Marfan syndrome, 10% Loeys-Dietz syndrome, and 10% bicuspid aortic valve; aortopathy was unrecognized until after dissection in 47% of women, with 97% survival.
A prospective nationwide Dutch cohort study of all deliveries over two years found a maternal mortality rate of 3 per 100,000 deliveries, with 45% of these deaths attributed to aortic dissection.

In a literature analysis of 75 pregnancy-related aortic dissection cases, 77% were Stanford type A, 49% had underlying connective tissue disorders, overall mortality was 22%, and fetal mortality was 36% when antepartum repair was required.

In a UK multicenter retrospective cohort of 151 women with Marfan syndrome and 258 pregnancies, only half received preconception counseling; 1.9% experienced aortic dissection (mostly type B), 1.9% required postpartum cardiac surgery, C-section rate was 50%, and aortic root size increased by 0.84 mm.

In the GenTAC registry, 10.6% of 184 women with Marfan syndrome experienced a pregnancy-related aortic complication, with most dissections and the coronary dissection occurring postpartum, and only 5 of 8 women with pregnancy-associated dissection aware of their diagnosis beforehand.

In 69 women with Marfan syndrome without dissection or surgery during pregnancy, aortic growth rate increased during pregnancy and did not return to baseline afterward, and prior pregnancy was associated with higher long-term prevalence of aortic dissection and elective aortic surgery.

In a natural history study of 90 patients with LDS type I/II from 52 families, mean age at death was 26 years, and pregnancy-related complications affected 6 of 12 women (dissection in four, uterine rupture in two).
In a case series, two-thirds of women with Loeys-Dietz syndrome who had undergone prophylactic aortic root replacement suffered acute dissection distal to the graft in the postpartum period.

In a review of pedigrees and interviews of families with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, pregnancy-related death occurred in 5.3% of deliveries, with life-threatening complications (arterial dissection/rupture, uterine rupture, surgical complications) in 14.5% of deliveries and maternal death in 6.5%.

In a study of 53 women with non-syndromic hereditary thoracic aortic disease and 137 pregnancies, 6% had aortic dissections during the third trimester or postpartum, including three ascending dissections at diameters less than 5.0 cm (3.8-4.7 cm).

Eleven genes (FBN1, LOX, COL3A1, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, TGFB2, ACTA2, MYH11, MYLK, and PRKG1) confer highly penetrant risk for heritable thoracic aortic disease, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with 50% inheritance risk.

A small randomized, multicenter, open-label trial found celiprolol significantly reduced the rate of arterial dissection and rupture in patients with vascular EDS, including normotensive women, though it is not available in the United States.

In a report of 11 pregnant women undergoing aortic surgery, there were no maternal deaths, but three pregnancies resulted in intrauterine fetal demise within a week of surgery; mean cardiopulmonary bypass and cross-clamp times were 105 and 89 minutes respectively.
Histologic analysis of arterial tissue from postpartum women who suffered aortic dissection demonstrated significant arterial degeneration and loss of structural integrity.
Postpartum women with ultrasound-confirmed urethral (bladder neck) hypermobility had a significantly higher incidence of stress urinary incontinence symptoms than women without hypermobility.
The study and control groups were demographically similar in age, weight, BMI, education, and occupation, indicating hypermobility findings were not confounded by these baseline demographic factors.
Body surface area was significantly lower in both juvenile and adult OI patients compared with age- and sex-matched healthy controls.

When corrected for body surface area, aortic diameter, left atrium diameter, interventricular septum thickness, left ventricular end-diastolic and end-systolic diameters, and fractional shortening were significantly larger in OI juveniles than in juvenile controls.
When corrected for BSA, AD, LAD, IVST, LVPWT, LVEDd, LVESd, LVEF and FS were significantly larger in OI adults compared with adult controls.
Uncorrected aortic diameter and left ventricular mass were significantly larger in adult controls than in OI adults.
Mild mitral regurgitation was found in 12% and mild tricuspid regurgitation in 36% of juvenile OI patients.

Among 23 OI adults, mild mitral regurgitation occurred in 13%, mild tricuspid regurgitation in 17%, mild aortic regurgitation in 4%, left atrium enlargement in 4%, and increased pulmonary artery pressure in 4%, with one patient (4%) having had aortic valve replacement.
Thirty of the 48 OI patients carried COL1A1 mutations, comprising 11 nonsense, 9 missense, 8 frameshift, one splice, and one gross deletion mutation.
Sixteen OI patients harbored COL1A2 gene mutations, including 14 missense and 2 splice mutations.
A pathogenic IFITM5 variant was detected in two OI patients.
One boy carried compound heterozygous WNT1 variants causing recessive OI.
A novel COL1A1 duplication variant (c.1865dupC) and a gross COL1A1 deletion, absent from the LOVD database, were identified as novel variants in this cohort.
A novel COL1A2 missense variant (c.1649G>C), absent from the LOVD database, was identified in this cohort.
Joint hypermobility assessment in juvenile OI patients showed 11% with no hypermobility, 33% with peripheral hypermobility, and 56% with generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥4).
Among 20 assessed adult OI patients, 40% had no joint hypermobility, 40% had peripheral hypermobility, and 20% had generalized joint hypermobility, a lower prevalence than in juveniles.
In juvenile OI patients, the degree of joint hypermobility was significantly greater in the echocardiographically abnormal group than the normal group.
In adult OI patients, the degree of joint hypermobility did not differ significantly between the echocardiographically normal and abnormal groups.
In multiple regression analysis, having OI was itself a significant predictor of left atrium diameter and fractional shortening among juveniles, independent of age, sex, and BSA.
In multiple regression analysis, OI was a significant predictor of left atrium diameter and left ventricular mass among adults, independent of age, sex, and BSA.

Two patients meeting diagnostic criteria for COL1-related overlap disorder (C1ROD), with blue sclera, generalized joint hypermobility, soft/hyperextensible skin, atrophic scars, and fracture history, carried a COL1A1 p.Arg1026* variant and a COL1A2 p.Cys1195Arg variant respectively.
Among 9 juvenile OI patients with echocardiographic abnormalities, 6 (67%) had moderate to severe clinical OI type 3-4, suggesting more severe phenotype correlates with cardiac abnormality.

A patient-specific finite element model showed that lower trapeziometacarpal joint passive stiffness (i.e., greater joint laxity/hypermobility) was significantly negatively correlated with contact pressure on the trapezium cartilage during a simulated pinch grip task.

The study concludes that trapeziometacarpal joint hypermobility may increase mechanical cartilage loading and thereby support its role as a risk factor for osteoarthritis, though prior evidence on this link had been controversial due to lack of quantitative validation.
In children with isolated (non-syndromic) high myopia and peripheral retinal degenerations who had a confirmed genetic diagnosis, COL2A1 mutations accounted for 77.4% of cases.
In children with isolated high myopia and peripheral retinal degenerations who had a confirmed genetic diagnosis, COL11A1 mutations accounted for 22.6% of cases.
Among children diagnosed with Stickler syndrome with confirmed genetic diagnosis, COL2A1 mutations were found in 33.3% of cases.
In children diagnosed with Marshall syndrome, a COL11A1 mutation was detected in 11.1% of cases.

In children with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome combined with high myopia and peripheral retinal degenerations, mutations were identified in the COL5A1 gene as part of a group of syndromic cases collectively accounting for 55.6% of confirmed genetic diagnoses.
A mutation in the COL18A1 gene was identified in a child with Knobloch syndrome type 1 presenting with high myopia and peripheral retinal degenerations.
A mutation in the VPS13B gene was identified in a child with Cohen syndrome presenting with high myopia and peripheral retinal degenerations.
A mutation in the FBN1 gene was identified in a child with Marfan syndrome presenting with high myopia and peripheral retinal degenerations.
A mutation in the VCAN gene was identified in a child with Wagner syndrome presenting with high myopia and peripheral retinal degenerations.

In one-third of cases of Knobloch syndrome type 1, Cohen syndrome, and Wagner syndrome, the causative gene mutation was found on both chromosomal copies (biallelic), which was associated with development of peripheral retinal degenerations combined with high myopia.
In a clinical trial of 100 fibromyalgia patients, 10 sessions of whole-body cryostimulation improved pain perception and quality of life compared to a no-WBC control group.
In a randomised, open-label crossover trial of 60 fibromyalgia patients, WBC produced similar positive results at a 1-month follow-up compared to no-WBC condition.

In 43 patients with obesity and fibromyalgia undergoing a multidisciplinary rehabilitation program, the group receiving 10 WBC sessions showed greater improvements in pain severity, depressive symptoms, disease impact, and sleep quality than the group receiving rehabilitation alone.
In a randomised controlled trial of 56 rheumatoid arthritis patients, WBC combined with multimodal treatment reduced pain and serum TNF and IL-6 levels compared to a no-treatment control group.

In a randomised single-blinded controlled trial, WBC as an adjunct to physiotherapy reduced pain more than other cryotherapies in some rheumatoid arthritis patients, but there was no significant difference in disease activity between groups or versus local cryotherapy, and heterogeneous small groups limited conclusions.

In a trial of 44 patients (25 WBC vs 19 traditional rehabilitation), both groups showed similar significant reductions in IL-6, TNF-α levels, pain, and physical function, showing no clear superiority of WBC.

A case report of a 74-year-old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica and central sensitization showed long-lasting (6-month) improvements in disease impact, fatigue, pain, sleep quality, and physical activity after a 10-session WBC cycle used as a stand-alone treatment, with reduced pharmacological treatment.

In an uncontrolled study of 30 patients with low back pain, a WBC cycle combined with exercise improved pain, suggesting an effect on the nervous and endocrine systems, though no control group was used.

In a quasi-experimental study without a control group involving 41 patients with chronic low back pain, WBC improved pain perception and disability after only four sessions and reduced serum inflammatory markers while increasing anti-inflammatory markers.
In myofascial pain syndrome, WBC was associated with reduced perceived pain and an increase in pain threshold shortly after treatment.

In a case study of an amputated paralympic athlete with phantom limb pain and central sensitization, WBC produced a clinically significant reduction in phantom limb pain intensity and paraesthesia lasting two weeks, with symptoms returning at lower intensity after one month and better sleep quality than before treatment.

Central sensitization is characterized biologically by increased excitatory neurotransmitters (glutamate, substance P) and decreased inhibitory transmitters (GABA), together with downregulated dopaminergic activity and opioid receptors.
The immune system contributes to central sensitization by increasing pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) in the spinal cord in response to stressors.
Cold exposure via WBC enhances anti-inflammatory responses and increases release of analgesic factors such as serum beta-endorphin and norepinephrine.
Some studies suggest WBC may transiently increase testosterone levels in response to cold stress, but results are inconsistent regarding significant long-term effects.
An initial increase in cortisol levels after WBC exposure can be found, which may decrease over time as part of an adaptation phenomenon.

In fibromyalgia, persistent impairment of pain modulation combined with an imbalance between inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α) contributes to central sensitization and sustains fibromyalgia-related hyperalgesia.
Patients with inflammatory sacroiliac joint disease and negative serologies are frequently misdiagnosed and mislabeled as having fibromyalgia.

The authors suggest that sacroiliac joint disease is generally overlooked and underdiagnosed, recommending greater focus on SIJ imaging when evaluating unexplained low back pain, morning stiffness, or buttock pain.
The authors hypothesize that SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein contributes to Long COVID-19, a syndrome that includes strokes, cardiopathies, neuralgias, fibromyalgia, and Guillain-Barré-like disease.

The authors propose that Spike-encoding mRNA (from infection or vaccination) may integrate into host DNA via retrotransposition mechanisms involving LINE-1 (L1) elements and ORF1/ORF2, altering genome integrity in mature cells and stem cells.
Oral UPE reduced OVA-induced sneezing and nasal rubbing behaviors in a dose-related manner compared with untreated OVA mice.

UPE at 100 and 200 mg/kg significantly decreased total and differential inflammatory cell counts (epithelial cells, eosinophils, neutrophils, lymphocytes, macrophages) in nasal lavage fluid compared with OVA-challenged mice.
UPE and dexamethasone treatment reduced OVA-induced sub-epithelial inflammatory cell aggregation and mucosal thickening in nasal and lung tissue on histology.
High-dose UPE (200 mg/kg) reduced OVA-induced goblet cell hyperplasia and mucus overproduction in bronchi and nasal cavity, while low-dose UPE (50 mg/kg) showed no significant improvement.
UPE administration dose-dependently lowered serum anti-OVA IgE levels compared with untreated OVA mice, which had markedly elevated IgE relative to controls.
UPE administration dose-dependently lowered serum anti-OVA IgG1 levels compared with untreated OVA mice.
UPE-treated mice had higher anti-OVA IgG2a levels than untreated OVA mice, similar to the dexamethasone group.
Oral UPE dose-dependently downregulated nasal lavage fluid IL-4 levels, which were significantly elevated in OVA-challenged mice versus controls.
Oral UPE dose-dependently downregulated nasal lavage fluid IL-13 levels, which were significantly elevated in OVA-challenged mice versus controls.
Oral UPE dose-dependently downregulated nasal lavage fluid IL-17 levels, which were significantly elevated in OVA-challenged mice versus controls.

UPE-treated mice showed a non-significant increase in Th1 cytokines IFN-γ and IL-12 in nasal lavage fluid compared with OVA-challenged mice, in contrast to the significant increase seen with dexamethasone.
UPE-treated mice showed a non-significant increase in the Treg cytokine IL-10 in nasal lavage fluid compared with OVA-challenged mice.
UPE and dexamethasone treatment dose-dependently reduced sub-epithelial eosinophil counts in the nasal mucosa, which were significantly elevated in AR mice compared with controls.
Eotaxin (CCL11) was significantly elevated in NALF of OVA-exposed mice and was inhibited dose-dependently by UPE treatment.
Total NF-κB p65 and phosphorylated NF-κB p65 in nasal lavage fluid were significantly elevated in OVA-challenged mice and significantly inhibited by UPE and dexamethasone treatment.
Phosphorylation of MAPKs (ERK, JNK, p38) in lung tissue was significantly elevated in OVA-challenged mice and significantly inhibited by UPE and dexamethasone treatment.
In vitro, UPE pretreatment (0.1, 1, and 10 mg/mL) inhibited compound 48/80-induced degranulation of rat peritoneal mast cells, preserving normal cell morphology.
UPE showed no significant cytotoxicity to rat peritoneal mast cells at concentrations up to 10 mg/mL by MTT assay.
UPE and dexamethasone treatment suppressed mast cell infiltration into the nasal mucosa, which was significantly increased in OVA-challenged mice compared with controls.
Histamine secretion in nasal lavage fluid was upregulated by OVA exposure and downregulated in a dose-dependent manner after UPE treatment.
SSL3 induced adhesion of murine bone marrow-derived mast cells to the culture substratum.
SSL3-induced mast cell adhesion was mediated by fibronectin in an RGD sequence-dependent manner, implicating integrins in the process.
SSL3 was found to bind directly to the anti-adhesive surface protein CD43.
SSL3 induced adhesion of HEK293 cells engineered to express exogenous CD43, indicating CD43 is the target molecule mediating SSL3-induced adhesion.
Mutational analysis showed that the C-terminal region (residues 253-326) of SSL3, specifically residues T285 and H307, is required to induce adhesion.
SSL3 augmented IL-13 production by mast cells in response to immunocomplex and to SSL12 stimulation, indicating a role for SSL3 in enhancing mast cell activation.

Unsupervised PCA of six vascular parameters showed lung vascular remodeling in neonatal mice as early as two weeks after allergen exposure, worsening by three weeks and driven mainly by loss of microcirculation.

Three weeks of HDM allergen exposure reduced pericyte coverage (protrusion volume around endothelial cells) by approximately 42% in the lung adventitia, which slowly recovered toward baseline during the resolution phase.

Adventitial pericyte cell number was not significantly changed during normal mouse development or by HDM allergen exposure, indicating that pericyte loss is driven by reduced protrusion coverage rather than cell number.
After three weeks of HDM exposure, the adventitial microcirculation showed reduced red blood cell (Ter119+) density, and this reduction persisted two weeks into the resolution phase.
HIF-1α expression in vasculature increased after three weeks of HDM exposure, indicating development of hypoxic areas, and slowly normalized during the resolution phase.

Re-exposing previously HDM-treated mice to a single allergen dose two weeks after the end of initial exposure caused a persistent ~26% reduction in pericyte coverage and elevated HIF-1α, despite no change in pericyte number, indicating long-lasting vascular consequences of early-life allergen exposure.

Adventitial CD45+ leukocyte numbers increased significantly after each HDM exposure (about 36% and 40% after 2 and 3 weeks respectively), remaining elevated into early resolution before returning to baseline.

The number of degranulated connective tissue mast cells (CTMCs) increased with each allergen exposure even though total CTMC numbers did not change, indicating allergen-driven mast cell activation rather than mast cell recruitment.
Degranulated mast cell (CTMC) numbers positively correlated with vascular HIF-1α expression, linking mast cell activation to local hypoxia.
The volume of extracellular CTMC granules was negatively correlated with pericyte coverage, showing that regions with larger mast cell granule deposits had greater loss of pericyte morphology.

In vitro, activation of IgE-sensitized mouse lung mast cells by increasing DNP-BSA concentrations caused a dose-dependent reduction in pericyte volume (~30% at 100 ng/ml) without changing pericyte number.
Small pericytes had higher surface avidin (mast cell granule) signal than large pericytes, indicating that direct contact with mast cell granules drives pericyte retraction.
Mast cell degranulation increased intracellular F-actin signal per unit volume within pericytes, consistent with pericyte retraction/polarization.

Contact with mast cell granules decreased N-cadherin surface expression on pericytes by approximately 20% at the highest stimulation dose, implicating loss of this adhesion molecule in endothelial cell-pericyte destabilization.
A general protease inhibitor did not affect mast cell degranulation but prevented pericyte volume loss and N-cadherin downregulation, showing that MC-derived proteases mediate pericyte retraction.

m-MCP6 (mouse mast cell tryptase) was detected in both intracellular and extracellular CTMC granules in the lung adventitia 24 hours after the last HDM challenge, colocalizing with avidin+ granule regions.

Direct exposure of lung pericytes to recombinant m-MCP6 (mouse tryptase) was sufficient to induce an approximately 62% reduction in pericyte volume, confirming tryptase as a direct mediator of pericyte retraction.

Spatial transcriptomic profiling of endobronchial biopsies from children with severe asthma showed increased cellular stress/hypoxia pathway signals and decreased extracellular matrix organization and PDGF signaling pathways in endothelial cell-rich regions compared to controls.
Mast cell FcεRI activation pathway genes were particularly enriched in endothelial cell-rich regions of endobronchial biopsies from children with asthma compared to controls.

Tryptase gene (TPSAB1) expression was increased in endothelial cell-rich regions correlating with higher mast cell proportion, though there was no difference in abundance between asthma and control groups specifically in these regions.

Activated human lung mast cells caused human pericyte retraction (volume loss) without affecting pericyte viability, and volume reduction was greater in pericytes in close contact with mast cell granules, replicating the murine findings.
Flow cytometry of extracellular human mast cell granules revealed heterogeneous content including IL-6 and TNF, with tryptase present in approximately 61.6% of extracellular granules.

The tryptase inhibitor APC-366 did not affect human mast cell degranulation but prevented loss of pericyte volume, demonstrating that tryptase specifically mediates human MC-induced pericyte retraction.

Most studies report lower circulating B-cell counts in idiopathic and connective-tissue-disease-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension compared with healthy controls, though this is not universally observed.

PAH patients show expansion of naive B-cells, plasmablasts and IgA+ plasma cells alongside contraction of the memory B-cell compartment, and these subset anomalies correlate with survival in heritable and idiopathic PAH.
A CD27/IgD double-negative, low-CD21 B-cell subset associated with autoimmunity is expanded in idiopathic PAH patients and correlates with clinical markers of pulmonary hypertension.

In monocrotaline-induced PAH rat lungs, B-cell activation and BCR signalling genes show the strongest correlations with hemodynamic and histological severity, with upregulation of CD79A/B, BTK, CD19 and CD21 that worsens with disease progression.

Intracellular BTK expression is increased in total, naive and memory B-cells from idiopathic and connective-tissue-disease PAH patients, and correlates with the presence of circulating autoantibodies.

B-cell-specific BTK overexpression in transgenic mice exposed to bleomycin induces a pulmonary hypertension phenotype with accumulation of memory B-cells and antibody-secreting cells in mediastinal lymph nodes and production of circulating antibodies against endothelial antigens.

In monocrotaline rats, a BTK inhibitor attenuates right ventricular systolic pressure elevation, pulmonary vascular remodelling, right ventricle hypertrophy and endothelial-mesenchymal transition, although effects may be mediated by macrophage rather than B-cell BTK.

Increased serum IgE levels and IgE+ B-cells are observed in the blood of PAH patients and lungs of experimental pulmonary hypertension models, reflecting Th2-driven class-switching to IgE, which primes mast cells via FcεRI.
In a hypoxia plus ovalbumin mouse model, CD294 deficiency or IL-4/IL-13 neutralisation decreased lung infiltration by IgE+ B-cells and attenuated pulmonary hypertension.

Mast cell inhibition in monocrotaline rats results in lower B-cell lung infiltration, lower circulating autoantibodies and normalised serum IgG levels, with similar effects seen with anti-IL-6 antibody treatment.

In systemic sclerosis patients, cTfh cell counts are higher in the presence of PAH, correlate with circulating plasma cell counts, and produce more IL-21 and CXCL13, driving plasmablast differentiation via an IL-21-dependent mechanism.

Serum BAFF concentrations are similar in systemic sclerosis patients with and without pulmonary hypertension but strongly correlate with clinical markers of pulmonary hypertension severity in SSc-PAH patients.
A pathogenic variant in the gene coding for TACI has been identified as a new causative mutation for PAH, possibly by promoting dysregulated vascular inflammation.

In the United Kingdom national iPAH cohort, serum IgG3 titres are significantly increased compared to healthy controls while other Ig isotypes (IgG, IgM, IgA, IgG1, IgG2, IgG4) are unchanged, possibly reflecting IL-21-driven preferential class-switching.

Unsupervised clustering of whole-blood transcriptome data from the UK iPAH cohort delineated three patient subgroups with incremental mortality risk, with immunoglobulin genes being the top discriminating genes and higher Ig gene expression associated with better survival.

BCR repertoire analyses of B-cells and plasmablasts from PAH patients show no shared CDR3 sequence but over/under-used VDJ recombinations and elevated mutation loads, and monoclonal antibodies derived from iPAH plasmablast clones are autoreactive and polyreactive, consistent with a persistent antigen-driven but patient-specific humoral response.
Older studies observed antinuclear antibody positivity in approximately 40% of idiopathic PAH patients.

Anti-endothelial cell antibodies are more prevalent and at higher titres in PAH patients than healthy controls, and stimulation of endothelial cell lines with seropositive PAH serum induces a pro-inflammatory and pro-adhesive phenotype (increased IL-6, IL-8, CCL2, CCL5, E-selectin, ICAM-1, VCAM-1) without effect on endothelin-1 or apoptosis.

Anti-AT1R and anti-ETAR antibodies are more frequent in SSc-PAH and CTD-PAH than in iPAH, show weak-to-nonexistent correlation with hemodynamics, but predict occurrence of PAH in SSc patients and mortality in SSc-PAH patients.

Anti-ETAR antibodies increase HUVEC permeability, VEGF-A and PDGF-B expression, and pulmonary artery smooth muscle cell proliferation and PDGF receptor-β expression, effects that are annulled by the endothelin receptor antagonist bosentan.

Anti-BMPR2 antibodies were detected in a small fraction of idiopathic PAH patients but none of the healthy controls, and these antibodies recognize the extracellular domain of BMPR2 and attenuate BMP4 signalling in pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells.

IgM and IgG deposits co-localise with C3 and C4 staining in lungs of hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension mice, and immunoglobulin-deficient mice are protected against complement activation, vascular changes and RVSP elevation, an effect restored by immune reconstitution with healthy-control polyvalent IgG.

In hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension mice and monocrotaline rats, treatment with anti-IgE antibodies or mast cell-specific FcεRI deletion normalises hemodynamics, pulmonary vascular thickening/muscularisation, and IL-6 and IL-13 lung expression.
Circulating CD24hi CD27+ regulatory B-cells are decreased in SSc-PAH patients compared to SSc patients without PAH.

In hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension mice, adoptive transfer of Bregs improves hemodynamics and pulmonary vascular remodelling, favours T follicular regulatory cell differentiation over Tfh, and inhibits hypoxia-induced pulmonary artery smooth muscle cell proliferation.

In an NIH multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial of rituximab as add-on therapy in SSc-PAH, the primary outcome (6-minute walk distance change at week 24) did not differ significantly between arms, though a secondary analysis at week 48 favoured rituximab, and a machine-learning-identified biomarker subgroup showed greatest benefit.

Anti-BMPR2 autoantibodies, detected in a small fraction of iPAH patients but none of the healthy controls, bind the extracellular domain of BMPR2 and reduce BMP4 signalling in pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells.
Anti-ALK1 antibodies are present in SLE-PAH patients but not in SLE-no PAH, MCTD-PAH or iPAH patients, indicating a disease-specific autoantibody pattern.
Anti-BMPR1A antibodies are present in SLE-PAH patients but not in SLE-no pulmonary hypertension patients or healthy controls.

IgM and IgG deposits co-localise with complement C3 and C4 staining in the lungs of hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension mice, and immunoglobulin-deficient animals are protected from complement activation, vascular changes and RVSP elevation caused by hypoxia.

In hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension mice and monocrotaline rats, blocking IgE with anti-IgE antibodies or deleting mast-cell FcεRI normalises haemodynamics, pulmonary vascular thickening/muscularisation and IL-6/IL-13 lung expression.
Circulating B-cells from systemic sclerosis patients produce more IL-6 than those from healthy controls.
In a P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1-deficient mouse model of SSc-PAH, IFN-γ-producing B-cells infiltrate the lungs in higher proportion than in control animals.

Circulating CD24hi CD27+ regulatory B-cells (Bregs) are decreased in SSc-PAH patients compared to SSc patients without PAH.

SSc B-cells produce more angiogenic mediators (angiogenin, angiopoietin 1) than healthy controls, but levels do not differ between SSc patients with and without PAH.
Various plasma cell proliferative disorders are characterised by elevated VEGF levels and vascular manifestations including PAH.

Fibroblastic reticular cells and follicular dendritic cells locally produce lymphorganogenic chemokines (CXCL13, CCL19, CCL20, CCL21) that recruit circulating CXCR5+ and/or CCR7+ T- and B-cells to form tertiary lymphoid organs in PAH lungs.

Lung tertiary lymphoid organs in PAH show active germinal-centre reactions, evidenced by Bcl2-Bcl6+Ki67+ germinal-centre B-cells, strong AID overexpression, and CD138+ plasma cells with IgG+/IgA+ cells.

Machine learning analysis of the rituximab SSc-PAH trial identified a subgroup with low rheumatoid factor, IL-12 and IL-17 levels that derived the greatest treatment benefit.

In SSc patients, ibrutinib reduces production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and autoantibodies by peripheral B-cells without altering their IL-10 secretion.

In hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension mice, anti-CD22 antibody treatment worsens haemodynamics, right ventricle hypertrophy and pulmonary vascular remodelling by specifically depleting regulatory B-cells.

TLO-targeted strategies in monocrotaline rats (CCR7 antagonism, LTβR antagonism, VEGFR3 antagonism) reduced pulmonary artery pressure elevation, remodelling and autoantibody production, with stronger effects when given preventively than curatively.

Vaccination against the second extracellular loop of endothelin receptor A generates inhibitory (rather than agonistic) antibodies in monocrotaline rats and improves haemodynamics, right ventricle hypertrophy, and pulmonary artery pathology with no obvious side-effects.

GI motility disorders including diabetic gastroparesis, IBS, and inflammatory bowel disease are frequently associated with reduced interstitial cell of Cajal (ICC) function.
Activated immune cells such as macrophages or dendritic cells may overstimulate enteric neurons, contributing to increased pain and visceral hypersensitivity in IBS patients.
Mucosal macrophages are generally proinflammatory while muscularis macrophages (MMs) tend to be anti-inflammatory under certain conditions.
In a mouse colitis model, monocytes preferentially differentiate into proinflammatory macrophages.
Muscularis macrophages regulate development of the enteric nervous system from birth via transforming growth factor-beta signaling.
Muscularis macrophages typically show high CX3C chemokine receptor 1 (CX3CR1) protein levels and are positive for the myeloid marker integrin alpha-M (ITGAM/CD11b).
Long-lived, tissue-resident muscularis macrophages of embryonic origin are identified by expression of CD4 and TIMD4.
Mucosal macrophages, unlike tissue-resident MMs, are typically replenished by monocytes and characterized by CD14 expression.

Muscularis macrophages are tissue-protective under normal conditions, evidenced by expression of β2 adrenergic receptors, linking β2-adrenergic signaling to anti-inflammatory M2-like macrophage polarization.
Enteric neurons secrete CSF1 to support MM development, while MMs regulate intestinal peristalsis through secretion of BMP2, illustrating bidirectional ENS-MM signaling.
Postnatal (but not earlier) absence of muscularis macrophages results in increased enteric neuronal density and enhanced GI motility, contrary to the MM role seen in mature development.
Csf1op/op mice, which lack muscularis macrophages, have more nitrergic neurons than wild-type mice but show no change in overall neuronal cell density.
Despite close anatomical proximity between MMs and ICCs/PDGFRA-positive cells, a definitive functional connection has not been established.

Inflammatory M1-like macrophages reduce the number of ICCs in vitro, potentially through TNF-alpha expression.

Reintroduction of GI microbiota via fecal transfer reverses antibiotic-induced MM/BMP2/CSF1 loss and improves dysmotility.
Blockade of serotonin signaling impairs the development of myenteric neurons in germ-free mice even after microbiota colonization.
Serotonin regulates ICC proliferation and ameliorates disrupted colonic motility through the 5-HT2B receptor (HTR2B), though direct links to MM involvement remain unclear.
Inflammation in the small intestine prompts macrophages to express inflammatory mediators at higher levels than in normal GI tissue, exacerbating the inflammatory milieu.

Reduced expression of FOXO3 correlates with a shift of macrophages from anti-inflammatory to proinflammatory phenotype in aged mice, and this shift together with FOXO3 deficiency is linked to enteric neuronal loss.
Denervation downregulates anti-inflammatory genes in MMs, suggesting neuronal loss triggers a proinflammatory shift in MMs and a potential feedback loop of further inflammation and neuronal death.
The blood-myenteric barrier is compromised specifically when MMs cluster near enteric ganglia during inflammation, paralleling blood-brain barrier disruption in neuroinflammation.

Reintroducing GI microbiota via fecal transfer reversed the antibiotic-induced macrophage/BMP2/CSF1 deficits and improved dysmotility.
Blockade of serotonin signaling impaired myenteric neuron development in germ-free mice even after microbiota colonization, implicating serotonin in microbiome-driven ENS maturation.

Denervation downregulates anti-inflammatory genes in muscularis macrophages, suggesting neuronal loss triggers a proinflammatory phenotypic shift in these macrophages.
The blood-myenteric barrier is compromised specifically when muscularis macrophages cluster near enteric ganglia during inflammation, paralleling blood-brain barrier disruption in neurodegeneration.

In non-obese diabetic (NOD/ShiLtJ) mice, interleukin-10 treatment increased heme oxygenase 1 (HO1) protein levels in muscularis macrophages and reversed oxidative damage in ICCs.

Patients with post-infectious IBS exhibit high expression levels of the chemokines CCL2 and CCL4.

Reduced expression of forkhead box protein O3 (FOXO3) correlates with a shift of macrophages from anti-inflammatory to proinflammatory phenotype in aged mice, and this shift is linked to neuronal loss in the enteric nervous system.

A prior study cited by the authors found that CFS patients' HRV signals show reduced fractal complexity compared to healthy subjects.

Prior work (Ohashi et al., Burton et al.) found CFS patients' 12-14 day activity signals show reduced fractal complexity compared to controls, though significance depended on the average activity level of the group studied.

Within individual CFS patients, the fractal dimension of activity patterns varied considerably across the three recorded weeks, in several cases exceeding the magnitude of the patient-vs-control difference reported in a prior study.

Spearman rank correlations between each patient's weekly high-level functioning ranking and weekly activity-complexity ranking were inconsistent across patients, so the hypothesis that decreased functioning is linked to lower complexity could not be confirmed.

Within-patient, higher total activity counts in a 3-day window were generally correlated with lower (or unchanged) fractal dimension, i.e. correlations were negative or close to zero for all patients.

Short-term high peaks in activity counts, identified via daily surveys as intensive sports such as fitness or running, momentarily increased the fractal dimension (reduced apparent complexity), contradicting the general trend of higher activity correlating with lower fractal dimension.
Weekly total activity counts were mostly negatively correlated with weekly functioning rankings, but the alignment was not consistent across patients.

A previously published study (Burton et al.) reported average fractal dimensions of 1.14 for healthy controls, 1.16 for active CFS patients, and 1.21 for pervasively inactive CFS patients, indicating progressively reduced complexity with greater CFS-related inactivity.

Prior studies (Ohashi et al., Burton et al.) only found statistically significant fractal-dimension differences versus healthy controls in pervasively inactive CFS patients, not in relatively active CFS patients.

Within each patient's activity sequence, the estimated fractal dimension increased (complexity decreased) at larger aggregation timescales, and this scale-dependence differed in relative ranking between patients depending on which timescale was examined.

Patients with aortic root dilation almost universally had only trivial mitral, tricuspid, or pulmonary valve regurgitation, indicating an absence of significant valvular complications associated with ARD.
Mild aortic regurgitation occurred more often in hEDS patients (2.4%) than HSD patients (0.5%) at first echocardiogram.
Genetic testing of 84 selected hEDS/HSD patients using a 92-gene connective tissue panel identified variants of uncertain significance in 19% of patients, with no pathogenic variants found.

Three hEDS/HSD patients carried polymorphisms in FLNA, with one having mild aortic regurgitation and another having mitral valve prolapse with moderate mitral regurgitation and mild aortic/pulmonary regurgitation.
Two hEDS/HSD patients were identified as carriers for variants in PLOD1, the gene associated with kyphoscoliotic EDS.

Among the 124 children with joint hypermobility, thumb apposition to the forearm was the most frequent Beighton variable (96%), followed by fifth-finger hyperextension (83.1%), elbow hyperextension (79.8%), knee hyperextension (61.3%), and anterior trunk flexion, which was the least frequent (29.8%).

Only 25.7% of children with joint hypermobility had involvement of the axial skeleton together with both upper and lower limbs, the pattern the authors define as true generalized joint hypermobility (GJH), while 39.5% had only upper- plus lower-limb combinations and 28.2% had upper-limb-only involvement.

Beighton scores of 6 and 8 were shown to reflect only upper-limb or combined upper- and lower-limb involvement without axial (trunk) involvement, meaning only BS=7 and BS=9 actually represented true generalized joint hypermobility.
A statistically significant sex difference was found for the anterior trunk flexion (ATF) Beighton variable, which was more frequent among girls than boys.
No statistically significant sex differences were found for the other four Beighton variables (thumb apposition, fifth finger, elbow, and knee hyperextension).
Overall, 81.4% of the children in the sample had a Beighton Score of 6 or higher.

A Beighton Score of exactly 6 was more common among boys (38%), whereas a score of exactly 8 was more common among girls (27%), which the authors interpret as suggestive of greater GJH frequency in females.
For the Beighton Score ≥ 7 category, girls were significantly overrepresented compared with boys.
For Beighton Score ≥ 8 and BS = 9, girls were more frequently represented than boys, but these differences did not reach statistical significance.
Considering the overall Beighton Score distribution, a Mann-Whitney U test showed a statistically significant difference between girls and boys.

Among children exhibiting anterior trunk flexion (ATF), the majority (54.1%) had the maximum Beighton Score of 9, indicating full generalized joint hypermobility involving the axial skeleton and all four limbs.
Among children with thumb-apposition hypermobility, 30.3% had a Beighton Score of 6, which the authors note reflects a localized (non-axial) pattern rather than true GJH.
Children with fifth-finger, elbow, and knee hyperextension had the greatest frequency of a Beighton Score of 8, at 31.1%, 32.3%, and 42.1% respectively.
Patients experienced a median 10-year delay from symptom onset to receiving a diagnosis of hEDS, with a 4-year gap before the initial medical evaluation.
The vast majority of hEDS patients (95.2%) rated receiving a diagnosis as important or highly important to them.
Most patients reported that receiving a diagnosis helped them cope better with their condition and manage symptoms and long-term care.
Patients reported a mostly positive emotional reaction and improved support from caregivers and healthcare providers after receiving an hEDS diagnosis.
Whole exome sequencing identified variants in 317 distinct genes across 906-967 EDS patients, supporting a polygenic/network basis for EDS rather than single-gene causation.
53 EDS patients (49 old enough for comparison) had COL5A1 or COL5A2 variants, the long-recognized classical EDS genes, providing a reference group supporting the relevance of the broader gene set.

Patients with COL5A2 variants had a significantly higher percentage meeting hypermobile EDS criteria and more child clumsiness, hypermobility awareness, and neuro-autonomic findings than patients with COL5A1 variants.
17 POLG variants in 13 EDS patients were linked to neuromuscular and dysautonomia symptoms, suggesting mitochondrial depletion with brain-muscle energy deficiency as a mechanism contributing to EDS.

FLG variants were found in 35 (6.2%) of 568 EDS patients versus 2 (2.4%) of 82 developmental disability patients and only 2.2% of the general population, supporting an autonomic-inflammatory and skin-fragility role rather than the isolated scaly-skin association typically assigned by commercial labs.

Mitochondrial DNA variants were far more prevalent in EDS patients (158) than in developmental disability patients (10), a surprising finding given mitochondrial variants' typical association with severe disability diseases like Leigh syndrome.

Primary nuclear DNA variants had maternal origin significantly more often in EDS patients (35%) than in developmental disability patients (18%), while de novo variants were far more common in DD (48%) than EDS (3.8%).

The novel clinical diagnostic-utility protocol qualified 566 of 568 (99.6%) EDS patients' DNA variants as relevant to their disease profile, compared to only 20 (3.5%) qualified as likely/definitely pathogenic by commercial testing laboratories using standard consensus criteria.

20 genes (24 variants in 21 developmental disability patients) overlapped with EDS patient variants, with different mutations in the same genes feasibly contributing to cognitive disability versus autonomic/neurologic EDS features.

69% of EDS females and 75% of EDS males met 2017 consensus criteria for hypermobile EDS, and comparable hypermobile-EDS majorities were found across almost all gene-variant groups, refuting the assumption that hypermobile EDS is gene-change-free.

Patients with COL1 gene variants had significantly more joint-skeletal problems and fractures (79%) than the overall EDS cohort (51%), consistent with COL1's prior association with brittle bone diseases.

Patients with COL2/9/11 variants (Stickler syndrome-associated) had more MCAS complications (rashes, asthma) than the overall cohort, suggesting Stickler-related arthritis has inflammatory as well as mechanical causes.

EDS patients with VWF and other clotting-related gene variants showed typical EDS profiles with more bruising, striae, and pedal blood pooling, indicating vessel fragility/distensibility from clotting-related connective tissue genes.

EDS patients with COL3A1 (vascular EDS), FBN1 (Marfan), or TGFB/TGFBR (Loeys-Dietz) variants had significantly higher IBS-MCAS finding frequencies than the general EDS cohort, and vascular EDS-related COL3A1 patients showed more bowel irregularity/bloating/dysphagia consistent with bowel ischemia risk.

EDS patients with SCN9A-11A sensory sodium channel gene variants, previously associated with erythromelalgia and hereditary sensory/autonomic neuropathy, showed congruent EDS profiles supporting a role for autonomic/small-fiber dysplasia reinforcing articular symptoms.

18 EDS patients with MT-ATP gene changes related to a disease with neuromuscular and dysautonomia symptoms, and 61 patients overall had changes in genes encoding all 4 mitochondrial respiratory complexes, each showing a similar EDS-dysautonomia finding profile.

Genes classified as impacting tissue laxity produced more increases than decreases not only in tissue laxity findings (67% vs 33%) but also disproportionately increased dysautonomia (61%) and neuromuscular (71%) findings, supporting a reciprocal articulo-autonomic cycle.

EDS females had significantly higher history/physical finding category totals than EDS males (37/19 vs 27/17) and higher frequencies of nearly all mechanism-related finding classes except deformation, confirming previously demonstrated greater disease severity in females.

The authors propose that a holistic diagnostic approach integrating joint, skin, autonomic (POTS, MCAS, IBS), and neuromuscular findings alongside broad genomic screening could shorten EDS diagnostic delays currently averaging 14 years.

The patient carried a pathogenic deletion of exon 1 in COL5A1, predicted to cause loss of transcription/translation of the affected allele and resulting COL5A1 haploinsufficiency, confirming a diagnosis of classic EDS.
Arteriopathy, including aneurysms, dissections, and rupture (as seen in this patient's bilateral iliac artery events), is described as a rare complication of classic EDS.

Genetic testing including deletion/duplication analysis found no pathogenic variants in COL3A1, excluding a diagnosis of vascular EDS despite the patient meeting clinical diagnostic criteria for VEDS.
In a prior multi-institutional Low Frequency Disease Consortium cohort of patients submitted for suspected VEDS, nearly 10% had nonpathogenic variants in COL3A1 and thus did not actually have VEDS.
COL5A1 variants have been described in cases presenting with an appearance resembling fibromuscular dysplasia.
Patients with classic EDS undergoing repair of arterial aneurysms or dissections should be counseled about a known increased risk of bleeding.

The patient underwent open surgical repair (Dacron interposition and end-to-side bypasses) of a right common iliac artery dissection/aneurysm, complicated postoperatively by a large retroperitoneal hematoma and ileus, but ultimately stabilized and remained well at 2-year follow-up.
Aortic root dilation, a recognized vascular manifestation of classic EDS, was not present in this patient.
Easy bruising (since childhood) and hernias, both minor diagnostic criteria for classic EDS, were observed in this patient.
Six other previously reported cases in the literature describe patients with genetically confirmed classic EDS who also had iliac artery arteriopathy, similar to the present case.
A man with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome developed recurrent hemothorax shortly after taking sildenafil obtained through an online prescription service.

The patient's underlying Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, characterized by collagen abnormalities and vessel fragility, is proposed as a predisposing factor for vascular complications from PDE-5 inhibitor use.
Prior case reports describe PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) associated with aortic dissection in men with predisposing factors such as hypertension and cocaine use.
In mouse models, pre-existing abdominal aortic aneurysms were shown to worsen after use of PDE-5 inhibitors.

Online prescription services investigated by researchers posing as patients with contraindications (e.g., coronary artery disease, nitrate use) still resulted in 20-30% receiving sildenafil prescriptions.
Pediatric patients undergoing minimally invasive sutured fixation for slipping rib syndrome reported significantly less pain at one-month follow-up compared to preoperative baseline.
Preoperative analgesic use decreased by 80% following minimally invasive sutured fixation.
Eight of the 31 pediatric patients diagnosed with slipping rib syndrome had joint hypermobility, identified alongside traumatic causes in three patients.
A substantial subset of patients required additional surgery after initial suture fixation, with seven undergoing a second operation, three a third, and one patient undergoing five total operations.
Recurrent pain after suture fixation surgery was reported in six patients.
Athletes with hyperextended (hypermobile) knees had significantly shorter leg length and shin length compared to athletes without knee hyperextension.

Athletes with hyperextended knees had a significantly lower hamstrings-to-quadriceps (H/Q) strength ratio at 60°/s compared to athletes without knee hyperextension, reflecting reduced hamstring strength relative to quadriceps.
The functional H/Q strength ratio measured at 180°/s did not significantly differ between athletes with and without knee hyperextension.
Discriminant analysis showed that leg length, shin length, and the H/Q ratio at 60°/s accounted for classifying athletes into hypermobile versus nonhypermobile groups.

A weak, statistically significant negative correlation was found between degree of knee hypermobility and H/Q ratio at 60°/s, such that athletes with a lower H/Q ratio had increased degrees of knee hypermobility.
Prior literature cited by the authors found no correlation between body mass index and knee hypermobility in a study of 96 girls aged 16-18.
Children with germline PTEN mutations showed overall adaptive behaviour levels below the typical range, with no marked relative differences between adaptive domains.

Children with PTEN mutations showed higher levels of autism spectrum condition (ASC)-related difficulties, including sensory experiences, compared with typically developing children, with restrictive/repetitive behaviour possibly most affected.
ASC-related difficulties and sensory processing atypicality strongly correlated with reported joint hypermobility in children with PTEN mutations.
Despite elevated ASC phenomenology, social motivation was relatively preserved in children with PTEN mutations.
Overall anxiety levels were elevated in children with PTEN mutations compared with normative data.
Social anxiety in children with PTEN mutations was comparable with normative data, unlike other anxiety domains.
Elevated anxiety in children with PTEN mutations was associated with greater sensory processing atypicality and higher levels of reported joint hypermobility.
Social anxiety in children with PTEN mutations was comparable to normative data, in contrast to overall elevated anxiety.
Self-injurious behaviour was reported as common among children with PTEN mutations.

In females, increasing severity of neonatal hip dysplasia on ultrasound was associated with a graded increase in the proportion of borderline or dysplastic hips (by center-edge angle) at skeletal maturity.
In males, no significant association was found between neonatal hip dysplasia phenotype and adult acetabular dysplasia at skeletal maturity.
In females, adult generalized joint hypermobility was associated with a history of sonographic neonatal hip instability.
In females, adult generalized joint hypermobility was associated with adult acetabular dysplasia at skeletal maturity.
FM patients showed significantly higher depressive symptom scores than healthy controls on the Beck Depression Inventory.
FM patients had markedly higher disease impact/severity scores (FIQ-R) than healthy controls, confirming greater functional and symptomatic burden.
FM patients scored significantly higher on the Widespread Pain Index and Symptom Severity Scale than healthy controls, consistent with diagnostic criteria.
FM patients reported significantly lower quality of life (SF-36) than healthy controls.
FM patients reported significantly greater fatigue, numbness, and pain intensity (previous week and month) than healthy controls on visual analogue scales.
Baseline pressure pain threshold (PPT) was similar between FM patients and healthy controls, indicating no group difference in basal mechanical pain sensitivity.
The sequential CPM paradigm did not distinguish FM patients from healthy controls, with similar (near-zero) CPM magnitude in both groups.
FM patients showed a significantly smaller (less efficient) parallel CPM effect than healthy controls, indicating impaired descending pain inhibition.
Across all participants, the parallel CPM paradigm produced a significantly greater pain-inhibitory (CPM) effect than the sequential paradigm.

There was a significant Paradigm x Group interaction, such that the difference between FM patients and healthy controls in CPM effect was significant only for the parallel paradigm, not the sequential one.
Using the parallel paradigm, a significantly greater proportion of healthy controls (87%) than FM patients (57%) were classified as CPM responders.
Using the sequential paradigm, the proportion of CPM responders did not differ significantly between FM patients (30%) and healthy controls (39%).

Binary logistic regression using the parallel CPM effect as the sole predictor correctly classified 69.6% of participants as FM patients or healthy controls, with the smaller CPM magnitude predicting FM status.
The sequential CPM effect did not significantly predict group classification (FM vs healthy control) in the logistic regression model.
Among FM patients, parallel-CPM responders had lower disease severity (FIQ-R) scores than non-responders, but this difference did not survive Bonferroni-Holm correction for multiple comparisons.
Parallel-CPM responder FM patients unexpectedly showed a more widespread pain distribution (higher WPI) than non-responders, a difference that also did not survive multiple-comparison correction.

Neither sequential nor parallel CPM magnitude significantly correlated with any clinical variable (depression, disease severity, symptom severity, widespread pain, quality of life, fatigue, numbness, or pain intensity) in FM patients.
Reserpine administration induced a fibromyalgia-like model characterized by reduced mechanical nociceptive threshold (mechanical allodynia).
Active tDCS reversed the reduction in mechanical nociceptive threshold induced by the fibromyalgia-like model.
Pregabalin had no effect on the mechanical nociceptive threshold in the fibromyalgia-like model.
Active tDCS reversed the fibromyalgia model-induced decrease in serum BDNF levels.
Neither pregabalin nor tDCS altered TNF-α levels in brainstem, cerebral cortex, or serum.
The fibromyalgia-like model induced an increase in grooming time, a decrease in unprotected head-dipping (NPHD), and a decrease in rearing, indicative of anxiety-like behavior.
Active tDCS reversed the fibromyalgia model-induced increase in grooming time, an anxiety-like behavior measure.
Pregabalin reversed the fibromyalgia model-induced decrease in unprotected head-dipping (NPHD), an anxiety-like behavior measure.
tDCS treatment reversed the reserpine-induced increase in grooming time, a marker of anxiety-like behavior, in the fibromyalgia-like model.
Pregabalin reversed the reserpine-induced decrease in unprotected head-dipping (NPHD), an anxiety-related behavior, in the fibromyalgia-like model.
Overall, tDCS was found to be more effective than pregabalin in controlling nociceptive and anxiety-like behaviors in the rat fibromyalgia-like model.
Muscle oxygen saturation increased after intervention in all four groups, with the largest increase in the Suit+VR group (15.6%) followed by Exercise (11.72%), Suit (4.7%), and Control (1.52%).
HHb decreased (1.97 g/dL in Suit+VR, 1.43 g/dL in Exercise) while O2Hb increased (1.77 g/dL in Suit+VR, 1.34 g/dL in Exercise) after intervention, proportionally to SmO2 changes.
Effect sizes for SmO2, HHb, and O2Hb changes were small/below threshold (<0.4) in the Control and Suit groups but large (0.88-0.98) in the Exercise and Suit+VR groups.

Numeric Rating Scale pain scores decreased in all groups post-intervention, with the largest decrease in Suit+VR (2.21 points), followed by Suit (1.46), Exercise (1.23), and Control (~1 point), with no significant between-group differences.
Pressure pain threshold at the knee significantly increased after the Suit+VR (0.61 kg) and Exercise (0.42 kg) interventions, with no significant change at other sites/groups except as noted.
FEV1 significantly decreased by 1.07 L after the Suit+VR intervention, while no significant changes were seen in other respiratory variables/groups.
Chest perimeter difference (inspiration vs expiration) significantly increased after the Suit (0.65 cm) and Exercise (0.54 cm) interventions.
Cortical arousal (CFFT) significantly increased by 1.4 Hz in the Control group and 1.7 Hz in the Exercise group after intervention.
Chair stand test repetitions significantly improved after the Suit (1.41 reps) and Exercise (1.58 reps) interventions.
Handgrip strength significantly increased in the Suit (0.44 kg) and Suit+VR (0.9 kg) groups, while it decreased in the Control group (0.53 kg).
One-leg balance time increased in Suit+VR (right leg, +11.79 s) and Exercise (left leg, +13.28 s) groups but decreased in the Suit group (right leg, -12.15 s).

Hand and index finger temperature decreased after intervention in the Control, Suit, and Suit+VR groups (significant for Control and Suit hand temperature), while it increased in the Exercise group, interpreted as reflecting a shift toward reduced sympathetic and increased parasympathetic activity.
Fibromyalgia patients typically exhibit higher baseline sympathetic nervous system activation compared to healthy controls, consistent with prior research cited by the authors.

Fibromyalgia patients' baseline data mirrored prior reports of lower SmO2 and O2Hb and higher HHb levels compared to healthy controls, consistent with theorized mitochondrial dysfunction and inadequate ATP production.
Mitochondrial dysfunction in fibromyalgia is associated with significantly lower muscle oxygen saturation, sometimes as low as 20% compared to a normal level of approximately 75%.
Anxiety disorders occur in approximately 60% and depression in 14-36% of fibromyalgia patients, compared to 6.6% in the healthy population.
Only about one in four fibromyalgia patients achieves a 30% reduction in pain with antidepressant treatment, and no single medication has shown efficacy in more than half of treated patients.

The combination of the EXOPULSE Mollii suit with VR or with a 1-hour exercise session showed augmented psychophysiological benefits over the suit used in isolation, particularly for muscle oxygenation and pain.
Serum levels of the microbial AhR ligand 3-IAld inversely correlated with multiple sclerosis disease duration in a cohort of 35 MS patients.
Serum 3-IAld and IAA levels did not significantly differ according to sex, age, MS type, treatment status, disease activity, or EDSS score in the MS cohort.

Using a published metagenome dataset, 3-IAld-producing bacteria (Arat+) were not less abundant in MS patients compared to healthy controls, despite previously reported lower Lactobacilli abundance in relapsing-remitting MS.

Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation showed that 3-IAld binds the AhR PAS-B domain via hydrogen bonds and π–π stacking with residues Gln377, Ser330, Tyr316 and His285, overlapping with residues required for L-kynurenine binding.
MEFs reconstituted with AhR mutants H285A, Y316A, or Y316A/Q377A lost 3-IAld-induced Cyp1a1 reporter activity compared to wild-type AhR.
In contrast to L-kynurenine, 3-IAld showed higher affinity for the Q377A AhR mutant than for WT AhR, resulting in increased reporter activity.
Systemic i.p. administration of 3-IAld in mice produced a peak serum concentration at 3 hours post-injection, with low brain levels not significantly different between treated and vehicle groups.

Systemic 3-IAld administration shifted tryptophan metabolism toward the serotonin (Tph1) branch rather than activating the IDO pathway (unlike L-kynurenine), particularly evident in serum of treated mice.
In bone marrow-derived mast cells, 3-IAld induced Tph1 expression via AhR, but only following IgE pre-incubation of the cells.
Ahr-deficient BMDMCs stimulated with 1 µM 3-IAld showed significantly downregulated Cyp1a1 expression, suggesting 3-IAld may act on other xenobiotic receptors besides AhR.
Treatment with 1 µM 3-IAld increased serotonin (5-HT) release from bone marrow-derived mast cells.

Tph1 expression was not induced by 3-IAld in mast-cell-deficient KitW/KitW–v mice compared to WT littermates in peripheral lymph nodes at 6 hours post-administration, confirming mast cells as the source of the Tph1 induction.
Human CD34-derived mast cells were more sensitive to 3-IAld than murine mast cells, with 0.1 µM 3-IAld sufficient to induce both Tph1 and Cyp1A1 expression.
Despite being more abundant in human serum than 3-IAld, IAA did not activate human mast cells (no induction of Cyp1A1/Tph1).
Cyp1a1, but not Tph1, was induced in CD4+ T cells in response to 3-IAld, indicating cell-type specificity of the Tph1 response to mast cells.
Western blot analysis confirmed nuclear translocation of AhR in bone marrow-derived mast cells exposed to 3-IAld, confirming AhR activation.
3-IAld treatment did not significantly alter mast cell degranulation as measured by β-hexosaminidase release.
3-IAld decreased ROS release from mast cells in an AhR-dependent manner.
3-IAld at concentrations from 1 to 100 µM did not bind murine PXR, excluding a role for this xenobiotic receptor in mast cell responses to 3-IAld.

In bone marrow-derived mast cells, 3-IAld induced Tph1 expression via AhR only after IgE pre-incubation, while AhR-deficient mast cells stimulated with 3-IAld showed a paradoxical significant downregulation of Cyp1a1 expression.
Treatment with 1 µM 3-IAld increased 5-HT release from bone marrow-derived mast cells and increased Tph1 expression in ex vivo sorted mast cells.
Tph1 expression was not induced by 3-IAld in mast-cell-deficient KitW/KitW-v mice compared to WT littermates in peripheral lymph nodes, demonstrating mast cells are required for the Tph1 response.

Human CD34-derived mast cells were more sensitive to 3-IAld than murine mast cells, with 0.1 µM 3-IAld inducing both Tph1 and Cyp1A1, whereas human mast cells were not sensitive to IAA despite its higher abundance in human serum.
In CD4+ T cells, 3-IAld induced Cyp1a1 but not Tph1 expression, contrasting with the dual induction seen in mast cells.
Western blotting confirmed nuclear translocation of AhR in mast cells exposed to 3-IAld, confirming that Cyp1A1 induction is due to genuine AhR activation.
3-IAld did not modulate mast cell degranulation but decreased ROS release in an AhR-dependent manner.
3-IAld induced Tgfβ and Il10 mRNA expression and protein release in mast cells, similar to the effect of L-Kynurenine.
3-IAld-induced mast cell activation increased IL-9 production, a key mediator of mast cell recruitment.
3-IAld increased IL-6 expression and release from mast cells in an AhR-dependent manner, a response that differs from what has been reported in monocytes.

Systemic 3-IAld treatment protected WT mice from EAE, with minimal clinical progression that resolved and no myelin loss or inflammatory infiltration in the spinal cord, whereas untreated WT mice and both treated and untreated Ahr-/- mice showed severe pathology with high inflammatory infiltration and demyelination.
