Reconstitution of mast cell-deficient KitW/KitW-v mice with WT mast cells restored the ability of 3-IAld to reduce EAE clinical signs, compared to non-reconstituted KitW/KitW-v mice.
Mast cell-deficient KitW/KitW-v mice exhibited delayed EAE onset compared to mast cell-competent WT littermates, confirming a pathogenic role for mast cells in EAE.
3-IAld treatment increased Cyp1a1 and Tph1 expression in cervical lymph nodes in vivo, along with increased Il10 and Il17 mRNA in the T cell cytokine signature.

In Tph1-/- mice, 3-IAld treatment failed to reduce EAE clinical scores and instead strongly promoted Il17 expression in cervical lymph nodes, explaining why 3-IAld exacerbated EAE symptoms in these mice.

Induction of Tph1 and Cyp1a1 expression, as well as 5-HT release, was not observed in the spinal cord upon 3-IAld treatment, indicating the AhR-Tph1 mast cell axis acts peripherally rather than within the CNS.
Ahr-deficient mice did not show a significantly susceptible or resistant phenotype to EAE compared to WT animals, reflecting the complex, context-dependent role of AhR in autoimmune inflammation.
Parents classified as High CI on the QEESI were 4.2 times more likely to report having a child diagnosed with autism than parents classified as Low CI.
Parents classified as High CI were 2.3 times more likely to report having a child diagnosed with ADHD than parents classified as Low CI.
Comparing the highest to lowest decile of total chemical intolerance scores among parents yielded a relative risk of 5.7 for reporting a child with autism.
Comparing the highest to lowest decile of total symptom scores among parents yielded a relative risk of 7.1 for reporting a child with autism.
Comparing the first and last deciles of chemical intolerance scores yielded a relative risk of 2.1 for reporting a child with ADHD.
Comparing the first and last deciles of total symptom scores yielded a relative risk of 2.8 for reporting a child with ADHD.
The odds ratio linking parental High CI to reported autism in offspring increased from 3.01 in the authors' 2015 study to 5.29 in the current study.
The odds ratio linking parental High CI to reported ADHD in offspring increased from 2.3 in the authors' 2015 study to 3.18 in the current study.
5.5% of Low CI parents versus 24.2% of High CI parents reported having a child diagnosed with autism.

Protracted antibiotic use for difficult-to-treat infections (prostate, skin, tonsils, GI tract, sinuses) was strongly associated with TILT/Chemical Intolerance in an earlier study cited by the authors.
The authors propose that toxic exposures alter mast cells (potentially via epigenetic mechanisms), and this mast cell alteration is the underlying biomechanism for chemical intolerance and TILT.

The authors state that xenobiotics with molecular weight below 10,000 Daltons, which includes most pesticides, plasticizers, fragrances, and food additives, initiate mast cell-mediated cell-mediated immunity (delayed-type hypersensitivity).
Mast cell-stabilizing medication (cromolyn) and H1/H2 antihistamines, which block mast cell inflammatory mediators, appear useful for treating some individuals with autism and ADHD.
Aripiprazole and risperidone are FDA-approved medications for autism that can alleviate self-aggressive, angry, and/or irritable behaviors.
Maternal use of artificial sweeteners during pregnancy has recently been shown (in a cited study) to increase the risk of autism in boys threefold.

In an earlier study by the authors, the most frequently cited initiating exposures for chemical intolerance were mold (15.6%), pesticides (11.5%), medical/surgical procedures (11.3%), remodeling/new construction (10.7%), fires/combustion products (6.4%), and implants (1.6%).
Sophoraflavanone G (SFG) directly inhibited Syk enzymatic activity with an IC50 of 2.2 μM.
SFG suppressed IgE/BSA-induced mast cell degranulation in RBL-2H3 cells in a dose-dependent manner without significant cytotoxicity below 10.0 μM within 24 h.
SFG reduced TNF-α production in RBL-2H3 mast cells following IgE/BSA stimulation.
SFG reduced IL-4 production in RBL-2H3 mast cells following IgE/BSA stimulation.
SFG inhibited PLCγ1 phosphorylation/activity downstream of Syk in mast cells in a dose-dependent manner.
SFG inhibited activation of AKT, Erk1/2, p38, and JNK downstream of Syk in mast cells in a dose-dependent manner.
In a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model, SFG reduced ear swelling.
SFG reduced COX-2 expression in the passive cutaneous anaphylaxis mouse model.
SFG dose-dependently reduced AKT activation/phosphorylation downstream of Syk in mast cells.
SFG dose-dependently reduced Erk1/2 activation downstream of Syk in mast cells.
SFG dose-dependently reduced p38 MAPK activation downstream of Syk in mast cells.
SFG dose-dependently reduced JNK activation downstream of Syk in mast cells.
In a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model, SFG treatment reduced IgE-mediated ear swelling.
SFG reduced mast cell degranulation in vivo in the PCA mouse model.
SFG reduced COX-2 expression in the PCA mouse model.
In the passive cutaneous anaphylaxis mouse model, SFG treatment reduced ear tissue expression of COX-2.
In the passive cutaneous anaphylaxis mouse model, SFG treatment reduced ear tissue expression of IL-4 in vivo.
The review proposes that mast cell activation is a key mediator linking Helicobacter pylori infection and metabolic syndrome to neuroinflammation, vascular dysfunction, and neurodegeneration.

H. pylori infection and metabolic syndrome are proposed to jointly activate mast cells, contributing to obesity, dyslipidemia, diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, vascular dysfunction and arterial stiffness.
Meningeal mast cells can be activated by triggers such as stress and toxins, leading to vascular changes and neurodegeneration.

H. pylori and metabolic syndrome-related mast cell activation is linked to vasculitis and thromboembolic events that increase risk of cardio-cerebrovascular and neurodegenerative disorders, as well as to gut dysbiosis-associated neurodegeneration.
Galectin-3 overexpression is cited as one of the mechanisms linking H. pylori infection and metabolic syndrome to cardio-cerebrovascular and neurodegenerative disease pathophysiology.
Using temperature threshold testing (TTT), 63% of type 2 diabetic patients screened positive for small fiber neuropathy.
Patients in the small fiber neuropathy group were significantly older than those in the non-neuropathy group.
Duration of diabetes was significantly greater in patients with small fiber neuropathy than in those without.
Systolic blood pressure was higher in the neuropathy group but did not reach statistical significance.
Postprandial blood sugar (PPBS) values were higher in the neuropathy group, though the difference was not statistically significant.
The lipid profile was similar between the neuropathy and non-neuropathy groups.
The MNSI Part B (clinical examination) score was significantly higher in the small fiber neuropathy group.
The MNSI Part A (symptom questionnaire) scores were similar between neuropathy and non-neuropathy groups, indicating symptomatic detection lagged behind the electrophysiological (TTT) findings.
Warm (hot) temperature thresholds were significantly higher in all four limbs in the small fiber neuropathy group compared to the non-neuropathy group.
Cold temperature thresholds were significantly lower in all four limbs in the small fiber neuropathy group compared to the non-neuropathy group.
Age and years since diabetes diagnosis were positively correlated with the presence of small fiber neuropathy.
Hot (warm) thresholds of both upper and lower limbs showed a strong positive correlation with neuropathy, more so than cold thresholds.
Cold thresholds of both upper and lower limbs showed a weak negative correlation with neuropathy, weaker than the association seen with hot thresholds.
HbA1c values were comparable between the small fiber neuropathy and non-neuropathy groups, contrary to some prior reports linking higher HbA1c to diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
Gastrointestinal symptoms were present in 85% of pediatric SFN patients, with constipation being the most common at 50%.
Autonomic dysfunction, including orthostasis and temperature dysregulation, was observed in 61.5% of pediatric SFN patients, which was not statistically significant.
Somatosensory symptoms such as pain or numbness were seen in 85% of pediatric SFN patients, a statistically significant finding.
SFN was diagnosed via skin biopsy showing epidermal nerve fiber density below the 5th percentile from the left distal leg (calf).
The high prevalence of constipation in SFN patients correlated with abnormal results on GI motility testing.
Absolute IENFD values were significantly lower in the DM1 group compared to a healthy reference group.
IENFD Z-scores, adjusted for age and gender, were also significantly lower in DM1 patients compared to reference values.
Chronic pain was reported by 17 of 20 (85%) DM1 patients in this study.

Six of the 17 patients with chronic pain described symptoms possibly indicating neuropathic pain (burning or lancinating pain in the feet), while 14 reported other pain qualities (deep, aching muscle/musculoskeletal pain), with three reporting both types.

Ten of 20 DM1 patients had abnormal findings on nerve conduction studies (NCS), quantitative sensory testing (QST), and/or IENFD (skin biopsy), individually or in combination, indicating large and/or small fiber neuropathy.
Only two patients (both female, aged 37 and 40) had mild depletion of intraepidermal nerve fibers on skin biopsy, and neither reported symptoms typical of neuropathic pain.

Patients with large fiber neuropathy on NCS had significantly lower mean muscle strength than those without, and CTG repeat number tended to be higher in the large fiber neuropathy group though this did not reach significance.
Patients with absent deep tendon reflexes (n=14) had significantly lower muscle strength compared to patients with normal reflexes.

Decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes were found in at least two sites in the lower extremities in 14 of 20 patients, and decreased distal sensibility to pinprick or light touch was found in 6 patients.
Of six patients reporting distal foot pain, two had pathological QST findings and one had abnormal NCS; these three also had clinical hyperalgesia for pinprick in the painful area.
None of the DM1 patients in this study met the Besta or Neurodiab diagnostic criteria for definite small fiber neuropathy, despite objective findings of reduced IENFD in some patients.

PGP9.5 immunoreactivity was concentrated in the varicose bulges of intraepidermal nerve fibers, confirming that discontinuous THG dot signals correspond to unmyelinated free intraepidermal nerve endings (FINEs).

The authors developed discontinuity third harmonic generation microscopy (dTHGM), a label-free imaging method exploiting the Gouy phase shift effect to detect discontinuous varicose structures of unmyelinated free intraepidermal nerve endings (FINEs) using a tightly focused 1,260-nm femtosecond laser beam.

In vivo dTHGM imaging showed that dot-like bead-string FINE signals in mouse toe tips disappeared completely 48 hours after spared nerve injury (SNI) surgery in all three mice tested, consistent with known FINE degeneration timelines.
The IENF index derived from in vivo dTHGM imaging was significantly lower in patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) compared to controls.
The IENF index from in vivo dTHGM imaging was highly correlated with IENF density from skin biopsies in patients with DPN.

Prior literature comparing corneal confocal microscopy (CCM) and skin biopsy showed low correlation between the two methods for detecting nerve fiber loss in patients with recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes, suggesting SFN does not develop simultaneously in different organs.
The vagus nerve mediates bidirectional gut-brain communication and its disruption is implicated in the pathogenesis of irritable bowel syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease.
Stress is described as playing a role in the pathogenesis of IBS and IBD, consistent with a biopsychosocial disease model.

Current pharmacological treatments for IBS and IBD are described as having side effects, being costly, not curative, and losing efficacy over time, contributing to poor patient satisfaction and adherence.
Vagus nerve stimulation is proposed as a non-drug therapy targeting the gut-brain axis for treating IBS and IBD.
Hypnosis is proposed as a non-drug therapy targeting the gut-brain axis for treating IBS and IBD.
Ketotifen reduced ACTA2 (αSMA) mRNA expression in TGFβ1-activated HDFa fibroblasts compared to TGFβ1 treatment alone.
Ketotifen also inhibited TGFβ1-induced upregulation of ACTA2 gene expression in WS1 dermal fibroblasts.
Ketotifen alone (without TGFβ1) considerably decreased ACTA2 expression in resting WS1 fibroblasts.
Ketotifen had no effect on ACTA2 expression in resting (unstimulated) HDFa fibroblasts.
Ketotifen reduced αSMA protein levels (western blot) in TGFβ1-activated HDFa fibroblasts compared to TGFβ1 alone.
Ketotifen did not alter COL1A1 mRNA expression in HDFa fibroblasts at rest or following TGFβ1 activation.
Ketotifen significantly reduced secreted pro-collagen 1α1 protein levels in TGFβ1-activated HDFa fibroblasts.
Ketotifen reduced fibronectin protein levels in TGFβ1-activated HDFa fibroblasts.
Ketotifen did not affect fibroblast viability or induce apoptosis (Annexin-V/7-AAD) compared to controls, indicating no cytotoxicity at doses used.

Immunofluorescence showed dose-dependent reduction in per-cell αSMA+ staining in ketotifen-treated TGFβ1-activated fibroblasts, accompanied by a shift from stellate to compact, spindle-shaped morphology.
Low-dose (10 μM) ketotifen decreased CNN1 expression in resting WS1 fibroblasts but had no effect in resting HDFa fibroblasts.
Higher-dose (25 μM) ketotifen decreased both CNN1 and TAGLN gene expression in unstimulated WS1 and HDFa fibroblasts.
In TGFβ1-activated fibroblasts, ketotifen reduced both CNN1 and TAGLN expression in both WS1 and HDFa cells, reversing the TGFβ1-induced increase in these cytoskeletal genes.
Ketotifen did not alter YAP1 mRNA levels in control or TGFβ1-treated fibroblasts.
Ketotifen increased YAP phosphorylation at serine 127 in both resting and TGFβ1-activated fibroblasts, promoting cytoplasmic retention of YAP.
Ketotifen reduced transcription of WWTR1 (TAZ) in TGFβ1-activated fibroblasts compared to TGFβ1 alone.
Total TAZ protein levels were reduced following ketotifen treatment of TGFβ1-activated fibroblasts compared to TGFβ1-activated controls.
Ketotifen impaired AKT phosphorylation at Ser473 in TGFβ1-activated fibroblasts compared to TGFβ1 treatment alone, suggesting a PI3K/AKT-dependent anti-fibrotic mechanism.
In a long-term model, ketotifen treatment given after cessation of TGFβ1 stimulation still decreased ACTA2 and CNN1 expression compared to control media post-TGFβ1.

Ketotifen reduced the contractile ability of fibroblasts in a fibroblast-populated collagen lattice (FPCL) assay; at 4h control gels contracted to <50% of original size while ketotifen-treated gels remained around 70%.
Ketotifen-treated TGFβ1-activated fibroblasts seeded into collagen gels showed reduced contractility at 4- and 8-hours compared to fibroblasts activated with TGFβ1 alone.
ACTA2 gene expression was significantly decreased as early as 4 hours after ketotifen treatment in TGFβ1-pretreated fibroblasts.
Oral ketotifen significantly reduced collagen density in bleomycin-induced fibrotic mouse skin compared to untreated fibrotic skin.
Ketotifen reduced Scar Elevation Index (dermal thickness) in bleomycin-treated fibrotic mouse skin compared to fibrotic skin without ketotifen.
There was no significant difference in the ratio of collagen type I to type III in bleomycin-induced fibrotic skin with or without ketotifen treatment.
Ketotifen did not alter fibroblast migration in an in vitro scratch assay compared to untreated resting fibroblasts.
Ketotifen did not affect fibroblast proliferation, as measured by cell proliferation dye dilution via flow cytometry.
In a bleomycin-induced mouse model of dermal fibrosis, oral ketotifen treatment significantly reduced collagen density in fibrotic skin compared to fibrotic skin from untreated mice.
Ketotifen-treated bleomycin-fibrotic mouse skin showed a reduced Scar Elevation Index (dermal thickness) compared to fibrotic skin without ketotifen.
Ketotifen treatment did not alter the ratio of type I to type III collagen in fibrotic mouse skin, as assessed by picrosirius red staining and birefringence imaging.
Ketotifen did not alter fibroblast migration in an in vitro scratch assay, with similar rates of scratch closure observed with or without ketotifen treatment.
Ketotifen did not affect fibroblast proliferation, as measured by cell proliferation dye fluorescence intensity via flow cytometry after 24 h.
Plasma TGF-β levels were found to significantly correlate with the occurrence of pulmonary fibrosis following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A meta-analysis of 2000 patients found the prevalence of post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis to be 44.9%, with higher rates among males than females and among patients with a history of COPD.

In a study of long-term pulmonary complications, 52.6% of COVID-19 survivors showed abnormalities on high-resolution CT six months post-infection, rising to 57% among those who had required high-flow nasal cannula, NIV, or invasive mechanical ventilation.

A CD163+ macrophage population expressing genes for TGF-β, osteopontin, and legumain acts as a profibrotic trigger in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients and strongly interacts with fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, and pericytes to promote lung fibrosis.
IL-4 and IL-13 levels were increased in patients with respiratory distress due to SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with healthy individuals, confirmed by RT-PCR.
Following anti-IL-13 treatment in patients with severe COVID-19, Arg1 expression was substantially downregulated, supporting a role for IL-13 in COVID-19-associated pulmonary fibrosis pathogenesis.

Treating human bronchial epithelial cells with IL-13 reduced COVID-19 viral RNA in these cells, suggesting a potential beneficial effect of IL-13 in some patients that contrasts with its profibrotic role.
A study by Maranatha et al. found a statistically significant correlation between elevated TNF-α serum levels in COVID-19 patients and subsequent development of pulmonary fibrosis.
Proudfoot et al. demonstrated that anti-TNFR1 antibodies may reduce pulmonary inflammation and endothelial injury, suggesting TNF-α signaling through TNFR1 contributes to lung disease.
Administration of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells reduced hyperinflammation in COVID-19 ARDS via TNFR2 signaling.
One author found no statistically significant relationship between EGFR overexpression and pulmonary fibrosis, contradicting the proposed EGFR–STAT1/STAT3 profibrotic mechanism.
COVID-19 patients showed higher levels of Galectin-1, Galectin-3, and prostaglandin E2 compared to healthy patients.
Galectin-1 was positively associated with IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10, IL-23, and IL-33 in COVID-19 patients, and its level was directly proportional to IL-10, especially in stage III COVID-19.

CRP levels were positively correlated with Galectin-9, a lectin shown to induce monocyte and NK cell production of IL-6 and TNF-α and to enhance viral spike protein affinity for type II alveolar epithelial cells.
Patients who developed pulmonary fibrosis after COVID-19 had lower plasma IFN-γ (2-fold), IFN-α2 (1.3-fold), and MCP-3 (1.3-fold) levels compared to those without fibrosis.
Patients who developed pulmonary fibrosis after COVID-19 had 2.6-fold higher plasma CRP levels compared to those without fibrosis.
D-dimer values above 1 µg/mL were significantly associated with pulmonary fibrosis compared to patients with normal D-dimer values.

Elderly patients (mean age 66 ± 15 years) with severe COVID-19 who developed pulmonary fibrosis had longer hospital stays (24 vs 19 days in controls) and a delayed hospital admission of approximately 2 days.

Mechanically ventilated ARDS patients were observed to develop lung fibrosis after five days of ventilation, consistent with ventilator-induced lung injury promoting collagen formation and TGF-β secretion.
Incessant hypoxia in type II alveolar epithelial cells caused by COVID-19-related hypoxemia upregulates HIF-1α and hypoxia-inducible profibrotic genes including TGF-β1, contributing to lung fibrosis.

Multiple risk factors for post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis were identified, including elderly age, smoking, diabetes, obesity, need for mechanical ventilation, hyperinflammation syndrome, and prior chronic interstitial lung disease.
Lung fibrosis can occur even in young, healthy individuals after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection with a short hospital stay, if high viral RNA levels persist.

Chronic alcohol intake is proposed as a risk factor for interstitial fibrosis after acute lung injury by inducing pulmonary TGF-β secretion, decreasing glutathione, and increasing oxidative stress and viral-induced inflammation.
In study period 1 (1 week, high-intensity), active tVNS did not significantly reduce upper GI symptoms (GCSI) compared with sham stimulation.
In study period 1, active tVNS did not significantly reduce lower GI symptoms (GSRS) compared with sham stimulation.
In study period 2 (8 weeks, medium-intensity), active tVNS did not significantly reduce upper GI symptoms (GCSI) compared with sham.
In study period 2, active tVNS did not significantly reduce lower GI symptoms (GSRS) compared with sham.
Treatment responder rates (≥30% symptom reduction) were similar between active and sham groups in study period 1.
Treatment responder rates were similar between active and sham groups in study period 2.
Active tVNS was associated with a paradoxical increase (prolongation) in gastric emptying time relative to sham, contrary to the anticipated therapeutic direction.
Small-bowel, colonic and whole-gut transit times were unchanged by active tVNS compared with sham.
Neither acute (immediately post first stimulation) nor long-term (post study period) changes in cardiac vagal tone were observed with active tVNS versus sham.

The expiration/inspiration ratio test component of the CAN score showed a greater decrease in the sham group than the active group in study period 1, an isolated significant difference among otherwise non-significant CAN sub-scores.
Adverse event rates did not differ significantly between active tVNS and sham groups, though one active-group participant experienced treatment-related hoarseness leading to discontinuation.

Multivariate regression models adjusting for demographic, autonomic, and compliance covariates confirmed no significant symptom score differences between active and sham groups in either study period.
Sensitivity analysis restricted to high-compliance (>80%) active participants versus sham showed similarly no significant symptom score differences.
Immunohistochemical staining showed significantly greater CD15 (neutrophil marker) expression in both peri-implantitis and periodontitis tissue compared to healthy controls.
Peri-implantitis tissue showed lower levels of connective tissue and collagen (Picro-Sirius red staining) than both periodontitis and control tissue, indicating greater connective tissue destruction.
Immunofluorescence showed significantly greater citrullinated histone H3 (citH3), a NET marker, expression in peri-implantitis tissue compared to periodontitis and control tissue.
Transmission electron microscopy directly visualized neutrophil release of nuclear content, consistent with NET formation, in peri-implant and periodontal tissue samples.
The paper's discussion of splenic artery aneurysm risk factors lists fibromyalgia alongside liver cirrhosis, portal hypertension, pregnancy, and congenital abnormalities.

The patient with a ruptured splenic artery aneurysm attributed to polyarteritis nodosa also tested positive for COVID-19 on PCR, with imaging showing bilateral ground-glass opacities, which initially led clinicians to treat him for sepsis secondary to pneumonia before the vascular etiology of his anemia and abdominal pain was identified.
Long-surviving multiple myeloma patients had a higher bone marrow neutrophil functional score than patients with progressive disease.
Among long-surviving patients, those with persistent MRD-positive status had a greater mast cell functional score than those who were MRD-negative.
Four genes (CTSG, IFIT2, S100B, and CHIT1) were significantly downregulated in long-surviving MM patients compared with patients with progressive disease.
Six genes including complement genes C4B and C2 were significantly upregulated in long-surviving MM patients compared with patients with progressive disease.
Among long-surviving patients, CMA1 was the only gene significantly upregulated in the MRD-positive group compared with the MRD-negative group.

Ten genes, five of which (ISG15, OAS3, MX1, IFIT2, DDX58) relate to the interferon response pathway, were significantly downregulated in the MRD-positive group relative to the MRD-negative group among long-surviving patients, suggesting interferon signaling activation is a feature of MRD-negative long-term survival.
Repeated water avoidance stress (WAS) for 10 days significantly increased fecal pellet output compared to controls in both male and female rats.
Female rats exposed to repeated WAS exhibited significantly higher fecal pellet output than male rats in the WAS group, indicating a sex difference in stress response.
In male rats, B. longum administration did not significantly reduce WAS-induced fecal pellet output compared to WAS alone.
In female rats, B. longum administration significantly reduced WAS-induced fecal pellet output compared to WAS alone.
Colonic submucosal mast cell infiltration was significantly increased in female rats exposed to repeated WAS compared to female controls.
Only in female rats was there a statistically significant positive correlation between fecal pellet output and colonic submucosal mast cell counts.
Colonic mucosal myeloperoxidase levels showed no significant differences among control, WAS, and WAS+B. longum groups in either sex.
Colonic mucosal IL-1β mRNA levels showed no significant differences among groups in either sex.
Colonic mucosal TNF-α mRNA levels showed no significant differences among groups in either sex.
Fecal microbiota alpha-diversity (Chao1 and Shannon's indices) showed no statistical differences among control, WAS, and WAS+B. longum groups.
Beta-diversity analysis (PCoA using generalized UniFrac distance) showed differences among groups in female rats' microbial communities, but not in males.
Female rats in control and WAS groups showed higher relative abundance of Bacteroidetes compared to corresponding male groups.
Firmicutes relative abundance showed no differences among groups in either male or female rats.

Predictive KEGG functional profiling (PICRUSt) showed significant differences in metabolism modules between control and WAS groups in females, which were mitigated by B. longum treatment toward a control-like pattern.
KEGG orthology analysis at the gene level showed no consistent differences among groups.
SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with an increased risk of incident psychotic disorders compared with the contemporary control group.
SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with a significantly increased risk of incident mood disorders.
SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with a significantly increased risk of incident anxiety disorders.
Depressive episodes were significantly more common in the infection group than in contemporary controls.
Panic disorder risk was increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with contemporary controls.
Generalized anxiety disorder risk was significantly increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
PTSD risk was significantly increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with contemporary controls.
Incident antipsychotic prescriptions were markedly increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Incident antidepressant prescriptions were increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection, including SSRI and SNRI subtypes.
Incident benzodiazepine prescriptions were increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Incident mood stabilizer prescriptions were increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Incident opioid prescriptions were increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with contemporary controls.
Alcohol use disorder risk was increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection, whereas tobacco use disorder was not.
Tobacco use disorder risk was not significantly different between the infection group and contemporary controls.
Sleep disorder risk was increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with contemporary controls.
Overall risk of any incident psychiatric diagnosis, any psychotropic prescription, and any mental health outcome was increased after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Incident or recurrent psychiatric diagnoses, psychotropic prescriptions, and any mental health outcome remained significantly elevated after SARS-CoV-2 infection when prevalent cases were included.

In fully vaccinated participants, breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection was not significantly associated with mental health diagnoses compared with vaccinated uninfected controls, except for a marginal increase in psychotropic prescriptions.

Non-breakthrough infection (unvaccinated or partially vaccinated at infection) was associated with increased risk of incident and prevalent mental health outcomes compared with the unvaccinated/partially vaccinated control group.
Risk of mental health outcomes increased with COVID-19 severity, being highest among those testing positive in a hospital setting compared with a community setting.

Compared with test-negative controls, the infection group had significantly lower risk of incident psychiatric diagnosis and any mental health outcome, with no significant difference in psychotropic prescriptions.
As a positive outcome control, SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with increased risk of established long-COVID symptoms fatigue and dyspnoea, validating the study design.
As negative outcome controls, SARS-CoV-2 infection showed no significant association with skin neoplasms or skin follicular cysts, supporting validity of the study design.

The authors propose that increased blood-brain barrier permeability, CNS infiltration by SARS-CoV-2, chronic systemic immuno-inflammatory responses, and microglial/astrocyte and synaptic dysregulation may underlie post-COVID-19 psychiatric sequelae.
Expression of the EBV latent protein EBNA-1 in endothelial cells is associated with increased IL-6 production, suggesting a proinflammatory endothelial phenotype.
EBNA-1 significantly increases reactive oxygen species production in infected host cells, contributing to DNA damage and inhibiting DNA repair.
Immune responses against EBNA-1 lead to production of autoantibodies, which the authors suggest may have relevance to autoimmunity in ME/CFS.
EBNA-1 is associated with upregulation of IL-8, HIF-1alpha, and VEGF, with the latter two promoting angiogenesis and affecting vascular integrity.
EBV LMP-1, acting through NF-kB, increases expression of COX-2, prostaglandin E2, and VEGF.
In endothelial cells, LMP-1 activates NF-kB and increases IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1, RANTES, ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and E-selectin, while inhibiting caspase-3 and reducing apoptosis.
LMP-1 upregulates endocan via NF-kB, and endocan levels correlate positively with LMP-1 levels in patient tissue samples; endocan promotes endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular disease.
LMP-1 interferes with mitochondrial regulation and cell metabolism by altering phosphorylation of the mitochondrial dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1).
LMP-2A exerts anti-apoptotic effects and aids EBV immune evasion by reducing CD8+ T cell reactivity to infected cells.
The HHV-6 latency protein U94 reduces endothelial cell migration and angiogenic potential by desensitizing the VEGF response, prolonging wound healing.
U94 increases expression of HLA-G, believed to underlie its effects on angiogenesis.

Skin perfusion was significantly reduced in patients with higher blood EBV loads compared to those with low or undetectable viral loads, indicating an inverse association between EBV load and blood perfusion.
HHV-6 encephalopathy is associated with reduced cerebral blood flow and frontal lobe perfusion, as well as coronary microcirculation perturbations.
Aortic (large-vessel) endothelial cells are more susceptible to HHV-6 infection than microvascular endothelial cells, which may be relevant to reduced cerebral blood flow in ME/CFS.

In a small histopathological study of penile tissue, SARS-CoV-2 RNA and virus particles were found near endothelial cells and eNOS expression was decreased in COVID-19-positive samples compared to controls, suggesting COVID-19-induced endothelial dysfunction.
EBV infection of endothelial cells causes a significant increase in VWF, VEGF, and PECAM-1 levels, contributing to procoagulant processes.
Supernatant from EBV-infected NK cells increases procoagulant activity in monocytes by upregulating tissue factor expression.
HHV-6 reactivation is accompanied by an increase in PAI-1, leading to reduced clot lysis and clearance.

HHV-6 infection is associated with thrombotic microangiopathy, potentially related to fibrinaloid microclots seen in both Long COVID and ME/CFS cohorts, though this link requires further investigation.
An older study reported a prothrombotic state associated with active HHV-6 infection in an ME/CFS cohort.
EBV has been detected in CNS tissue from deceased ME/CFS patients, suggesting cerebrovascular endothelial cells could be a reservoir/latent site in patients.
HHV-6 has been detected in CNS tissue from deceased ME/CFS patients, suggesting cerebrovascular endothelial cells could be a reservoir/latent site in patients.
The authors' prior work found significant levels of amyloid fibrin(ogen)/microclots in platelet-poor plasma from ME/CFS patients, the same clotting material implicated in Long COVID.
Reduced cerebral blood flow has been repeatedly demonstrated in ME/CFS patients, even in those without tachycardia or hypotension.
Orthostatic symptoms in ME/CFS are not attributable to deconditioning, implying an underlying defect in blood flow regulation possibly related to autonomic dysfunction.

An XGBoost classifier trained on the top 50 ANOVA-selected plasma metabolites achieved 98.18% accuracy, 98.85% AUROC, a 0.023 Brier score, 98% F1-score, and 100% sensitivity for distinguishing ME/CFS patients from healthy controls.

When all 832 metabolomic features were used without feature selection, logistic regression performed best among classifiers but only reached 80.36% accuracy with a Brier score of 0.143, substantially lower than the ANOVA-reduced XGBoost model.
Alpha-CEHC sulfate, a vitamin E metabolite, was identified by SHAP as the single most important metabolite for predicting ME/CFS, with decreased levels associated with increased risk of ME/CFS.
Decreased plasma hypoxanthine levels were found to increase the modeled risk of ME/CFS, implicating disturbed purine metabolism.
Decreased levels of phenylacetylglutamine were found to increase the modeled risk of ME/CFS.
Increased levels of N-delta-acetylornithine, a urea cycle/amino-acid metabolism metabolite, were found to increase the modeled risk of ME/CFS.
Increased levels of the diacylglycerol lipid oleoyl-linoleoyl-glycerol (18:1/18:2) [2] were found to increase the modeled risk of ME/CFS.

1-Arachidonylglycerol (20:4), an endocannabinoid involved in energy balance, emotion, pain sensation, and neuroinflammation, was identified among the candidate biomarker metabolites distinguishing ME/CFS patients from controls.
Alpha-hydroxyisovalerate (AHIV) was identified as another important candidate biomarker metabolite in the ME/CFS classification model.
Post-COVID small fiber neuropathy was associated with a constellation of dysautonomia symptoms including orthostasis, altered sweating, and labile heart rate.
The majority of patients with post-COVID small fiber neuropathy had comorbid ME/CFS (89% in IVIG group, 86% in control group).
A subset of patients with post-COVID small fiber neuropathy also had comorbid POTS (33% in IVIG group, 43% in control group).
CRP was elevated in both the IVIG and control groups, with no significant difference between groups.
Three of ten tested patients were positive for IgM TS-HDS sensory neuropathy autoantibody.
Three of ten tested patients were positive for IgG FGFR3 sensory neuropathy autoantibody.

All 7 patients tested with invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing showed abnormal results consistent with ME/CFS, including depressed aerobic capacity, elevated peak mixed venous oxygen saturation, depressed arterial-venous oxygen content difference, and low biventricular filling pressures.
IVIG treatment resulted in resolution or improvement of neuropathic symptoms in all treated patients within 6 months, significantly more than in untreated controls.
Prior to IVIG, all patients were trialed on gabapentin, pregabalin, and/or duloxetine without resolution of neuropathic symptoms.
One patient received a 10-day course of prednisone with temporary improvement in symptoms before IVIG.
Some patients who achieved resolution or improvement with IVIG experienced return of neuropathic symptoms during attempts to wean or space out infusions ('wearing-off' phenomenon).
The patient who experienced improvement but not full resolution with IVIG had a comorbid diagnosis of diabetes.

The authors propose that post-COVID SFN has an autoreactive, dysimmune etiology, supported by symptom onset within 6 weeks of viral illness, persistently elevated CRP, response to immunotherapy, female predominance, comorbid autoimmune disease, and presence of autoantibodies.
Control-group patients with positive sensory neuropathy autoantibodies (TS-HDS or FGFR3) who did not receive IVIG experienced unchanged or worsening symptoms.
All patients tested negative for a panel of additional neuropathy-associated autoantibodies (IgM GD1b, IgG GM1, IgG/IgM sulfatide, IgM MAG, IgM Histone H3, IgM GD1a, IgG Hu, IgG CRMP-5).
Multiple studies found that plasma, urine, and saliva cortisol concentrations were significantly lower in CFS patients than in healthy controls.
In CFS patients, saliva cortisol levels were lower in the morning and higher in the evening, indicating attenuated diurnal variability compared with normal controls.
Intensive plasma sampling showed that the secretion rhythm of ACTH in CFS patients differed significantly from healthy controls, with reduced release during the normal morning peak.

Using the Trier Social Stress Test, CFS patients showed a significantly reduced area under the ACTH response curve compared with healthy controls, while the cortisol response curve area did not differ significantly.
CFS patients with childhood trauma showed a significantly reduced and flatter cortisol awakening response curve compared with healthy controls.
Women with CFS had significantly lower cortisol awakening response levels and a smaller increase in the area under the response curve than healthy women.

An insulin tolerance test showed significantly reduced area under the ACTH response curve in CFS patients, while cortisol response was not significantly different from controls, confirming a blunted HPA axis response.
After a 0.5 mg dexamethasone suppression test, saliva cortisol output was significantly lower in CFS patients than in healthy controls, indicating enhanced negative feedback of the HPA axis.

After 5 mg prednisolone administration, saliva cortisol and urine cortisol metabolite levels were significantly lower in CFS patients than controls, with a significantly higher percentage of suppression, demonstrating enhanced HPA axis negative feedback.
Several studies found no significant difference in cortisol levels between CFS patients and healthy controls, contradicting the mainstream hypocortisolism finding.

Another study found no significant differences between a CFS group and healthy controls in cortisol awakening response, daily cortisol secretion curve, or CAR after dexamethasone suppression testing, and childhood trauma was not significantly associated with cortisol output on TSST.

In CFS patients, the peak phase of cortisol secretion is advanced while the peak phase of melatonin secretion is delayed, with abnormalities in these opposing circadian rhythms proposed to underlie sleep disturbances.
In CFS patients treated with pestle needle therapy combined with electric acupuncture, cortisol levels were lower after treatment than before treatment.

Five TCM RCTs (Fuyang cupping, five-element gongdiao music with Lixujieyu decoction, acupoint sticking, Lixujieyu decoction, and electric acupuncture) reported that treatment effectively increased cortisol levels in CFS patients, with electric acupuncture also restoring the CORT peak phase.
Three TCM RCTs using pestle needle therapy with electric acupuncture, scalp acupuncture, and acupoint sticking all reported that treatment effectively increased ACTH levels in CFS patients.
Electric acupuncture treatment increased salivary melatonin levels and diurnal secretion variation, restoring the melatonin peak phase that had previously shifted backward.

Randomized controlled trials showed beneficial effects of hydrocortisone in some CFS patients, but overall evidence of efficacy was insufficient, and it was excluded from CDC guidelines due to long-term adverse effects.

The largest study on CBT and graded exercise therapy initially provided favorable evidence of efficacy and safety, but re-analysis of the data changed the results significantly, and subsequent studies questioned their efficacy and safety, leading the CDC to no longer recommend either treatment.
EEG spectrograms from a visuomotor Cognitive-Motor Integration task differed between healthy participants and those with PASC or ME, enabling machine learning classification.
PASC and ME participant groups were combined for analysis because their kinematic behavioral performance on the visuomotor task did not significantly differ from each other.
A prior study found that 58% of 465 PASC patients met criteria for ME, indicating substantial overlap between post-viral conditions after COVID-19.

Among traditional machine learning models, Random Forest achieved the best classification accuracy (77%) for distinguishing healthy participants from those with PASC/ME based on EEG spectrogram features.

Among deep learning models, CNN-LSTM achieved the highest classification performance (83% accuracy, 85% precision, 82% recall, 83% F1-score) in distinguishing healthy from PASC/ME participants using EEG spectrograms.

Statistical comparison via Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed no significant differences in classification accuracy among CNN-LSTM, ConvLSTM, and GRU models, but BiLSTM performance significantly differed from all three.

Training the CNN-LSTM model on WGAN-generated synthetic EEG spectrograms improved average classification accuracy to 93% across five runs, compared to 83% accuracy when trained on original data alone.
In the intention-to-treat analysis, SJZD produced a greater reduction in Chalder fatigue questionnaire score than placebo, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant.
In the per-protocol population with good medication adherence, SJZD showed a statistically significant greater reduction in fatigue score compared with placebo.
SJZD significantly improved overall health status compared with placebo in the per-protocol population.
No significant difference was found between SJZD and placebo groups in change of SF-36 physical function score.
No significant difference was found between SJZD and placebo groups in change of spleen deficiency scale score.
No significant difference was found between SJZD and placebo groups in clinical global impression (CGI) evaluation.
Fecal metagenome sequencing and correlation analyses suggested that the beneficial fatigue effect of SJZD may be related to a change in abundance of the gut bacterium Pediococcus acidilactici.
No serious adverse events or abnormal laboratory test results were observed in either the SJZD or placebo group during the two-month trial, indicating the formula was well tolerated.
In a general-population cohort, 3.1% of participants met CDC diagnostic criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome.
In the same cohort, 6.6% of participants met American College of Rheumatology diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia.
In the same cohort, 5.5% of participants met Rome IV diagnostic criteria for irritable bowel syndrome.
The number of participants who met diagnostic criteria for all three functional somatic syndromes (CFS, FM, and IBS) simultaneously was 45 times higher than would be expected by chance.

When chronicity and symptom-interference criteria were aligned across the three syndromes to remove differences in diagnostic thresholds, the overlap among CFS, FM and IBS increased to 152 times higher than chance.
Participants meeting diagnostic criteria for CFS and FM showed a similar pattern of symptom occurrence, suggesting shared underlying symptomatology between these two functional somatic syndromes.

In a randomized open-label trial in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS/ME_CFS), daily supplementation with acetyl-L-carnitine (ALC), propionyl-L-carnitine (PLC), or their combination for 24 weeks improved mental fatigue and quality of life.
A 2012 double-blind randomized controlled trial found that 500 mg/day of L-carnitine for 12 weeks was effective in alleviating symptoms in migraine disorder patients.
A 2015 triple-blind crossover controlled trial using the same L-carnitine intervention as the earlier 2012 trial found no significant improvement in migraine disorder symptoms.

Among all trials reviewed across conditions, the L-carnitine migraine trial had the highest reported adverse event rate, with about a third of subjects experiencing mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal and neurological adverse events.
Women with endometriosis reported significantly greater pelvic pain severity than women with pelvic-abdominal pain not associated with endometriosis.
Women with endometriosis reported significantly greater pain interference with daily functioning compared to women with pelvic pain without endometriosis.
Women with endometriosis reported significantly greater pelvic pain impact (on social life, career, family planning, sexual intercourse, healthcare interactions) than those without endometriosis.

Endometriosis was associated with a higher number of chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPCs), with 25% of women with endometriosis reporting three or more COPCs compared to 12% of women without endometriosis.
Women with endometriosis had significantly higher rates of comorbid chronic fatigue syndrome than women with pelvic pain without endometriosis.
Women with endometriosis had significantly higher rates of comorbid fibromyalgia than women with pelvic pain without endometriosis.
Women with endometriosis had significantly higher rates of comorbid temporomandibular disorder than women with pelvic pain without endometriosis.
A greater number of overlapping pain conditions was significantly associated with greater pelvic pain severity across the sample.
A greater number of overlapping pain conditions was significantly associated with greater pain interference across the sample.
A greater number of overlapping pain conditions was significantly associated with greater pain impact across the sample.

The association between number of overlapping pain conditions and pain outcomes did not significantly interact with endometriosis diagnosis, indicating the effect of COPCs on pain outcomes was independent of having endometriosis.
Women with endometriosis tended to have an earlier age of pelvic pain onset compared to women without endometriosis.
Nearly all women with hEDS in this cohort reported temporomandibular disorder (TMD) symptoms.
TMD pain was reported by 95% of women with hEDS, making it the most common specific TMD symptom.
TMJ clicking was reported by 90% of women with hEDS.
Jaw fatigue was reported by 80% of women with hEDS.
TMJ crepitation and luxation were reported less frequently than other TMD symptoms among women with hEDS.

Among 27-50 year-old women with hEDS, being born in Finland, living alone, and self-reported worst pain being located elsewhere in the body rather than in the joints were significant risk factors for TMD symptoms.
Among 51-78 year-old women with hEDS, being born in Finland, having a family history of EDS, tinnitus, and regularly taking contraceptives were significant risk factors for TMD symptoms.
Among younger women (27-50 years) with hEDS, being born in Finland was associated with increased risk of TMD symptoms.
Living alone was identified as a risk factor for TMD symptoms among younger women (27-50 years) with hEDS.
Self-reported worst pain located elsewhere in the body (not the joints) was associated with increased risk of TMD symptoms among younger women (27-50 years) with hEDS.
Among older women (51-78 years) with hEDS, being born in Finland was associated with increased risk of TMD symptoms.
Family history of EDS was a risk factor for TMD symptoms among older women (51-78 years) with hEDS.
Tinnitus was associated with increased risk of TMD symptoms among older women (51-78 years) with hEDS.
Regular use of contraceptives was associated with increased risk of TMD symptoms among older women (51-78 years) with hEDS.
The collagen receptor integrin α2β1 is downregulated in EDS/HSD cells, consistent with disrupted collagen-cell adhesion.
The fibronectin receptor α5β1 integrin is downregulated in EDS/HSD fibroblasts.
The vitronectin receptor αvβ3 integrin is upregulated in EDS/HSD cells and acts as an alternative fibronectin receptor, driving an 'integrin switch' that alters downstream signaling.
Transcriptome profiling of EDS/HSD fibroblasts revealed differential expression of multiple cadherin, protocadherin, claudin, and desmosomal genes involved in cell-cell junction formation.

EDS/HSD fibroblasts transform into migrating myofibroblast-like cells marked by increased α-SMA, cadherin-11, and MMP9, with altered CYR61/CTGF expression, driven by αvβ3-integrin/ILK/Snail1 signaling.
Dermal fibroblasts from EDS patients show dysregulation of calcium signaling sensors CALM1 and CALM2 compared to controls.
Differential expression of several annexin family members, involved in signaling, proliferation, and inflammation, was noted in EDS dermal fibroblasts.

Among 20 heterozygous individuals with TNX haploinsufficiency, 45% (9 individuals) presented with generalized joint hypermobility, recurrent joint dislocations, and chronic joint pain resembling JHS/EDS-HT.
Of 80 patients with EDS-HT, 7.5% (6 individuals) exhibited TNX haploinsufficiency with significantly reduced serum TNX levels.
TNX-null mice showed a 30% reduction in skin collagen content compared to wildtype littermates, despite normal fibril size/shape but reduced fibril density.
Vitronectin was among six proteins with increased serum levels in JHS patients compared to controls in a proteomic study.
C4BPA showed increased serum expression in JHS patients compared to controls, suggesting complement system involvement in local inflammation.
Serum TNX was undetectable in patients with classical EDS while control individuals had a mean of 144 ng/mL, suggesting a quantification method useful for EDS diagnosis and risk stratification.

In half of hEDS patients studied, serum TNX concentration was significantly lower (mean 69.3 ng/mL) than healthy controls (mean 110 ng/mL), with no association found between reduced sTNX and TNXB mutations, suggesting epigenetic regulation.

S100A4 was found elevated in hEDS dermal myofibroblasts compared to control fibroblasts in a proteomic study identifying 183 differentially expressed proteins, and is proposed to drive pathological ECM remodeling via MMP modulation.
IL6 gene expression was found downregulated in a functional study of hEDS fibroblasts.
Elevated serum prolactin concentration has been hypothesized to relate to chronic pain in EDS patients with hypermobile joints, though this remains unverified.

MTHFR C677T and A1298C polymorphisms, present in about 30% of the population and reducing enzyme function by up to 80%, are proposed to underlie a folate-dependent hypermobility syndrome via altered folate metabolism and downstream ECM effects.
A mutation in type III collagen (COL3A1) has been documented in JHS/EDS-HT, resulting in the severe vascular type of EDS.

Kyphoscoliotic EDS (kEDS) results from PLOD1 mutations causing lysyl hydroxylase 1 deficiency, leading to under-hydroxylation of collagen lysyl residues and abnormal urinary crosslink patterns diagnosable via fibroblast enzyme activity assay.

Among EDS patients presenting with back pain, joint pain, and joint laxity, 67.1% received a diagnosis of at least one rheumatological condition after thorough serological, radiographic, and physical examination.

A clinical case definition has emerged for fibromyalgia syndrome with hypermobility developing after COVID-19 infection, with an 80% overlap between JHS and fibromyalgia, hypothesized to involve immunologic responses to connective tissue proteins triggered by COVID-19.
Genetic mutations in COL1A1 and COL3A1, governing collagen types I and III, have been linked to benign joint hypermobility syndrome (BJHS).

A novel homozygous frameshift variant, c.2923del, was identified in AEBP1 in the patient, predicted to cause a premature termination codon (p.Ala975Profs*22) that truncates the ACLP protein by 163 amino acids and reduces peptide length by over 10 percent.

A maternally inherited heterozygous COL11A1 variant of uncertain significance was found but assessed as unlikely to contribute to the patient's phenotype since neither she nor her mother showed features of Stickler or Marshall syndrome.

The patient exhibited widespread joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 9/9, along with marked skin hyperextensibility, translucency, tissue-paper scarring, and easy bruising consistent with clEDS2.

The patient and one other previously reported clEDS2 individual with premature birth (32 and 30 weeks gestation, respectively) both showed significant short stature well below their mid-parental heights.

Across all 15 reported clEDS2 patients, skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring/delayed wound healing, and easy bruising were each present in 100%, excessive skin in 93%, generalized joint hypermobility, pes planus, and dislocation/subluxation each in 93%, and cardiovascular features in 86%.

Three of the reported clEDS2 patients presented with subtle signs of autonomic dysfunction including urinary retention, bowel immobility, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and chronic fatigue, while two additional patients presented with chronic fatigue alone.
Forty-seven percent of all reported clEDS2 patients were born prematurely, between 30 and 36 weeks gestation.
Fifty percent (3 of 6) of male clEDS2 patients presented with cryptorchidism.
Fourteen of 18 unique AEBP1 variants identified across clEDS2 patients were nonsense, frameshift, or splice-site variants predicted or confirmed to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

Transmission electron microscopy of skin biopsies from previously reported AEBP1-variant patients showed abundant collagen flower deposits in the dermis, with elastin deposits ranging from normal to decreased.
Biochemical analysis in a previously reported clEDS2 patient showed reduced secretion of type I and type III procollagen.

Unlike most previously reported AEBP1 variants that trigger NMD, the patient's p.Ala975Profs*22 variant is located downstream and is predicted to escape NMD; because it lacks residue N1030, important for ACLP secretion, the truncated protein may be retained intracellularly, limiting its downstream function.

Rare critical complications reported in clEDS2 include superior mesenteric artery aneurysms/ruptures, aortic root aneurysm or dissection requiring surgery, spontaneous pneumothorax, and bowel rupture requiring surgical repair, each occurring in only one or two patients.

Other cardiovascular features reported in clEDS2 patients include aortic root dilation, carotid stenosis, and mitral valve regurgitation/prolapse (ages 33-58 years) and varicose veins with arterial dissection, dilation, and tortuosity (ages 53 and 63 years).

Two clEDS2 patients who gave birth to healthy children experienced significant postpartum bleeding, with one also developing severe paralytic ileus post-caesarean section and postoperative abdominal hernia.
Less common features across clEDS2 patients included dental abnormalities (60%), hernias (60%), alopecia (53%), scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis (53%), neuromuscular features (53%), and osteopenia (47%).
P100 latency of visual evoked potentials was significantly longer in patients with generalized joint hypermobility compared with healthy controls.
VEP amplitude was slightly higher in the GJH group than controls but the difference was not statistically significant.
Within the GJH group, higher Beighton scores were significantly positively correlated with longer P100 latency.
Within the GJH group, higher Beighton scores were significantly positively correlated with higher VEP amplitude.
In the control group, Beighton score was not significantly correlated with either VEP latency or amplitude.
Bilateral symmetric joint mobility tests (same test performed on left and right side) were the most strongly correlated of all joint mobility measures.
Some anatomically 'body-close' joint pairs (fifth finger extension/thumb apposition left-right, patella medial-lateral and knee extension right) showed only moderate correlation with each other.
Most other (non-bilateral, non-body-close) joint mobility test pairs showed weak correlation, indicating that mobility at one joint does not predict mobility at another.

Principal component analysis of 13 non-dominant-side joint mobility tests could not identify a subset of tests that accounted for the overall variation in joint mobility, so no reduced test battery could define generalized joint hypermobility.

Using eight systematically developed combinations of major/minor joints across upper limb, lower limb, and axial skeleton, and five different standard-deviation cut-off levels, the estimated prevalence of GJH varied widely depending on the definition used.

The proportion of women classified as having GJH under at least one of the eight combination definitions decreased substantially as the standard-deviation cut-off for defining joint hypermobility became stricter.

Among women meeting any of the eight combination-based GJH definitions, there was substantial variation in which specific joints were hypermobile, indicating GJH is not concentrated in a fixed set of joints across individuals.
Histopathology of the affected hamster's skin showed disorganized, haphazardly arranged dermal collagen fibres consistent with cutaneous asthenia (a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome).
The affected hamster presented with hyperextensible skin, glaucoma, and lens dislocation, phenotypic features associated with cutaneous asthenia/Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in this animal.
Surgical reduction of the excess skin folds was performed but provided only temporary relief of the hamster's cutaneous asthenia symptoms.
Children with EDS had over twice the risk of being diagnosed with hearing loss compared to matched non-EDS controls.
Children with EDS were 1.6 times more likely than matched controls to be diagnosed with allergic rhinitis.
Children with EDS were 1.52 times more likely than matched controls to develop sinusitis.
Children with EDS were 4.24 times more likely than matched controls to be diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea.
Children with EDS were less likely than matched controls to develop acute tonsillitis.
No statistically significant difference in risk of otitis media was found between children with EDS and matched controls.

Rare, largely missense HOXD12 variants are enriched in clubfoot cases relative to two independent control cohorts and segregate with highly penetrant autosomal dominant clubfoot in multiplex families, establishing HOXD12 as a novel clubfoot disease gene.
Rare, predominantly missense variants in the Ehlers-Danlos-associated collagen gene COL9A3 are enriched in clubfoot cases and expand its phenotype to include isolated (non-syndromic) clubfoot.

Previously reported disease-causing COL9A3 variants were mostly deletions, splice-site, or nonsense, whereas 14 of 16 COL9A3 variants found in the clubfoot cohort were missense (including 6 glycine substitutions), suggesting a distinct genotype-phenotype correlation for the clubfoot presentation.

Rare COL12A1 variants, previously linked to myopathies, are enriched in clubfoot cases and segregate with clubfoot in multiple multiplex families, expanding the COL12A1 disease phenotype to isolated clubfoot.

Rare variants within the unique region of COL12A1 encoding the early-embryonic long collagen XII isoform are enriched in clubfoot cases compared with gnomAD controls, though not significantly compared with the smaller in-house control cohort.

Rare LMX1B variants, which normally cause nail-patella syndrome, are enriched in clubfoot cases and segregate with clubfoot as a dominant trait in three families, often without other clinical features of nail-patella syndrome, expanding the LMX1B phenotype to isolated clubfoot.

Collapsed rare, deleterious variants across posterior (limb-expressed) HOX genes HOX9-13 are significantly enriched in clubfoot cases relative to both control datasets, whereas non-limb-expressed HOX1-8 genes and autism genes used as negative controls show no such enrichment.

Segregation analysis identified a de novo HOXD11 variant and two HOXC11 variants that segregate with clubfoot in two multiplex families, with additional variants in HOXC9, HOXC12 and HOXD11 potentially segregating in three more families.

Rare deleterious PITX1 variants, used as a positive control given its known clubfoot disease-gene status, were confirmed enriched in the burden analysis, identifying 7 candidate variants in 8 of 1190 probands.

Across the entire cohort, rare and predicted deleterious variants in PITX1, LMX1B, COL9A3, COL12A1, HOXD12 and other posterior HOX genes were found in only 8.4% (100/1190) of clubfoot cases, highlighting the strong genetic heterogeneity of non-syndromic clubfoot.

Although COL15A1 showed rare-variant enrichment in the burden analysis, segregation data (non-segregating variants, one variant seemingly inherited from an unaffected distal relative) did not provide strong support for a causal role in clubfoot.
The clubfoot cohort showed a male-to-female ratio of approximately 2:1 (822 male, 368 female), consistent with previously reported sex skew in clubfoot across ethnicities.

Among the 1190 clubfoot probands, 35% (416/1190) reported a family history of clubfoot, and 13.8% (164/1190) had an affected first-degree relative, consistent with prior estimates of familial clustering.

Gene burden analysis using TRAPD identified 29 genes with significant enrichment (p<0.05 against both in-house and gnomAD control datasets) of rare deleterious variants in non-syndromic clubfoot cases, including known limb-development and connective-tissue disease genes.
In hallux valgus feet, the talonavicular joint showed significantly greater eversion than in healthy control feet under weightbearing conditions.
The talonavicular joint in hallux valgus feet showed significantly greater dorsiflexion and eversion compared with hallux rigidus feet.
The medial cuneiform joint in hallux valgus feet showed significantly greater eversion and abduction than in healthy control feet.
The first tarsometatarsal joint in hallux valgus feet showed significantly greater dorsiflexion, inversion, and adduction compared with healthy control feet.
The first tarsometatarsal joint showed significantly greater inversion and adduction in hallux valgus feet compared with hallux rigidus feet.
Dorsiflexion of the first tarsometatarsal joint was significantly greater in hallux rigidus feet compared with healthy control feet.
Fibromyalgia affects upwards of 2% of the U.S. population, and women are diagnosed at roughly twice the rate of men.
FMS patients show significantly higher lifelong rates of anxiety and depression than controls, with suicide risk reported as nearly ten-fold higher in some countries.
The revised ACR criteria diagnose FMS via a Widespread Pain Index (WPI) ≥7 with Symptom Severity (SS) ≥5, or WPI 4-6 with SS ≥9, formally embedding affective/cognitive/sleep symptoms into diagnosis.
Higher Symptom Severity (SS) scale scores correlate with higher rates of anxiety and depression diagnoses, higher pain scores, and greater sleep disturbance in FMS patients.

A cited meta-analysis found duloxetine most effective among FDA-approved FMS drugs for improving pain and depression, whereas off-label amitriptyline was most effective for sleep, fatigue, and quality of life.

In the original reserpine model, doses of 0.1-1 mg/kg s.c. for 3 days dose-dependently reduced muscle and mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds, with 1 mg/kg producing the most pronounced threshold reduction and the greatest depletion of dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine in spinal cord, thalamus, and prefrontal cortex.

Pregabalin and pramipexole restored muscle and mechanical withdrawal thresholds in the reserpine model, duloxetine restored mechanical thresholds only, and diclofenac produced no change in either threshold.
Across the reviewed literature, all studies using the Forced Swim Test found the reserpine model reliably produced depression-like immobility behavior in animals.
The reserpine model's ability to reliably produce anxiety-like behavior (EPM, OFT) is unclear, with many studies finding effects and many others failing to find them.

All identified studies using the Morris Water Maze found cognitive deficits associated with the reserpine model, with additional deficits found in discrimination/fear conditioning and passive avoidance.
All studies investigating sleep in the reserpine model identified significant alterations in sleep patterns, durations, or intensities, mirroring the sleep disturbances reported by FMS patients.

Bilateral hyperalgesia induced by repeated intramuscular acidic saline injections is understood to involve activation of muscle afferent ASIC3 channels during induction, though these peripheral channels are not implicated in the 4-week maintenance phase, which instead involves spinal/supraspinal glutamatergic central sensitization.
The acidic saline model produced mixed and inconsistent results for negative emotionality across EPM, OFT, sucrose preference, and FST assays.
Mirogabalin alleviated negative affect (EPM, OFT) and was the only treatment found effective for cognitive deficits in the acidic saline model, though it did not improve pain thresholds.
In the fatigue-enhanced muscle pain model, female mice show greater magnitudes of hyperalgesia than males, an effect not altered by ovariectomy.

The single study assessing affect and cognition in the fatigue-enhanced muscle pain model found no evidence of negative affectivity or cognitive deficits in escape-avoidance and learned avoidance tasks.

In the subchronic swim stress model, pretreatment with clomipramine or fluoxetine reduced immobility behavior by the third swim session, and clomipramine, fluoxetine, and tryptophan improved thermal withdrawal latencies and reduced formalin-evoked pain scores versus vehicle, supporting a serotonergic mechanism.

The subchronic swim stress model consistently produced increased immobility (depression-like behavior) across studies, but its ability to produce anxiety-like behavior was inconsistent, with OFT results repeatedly failing to show anxiogenic locomotor changes.

Cold stress (intermittent -3°C exposure) produced persistent bilateral mechanical hyperalgesia lasting up to 42 days post-exposure, and is associated with reduced 5-HT and its metabolites across multiple supraspinal regions.
Gabapentin improved evasion behaviors (depression-like) and evoked pain in the cold stress model, and Valeriana fauriei extract improved both evoked pain and depression-like behaviors.

The sound stress model produces hyperalgesia via a sympathetic-independent mechanism involving increased epinephrine release from the adrenal medulla, together with peripheral catecholamine-synthesizing enzyme activity.

Most studies of the sound stress model show anxiety-like behavior changes in EPM, OFT, and grimace scale, though one study found contrasting EPM results; riparin III and the CGRP antagonist olcegepant significantly improved these negative affective measures.

Coumarins (imperatorin, esculetin, daphnetin), Angelica archangelica extract, and gabapentin were highlighted as attenuating reserpine-induced nociceptive, affective, and cognitive deficits across all three pain dimensions.
Women with ≤9 years of education had more than double the risk of self-reported fibromyalgia compared to those with ≥13 years of education.
Women with 10-12 years of education had a moderately elevated risk of self-reported fibromyalgia compared to those with ≥13 years of education.
Lifestyle factors (BMI, physical activity, smoking, alcohol consumption) jointly mediated 17.3% of the total effect of low education (≤9 years) on self-reported fibromyalgia risk.
Lifestyle factors jointly mediated 14.1% of the total effect of moderate education (10-12 years) on self-reported fibromyalgia risk.

Alcohol consumption was the largest single mediator among lifestyle factors in the education-fibromyalgia association for women with the lowest education level, consistent with an alcohol-harm paradox.
Smoking was the largest single mediator among lifestyle factors in the education-fibromyalgia association for women with moderate education (10-12 years).
BMI mediated a small proportion of the education-fibromyalgia association, contributing least along with physical activity.
Physical activity contributed the least of all lifestyle mediators, with an almost negligible indirect effect on the education-fibromyalgia association.
The prevalence of self-reported fibromyalgia showed a negative educational gradient, with 4.5% reporting FM among those with ≤9 years of education compared to 1.7% among those with ≥13 years.
The overall incidence rate of self-reported fibromyalgia in the cohort was 235.1 per 100,000 person-years over 1,005,169 person-years of follow-up, with 2,363 incident cases.
Two independent saliva proteomics studies both found transaldolase (TALDO) over-expressed in patients with FMS compared to controls.
PGAM1, a glycolysis enzyme, was found elevated in saliva of FMS patients in two studies, potentially linking FMS to glucose metabolism disorders and autoimmune processes.
Calgranulin A (S100-A8) was elevated in saliva of FMS patients compared to healthy controls, but this difference disappeared when compared with rheumatoid arthritis or migraine patients.
Calgranulin C (S100-A12) concentrations were elevated in both saliva and serum of patients with FMS compared to controls.
Apolipoprotein C-III levels differed between FMS patients and controls in both CSF and plasma, with inconsistent direction across biological fluids and comparator groups.
Complement C4-A was found elevated in both CSF and serum of FMS patients, implicating the classical complement pathway in FMS pathophysiology.
Malate dehydrogenase, an enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis and muscle energy production, was decreased in CSF of FMS patients.
PCSK1 (ProSAAS), involved in neuropeptide processing, was elevated in CSF of FMS patients, possibly reflecting endocrine disturbances.

Transferrin was the most prevalent protein identified across included studies, over-expressed in both plasma and saliva of FMS patients compared to healthy and pain controls, suggesting altered iron metabolism.

Haptoglobin, an acute phase antioxidant protein, was elevated in plasma of FMS patients, possibly as a coping mechanism against oxidative stress; conventional methods have also linked elevated haptoglobin to depression, hyperalgesia, exhaustion, and sleep disturbance.
Plasma α2-macroglobulin, a protease inhibitor involved in coagulation and immune response, was elevated in FMS patients compared to healthy controls.

Fibrinogen alpha, beta, and gamma chain concentrations differed between FMS patients and controls in serum and plasma across studies, with direction varying by investigator, though overall research leans toward elevated fibrinogen indicating a prothrombotic state.

Profilin-1, an actin-binding cytoskeletal protein, was found decreased in serum but increased in saliva across three studies of FMS patients, and was proposed as a discriminating marker between pain-predominant and stiffness-predominant FMS subgroups.
Serum amyloid P component, an acute phase immune-regulatory protein, was elevated in both plasma and serum of FMS patients.
Serum amyloid A4, a procoagulant acute-phase reactant, was elevated in plasma but decreased in serum of FMS patients relative to controls.
Thrombospondin-1 concentrations differed between FMS patients and controls in both serum and plasma, implicated in coagulation/fibrinolysis disturbance linked to CNS degeneration.
C1qC was observed at high levels in plasma and serum samples of FMS patients, supporting complement cascade involvement.

A broad panel of pro-inflammatory, anti-inflammatory, and regulatory cytokines/receptors (including IL-8, TNF, IL1RAP, TNFSF14, CCL3) was found elevated in the serum of FMS patients using targeted (Olink) proteomics.
A decision tree model using serum expression levels of HMPT1, IL1RAP, and Ig lambda chain V-IV region (IGL3-25) differentiated FMS patients from controls with an accuracy of up to 0.97.
In women with FMS and low ferritin who had failed oral iron supplementation, intravenous ferric carboxymaltose treatment reduced pain sensation and improved quality of life.

In an RCT, women with FMS treated with 50 mL of EVOO or refined olive oil for 3 weeks showed improved antioxidative profiles, reduced pain (FIQ), and improved quality of life, with antithrombotic and anti-inflammatory effects.
A prior systematic review found that supplementation with antioxidant vitamins and coenzyme Q10 for at least 6 weeks was associated with reduced pain perception in 80% of FMS patients.
Serum KRT80 was negatively correlated with depressive symptoms (BDI score) in FMS patients.
The GHV1-46 immunoglobulin heavy chain V-I region segment showed a mild positive correlation with pain intensity (VAS) in FMS patients.
Elevated plasma α2-macroglobulin and transferrin concentrations were correlated with moderate-to-severe pain intensity in FMS patients.
Using serum proteomics, FMS patients could be discriminated into pain-predominant versus stiffness-predominant phenotype subgroups based on differing proteomic marker concentrations.

FMS patients show increased pro-oxidative markers (nitric oxide, malondialdehyde, lipid hydroperoxide) alongside decreased xanthine oxidase and reduced endogenous antioxidants (glutathione, superoxide dismutase, total antioxidant status), supporting a role for oxidative stress in disease pathophysiology.
Small-fiber neuropathy has been reported as a consistent comorbid finding in FMS, suggestive of CNS/peripheral nerve degeneration.
An increased incidence of immunodeficiency has been observed in FMS patients, and conversely, FMS occurs more commonly in patients with primary immunodeficiency.

Complement C1QC and C4A concentrations were elevated across multiple biological fluids (CSF, plasma, serum) in patients with FMS compared to controls, implicating classical complement pathway activation.
Plasma levels of the hormone transport proteins TBG and CBG, and of angiotensinogen (linked to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system), were decreased in FMS patients compared with controls.
Plasma gelsolin and actin cytoplasmic 1 levels were increased in patients with FMS compared with controls across two plasma proteomics studies.

A panel of inflammatory, anti-inflammatory and regulatory serum immune markers (including IL-8, TNF, TNFSF14, CCL3, IL-10RB, IL-18R1, CD5, TNFRSF9) was found elevated in the serum of FMS patients using targeted proteomics.
Fibroblast growth factors FGF-21, FGF-19, FGF-23 and colony stimulating factor 1 (CSF-1) were increased in the serum of FMS patients compared with controls.
Serum keratin type II cytoskeletal 80 was increased while profilin-1 was decreased in patients with FMS compared with controls.
Serum sirtuin 2, sulfotransferase 1A1, stromelysin-2 (MMP10), and histidine protein methyltransferase 1 homolog were increased in patients with FMS.
Serum alpha1-antitrypsin was increased while serpin B3 was decreased in patients with FMS versus controls.
Serum thrombospondin-1 and thrombospondin-2 levels were decreased in patients with FMS compared with controls, potentially reflecting impaired coagulation/fibrinolysis relevant to CNS degeneration.
Serum LYVE1 and hornerin were increased while galectin-7 was decreased in patients with FMS.
Serum transthyretin and retinol binding protein 4 were increased in patients with FMS compared with controls.
A decision tree model using expression levels of HMT1, IL1RAP, and an immunoglobulin lambda chain V-IV region segment differentiated FMS patients from controls with accuracy up to 0.97.
A Taiwan nationwide study found that adults with iron deficiency anemia had increased odds of developing fibromyalgia syndrome.
In women with FMS and low ferritin who had failed oral iron supplementation, intravenous ferric carboxymaltose treatment reduced pain sensation and improved quality of life.
A blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trial supported a beneficial role for iron supplementation in FMS treatment among patients with low iron stores.

In an RCT, women with FMS consuming 50 mL of extra-virgin or refined olive oil for 3 weeks showed improved antioxidative profiles, reduced pain (FIQ), and improved quality of life, with antithrombotic and anti-inflammatory effects.

A preliminary single-patient study found that high-hydroxytyrosol nutritional treatment normalized dermal fibroblast protein expression involved in extracellular matrix turnover and oxidative metabolism in a patient with FMS compared with a healthy control.

Patients with FMS show increased prooxidative markers (nitric oxide, malondialdehyde, lipid hydroperoxide) and decreased xanthine oxidase, along with reduced endogenous antioxidants (glutathione, superoxide dismutase, total antioxidant status).
A systematic review found that supplementation with antioxidant vitamins and coenzyme Q10 for at least 6 weeks was associated with reduced pain perception in 80% of FMS patients.
Serum keratin type II cytoskeletal 80 concentration correlated negatively with depressive symptoms measured by the BDI scale in patients with FMS.
An immunoglobulin heavy chain V-I region segment (GHV1-46/HG3) showed a mild positive correlation with pain severity (VAS) in patients with FMS.
Higher serum total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglyceride levels have been reported in women with FMS, in parallel with increased cardiovascular risk and obesity.
