Increased skin mast cells, substance P, and CRH in FMS appear to activate release of IL-8 and MCP-1, elevating their plasma concentrations and supporting both as candidate inflammatory diagnostic biomarkers.
Small-fiber neuropathy is noted as a consistent finding in FMS, indicative of CNS/peripheral nerve degeneration relevant to the pain phenotype.
Consumption of refined olive oil in FMS patients reduced fibrinogen levels, platelet distribution width, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
α2-macroglobulin has been proposed as a treatment for neuropathic pain and is used in knee osteoarthritis injections to inhibit catabolic enzymes and cytokines and prevent cartilage degeneration.

An early survey found that approximately 30% of patients with FMS reported taking dietary supplements or making holistic dietary changes, all achieving improved pain relief according to healthcare professionals.
Two studies assessing sleep quality with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index in FMS patients converged on findings of poor sleep quality, frequent sleep interruptions, and fatigue.
One study quantifying anxiety and depression using BAI and BDI scales revealed an increased incidence of anxiety and depression among patients with FMS.

A patient with severe fibromyalgia comorbid with ME/CFS experienced considerable relief of widespread pain after 20 days of gradually escalating Kanshoho, a low-force (100-400g) muscle relaxation technique applied progressively from the superior nuchal line outward.
Standard pharmacological treatment with eperisone, pregabalin, and tramadol failed to control the patient's pain, which persisted and spread to the entire body over 6 months.
The patient exhibited severe allodynia, perceiving a mere 100 g of applied force as intensely painful ('being stabbed by a bed of nails').

The patient met American College of Rheumatology diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia with a Widespread Pain Index of 12 and a Symptom Severity Score of 9, including severe fatigue, unrefreshed wakening, mild cognitive symptoms, headaches, and depression.
The paper cites a systematic review indicating that almost half of reported ME/CFS cases overlap with fibromyalgia.
An electronic survey cited in the introduction found that more than half of respondents with fibromyalgia also suffer from migraine headache.
A cited study found that intramuscular force/pressure of the trapezius muscle was significantly higher in patients with fibromyalgia, suggesting trapezius stiffness may trigger FM.
A cited tender-point study (Simms et al) found that pressure intolerance above the nuchal line was not significantly different between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Barometric pressure is widely recognized as being associated with fibromyalgia symptom fluctuation, and the patient's pain flare from day 11 coincided with the onset of rainfall.
Acute and prolonged treatment with the hydroalcoholic extract of E. brasiliensis leaves (HEEb) reduced mechanical nociception in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia mouse model.
HEEb treatment reduced thermal nociception in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model, similar to duloxetine positive control comparisons.
HEEb-treated animals showed increased muscular strength compared to controls, without altering locomotion or motor coordination.
HEEb treatment did not significantly change locomotion or motor coordination parameters in the fibromyalgia model animals.
Treatment with HEEb reduced anxiety-like behaviors in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model.
Treatment with HEEb reduced depressive-like behaviors in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model.
HEEb treatment reduced hippocampal inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β and IL-6) in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model.
Treatment with the hydroalcoholic extract of E. brasiliensis leaves (HEEb) reduced IL-1β levels in the hippocampus of reserpine-treated mice.
Treatment with HEEb reduced IL-6 levels in the hippocampus of reserpine-treated mice.
HEEb treatment increased BDNF levels in the prefrontal cortex of reserpine-treated mice.
HEEb treatment did not alter total TrkB receptor expression in the brain of reserpine-treated mice.
HEEb treatment did not alter phosphorylated TrkB receptor expression in the brain of reserpine-treated mice.
Serum BDNF levels were significantly lower in both active and non-active RA patients compared with healthy controls.
Abnormal cognitive function was detected in a higher proportion of both active and non-active RA patients compared with healthy controls.
Serum BDNF level was not significantly associated with disease duration or with presence of cognitive dysfunction within RA patients.

One paper using a clinical symptom-based definition found LC patients had similar Mast Cell Mediator Release Scores to clinically confirmed mast cell activation patients, though there is no accepted international definition of mast cell activation.

IBS-D model rats exhibited significantly lower body weight and growth rate than control rats.
SYNC decoction and Pinaverium Bromide treatments ameliorated the weight loss caused by IBS-D modeling.
Fecal water content and AWR (abdominal withdrawal reflex) scores, markers of diarrhea and visceral hypersensitivity, were significantly elevated in IBS-D model rats versus controls.

Colonic histology of IBS-D model rats showed substantial inflammatory cell infiltration and submucosal edema compared with the smooth, intact mucosa of controls.
High-dose SYNC (SYNC-H) and Pinaverium Bromide restored colonic mucosal structural integrity with regular glands and normal goblet cell numbers, more effectively than low/medium-dose SYNC.
IBS-D model rats showed anxiety-like behavior in the open field test, with fewer entries into central/peripheral zones, shorter travel distance, and reduced grooming and upright behaviors.

SYNC treatment (especially high-dose SYNC-H) increased central-zone entries, grooming, and upright behaviors in the open field test, whereas Pinaverium Bromide showed no significant improvement in peripheral-zone entries, grooming, or upright behaviors.
IBS-D model rats showed significantly lower sucrose preference (sugar-water bias rate) than controls, indicating a depression-like phenotype.

Colonic mast cell infiltration (toluidine blue staining) was elevated in IBS-D model rats and significantly reduced in normal, SYNC-medium, SYNC-high, and Pinaverium Bromide groups.
Colonic mast cell tryptase (MCT) expression, a marker of mast cell degranulation, was elevated in the IBS-D model group and significantly reduced in the normal, SYNC-M, SYNC-H, and PI groups.
Serum IL-6 was elevated in IBS-D model rats compared with controls, consistent with intestinal inflammation.
Serum corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) was elevated in IBS-D model rats compared with controls.
Serum calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) was elevated in IBS-D model rats compared with controls.
Serum serotonin (5-HT) was elevated in IBS-D model rats compared with controls.

Nr4a3 gene expression was significantly upregulated in colon tissue of the IBS-D model group compared with controls, and was subsequently downregulated after medium-dose SYNC treatment.

CRH-R1 expression was upregulated in both colon and hypothalamus of IBS-D model rats compared to controls.

In post-COVID SFN, innate immune factors including NK cells, dendritic cells, activated macrophages, and cytokines are prominent and may trigger immune-mediated nerve injury.

Among idiopathic SFN cases, nearly 20% occur alongside another autoimmune disease such as Sjögren syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, or sarcoidosis, termed 'apparently autoimmune SFN.'
Fibromyalgia commonly seen in connective tissue diseases may in many cases be attributable to underlying small fiber neuropathy based on skin biopsy findings.
Anti-Plexin-D1 antibodies, detected in less than 13% of SFN patients, may contribute to neuropathic pain by binding to dorsal root ganglion sections.
Controlled neuropathy trials are known to show a 30%-40% placebo effect, complicating interpretation of subjective IVIg efficacy assessments in SFN.

The modified epidermal nerve fiber density counting protocol using PGP9.5 immunostaining on thin FFPE sections showed excellent intraobserver and interobserver reliability.

FSP-1 expression was negatively correlated with SMAD7 expression in AS sacroiliac joint tissue.
PAR-2 knockout mice showed a more severe decrease in body temperature than wild-type mice during IgE-dependent passive systemic anaphylaxis.
PAR-2 knockout mice showed a more severe decrease in body temperature than wild-type mice during IgE-independent (compound 48/80-induced) anaphylaxis.
There was no significant difference in the number of skin mast cells between wild-type and PAR-2 knockout mice.
Plasma histamine levels after compound 48/80 injection did not differ significantly between wild-type and PAR-2 knockout mice, indicating comparable mast cell degranulation.
Plasma mMCP-6 (mast cell tryptase) levels after compound 48/80 injection did not differ significantly between wild-type and PAR-2 knockout mice.

PAR-2 deficiency did not significantly affect hematocrit changes, pulmonary Evans blue dye extravasation, or local ear vascular permeability following compound 48/80-induced anaphylaxis, indicating PAR-2 has little effect on vascular hyperpermeability during anaphylaxis.
PAR-2 knockout mice showed significantly lower blood pressure than wild-type mice at 15 and 20 minutes after compound 48/80 injection, indicating impaired recovery from anaphylactic hypotension.
In PAR-2 knockout mice, lung eNOS mRNA expression after compound 48/80 injection was significantly higher than baseline, an effect not seen in wild-type mice.
At 120 minutes after compound 48/80 injection, lung eNOS protein expression was significantly higher in PAR-2 knockout mice than in wild-type mice.
At 10 minutes after compound 48/80 injection, lung eNOS phosphorylation was significantly higher in PAR-2 knockout mice than in wild-type mice.
mMCP-6 (mast cell tryptase)-deficient mice showed no significant difference in body temperature decrease compared to wild-type mice after compound 48/80-induced anaphylaxis.
Pharmacological PAR-2 antagonism with ENMD-1068 exacerbated the decrease in body temperature during compound 48/80-induced anaphylaxis in wild-type mice.
PAR-2 antagonism with ENMD-1068 did not affect the decrease in body temperature during anaphylaxis in mMCP-6-deficient mice, indicating the antagonist's effect requires mMCP-6.
Wild-type mice pre-treated with the PAR-2 antagonist ENMD-1068 showed increased lung eNOS phosphorylation compared to vehicle-treated mice 10 minutes after compound 48/80 administration.
CGRP-immunoreactive fine, varicose nerve endings were localized within motor endplates on a small proportion (4%) of esophageal striated muscle fibers in the rat.

Most of the CGRP-positive nerve endings in the motor endplates were co-localized with nitric oxide (NO) synthase-containing nerve terminals, suggesting a spatial relationship between sensory and intrinsic nitrergic nerve endings.
Most CGRP-positive nerve endings in esophageal motor endplates co-expressed substance P (SP) and TRPV1, indicating a sensory/nociceptive phenotype for these terminals.

Retrograde tracing with Fast Blue injected into the esophagus revealed many Fast Blue-labeled CGRP-positive sensory neurons that were also SP- and TRPV1-positive in the nodose ganglion and the T10 dorsal root ganglion, identifying the vagal and spinal origin of the CGRP nerve endings.

The authors propose that a subset of esophageal striated muscle fibers are triply innervated (vagal motor, enteric nitrergic, and sensory CGRP/SP/TRPV1 nerves), with the sensory terminals potentially detecting acetylcholine-derived acetic acid and NO within motor endplates to help regulate esophageal motility.
Oral GBE (100 and 200 mg/kg) significantly reduced bleomycin-induced dermal thickening in mice.
GBE reduced collagen deposition (Masson's trichrome) compared to the BLM group.

CKF treatment decreased 5-HT and substance P concentrations in serum and colon tissues of IBS-D model rats, correlating with symptom improvement.

TEA/ST36-100 Hz, but not other stimulation modalities, significantly increased rectal sensation thresholds for first sensation and urge to defecate.

MVPA was positively correlated with gait velocity after adjusting for age and height.
MVPA was positively correlated with step length after adjusting for age and height.
Sedentary time was negatively correlated with gait velocity.
Sedentary time was negatively correlated with step length.

Serum TGF-beta concentration, a marker of lung fibrosis, did not differ between COVID-19 convalescents and never-infected controls.
Soluble CD163, a marker of pulmonary macrophage activation, showed no significant difference between convalescents and never-infected subjects.
COVID-19 convalescents had a significantly lower serum Lp-PLA2 concentration, a marker of vascular/endothelial risk, than never-infected subjects.

Serum creatinine concentration did not differ between COVID-19 convalescents and never-infected controls.
Serum NGAL concentration, a marker of acute kidney injury, did not differ between COVID-19 convalescents and never-infected controls.

Sequence analysis and clustering of return-to-work (RTW) trajectories in breast cancer survivors identified four distinct clusters: slow RTW, quick RTW, partial RTW, and part-time work.
Breast cancer survivors in the quick and slow RTW clusters showed slightly lower baseline anxiety levels compared to other clusters.
Breast cancer survivors in the quick and slow RTW clusters showed higher baseline health-related quality of life (HRQoL) levels compared to other clusters.
Breast cancer survivors in the quick RTW cluster reported higher functioning-related HRQoL and fewer symptoms of pain and fatigue over the 4 years following diagnosis compared to other clusters.
Breast cancer survivors in the partial RTW cluster showed lower HRQoL on almost all dimensions compared to other RTW clusters.
All RTW clusters showed an increase in pain and fatigue symptoms until 6 months post-diagnosis, followed by a tendency to return toward baseline levels.

Breast cancer survivors who returned to full-time work via slow or quick RTW patterns recovered better psychosocially and in HRQoL than those who returned to part-time work via partial or part-time RTW patterns.

Atopic dermatitis was associated with increased risk of post-COVID-19 condition.

Low educational attainment showed a non-significant negative association with ME/CFS risk relative to medium educational attainment when compared to hospital chronic-disease controls.
Low educational attainment was associated with a 68% reduction in the risk of ME/CFS diagnosis relative to medium educational attainment when comparing to a randomly selected healthy population.
High educational attainment showed no statistically significant association with ME/CFS risk relative to medium attainment when compared to the random healthy population.

High household income showed no statistically significant effect on ME/CFS risk relative to medium income when compared to the random healthy population.
Employment status showed no significant association with ME/CFS risk when compared to hospital chronic-disease controls.

Being married was associated with a 23% decreased risk of ME/CFS diagnosis relative to being single, compared to hospital chronic-disease controls.

Both female and male ME/CFS patients showed significantly reduced scores on Fatigue Severity Scale, Pain and Fatigue Analog Scale, and SF-36 quality-of-life measures compared to their respective healthy controls.

An estimated 15-20% of adults with confirmed or suspected SARS-CoV-2 infection develop long-term symptoms lasting more than 3 months, termed post-COVID-19 condition.
Beta-endorphin, an endogenous opiate-like molecule whose circulation is increased by low-dose naltrexone, has been reported to be reduced in patients with ME/CFS.
Low-dose naltrexone antagonises toll-like receptors on neuroglia and peripheral blood mononuclear cells, resulting in reduced production of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF.
Increased IL-6 and TNF signaling, along with neuroinflammation, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of post-COVID-19 condition and ME/CFS.

In a prior single-centre study, 52 patients with post-COVID-19 condition treated with low-dose naltrexone had, on average, overall improvement in activities of daily living, energy levels, pain, concentration and sleep disturbance.
In a retrospective study, 37 of 59 (62.7%) patients with post-COVID-19 condition treated with low-dose naltrexone reported improvement in at least one symptom.

Prior clinical trials and case series in related conditions (e.g., fibromyalgia, ME/CFS) and clinical experience indicate that low-dose naltrexone is generally safe and well tolerated with a limited side-effect profile.
Almost a quarter of ME/CFS patients reported having been ill for 6 to 10 years before diagnosis.
62% of ME/CFS patients received a diagnosis within 10 years of disease onset, while 6.4% waited 21-40 years for diagnosis.

75% of participants consulted 6 to 15 different doctors across a wide range of specialties, particularly general medicine, neurology, internal medicine and psychosomatics/psychiatry, during the course of their illness.
ME/CFS diagnosis was made in particular by general practitioners and immunologists.
On average, participants reported 11 symptoms, mostly of a neuroregulatory nature.

The pattern of specialist referral in the diagnostic pathway for ME/CFS in Germany appears driven by individual symptoms or arbitrary contacting of doctors across disciplines rather than a systematic referral pathway.
Among 14 included publications on multimodal treatment for homebound ME/CFS patients, home visits (n=5) and telemedicine formats (n=7) were the predominant treatment delivery methods.
Individualisation and flexibility of treatment methods, allowing adaptation to day-to-day impairment levels, was identified as an important factor in eight of the included studies.
Explicit involvement of the patients' families in the treatment plan was described in six of the included studies.

Treatment concepts were evaluated in ten of the fourteen articles, predominantly using questionnaires (n=7) that were not consistent across studies, while qualitative evaluations invariably used Brown and Clarke's thematic analysis (n=3).

The review concludes that publications on multimodal treatment strategies specifically for homebound ME/CFS patients are rare, highlighting a research gap and specific care challenges for severely affected patients.
The paper's title poses whether post-infectious ME/CFS resembles or 'recalls' the clinical picture of post-COVID (PASC) syndrome, suggesting shared pathophysiology between the two conditions.

Usability testing of the developed HOPE program using the System Usability Scale showed a score corresponding to high acceptability.
Molecular testing of all three affected brothers revealed a homozygous deletion of exon 2 of the PLOD1 gene, confirming the diagnosis of kyphoscoliotic EDS, with both parents identified as carriers.

Patient 1, a 13-year-old boy with PLOD1-kEDS, developed a spontaneous celiac artery aneurysm rupture presenting with severe abdominal pain and a precipitous hemoglobin drop requiring massive transfusion and emergent laparotomy with celiac artery ligation.
Patient 2, the 10-year-old brother, developed a rapidly growing 1.7-cm celiac artery aneurysm without rupture, requiring urgent laparotomy and celiac artery ligation.

Eight months after celiac artery ligation, patient 2 developed a recurrent 9.5-mm pseudoaneurysm at the ligation site detected on surveillance imaging while asymptomatic, requiring reexploration and primary ligation.
Patient 2 experienced ocular fragility with scleral rupture of the right eye after minimal trauma at age 7, complicated by retinal detachment.

PLOD1-kEDS results from lysyl hydroxylase-1 deficiency, an enzyme critical for post-translational collagen cross-link formation, leading to vascular fragility and aneurysm/rupture susceptibility in medium-sized arteries.

PLOD1-kEDS carries a lower, yet still significant, risk of life-threatening vascular complications (aneurysms, arterial dissections, intracranial hemorrhages) compared with COL3A1-related vascular EDS.
Both patients were managed with a target systolic blood pressure below 110 mm Hg to reduce arterial rupture risk, achieved without antihypertensive medication.
The authors recommend annual surveillance with CT angiography or MR angiography for patients with PLOD1-kEDS to detect vascular complications.

The cumulative prevalence of EDS was estimated at 1 in 5,000 in a 2002 estimate, though true prevalence remains uncertain due to evolving diagnostic criteria and underdiagnosis.

The symptom subscale score of the EDS Disability Index showed a statistically significant improvement between initial and follow-up visits.

A few index variables did not show significant pre-post changes with treatment, raising the possibility of insensitivity to certain interventions though longitudinal and diverse-cohort testing is needed before concluding insensitivity.

Joint hypermobility prevalence in the lower limb followed the pattern knee > ankle > hip, which mirrors the pattern of contracture development seen in type II but differs from that in type III SMA.

Small fiber neuropathy has a low reported general population incidence and prevalence.

Epinephrine depletion via adrenodemedullation in animals under baseline conditions induced mechanical hyperalgesia and increased muscle proteolysis.
Overall, reduced sympathetic nervous system activity is implicated in the development of both pain and muscle atrophy in this female rat model of fibromyalgia.

Primary human mast cell viability was unaffected after 1 hour of exposure to either BD-MoS2 or BS-MoS2 at low (5 μg/mL) or high (50 μg/mL) doses.
MoS2 exposure did not induce mast cell degranulation as measured by β-hexosaminidase release in primary human mast cells, unlike the positive control C48/80.
MoS2 exposure at all tested concentrations and timepoints did not change expression of the activation markers CD63 and CD203c on primary mast cells, whereas C48/80 significantly increased CD63.
A non-significant increase in the late-activation marker CD107a was observed at 1 hour with molybdate and with both MoS2 materials at all tested doses in primary mast cells.

Expression of the IgE receptor FceRI on primary mast cells was increased compared to control only by soluble molybdate ion, not by either MoS2 material, with a stronger increase seen with the C48/80 positive control.
A non-significant increase in the non-IgE receptor MRGX2 was seen with molybdate and high-dose BS-MoS2 at 6 hours in primary mast cells.

LAD2 mast cell line viability at 6 hours was decreased only by the positive control C48/80, not by either MoS2 material, and a much lower C48/80 concentration was needed in LAD2 than in primary cells.
MoS2 did not induce degranulation in LAD2 cells as measured by β-hexosaminidase release, similar to primary mast cells.
In LAD2 cells, a non-significant increase in CD63 was seen with molybdate at 1 hour and with high-dose BD-MoS2 and BS-MoS2 at 6 hours.

No differences in ROS production at 1 hour were observed for any of the tested materials or controls in primary mast cells.

Electron microscopy showed that most MoS2 material remained outside mast cells or surface-associated, with minimal intracellular uptake in either primary mast cells or LAD2 cells, suggesting observed effects arise from surface contact rather than internalization.

In study 1, PTX induced significant mechanical allodynia at the end of treatment that resolved during the follow-up period.
In study 1, PTX induced significant thermal hyperalgesia at the end of treatment that resolved by the end of follow-up.
In study 2, PTX induced mechanical allodynia at the end of treatment (reversible), but did not induce thermal hyperalgesia at any time point.

Morphological analysis in study 1 showed mild, largely reversible axonopathy in sciatic nerve but severe, poorly reversible axonopathy with degenerated and lost myelinated fibers in proximal and distal caudal nerve segments after PTX.

Overall comparison showed that the chronic i.v. weekly high-cumulative-dose paclitaxel model (study 1) recapitulates the full clinical spectrum of human PIPN (pain, small fiber loss, large fiber axonopathy, elevated NfL), while the intermittent i.p. lower-dose model (study 2) reproduces only the acute painful phase without significant large-fiber pathology.

The authors propose that loss of oral tolerance to food antigens after an insult such as enteric infection leads to localized activation of mast cells and eosinophils with release of histamine and cytokines in patients with IBS or FD.

Inflammatory mediators such as histamine and cytokines released locally are proposed to have systemic effects, including triggering nociceptive nerves and altering mood, in patients with disorders of gut-brain interaction.

Dietary interventions including low-FODMAP diet, food antigen or gluten elimination, IgG food sensitivity diets, and salicylate restriction may benefit some patients with IBS or FD, potentially by modulating the proposed immune-mediated postprandial symptom pathway.

Drugs including proton pump inhibitors, histamine-receptor antagonists, mast cell stabilisers, and tricyclic or tetracyclic antidepressants with anti-histaminergic actions are proposed as potential treatments for FD and IBS acting on the immune-mediated postprandial symptom pathway.

The authors note that food antigen-driven intestinal immune activation is unlikely to fully explain postprandial symptoms, and that carbohydrate fermentation with gas release, adverse reactions to food chemicals, central mechanisms or nocebo effects may dominate in other patients.

Among 107 Fabry disease patients followed at a French tertiary center, four (3.7%) had at least one episode of aseptic meningitis.
Pooled analysis of 29 patients with FD-associated aseptic meningitis (4 center cases + 25 from literature) showed a median age of 29.0 years and male predominance (58.6%).

Among the 29 pooled patients, clinical course varied: 41.4% acute meningitis with meningeal syndrome, 24.1% acute meningitis with focal deficits without meningeal syndrome, 13.8% chronic meningitis with meningeal syndrome, 13.8% chronic meningitis with focal deficits without meningeal syndrome, and 6.9% recurrent meningitis with meningeal syndrome.
CSF pleocytosis in FD-associated meningitis was usually mild (median 24 cells/mm3), predominantly lymphocytic (64.7%), with elevated protein.

A large majority of patients with FD-associated aseptic meningitis had cerebrovascular involvement: 57.1% had a recent stroke on MRI, 62.1% had a stroke at some point during follow-up, and 75% of those with recent stroke had CSF leukocyte counts ≥20/mm3.
Large artery stenosis was found in 17.2% (n=5) and white-matter lesions in 40.7% of the pooled patients; basilar dolichoectasia was less common (7.7%, n=2).

Enzyme replacement therapy did not reliably resolve meningitis or prevent stroke: of 14 ERT-treated patients, 2 had a new stroke, and among 9 who had a repeat lumbar puncture, meningitis persisted in 5.
In the single reported case treated with migalastat, initiation of therapy did not prevent further strokes, while CSF (already normal before treatment) remained normal under migalastat.
In 82.8% of pooled patients, Fabry disease was undiagnosed prior to the discovery of aseptic meningitis, and 82.8% had the classic FD phenotype.
Aseptic meningitis in FD is frequently misattributed to other diseases, most often multiple sclerosis (31.0%), infectious meningitis (22.2%), and CNS vasculitis (17.9%).

Patient 1 (female) was confirmed to have classic Fabry disease via a pathogenic GLA variant (c.123delC), presenting with recurrent lymphocytic meningitis, chronic intracranial hypertension, and ischemic stroke.

Patient 2 was ultimately diagnosed with Fabry disease (GLA c.950T>C) after years of presumed idiopathic CNS vasculitis with recurrent stroke, arterial stenoses, and persistent lymphocytic meningitis unresponsive to multiple immunosuppressive regimens.

Patient 3 (male) had reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity and a pathogenic GLA variant (c.279C>G), presenting with recurrent stroke, lymphocytic meningitis, angiokeratoma, hypohidrosis, and proteinuria.

Patient 4 (male) had markedly reduced alpha-galactosidase A blood level, consistent with Fabry disease presenting with vestibular syndrome, meningitis, recurrent stroke, and basilar artery dolichoectasia.
A previously published case of meningitis-like CSF findings in a woman with the GLA c.937G>T (p.D313Y) variant was excluded from the review because the pathogenicity of this variant is debated.

Young FD patients have a markedly higher stroke incidence than the general population, with mean age at first ischemic stroke of 39.2 years in men and 51 years in women, and stroke frequency ~12-fold higher in men and ~10-fold higher in women aged 25-44 versus the general population.
In a prior retrospective study of 50 FD patients, 52% had white-matter lesions, and these were systematically present after age 55.
Strokes in Fabry disease are proposed to result mainly from Gb3 accumulation in vascular endothelium, reducing vascular compliance and causing cerebral hypoperfusion.

Excess Gb3 may generate pro-inflammatory signals by disrupting lipid raft organization and dysregulating toll-like receptor 4 pathway activation, promoting TNF and IL-1beta secretion, and may also generate reactive oxygen species via NO synthase inhibition; dysregulated autophagy is proposed as another pro-inflammatory mechanism in FD.

Stroke alone rarely produces substantial CSF pleocytosis in the general population, arguing against reactive post-stroke inflammation as the sole explanation for the elevated CSF cell counts seen in FD-associated meningitis.

Enzyme replacement therapy is accepted to stabilize renal disease and cardiomyopathy in FD, but its benefit in reducing stroke risk and white-matter lesion progression is unclear, possibly because it does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
Peripheral nervous system involvement in Fabry disease combines autonomic dysfunction and small fiber neuropathy, manifesting as neuropathic pain (acroparesthesia) and hypohidrosis.
The authors conclude that, in the absence of an alternative diagnosis in the reviewed cases, there is a high probability of a causal relationship between Fabry disease and aseptic meningitis.

NK cells from post-COVID-19 condition patients were significantly more resistant to the TRPM3 inhibitor ononetin than healthy control cells.

Constipation was the most commonly reported GI symptom, affecting 61% of the hEDS/JHS cohort.
Dysphagia was the second most commonly reported symptom, occurring in 32% of patients.
A quarter of the cohort reported symptoms of dyspepsia/gastroparesis spectrum, including abdominal pain, post-prandial nausea, vomiting, early satiety, or weight loss.
Upper endoscopy was performed in 67% of patients and had histological abnormalities in 34% of those tested.
Eosinophilic esophagitis was found in 21% of the hEDS/JHS cohort, markedly higher than the estimated general population prevalence of 1 in 1000.
Celiac disease was diagnosed in 4% of the hEDS/JHS cohort, an increased prevalence compared to the general population, though lower than the 16% reported in a prior adult hEDS study.
Colonoscopy was performed in 111 patients, with 24% having abnormal histological results including eosinophilic colitis, microscopic colitis, and inflammatory bowel disease.

Contrast imaging of the upper GI tract was abnormal in 14 of 108 patients, with esophageal dysmotility as the most reported abnormality.

Gastric scintigraphy showed delayed gastric emptying at 4 hours in 50 of 80 patients tested, with none showing accelerated emptying.

Among constipated patients who underwent anorectal manometry, half had manometric evidence of rectal evacuation dysfunction, with no evidence of rectal hyposensitivity or high prevalence of colonic dysmotility.

Valvular heart disease was notably prevalent in female hEDS patients, with about one-fourth reporting issues with one or more heart valves, an enrichment relative to general population data.
Abdominal hernias and pelvic organ prolapse were observed in nearly 20% of female hEDS patients.

Pelvic organ prolapse and mitral valve prolapse were less frequent in male hEDS patients than in females, while abdominal hernias and other heart valve conditions were similar between genders.
Gastrointestinal issues were the most frequently reported comorbidity across all gender groups in the hEDS cohort.

Tethered cord syndrome showed a 2-fold increase in occurrence among nonbinary patients with hEDS.

Beighton score (mean 7.4, range 7.0-7.6 across ages) did not correlate with number of comorbid conditions, gender, or age in the hEDS cohort.
On average, hEDS patients reported 11 conditions, and nearly all (98.6%) had at least 4 comorbid conditions, indicating substantial multimorbidity.

K-means clustering of hEDS diagnostic and comorbid condition data identified 3 distinct patient clusters independent of age, differing mainly in total condition burden and neurologic/MCAS comorbidities.

Cluster 3 patients showed a notably higher rate of neurologic comorbidities (craniocervical instability/atlantoaxial instability, Chiari malformation, tethered cord syndrome) and increased MCAS prevalence compared with Clusters 1 and 2.

Integrating Beighton scores into the k-means clustering analysis dissolved the previously identified clusters, suggesting the Beighton score is not a reliable criterion for hEDS multimorbidity phenotyping.

The 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria phenotypes (aside from joint subluxations and chronic pain) were less prevalent than the top comorbidities (gastrointestinal manifestations, anxiety, dysautonomia/POTS, migraine), raising questions about the adequacy of current diagnostic criteria.
Among children diagnosed with EDS, fracture prevalence was 34.6% (9 of 26).
Among children diagnosed with Generalized Joint Hypermobility, fracture prevalence was 25.4% (15 of 59).
No fractures occurred in infants under 1 year of age among children with EDS or GJH, arguing against these diagnoses as a cause of infant fractures.

IKDC functional score improved significantly after MPFL reconstruction with synthetic suture tape.
Tegner activity score improved significantly after MPFL reconstruction with synthetic suture tape.

One knee experienced suture-tape rupture as a postoperative complication following MPFL reconstruction.
One knee developed a surgical wound infection as a postoperative complication following MPFL reconstruction.
One patient reported residual pain postoperatively and did not experience the improvement seen in the rest of the cohort.

People with functional neurological disorder scored higher on the 5-Part Questionnaire for joint hypermobility than controls, with 74% meeting the common cut-off for joint hypermobility syndrome compared with 45% of controls.
Anxiety scores measured by GAD7 were higher in people with FND compared to controls.
Depression scores measured by PHQ9 were higher in people with FND compared to controls.
In a regression model, anxiety, depression, and joint hypermobility scores all predicted FND status, with joint hypermobility being the strongest predictor.
