COL4A1 mutations, affecting the α1 chain of type IV collagen in basement membranes, were the most frequently cited genetic cause of pediatric hemorrhagic stroke among the reviewed studies and can present as intracranial hemorrhage mimicking non-accidental head injury.

COL4A2 variants, affecting the α2 chain of type IV collagen, are associated with familial porencephaly and fetal/neonatal intracranial hemorrhage, with markedly variable neurological phenotypes even among relatives carrying the same deletion.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS type IV), caused by COL3A1 variants affecting procollagen III, predisposes to arterial fragility with cerebrovascular manifestations including subarachnoid hemorrhage, carotid-cavernous fistulae and intracranial aneurysms.

A case report described a 4-month-old girl with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (variant of unknown significance) who presented with subdural hemorrhage, retinal hemorrhage and bone fractures with no history of trauma, illustrating how EDS can mimic abusive head trauma.

A case report of a 13-year-old girl with kyphoscoliotic-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (PLOD1 variant) described a perinatal white-matter hemorrhage present at birth that progressed with gliotic changes over subsequent years, alongside generalized hypotonia and skin hematomas.
Children with neurofibromatosis type 1 have a substantially increased risk of hemorrhagic stroke compared with the general pediatric population.

A retrospective study by Rosser et al. identified eight NF1 patients with cerebral vasculopathy (stenosis, ectasia, aneurysm, Moyamoya pattern), including asymptomatic aneurysm and Moyamoya findings in children as young as 1-2 years old.
Rea et al. found at least a 6% prevalence of cerebral arteriopathy, including intracranial hemorrhage, among children with NF1.

Moyamoya disease, associated with RNF213 gene variants, causes progressive stenosis of the distal internal carotid artery with fragile collateral vessel formation, and accounts for hemorrhagic stroke in about 20% of pediatric Moyamoya-related strokes.
Homozygous GUCY1A3 variants cause a rare syndrome combining neonatal-onset achalasia with Moyamoya angiopathy, stroke and coronary artery disease.
Heterozygous ACTA2 variants are associated with a broad vasculopathy phenotype including Moyamoya disease, aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection and premature coronary artery disease.

Sickle cell disease, caused by homozygous variants in the β-globin gene (HbSS), markedly increases risk of intracranial hemorrhage, which is about 200 times more frequent than in the general population and carries high mortality.

Al-Jarallah et al. analyzed 68 children with nontraumatic intraparenchymal hemorrhage and found three had sickle cell disease (aged 6, 4 and 2.5 years), with at least one case following ischemic infarction.

Cerebral cavernous malformations, caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in KRIT1 (CCM1), CCM2, or PDCD10 (CCM3), present intracranial hemorrhage in 25-40% of cases; two pediatric case reports (18-month-old and 3-year-old) described bleeding cavernomas due to CCM1 mutations.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, caused predominantly by ACVRL1 (55%) or ENG (44%) variants (rarely SMAD4), is associated with cerebral arteriovenous malformations in about 10% of cases, with cerebral hemorrhage as the first manifestation in about 20% of HHT patients with AVMs.

Marfan syndrome, caused by FBN1 variants affecting microfibrils, is associated with increased risk of intracranial aneurysms and neurovascular complications even in childhood; a case series reported a female infant under 1 year old with Marfan syndrome presenting with subdural hematoma while on anticoagulation for valve prolapse.
Low expression of miR-126 has been associated with increased perihematomal edema after intracerebral hemorrhage, a major driver of morbidity and mortality.
miR-130a has been proposed as a non-invasive biomarker for cerebral edema following hemorrhagic stroke, useful in predicting disease progression.
miR-502-5p, miR-1297 and miR-4320 have been proposed as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for severity of subarachnoid hemorrhage due to ruptured aneurysm, AVM or cranial trauma.

Bleeding disorders such as hemophilia, von Willebrand disease, vitamin K deficiency and Factor XIII deficiency can cause intracranial and retinal hemorrhage following minor trauma or spontaneously, and may be misinterpreted as abusive head injury if not properly investigated.
Cecal volvulus after gynecological surgery is extremely rare, with only one prior reported case (open hysterectomy for endometrial clear cell carcinoma) identified in the literature.

Previous abdominal surgery is an important risk factor for cecal volvulus, with 23-53% of patients in a case series having a history of prior abdominal surgery, via adhesion formation creating a fulcrum for cecal rotation.

The patient developed a cecal volvulus with high-grade bowel obstruction on postoperative day 3 following a robotic-assisted total laparoscopic hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and sentinel lymph node dissection for endometrial carcinoma.
Cecal hypermobility, identified on preoperative CT imaging as impaired mesenteric fixation to the retroperitoneum, placed this patient at higher risk for developing a volvulus.

Prior appendectomy has been shown to increase cecal mobility as a result of freeing peritoneal attachments, and the patient's remote appendectomy may have promoted volvulus development by providing a fixation point for rotation.
Extensive right pelvic sidewall dissection performed during the hysterectomy to manage retroperitoneal fibrosis may have contributed to increased cecal mobility and subsequent volvulus.

The authors propose that steep Trendelenburg positioning during laparoscopic surgery may be a previously undescribed risk factor for volvulus in patients with pre-existing or surgically induced colonic hypermobility, though this cannot be definitively attributed as causal.

Preoperative CT imaging identified a malpositioned, redundant cecum in the left upper quadrant, but intraoperatively the cecum had returned to the right abdomen, suggesting cecal location on CT is positioning-dependent and CT alone may not reliably assess postoperative volvulus risk.

Symptoms of mobile cecal syndrome, such as colicky right-sided pain or distention that resolves after flatus, are present in about half of patients who go on to develop volvulus and should prompt consideration of concurrent prophylactic cecopexy.
Emergent exploratory laparotomy with ileocecectomy and primary ileocolic anastomosis successfully resolved the ischemic, massively dilated cecal volvulus.
S100A8 was reported to be upregulated in saliva samples of fibromyalgia patients.
S100A12 (calgranulin C) was reported to be upregulated in saliva samples of fibromyalgia patients.
Expression of S100A8 was increased in peripheral B cells of fibromyalgia patients.
Expression of S100A9 was increased in peripheral B cells of fibromyalgia patients.
S100B was found to be significantly elevated in serum of women with several chronic pain conditions, including fibromyalgia.
Serum levels of S100A7 were found to be lower in fibromyalgia patients than in controls.

S100 proteins such as S100A7, S100A8, S100A9, S100A8/A9 dimer, S100A12, and S100B act as DAMPs binding RAGE and/or TLR4 on macrophages, activating JNK/ERK/p38 signaling to AP-1 and NF-κB and inducing release of proinflammatory cytokines.
Serum IL-6 concentrations were increased in fibromyalgia patients and positively correlated with Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores.
Serum IL-8 concentrations were increased in fibromyalgia patients and positively correlated with Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores.

IL-6 has been shown to alter the resting membrane potential threshold and cause neuronal hyperexcitability secondary to phosphorylation of the sodium channel Nav1.7, increasing pain signal transmission.
S100A4 has been implicated in the modulation of neuropathic pain in rodent models.
Increased levels of S100B, together with BDNF, may be associated with changes in neuronal plasticity that translate to chronic pain in fibromyalgia patients.
FM participants had higher normalized pain scores and higher initial pain ratings to the first heat contact than healthy controls, indicating greater pain sensitivity.
The excitatory PBN→thalamus signaling connection was weaker in fibromyalgia participants than in healthy controls.
The LC→hypothalamus signaling connection was stronger in fibromyalgia participants than in healthy controls in both Pain and No-Pain conditions.
The LC→thalamus signaling connection was stronger and more significant in healthy controls than in fibromyalgia participants in both Pain and No-Pain conditions.
The hypothalamus→LC signaling connection was consistently higher in fibromyalgia participants than healthy controls in both Pain and No-Pain conditions.
The LC→PBN signaling connection had lower values in fibromyalgia participants compared to healthy controls in both Pain and No-Pain conditions.

In the FM group during the Pain condition, LC→thalamus connectivity values were correlated with pain ratings, being higher in participants with lower initial pain ratings and decreasing as pain ratings increased.
ANCOVA analysis showed the C6RD (right dorsal horn, C6 spinal segment)→thalamus connection had significantly higher connectivity values in FM than in HC.
Group interaction effects for the C6RD→thalamus and PAG→NTS connections were noted between FM and HC but did not reach significance after multiple-comparison correction.

The LC→DRt connection was the only group-level significant connection with predominantly inhibitory (negative) signaling, and its pattern of difference between FM and HC groups/conditions was unclear.
The PBN→hypothalamus connection had higher values during the No-Pain condition than the Pain condition in both FM and HC groups.

The authors note that previously proposed mechanisms underlying fibromyalgia include dysregulation of norepinephrine signaling, diminished serotonin transporter function, and hyperactivity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis.
Reserpine treatment induced mechanical and cold hypersensitivity along with early anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in mice, modeling fibromyalgia.
Reserpine-treated mice showed increased oxidative stress markers in sciatic nerve tissue compared to controls.
Pharmacological blockade or global genetic deletion of TRPA1 prevented reserpine-induced pain-like and mood-related behaviors and oxidative stress increases.
Macrophage depletion abolished reserpine-induced pain-like and mood-related behaviors, implicating macrophage recruitment in the mechanism.

Selective silencing of TRPA1 in Schwann cells reduced reserpine-induced neuroinflammation, including NADPH oxidase 1-dependent ROS generation and macrophage increase in the sciatic nerve, and attenuated fibromyalgia-like behaviours.

Activated Schwann cells expressing TRPA1 promote an intracellular pathway culminating in NADPH oxidase 1-dependent ROS release and macrophage recruitment in the sciatic nerve, sustaining mechanical and cold hypersensitivity.
Hispidulin (HPD) treatment attenuated the OVA-induced increase in splenic weight, a marker of systemic immune activation.
Serum total and OVA-specific IgE were elevated in OVA-sensitized mice, and HPD treatment inhibited secretion of both.
HPD treatment decreased the number of eosinophils and neutrophils infiltrating the BALF in the OVA-induced asthma model.
HPD treatment reduced BALF eosinophil peroxidase release, an enzyme released by activated eosinophils.
Histopathological (H&E) analysis showed increased immune cell infiltration in OVA-treated lung tissue that was decreased with HPD treatment.
Type 2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) were elevated in BALF of OVA-treated mice, and HPD alleviated their production.
Lung gene expression of type 2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, and IL-13 increased with OVA exposure and was suppressed by HPD treatment.
Lymph node gene expression of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and STAT6 increased in OVA-exposed mice and was suppressed by HPD treatment.
Gene expression of mast-cell-released chemokines CCL2, CCL3, and CXCL8 was increased in the OVA-treated lung and effectively suppressed by HPD treatment.
HPD treatment did not suppress c-kit gene expression in the OVA-induced asthmatic lung, indicating no effect on mast cell differentiation marker.
HPD treatment effectively suppressed the expression of the mast-cell-specific marker Tpsg1 in the OVA-induced asthmatic lung.
β-hexosaminidase activity (a mast cell degranulation biomarker) was increased in OVA-induced allergic asthma and reduced by HPD treatment.
Toluidine blue staining showed HPD treatment reduced mast cell infiltration into lung tissue in the OVA-induced asthma model.
In DNP-IgE-sensitized RBL-2H3 mast cells challenged with DNP-HSA, HPD reduced β-hexosaminidase and histamine release in a concentration-dependent manner.
In PMA/A23187 (PMACI)-stimulated HMC-1 human mast cells, HPD treatment alleviated β-hexosaminidase and histamine release.
HPD treatment reduced intracellular calcium influx in DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells, as measured by Fluo-4 AM fluorescence.
HPD treatment suppressed phosphorylation of the FcεR1 downstream signaling cascade from Lyn through PI3K to PLCγ in challenged RBL-2H3 cells.
TNF-α and IL-4 secretion increased in DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells, and HPD produced a concentration-dependent reduction in secretion of both cytokines.
HPD treatment reduced gene expression of TNF-α, IL-4, IL-6, and IL-13 in DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells.
HPD inhibited phosphorylation of Akt, NF-κB, and IKKαβ in challenged RBL-2H3 cells and increased total IκBα, which had decreased upon activation.
iNOS levels, increased in OVA-induced lung tissue, were suppressed by HPD treatment as shown by IHC.
Diminished catalase gene expression in the asthmatic lung was restored by HPD treatment.
DNP-HSA stimulation decreased SOD2 and CAT (but not GPx) expression in RBL-2H3 cells; HPD treatment restored SOD2/CAT expression, increasing CAT above control level, but was less effective on GPx.
Intracellular ROS levels increased in DNP-HSA-challenged RBL-2H3 cells and were effectively reduced by HPD treatment.

DNP-HSA stimulation decreased gene expression of SOD2 and CAT (but not GPx) in RBL-2H3 mast cells, and HPD treatment restored and even increased SOD2/CAT expression above control levels while being less effective for GPx.
Intracellular ROS levels increased in DNP-HSA-challenged RBL-2H3 mast cells, and HPD treatment effectively reduced these ROS levels.
Total Nrf2 levels decreased in whole-cell lysate of DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells, but HPD treatment enhanced total Nrf2 while reducing HO-1 levels; HPD also reduced Nrf2 nuclear translocation.
HO-1 protein levels were increased in activated mast cells (DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3), and HPD treatment reduced nuclear Nrf2 translocation to confirm downstream reduction of HO-1 expression.
H2O2 stimulation reduced antioxidant gene expression (SOD2, CAT, GPx) in RBL-2H3 cells, and HPD treatment restored and further increased this expression beyond control levels.
In H2O2-treated RBL-2H3 cells, HPD treatment reduced the expression of the proinflammatory cytokine TNF-α under conditions of excessive oxidative stress.

MPO and IL-6 production increased in OVA-induced asthmatic mice, indicating a neutrophilic/proinflammatory response alongside the type 2 response, and HPD treatment alleviated the production of these inflammatory mediators.
Gene expression of proinflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 increased in lungs of OVA-exposed mice, and decreased following HPD treatment.
In the LPS-induced acute lung injury (ALI) model, HPD treatment reduced the total number of immune cells in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.
LPS-induced acute lung injury increased secretion of MPO and proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), which was decreased by HPD treatment.
Gene expression of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 increased in lung tissue of LPS-induced ALI mice and was reduced by HPD treatment, similar to the secretion-level results.
MOD000001 showed higher selectivity for KIT compared with imatinib, sunitinib, and staurosporine when profiled against 468 human kinases.
In cell-free kinase assays, MOD000001 inhibited KIT with an IC50 of 2 nM, while requiring much higher concentrations to inhibit the related receptors PDGFRA (1400 nM) and PDGFRB (218 nM).
MOD000001 inhibited SCF-stimulated autophosphorylation of KIT tyrosine residues 703 and 719 in NCL2 mouse mast cells expressing wild-type KIT.
MOD000001 decreased SCF-dependent growth of M-07e cells (wild-type KIT) and GIST-T1 cells (constitutively active KIT) in a dose-dependent manner.
MOD000001 exhibited 89.7% oral bioavailability and an approximate plasma half-life of 3 hours after a single oral 3 mg/kg dose in mice.
Oral MOD000001 (3-100 mg/kg) dose-dependently inhibited SCF-induced plasma histamine increases in mice.
MOD000001 dose-dependently inhibited SCF-dependent KIT, AKT, and ERK1/2 phosphorylation in mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs).
MOD000001 did not affect IgE-dependent PI3K and AKT phosphorylation in BMMCs, indicating pathway selectivity for SCF/KIT over FcεRI signaling.
MOD000001 inhibited SCF-dependent chemotaxis of BMMCs in a dose-dependent manner across 0.1, 1.0, and 10 μM.
Pretreatment with 1 or 10 μM MOD000001 inhibited the SCF-dependent potentiation of IgE-mediated degranulation in BMMCs, as measured by β-hexosaminidase release.
Treatment of BMMCs with 1 or 10 μM MOD000001 for at least 24 hours did not affect cell viability, assessed by cell counting, WST assay, and Annexin V staining.
Addition of MOD000001 (1 or 10 μM) at the start of human CD34+ cell differentiation with IL-6 and SCF induced apoptosis and reduced the number of KIT-positive cells by culture day 28.
Addition of MOD000001 (0.3 or 3 μM) to mature (day 84) human PBMC-derived mast cell cultures induced apoptosis and reduced the number of KIT+FcεRI+ cells by day 89.

Oral MOD000001 (100 mg/kg daily for 7 days) inhibited the passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) reaction as effectively as imatinib, shown by decreased ear thickness, Evans blue extravasation, and serum CCL2 levels.

Despite attenuating the PCA reaction, 7-day oral MOD000001 treatment did not change skin mast cell numbers compared with vehicle, indicating short-term efficacy is not mediated by mast cell depletion.
Oral administration of 100 mg/kg MOD000001 for 7 weeks, but not 3 or 5 weeks, reduced the number of skin and peritoneal mast cells in mice.
3D tissue-clearing and light-sheet fluorescence microscopy in Mcpt5-Cre TdTomato reporter mice visually confirmed a reduction in skin mast cells after 7-week MOD000001 treatment.
PCA reaction was attenuated in mice treated orally with 100 mg/kg MOD000001 daily for 7 weeks compared with vehicle-treated controls.
Ultravist concentrations above 150 mg/ml induced significant cytotoxicity/cell death in P815 mast cells, establishing a non-toxic dose range for subsequent experiments.
Histamine levels in the supernatant of P815 mast cells increased in a dose-dependent manner with increasing ultravist concentration, indicating mast cell activation.
Intracellular β-hexosaminidase concentration decreased in a dose-dependent manner with increasing ultravist concentration, consistent with degranulation and release of this lysosomal enzyme.
Small RNA sequencing of ultravist-stimulated P815 mast cells identified 20 miRNAs that were differentially upregulated or downregulated compared with control.
miR-19a-3p was upregulated in P815 mast cells upon ultravist stimulation and was associated with activation of the mTOR signaling pathway.
miR-362-3p was upregulated in P815 mast cells upon ultravist stimulation and was associated with activation of the mTOR signaling pathway.

KEGG pathway mapping of miR-19a-3p and miR-362-3p targets showed upregulation of key mTOR pathway components including mTOR, AMP-activated protein kinase, PTEN and protein kinase C in contrast-medium-stimulated mast cells.
RT-qPCR confirmed a dose-dependent increase in miR-19a-3p expression with increasing ultravist doses, validating the sequencing data.
RT-qPCR confirmed a dose-dependent increase in miR-362-3p expression with increasing ultravist doses, validating the sequencing data.

Network analysis identified Atxn1, Akap2, and Uba2pl as candidate genes co-regulated by both miR-19a-3p and miR-362-3p, implicating them in mTOR pathway modulation during contrast medium-induced mast cell activation.
One of three replicate qPCR validation experiments for the miRNAs failed due to absence of detectable signal, so conclusions were drawn from only two of the three datasets.

The mast-cell related G-protein coupled receptor MRGPRX2 pathway has been identified as a mechanism of direct mast cell degranulation independent of IgE/FcεRI signaling, contributing to perioperative anaphylaxis.
The review notes ongoing investigations into a possible connection between the microbiota and anaphylaxis, with implications for future treatment strategies.
Serum tryptase levels serve as an indicator of mast cell activation during perioperative anaphylaxis, though identifying the specific trigger remains difficult.

A broad range of mediators including vasoactive peptides, proteases, lipid molecules, cytokines, chemokines, interleukins, complement components, and coagulation factors have been associated with anaphylaxis.
Early life exposure to acrylic acid was associated with an increased likelihood of developing allergic rhinitis.
Early life exposure to phosphine was associated with increased risk of developing allergic rhinitis.
Early life exposure to antimony compounds was associated with increased risk of developing allergic rhinitis.
Early life exposure to benzyl chloride was associated with increased risk of developing allergic rhinitis.
Air toxic exposures were found to alter nasal DNA methylation and gene expression of genes involved in mast cell activation, which mediated their effect on allergic rhinitis risk.
Pro-inflammatory TGF-β1 signaling gene expression/methylation in nasal mucosa was altered by air toxic exposure and mediated its effect on allergic rhinitis.
Genes involved in respiratory ciliary function in nasal mucosa were altered by air toxic exposure and mediated the effect on allergic rhinitis.

Nasal DNA methylation and gene expression changes linked to early-life air toxic exposure included alterations in genes involved in mast cell activation, implicating this pathway in mediating air pollutant effects on allergic rhinitis.
Pro-inflammatory TGF-β1 signaling genes in the nasal mucosa showed altered DNA methylation and expression associated with early-life air toxic exposure and allergic rhinitis.
Genes regulating myeloid immune cell function in the nasal mucosa were among those altered by early-life air toxic exposure and linked to allergic rhinitis risk.

Oral administration of aspalathin dose-dependently suppressed IgE-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis responses in mice, including Evans blue extravasation, ear thickening, and mast cell degranulation.
Aspalathin significantly mitigated ovalbumin-induced active systemic anaphylaxis responses in mice, including hypothermia, histamine secretion, and IgE and interleukin-4 production.
Aspalathin was more effective at suppressing allergic inflammation than nothofagin, another major rooibos flavonoid known for anti-allergic activity.

In RBL-2H3 mast cells and mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells, aspalathin reduced IgE-stimulated degranulation and intracellular calcium influx by inhibiting the FcεRI signaling pathway components Lyn, Fyn, and Syk.
Aspalathin reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in mast cells by inhibiting the transcription factors nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB).
Aspalathin decreased activation of the tyrosine kinase Lyn as part of its inhibition of the FcεRI signaling cascade in IgE-stimulated mast cells.
Aspalathin decreased activation of the tyrosine kinase Fyn as part of its inhibition of the FcεRI signaling cascade in IgE-stimulated mast cells.
Aspalathin decreased activation of the tyrosine kinase Syk as part of its inhibition of the FcεRI signaling cascade in IgE-stimulated mast cells.
Aspalathin reduced IgE-stimulated intracellular calcium influx in mast cells, contributing to reduced degranulation.
Aspalathin inhibited the transcription factor nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT), reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in mast cells.
Aspalathin inhibited nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB), reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in mast cells.
At 10 μM, kamebakaurin partially inhibited antigen-induced degranulation, histamine release, and IL-4 production in bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs).

At 30 μM, kamebakaurin further reduced leukotriene B4 (LTB4) and cysteinyl leukotriene production and fully suppressed degranulation, histamine release, and IL-4 production in antigen-triggered BMMCs.
Kamebakaurin reduced phosphorylation of Syk at Y519/520 in antigen-stimulated BMMCs, with complete inhibition observed at 30 μM.
Phosphorylation of Gab2, a downstream target of Syk, was reduced by kamebakaurin treatment.
In contrast to Syk and Gab2, phosphorylation of Erk was only partially inhibited by kamebakaurin even at the highest tested concentration (30 μM).
Docking simulation indicated that kamebakaurin blocks ATP binding to the ATP-binding site of Syk kinase, explaining the observed inhibition of Syk auto-phosphorylation.
Kamebakaurin inhibited antigen-induced vascular hyperpermeability in a dose-dependent manner in a mouse model.
Kamebakaurin reduced phosphorylation of Syk at Y519/520, with complete inhibition observed at 30 µM.
Kamebakaurin reduced phosphorylation of Gab2, a downstream target of Syk, with complete inhibition observed at 30 µM.
Erk phosphorylation was only partially inhibited by kamebakaurin even at the highest tested dose of 30 µM, unlike the complete inhibition seen for Syk and Gab2.
Docking simulation indicated that kamebakaurin blocks ATP binding to the ATP-binding site of Syk, explaining its inhibition of Syk auto-phosphorylation.
Kamebakaurin inhibited antigen-induced vascular hyperpermeability in a dose-dependent manner in a mouse model.
Kamebakaurin did not reduce histamine-induced vascular hyperpermeability, indicating its effect is upstream of histamine action and specific to antigen-triggered (FcεRI-dependent) signaling.
Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous pathogenic KRT5 variant, c.482T>G (p.Ile161Ser), consistent with autosomal dominant epidermolysis bullosa simplex in the patient.

A skin biopsy from the left lower leg above the lateral malleolus showed decreased epidermal nerve fiber density confirming severe small fiber neuropathy, in contrast to normal density seen in thigh skin.

Electromyography of both lower extremities showed no evidence of large-fiber neuropathy, and extensive laboratory workup (B12, TSH, SPEP, CPK, folic acid, B1, ANA, ESR, CBC, CMP, HbA1c) was unremarkable, supporting an isolated small fiber neuropathy without alternative systemic cause.

The authors report what they believe is the first documented case of concurrent epidermolysis bullosa simplex and small fiber neuropathy, suggesting a possible but unproven correlation between the two conditions.

Citing prior literature, the authors note that SFN was reported in the majority of patients with recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, a severe EB subtype caused by COL7A1 mutations, with dermoepidermal junction derangement proposed to injure small nerve fibers and cause neuropathic pain.

The authors cite a prior study of 58 patients with SFN in which several autoantibodies, including anti-KRT8, MX dynamin-like GTPase 1, and Drebrin-like protein, were found at significantly higher fold-changes in SFN patients compared with healthy controls.

The authors cite a rat model study in which human hair keratin promoted regeneration of peripheral sciatic nerves and axonal extension, suggesting a possible keratin-nerve interaction relevant to SFN pathophysiology.
The authors cite that in a prior study of patients with pure small fiber neuropathy, skin biopsy served as a diagnostic tool confirming the diagnosis in 88% of cases.
Percent female differed significantly among TS-HDS seropositive, FGFR-3 seropositive, and seronegative small fiber neuropathy patients.
The frequency of neuropathic pain symptoms differed significantly across TS-HDS seropositive, FGFR-3 seropositive, and seronegative small fiber neuropathy groups.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate values differed significantly between TS-HDS seropositive, FGFR-3 seropositive, and seronegative small fiber neuropathy groups.
Vitamin D levels differed significantly between TS-HDS seropositive, FGFR-3 seropositive, and seronegative small fiber neuropathy groups.
Vitamin B12 levels differed significantly between TS-HDS seropositive, FGFR-3 seropositive, and seronegative small fiber neuropathy groups.
Skin biopsy results were more frequently normal in both the FGFR-3 seropositive and TS-HDS seropositive cohorts compared with seronegative controls.
IgM autoantibodies against FGFR-3 and against TS-HDS each define distinct clinical phenotypes among small fiber neuropathy patients, differing from both controls and from one another.
Among 91 patients with pure small fiber neuropathy tested for TS-HDS, FGFR-3, and Plexin D1 antibodies, 60 (66%) were seropositive for at least one antibody.
Following IVIG treatment, 11 of 12 evaluable seropositive SFN patients (92%) showed a statistically significant 55.1% improvement in mean composite epidermal nerve fiber density.
Non-length-dependent epidermal nerve fiber density specimens improved by 42.3% after IVIG treatment.
Length-dependent epidermal nerve fiber density specimens improved by 99.7% after IVIG treatment.
In the subgroup of patients with Plexin D1 antibody-associated SFN, composite epidermal nerve fiber density improved by 139% after IVIG treatment.
Average pain scores decreased by 2.7 points after IVIG treatment in 14 patients with pre- and post-treatment questionnaires.
Two of the 17 seropositive patients who started IVIG treatment discontinued it due to side effects.
Among 17 seropositive patients who began IVIG, 2 discontinued treatment due to side effects, while 15 completed at least 6 months of therapy.
Of 91 patients with pure SFN tested for TS-HDS, FGFR-3, and Plexin D1 antibodies, 31 (34%) were seronegative.
Among 14 patients who completed SFN-specific questionnaires before and after IVIG, average pain scores decreased significantly by 2.7 points.

Applying the magnetic tape (TMP) to the lumbar scar produced an abrupt, statistically significant drop in dermal temperature near the scar within the first minute, which was maintained at 12 hours, whereas the control tape produced only normal thermal oscillation.

Numerical Pain Rating Scale (NPRS) scores with posteroanterior algometer pressure on lumbar spinous processes decreased after TMP application (L2: 9→7, L4: 8→3, L5: 10→5), while the placebo tape produced no change.
Pressure pain threshold (PPT) increased after TMP application, allowing higher tolerated pressure at L2, L4, and L5, while the placebo tape produced no significant change.
At 12 hours post-treatment, PPT remained elevated above baseline (though pain scores had partially rebounded), indicating a sustained but partially waning analgesic effect of TMP.

Patients with small-fiber neuropathy (SFN) show reduced thalamic connectivity with sensory-motor areas along with cutaneous nerve degeneration, correlating with diminished thalamic connectivity to pain-related regions across neuropathic pain phenotypes.
A prior meta-analysis found that kinesiology tape (KT) did not provide significantly greater pain relief than sham/placebo control in patients with chronic low back pain.
A cited study found that more than 70% of women with low back pain had painful surgical scars, supporting a correlation between scarring and LBP.

Duodenal food challenge increased the proportion of patients showing fluorescein leakage into the duodenal lumen compared to before challenge, in both patients with and without gastrointestinal adverse reaction to food.
Soy and wheat were the most frequent food components inducing a mucosal fluorescein leakage response during duodenal food challenge, followed by egg, milk, and yeast.

Duodenal biopsy histology, including intraepithelial lymphocyte number/distribution and mucosal mast cell number and function, was normal in patients with disorders of the gut-brain axis regardless of GARF status.
A significantly higher proportion of patients with GARF (group II) reported main symptom benefit from food exclusion therapy guided by eCLE/DFC results compared to patients without GARF (group I).
Administration of LPS to rats to mimic systemic bacterial infection increased colonic contraction frequency.
Transient depletion of intestinal macrophages using the Cx3cr1-Dtr rat model did not affect the colonic motility disruption caused by LPS-induced systemic inflammation.
Inhibiting nitric oxide synthase (inhibitory enteric neurotransmission) with Nω-nitro-L-arginine (NOLA) did not alter the colonic motility disruption induced by LPS.
In HAE with normal C1-INH, laboratory testing typically shows normal C4, normal C1-INH level and function, and normal Complement 1q.
The clinical presentation of HAE with normal C1-INH overlaps substantially with HAE types I and II, and heterogeneity of symptoms creates diagnostic challenges.
Presence of urticaria or other mast cell mediator release symptoms in patient history strongly suggests a mast cell-mediated pathway rather than bradykinin-mediated HAE.

A stepwise treatment approach is proposed: first trial histamine/mast cell-targeting treatments, then follow HAE type I/II bradykinin-pathway treatment guidelines if patients fail those trials or carry a mutation suggesting bradykinin pathway involvement.
A patient's response to medications approved for HAE types I/II is considered compelling support for a high clinical suspicion of HAE-nl-C1-INH diagnosis.
Key unmet needs in HAE-nl-C1-INH include the lack of confirmatory biomarkers for diagnosis and the lack of prospective controlled clinical studies of pharmacologic treatments in this population.

BL/6NTac mice developed significantly greater visceromotor response (visceral hypersensitivity) to colorectal distension at 60 mmHg after zymosan treatment compared with all other strain/treatment conditions, while BL/6J mice were resistant.

Zymosan instillation decreased colonic transit time regardless of substrain, indicating dysmotility (faster transit) developed in both strains even though only BL/6NTac also developed visceral hypersensitivity.
Both BL/6J and BL/6NTac mice showed significant changes in stool consistency (fecal water retention) 21 days after zymosan treatment.

No significant differences in body weight were found between strains or as a result of zymosan treatment during the visceral hypersensitivity development period, suggesting dehydration/calorie effects were minimal.

Whole-genome sequencing comparison of BL/6J and BL/6NTac substrains identified Avpr1a as the highest-priority candidate gene for visceral hypersensitivity susceptibility, as it was the only one of 5 candidate genes associated with variability in more than one pain assay.

The differentiating SNV between BL/6J and BL/6NTac lies in the 5' flanking/regulatory region of Avpr1a and represents an exon variant within an uncharacterized long intergenic noncoding RNA, implicating a regulatory rather than coding effect.
Avpr1a mRNA expression was increased in the colorectum of VH-susceptible BL/6NTac mice treated with zymosan compared with all other strain/treatment conditions.

Avpr1a mRNA expression was not significantly altered in colon-specific thoracolumbar or lumbosacral primary sensory (DRG) afferents by strain or zymosan treatment, indicating the expression change is restricted to colonic tissue rather than extrinsic sensory neurons.
Colorectal Avpr1a protein levels, measured by ELISA, were significantly higher in BL/6NTac mice compared with BL/6J mice 21 days after zymosan treatment.

No histological differences in inflammatory cell presence (H&E staining) were found between strains or conditions at day 21 post zymosan/saline, consistent with prior reports that zymosan-induced neutrophilic inflammation resolves before VH emerges.
No changes in percent mucin (Alcian Blue) staining area were found regardless of strain or zymosan/saline condition, indicating mucus-producing cells remained present and functional.

Exogenous AVP application to distal colon tissue produced a greater force-displacement response (AUC) in BL/6NTac-ZYM mice than BL/6J-ZYM mice, with longitudinal stretch eliciting the largest response in BL/6NTac-ZYM mice, indicating functional consequences of increased Avpr1a expression on colorectal mechanics.

Immunofluorescent colabeling of distal colon with PGP9.5 (pan-neuronal marker) and Avpr1a antisera showed overlap, suggesting Avpr1a is expressed on colon-innervating neurons (either enteric or extrinsic afferent terminals).

Colon-specific DRG and nodose ganglion neurons from BL/6NTac ZYM-VH mice did not show altered calcium influx or changes in percentage of cells responding to AVP or capsaicin compared with saline-treated controls.

Enteric neurons isolated from the myenteric plexus of BL/6NTac ZYM-VH mice showed increased calcium responses to both the Avpr1a agonist AVP and the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin compared with saline controls, implicating enteric neuron hyperresponsiveness in amplification of visceral pain signaling.

In pediatric IBS patients, those reporting high abdominal pain burden (Pain Burden Inventory) trended toward higher rectal biopsy AVPR1A mRNA expression than low-pain patients or healthy controls, but the difference was not statistically significant.

In adult ulcerative colitis patients, rectal biopsy Avpr1a mRNA expression was significantly higher in those with abdominal pain compared with those without pain, regardless of disease activity status (active vs inactive UC).

The relationship between Avpr1a expression and pain observed here for visceral pain is opposite to prior findings in somatic inflammatory pain models, where increased Avpr1a expression in DRG was associated with hypo-sensitivity (lower pain), an effect reported as sex- and stress-dependent.

Whole-exome and Sanger sequencing identified a novel haplotypic missense mutation (c.2657C>A/p.T886K) in exon 16 of LTBP2 on the same chromosome as a large deletion spanning exons 25-36, segregating with autosomal dominant Weill-Marchesani-like syndrome in the family.
Family members carrying the LTBP2 haplotypic mutations presented clinically with ectopia lentis, short stature, and obesity, consistent with a Weill-Marchesani-like phenotype.
SSc incidence varies by population, with the highest reported occurrence in Canadian First Nations.
SSc is roughly four times more prevalent in females than males.
Pulmonary fibrosis, the major cause of death in diffuse cutaneous SSc, has a prevalence of about 30% with roughly 40% 10-year mortality.
Among SSc subtypes, limited cutaneous SSc accounts for 64%, diffuse cutaneous SSc 28%, and sine scleroderma 8% of cases.
Microstomia (reduced mouth opening) is common in SSc, observed in more than half of patients and related to disease severity.

Microstomia is significantly more evident in diffuse cutaneous SSc than limited cutaneous SSc, with 2.5-fold higher Mouth Handicap in Scleroderma Scale (MHISS) scores impacting oral health-related quality of life.
Advanced periodontitis (stage III/IV) frequency was higher among diffuse cutaneous SSc patients than limited cutaneous SSc patients.
Gingival inflammation is specifically exacerbated in limited cutaneous SSc, whereas in diffuse cutaneous SSc it is not a constant finding, possibly masked by fibrosis.
Widening of the periodontal ligament (PDL) affects more than one-third of SSc patients, potentially due to collagen deposition and increased occlusal force.
Sicca syndrome occurs in 70% of SSc patients, and secondary Sjögren's syndrome affects up to 14% of SSc patients, significantly associated with the limited cutaneous subtype.
Trigeminal neuralgia is more prevalent in SSc patients than the general population and can present prior to SSc diagnosis.
Mandibular condyle resorption occurs in 10% to 50% of SSc patients, with rare cases of secondary apertognathia.

Subgingival Eikenella corrodens levels were significantly higher in lcSSc patients compared to healthy controls, and Porphyromonas gingivalis correlated with severe periodontitis in lcSSc, while Prevotella intermedia was exclusively associated with specific IL-1 gene polymorphisms in lcSSc.
Tongue swabs from SSc patients showed notably lower Lactobacillus amounts compared to healthy individuals, whereas gut microbiota Lactobacillus was increased in SSc, especially lcSSc.
IL-6 and IL-10 serum levels are elevated in SSc patients in the early disease phase and correlate with the extent of skin fibrosis.

Tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor alpha inhibitor, alleviated the persistent fibrotic phenotype of lesional SSc dermal fibroblasts in explant culture and reduced bleomycin-induced skin fibrosis in an animal model.
SSc patients show elevated IL-6 levels in gingival crevicular fluid, but these levels do not correlate with any clinical parameters of periodontitis.
Increased IL-1β levels in serum and skin biopsies from SSc patients positively correlated with fibrotic and inflammatory skin scores.
In lcSSc patients with periodontitis (31 of 38), an IL-1β C3953 allele polymorphism was linked to the presence of pathogenic Prevotella intermedia bacteria.
Elevated IL-17 mRNA and protein expression have been reported in lesional skin and peripheral blood mononuclear cells of SSc patients, though its role in oral complications remains uninvestigated.

CXCL-4 levels in gingival crevicular fluid of SSc patients are markedly elevated compared to controls and correlate with increased periodontitis measures including clinical attachment level, probing depth, and gingival index.
Elevated serum MMP-9 levels in diffuse cutaneous SSc correlate with serum TGF-β1 levels and degree of skin fibrosis, likely via activation of latent TGF-β.
MMP-9 and CXCL-4, but not IL-6, levels in gingival crevicular fluid significantly correlated with early-onset (<2 years) SSc disease.
No correlation was observed between skin thickness score and oral features, suggesting skin thickness is not an adequate proxy for oral disease severity in clinical trials.

An anti-IL-6 antibody was found not to improve skin fibrosis in SSc clinical trials, yet the same class of treatment improved periodontal outcomes in rheumatoid arthritis patients, highlighting divergent tissue-specific effects.
Dental implants can be placed successfully in SSc patients without exacerbating overall morbidity, with implant survival rates unaffected by SSc, improving oral health-related quality of life.
Four of 11 patients with functional gastrointestinal disorders (FD/IBS) were seropositive for gnAChR α3 and/or β4 antibodies by LIPS assay.
Sicca symptoms (dry mouth/eyes) were significantly more frequent in gnAChR antibody-positive FGID patients than in antibody-negative patients.

Aside from sicca symptoms, most clinical items including epidemiological features, individual autonomic symptoms, and total/domain COMPASS-31 scores did not differ significantly between gnAChR antibody-positive and negative FGID patients.
The LIPS assay for anti-gnAChRα3 antibody had an AUC of 0.849, with 46.9% sensitivity and 99.2% specificity at a cut-off antibody index of 1.0.
The LIPS assay for anti-gnAChRβ4 antibody had a lower AUC of 0.72, with 14.3% sensitivity and 100% specificity at a cut-off antibody index of 1.0.
Among seropositive FGID patients, isolated α3 seropositivity occurred in two patients, no patient had isolated β4 seropositivity, and two patients were double-positive for both α3 and β4 antibodies.
One of the two patients with double positivity for gnAChR α3 and β4 antibodies had particularly treatment-refractory IBS symptoms.

Prior animal and in vitro studies showed that autoantibodies against the nAChRα3 subunit cross-link and internalize the postsynaptic receptor, leading to its degradation, as the proposed pathogenic mechanism in autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy.
A novel murine model of autoimmune dysautonomia generated by nAChRα3 immunization showed delayed intestinal transit and ileus due to intestinal accumulation in one immunized mouse.
The authors cite prior epidemiological reports that atopic and autoimmune diseases, particularly psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis, are independent risk factors for IBS.

This is a study protocol describing a planned randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial testing faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) versus autologous placebo in 80 Norwegian ME/CFS outpatients, with no results reported yet.
The authors state that intestinal microbiota alteration has been observed in patients with ME/CFS, motivating the trial of gut flora transfer via FMT.
Across 60 RCTs comprising 7,088 ME/CFS patients, the pooled baseline fatigue severity (normalized to a 0-100 scale) was 77.9, indicating a high overall fatigue burden.
Fatigue severity was similar between adult (77.7) and adolescent (79.6) ME/CFS patients, with adolescents showing a slightly higher score despite general expectation of lower fatigue in youth.
Among three fatigue domains, mental fatigue scored lowest (70.1) compared to physical (74.3) and cognitive (74.2) fatigue in ME/CFS patients.
Physical and mental fatigue domains were strongly positively correlated across studies.
Baseline fatigue severity was slightly higher in RCT participants enrolled in non-pharmacological intervention trials than pharmacological intervention trials.

Among pharmacological intervention subtypes, patients enrolled in nutrient-supplement RCTs had the highest baseline fatigue severity, followed by antiviral drugs, mitochondrial modulators, and psychiatric drugs.

Among non-pharmacological intervention subtypes, patients enrolled in self-care RCTs had the highest baseline fatigue severity, followed by cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) and graded exercise therapy (GET).

Fatigue severity did not notably differ between ME/CFS patients diagnosed by the 1994 CDC criteria and Oxford criteria, but patients diagnosed by Canadian criteria showed the highest fatigue severity and those by International Consensus Criteria (ICC) the lowest.
Fatigue severity varied by continent, being highest in Africa and Europe and relatively lower in Asia and North America.
Fatigue severity scores differed substantially by assessment tool used, with CIS yielding the highest scores and MFS/MFI the lowest.
RCTs published before 2010 reported higher baseline fatigue severity than those published from 2010 onward.
Female-only ME/CFS RCTs reported higher fatigue severity than the remaining mixed-sex RCTs.
In a linear mixed-effects model, age had no significant influence on fatigue severity, whereas intervention type significantly influenced fatigue severity.
In a linear mixed-effects model, fatigue assessment tool significantly influenced fatigue severity scores, but case definition did not.

Sensitivity analyses adjusting for publication bias and removing high-risk-of-bias studies produced somewhat lower and higher overall fatigue severity estimates, respectively, but overall confirmed the robustness of the main finding.

A comparator study with an MFI-derived fatigue score of 73.8 in 150 ME/CFS patients showed severe functional impact: 92% had reduced activity by 50%, 82% could not maintain full-time work or school, and 48% were bedridden or unable to perform productive tasks during peak fatigue.

Comparison across disease populations using MFI-assessed fatigue scores showed ME/CFS-comparable severity in fibromyalgia (73.4) and Parkinson's disease (clinically severe fatigue threshold of 60), but lower fatigue in major depressive disorder (50.5) and Critical Illness Polyneuropathy patients (55.9).
Astragalus root extract (500 mg twice daily) significantly reduced chronic fatigue syndrome prevalence in nurses at the end of treatment and at 1-month follow-up compared to baseline.
In the placebo control group, chronic fatigue syndrome prevalence remained statistically significantly different (high, 72.2%) between before and after the trial period.
Having an underlying disease was associated with increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome among the nurses studied.
Being assigned to the control (placebo) group increased the risk of chronic fatigue syndrome compared to receiving Astragalus root extract.
Increasing length of time was associated with decreased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome in the generalised estimating equations model.
Longer duration of time since baseline was associated with a decreased likelihood of chronic fatigue syndrome.
The Mini-BESTest showed significant correlations with force plate balance measures, the 6MWT, and the LEFS in patients with hEDS/HSD, supporting its construct validity.
Test-retest reliability across two visits one to two weeks apart was excellent for the Mini-BESTest, 6MWT, and LEFS in patients with hEDS/HSD.
Minimal detectable change with 95% confidence (MDC95) values were calculated as 4 points for the Mini-BESTest, 77 meters for the 6MWT, and 11 points for the LEFS in this population.
The Mini-BESTest may show a potential ceiling effect for high-functioning patients with hEDS/HSD, limiting its sensitivity in this subgroup.

Shoulder external rotation active range of motion significantly increased over time in the experimental K-Tape group (tape crossing the glenohumeral joint) from baseline to immediately post-taping and to 48 hours post-taping, but not in the control group.

Shoulder internal rotation active range of motion significantly improved in the experimental K-Tape group from baseline to immediately post-taping and to 48 hours post-taping, with no significant improvement in the control group.

Shoulder flexion active range of motion showed no statistically significant differences at any time point or between K-Tape groups, though the experimental group showed non-significant improvements exceeding measurement error.
Active joint reposition (AJR) error, a measure of shoulder proprioception, showed no significant differences at any time point in either the experimental or control K-Tape groups.
Patients with hEDS demonstrated a baseline shoulder proprioceptive deficit (elevated AJR error) compared with normative values reported in healthy populations in prior literature.
Skin fragility-related minor adverse skin reactions occurred in 5 of 58 shoulders (5.2%) taped, all of which resolved by 4 days after tape removal.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is most commonly caused by defects in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes components of type III collagen, an important structural protein in skin, bowel wall, and blood vessels.
A less common cause of vEDS is a specific amino acid substitution in the COL1A1 gene encoding type I collagen, which produces vascular fragility mimicking classic COL3A1-related vEDS.

Major clinical complications of vEDS (arterial or uterine rupture, sigmoid colon perforation, family history, or cavernous sinus fistula) were the presenting sign in 70% of adults with the COL3A1 variant.
Gastrointestinal tract perforation occurs in approximately 15% of vEDS patients with the COL3A1 variant.
The median survival in studied vEDS patients was reported to be 50 years.
In this vEDS patient, nasogastric tube insertion in the emergency department was extremely difficult, requiring eight attempts before successful placement.

Attempted re-insertion of the nasogastric tube under direct laryngoscopy with Magill forceps caused an inadvertent laceration of the posterior pharynx, later shown by imaging and endoscopy to have created a traumatic false passage extending from the cricoid cartilage to approximately C7, which subsequently resolved by two months.

The patient presented with a spontaneous long-segment small bowel obstruction with a perforation site in the distal small bowel showing marked oedema concerning for ischemia, requiring laparotomy and small bowel resection, in the context of prior recurrent small bowel perforations attributed to vEDS.
Histopathology of the resected small bowel showed a perforation site with associated necrosis and serositis, with unremarkable mucosa, non-devitalized margins, and no malignancy.
Most deaths in the vEDS patient population result from vascular complications such as arterial rupture in the thorax and abdomen, whereas gastrointestinal rupture rarely leads to death.

Iatrogenic bowel perforation during colonoscopy has previously been reported in vEDS patients, suggesting that invasive procedures such as NGT insertion or colonoscopy may plausibly carry increased procedural risk in this population.

The most common gastrointestinal manifestation of vEDS is spontaneous sigmoid colon perforation in the absence of underlying bowel pathology such as diverticulosis, with small bowel and stomach perforations reported much less frequently.
Patients with hEDS use social media to connect with others who share their disease, describing it as a way of befriending peers with the same condition.
Patients with hEDS use social media to seek and vet health-related information about their condition.
Patients with hEDS reported risks and downsides associated with their social media use.
Patients with hEDS expressed a desire for clinicians to proactively discuss social media use with them as part of their care.
The patient presented with microcornea, distal joint laxity of the fingers and wrist, hypotonia, and a broad-based limping gait, an unusual combination of features for Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Neuroimaging revealed cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, described as an atypical finding in this case of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome musculocontractural type 1.
Whole exome sequencing was used to confirm the diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome musculocontractural type 1.
The patient's fracture dislocation of the right hip, likely related to tissue/joint fragility from the syndrome, was managed surgically with fixation.
The child was born of a second degree consanguineous marriage, consistent with an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern typical of musculocontractural EDS.

The patient with a rare EDS subtype developed bilateral secondary calcification of hydrophilic-acrylic IOLs fourteen years after implantation, presenting as floret-like surface lesions causing progressive visual deterioration.

Genetic testing for the major EDS subtype-associated genes (FKBP14, COL1A1, COL5A1/5A2, COL1A2, COL3A1) and multiple epiphyseal dysplasia genes (COL9A1/9A2/9A3) was negative, consistent with an undiagnosed rare EDS subtype.

EDS has been reported in prior literature to be associated with abnormal calcification of joints, breast, soft tissue, and teeth, supporting a plausible link between EDS and the ocular lens calcification observed in this patient.
The floret-like IOL surface opacities were resistant to Nd:YAG laser treatment, indicating this modality does not resolve secondary IOL calcification and may complicate future surgery.
Surgical exchange of the calcified left IOL for a 3-piece hydrophobic sulcus IOL resulted in improved visual acuity and good postoperative recovery two weeks later.

Histological staining of the explanted IOL showed diffuse Alizarin red staining across the anterior and posterior lens surfaces and haptics, and von Kossa staining confirmed calcium phosphate deposits beneath the whole IOL surface, consistent with secondary calcification.
Across studies worldwide, the pooled prevalence of a Beighton score of ≥4 in children was 33%, ranging from 11.7% to 64.6% between studies.
At a Beighton cut-off of ≥4, prevalence of generalised joint hypermobility was significantly higher in females than males, with a mean difference of 14.6%.
At a Beighton cut-off of ≥5, pooled prevalence of generalised joint hypermobility in children was 18%, ranging from 4.5% to 45.9% across studies.
At a Beighton cut-off of ≥5, prevalence was significantly higher in females than males, with a mean difference of 11.5%.
At a Beighton cut-off of ≥6, pooled prevalence of generalised joint hypermobility in children was 11%, ranging from 2.6% to 44.4% across studies.
At a Beighton cut-off of ≥6, prevalence was significantly higher in females than males, with a mean difference of 7.3%.
At a Beighton cut-off of ≥7, pooled prevalence of generalised joint hypermobility in children was 7%, ranging from 0.5% to 23.3% across studies, and was low overall for both sexes.
Mean Beighton-score-based hypermobility prevalence did not differ significantly between world regions at any cut-off score.

The meta-analysis supports rejecting a Beighton cut-off of 4 or 5 for identifying generalised joint hypermobility in children, recommending a minimum threshold of 6 or more, consistent with the recent Pediatric Joint Hypermobility Diagnostic Framework.
The analysis suggests that a Beighton cut-off of 7 or greater may be a more appropriate threshold, particularly for identifying generalised joint hypermobility in females.

Patients with EDS undergoing primary total knee arthroplasty had significantly higher rates of wound complications at 90 days compared to matched controls, both in unadjusted and comorbidity-adjusted analyses.

Rates of instability, manipulation under anesthesia, periprosthetic joint infection, aseptic loosening, and aseptic revision arthroplasty did not significantly differ between EDS patients and matched controls.
Creatine monohydrate supplementation (loading then maintenance dose) produced a significant improvement in muscle weakness, myalgia, and overall pain in a patient with hypermobile EDS.
After creatine supplementation, the patient's walking tolerance increased from 10-15 minutes to 20-25 minutes before needing to rest.
When the concurrent anti-inflammatory (diclofenac) was stopped, the patient's pain returned, but her muscular fatigue improvement persisted and her functional ability did not regress.

A cited Dutch study found a positive correlation between muscle weakness and fatigue severity in patients with EDS, potentially due to associated myopathy and/or polyneuropathy and resultant deconditioning.
A cited study reported that one week of creatine supplementation in healthy adults increased skin capillary density, which is important for exercise tolerance via improved tissue oxygenation.

The paper states that creatine monohydrate has a well-established safety profile with no known severe adverse effects in healthy individuals, and that concerns about renal damage are not supported by the data, though caution is advised in patients with existing renal disease.

The patient presented with a past medical history including hypermobile EDS, dysautonomia, obesity, and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), indicating comorbidity among these conditions.
A 36-year-old man presented with an anterior myocardial infarction due to spontaneous coronary artery dissection and was subsequently diagnosed with vascular type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection is described as an atypical cause of myocardial infarction predominantly affecting women, with genetic vasculopathies such as connective tissue diseases being significant contributing predisposing factors.
Isolated MPFLR resulted in a 19.1% recurrent instability rate (9 of 47 knees) requiring revision stabilization surgery at a mean 7.2-year follow-up in patients with EDS.
The total reoperation rate after isolated MPFLR in the EDS cohort, including chondroplasty and other unplanned surgeries, was 38.3% (18 of 47 knees).
Patients who developed recurrent instability after isolated MPFLR were significantly younger than those who did not.
The ability to place the palm on the floor with knees extended (a marker of hamstring/tendon hyperlaxity) was significantly associated with recurrent instability after isolated MPFLR.
Bilateral knee involvement showed a nonsignificant trend toward higher failure rate after isolated MPFLR compared with unilateral involvement.
Autograft MPFLR had a numerically higher failure rate than allograft MPFLR, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Among autograft failures, gracilis autografts failed significantly more often than semitendinosus autografts.
Preoperative patellar height and patellar tilt were significantly greater in knees that subsequently failed isolated MPFLR compared with those that did not fail.
High-grade trochlear dysplasia was present in 42.6% of knees preoperatively but was not significantly different between the failure and non-failure groups.

Postoperative patient-reported outcome scores after isolated MPFLR in EDS patients (Pedi-IKDC, Kujala, HSS Pedi-FABS, BPII, KOOS subscales) were suboptimal and inferior compared with published outcomes in non-EDS MPFLR patients.
Postoperative PRO scores did not significantly differ when patients were stratified by age, laterality, Beighton score, or graft type, likely due to small subgroup sample sizes.
Despite suboptimal PRO scores, nearly all patients reported satisfaction with their outcome after isolated MPFLR, regardless of need for subsequent surgery.
The EDS cohort had a high mean Beighton score (6.8 ± 1.5), with 26 of 31 patients scoring the maximum 9 of 9, reflecting substantial generalized joint hypermobility.

In a prior study of generalized joint hyperlaxity (GJH) patients undergoing isolated MPFLR, recurrent instability rates were low and similar regardless of Beighton score status, contrasting with the markedly higher failure rate seen in the current EDS cohort.
Skeletally immature patients who underwent MPFLR with the femoral attachment point moved distal to the physis showed no growth disturbances at final follow-up.
Wound healing complications and infection were rare in this cohort of hypermobile-type EDS patients, contrasting with higher rates reported for EDS surgical patients generally in the literature.

Prior literature cited in the discussion indicates that in EDS, tendon elongation is much greater and tendon stiffness much lower compared with controls, providing a biomechanical rationale for graft failure risk.
The Foot and Ankle Flexibility Index (FAFI), based on the last 7 items of the Lower Limb Assessment Score, showed high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.82).
Inter-item correlations for the FAFI items averaged 0.59, ranging from 0.43 to 0.74.
A discrimination cut-off score of 4 points on the ROC curve was found to identify children with joint hypermobility of the foot and ankle, with high sensitivity and specificity reported.
The FAFI showed largely good inter-rater reliability, with an ICC of 0.89.
The FAFI showed excellent intra-rater reliability, with an ICC of 0.96.

Lower extremity inter-joint coupling angles (hip-knee, hip-ankle, knee-ankle) during the stance phase of walking did not significantly differ between children with hypermobility spectrum disorder and non-HSD children.

Coupling patterns (assessed via permutational multivariate analysis of variance) between hip-knee, hip-ankle, and knee-ankle joint pairs during walking did not significantly differ between HSD and non-HSD groups.

Variability of inter-joint coupling angles during the stance phase of walking, assessed using statistical non-parametric mapping two-sample t-tests, showed no significant difference between children with HSD and non-HSD children.
Sixty-two percent of the athlete cohort with TOS had a Beighton score ≥4, indicating joint hyperlaxity, substantially higher than the ~26% prevalence estimated in the general population.
Joint hyperlaxity did not appear to affect whether athletes returned to sport after thoracic outlet decompression.
Return to sport after decompression did not significantly differ by sex.
Abnormal hypertrophy or insertion of the anterior scalene muscle was the most common musculoskeletal abnormality identified intraoperatively in the athlete TOS cohort.
A broad first rib with abnormal scalene tubercle development was the most common bony abnormality found in the athlete TOS cohort.
Supernumerary cervical rib was identified in a subset of athlete TOS patients, including one case with cervical-first rib fusion contributing to combined arterial and neurogenic compression.
Prior clavicular fracture, a known TOS risk factor, was found in nearly a quarter of the athlete cohort, associated with both venous and neurogenic TOS.
Among the athlete TOS cohort, venous TOS was the most common subtype, followed by neurogenic TOS, with arterial TOS being rare.
Most athletes were able to return to competitive athletics after supraclavicular thoracic outlet decompression, with the majority having no limitations.
Postoperative Derkash functional scoring showed that the majority of athletes had excellent or good results after thoracic outlet decompression.
Most patients with venous TOS required additional venoplasty at interval venogram follow-up after decompression surgery, but none had recurrent thrombosis.
One postoperative complication, a pneumothorax, occurred and resolved with conservative management.
Mean time to return to competitive athletics after decompression was approximately seven months, shortly after the mandated 6-month recovery period.
MRI showed bilateral scalene muscle hypertrophy in a rock-climber athlete with combined neurogenic and venous TOS, a finding absent in a non-athlete patient with the same combined TOS presentation.
Women with fibromyalgia showed autonomic dysregulation characterized by low parasympathetic activity and high sympathetic activity at rest compared with pain-free controls.
Women with fibromyalgia exhibited higher levels of psychological distress than pain-free controls, and this variable had a greater weight in the discriminant function distinguishing groups.

Women with fibromyalgia showed disorder-level social stress that, along with psychological distress, contributed most strongly to discriminant classification between fibromyalgia patients and controls.
A discriminant function combining heart rate variability, psychological distress, and social stress markers correctly classified 70%-74.5% of fibromyalgia cases and 85%-87% of pain-free controls.
Astaxanthin administration significantly reduced mechanical and thermal pain hypersensitivity in a mouse model of fibromyalgia.
Astaxanthin mitigated sleep disturbances induced by chronic pain, as monitored via electroencephalogram-recorded sleep stages in fibromyalgia model mice.
Astaxanthin reduced depressive-like behaviour induced by chronic pain in the fibromyalgia mouse model.
The analgesic and antidepressant-like effects of astaxanthin are proposed to be mediated through inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway.

Levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in brain and spinal cord were assessed in relation to astaxanthin's anti-inflammatory effect in the fibromyalgia model, alongside c-Fos activation in the anterior cingulate cortex and spinal glial cell activation.
Astaxanthin reduced c-Fos activation in the anterior cingulate cortex of fibromyalgia model mice, indicating decreased central pain-related neuronal activation.
Astaxanthin decreased activation of spinal glial cells in fibromyalgia model mice, consistent with an anti-neuroinflammatory effect.
Astaxanthin reduced levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in the brain and spinal cord of fibromyalgia model mice.
Astaxanthin increased expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 in the fibromyalgia mouse model.
Astaxanthin decreased expression of the inflammasome components ASC (Apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing CARD) and Caspase-1, consistent with NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition.

Pregabalin binds double-stranded fish sperm DNA via minor groove binding, as shown by electrochemical, UV-Vis absorption spectroscopy, and dye-replacement studies with ethidium bromide and Hoechst-32588.
The binding constant (Kb) of pregabalin with dsDNA, determined via the Benesi-Hildebrand plot, was 2.41×10^4 ± 0.30 at 298 K.
Fluorescence spectroscopy indicated a binding stoichiometry (n) of 1.21 ± 0.09 between pregabalin and dsDNA.

A differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) dsDNA biosensor detected pregabalin via decrease in deoxyguanosine oxidation signal, showing a linear response between 2 and 16 μM with LOD of 0.57 μM and LOQ of 1.91 μM in pH 4.80 acetate buffer.

tDCS was found to reduce migraine-related pain with high-certainty evidence in this umbrella review of RCT meta-analyses.
Across broader chronic pain conditions (not fibromyalgia- or migraine-specific), tDCS showed a treatment effect on pain but with very low certainty of evidence.
